en: Now begins the third maṇḍala.
In the third [book] of Vaiśvāmitra, there are five anuvākas.
In that regard, there are twelve hymns (*sūkta*) in the first anuvāka.
Among them, the first hymn, consisting of twenty-three verses, begins with "Somasya mā."
And thus it has been listed in the Anukramaṇī: "Of Soma, [the hymn] exceeds by three.
Its seer (ṛṣi) is Viśvāmitra, the beholder of the maṇḍala.
Since no other meter is specified, the metre (chandas) is Triṣṭubh.

By the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "in the *maṇḍala*s and so forth, [the deity is] Āgneya," Agni is the deity. Their application (*viniyoga*) is in the *prātaranuvāka* and the *āśvina-śastra* within the *Taittirīya* Veda. Thus it is stated in the Sūtra: "The three [verses] beginning with 'somasya mā tavasaṃ patyabhirūpasaḥ'" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.13).

O Agni, carry me, the powerful one, as a draught-horse to the sacrifice; perform the rite in the assembly to worship the gods. Shining toward them, I yoke the pressing-stone; O Agni, take pleasure in my body for the sake of well-being.

O Agni, bring hither for me the powerful one, the mighty, whom you must serve at the sacrifice to worship the gods. Shining toward them, I yoke the pressing-stone; O Agni, take pleasure in your own body for the sake of well-being. 1.

O Agni, in this sacrificial assembly (*vidatha*), you have made me the one to worship, the bearer and carrier of the *soma* for the sacrifice; as such, desire me—that is, favor me—who am powerful, vigorous, and strong. Furthermore, O Agni, shining forth toward the gods, I yoke the pressing-stone for the sake of the extraction, and I prepare it for the sake of well-being (*śam*). Thus says another mantra: "By the Truth, the god Savitṛ prepares himself for well-being" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 4.86.5).
Alternatively, I praise for the sake of *śam* (tranquility), because it is listed among the words for the act of praising in [the passage]: "The one striving (*śaśamānaḥ*) sings" (*śaśamāno jarati*).
And so there is another mantra: "That mortal has indeed exerted himself and performed his service" (*so anna iṃje śaśame ca martaḥ*; Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 6.1.9).
Furthermore, O Agni, "juṣasva" means: enjoy—that is, protect—your own body (tanvam);
or alternatively, it means: enjoy me as I extend my ritual acts (karmāṇi).
We have performed the sacrifice directed eastward; may the song increase. They have honored Agni with fuel and with reverence.
From heaven they have ordained the assemblies of the sages; they have sought a path for the wise one who possesses mental power.

We have performed the sacrifice facing forward; may the song of praise increase. With fuel and with reverence, they have honored Agni. They have proclaimed the sacred rites of the seers from heaven; they have sought a path for the wise and powerful one.
O Agni, we have performed this sacrifice that proceeds forward;
may my song of praise increase and flourish.
Let them honor Agni with fuel, with reverence, and with oblations; let our people serve him.
Furthermore, having come from the sky—the heavenly world—the gods instructed, that is, they taught, the *vidathas*—the acts of knowledge or hymns of praise—of the *kavis*, the singers;
moreover, [they taught them] for the sake of the skillful one (*gṛtsa*).
This is a form derived from the root *gṛ* (to praise).
They have sought a path to praise Agni—the powerful, the increased one—who is worthy of praise;
and the praisers indeed desire him.
*Cit* is used here in the sense of *ca* (and).

1. In the third maṇḍala of *jha* and *ma*. 2. The observer of the *ca*, *ma*, and *maṇḍala*. 3. The sūtra of *ka*, *kha*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *tha*, *na*, *ma*, *va*. 4. I shall [recite] *ka*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *tha*, *va*, *śam*; I shall [recite] *kha*, *ṇa*, *la*, *śa*. (Ṛgveda 2.23)

The wise one, of purified will, has established me—the close kinsman by birth of heaven and earth—as the one to be praised by enemies, O gods, as the beautiful Agni within the waters, in the work of the sisters. mayeḥ | dadhe | medhiraḥ | pūtadakṣaḥ | divaḥ | subandhuḥ | januṣā | pṛthivyāḥ | arivandan | om iti | darśatam | apsu | antaḥ | devāsaḥ | agnim | apasi | svasṛṇām ||3||

The wise one, the intelligent, the sagacious; the one of purified strength, whose power is cleansed; the one who by birth alone—that is, by the mere fact of his being—is a good kinsman, meaning he is a kinsman by his very nature;
that Agni who bestows, or provides, bliss (*mayaḥ*) for both heaven (*divaḥ*) and earth (*pṛthivyāḥ*).

Insofar as he brings happiness to both gods and humans—him, that beautiful and lovely Agni, the gods (devāsas) [have brought forth] from within the waters of the flowing rivers (svasṛṇām), which remain hidden; for the purpose of the rite consisting in the carrying of the sacrifice (apasi), purifying his brilliance (śociḥ)—which serves as his garment—he clothes himself all around (pari vasānaḥ) with it; and he measures out (mimīte), that is, produces, the life-span (āyuḥ) of the active ones (apām), their food, and abundant, undiminished, and perfect glories (śriyaḥ).

The seven sisters, the daughters of the mountain, who dwell upon the banks of the Sīmanadī, have clothed themselves in the hero [Agni] as they are naked; there, the ancient maidens of common origin have conceived one embryo, the seven voices.
The seven voices, moving in a line, unassailable, unconsuming, from heaven, wide-reaching, unclothed yet not naked, ancient yet youthful, sharing a common womb, have here conceived one embryo. 6.

The waters—those which do not consume, those which do not devour, the undeceived, and the unharmed, acting as mothers—the fire has gone forth from them and moves everywhere. Fire is the dryer of the waters, yet the waters pacify it; thus it is said that neither of these two exists here [in this state].
Of what nature are they?
Since they have become the offspring of heaven and the mid-region, they clothe themselves in garments; for water, which serves as their covering, is present there,
and for that very reason, they are unclothed.
Furthermore, those ancient ones— eternal, youthful (meaning ever-youthful, i.e., eternally aged)—
the seven rivers with common origin, whose place is the same intermediate space, have held, do hold, Agni as their embryo situated within them.
His two joined hands, assuming every form, are spread out in the womb of clarified butter, in the flow of honeyed streams;
there stand the swelling milch-cows, the two great, united mothers of the wondrous one.

Spread out are his [fires], compacted, possessing all forms, in the womb of ghee, in the flow of honeyed drops; there they have stood, the swelling milch-cows. The two great, united mothers of the wondrous one stand facing each other. 7.

In the womb of ghee—that is, in the intermediate space which is their source—they are gathered together, forming a mass. Having various forms (*viśvarūpāḥ*), meaning manifold in appearance, they are spread out, extending everywhere. These rays of this Agni stand—meaning they remain—during the flowing, the streaming forth, of the honey-like waters.

Swelling and being filled here in this fire, the waters have become milch-cows for the gratification of all. The two great ones, Heaven and Earth—the two mothers of the wondrous and beautiful Agni—become united, mutually anointing each other, and resplendent.
O Son of Strength, as you spread across the sky, assuming brilliant and impetuous forms, streams of honeyed ghee flow forth where the Bull has grown great through wisdom.
Being carried forth, O Son of Strength, he has shone out widely, assuming brilliant and impetuous forms. The streams of honey and ghee flow where the Bull has grown strong through poetic wisdom.
1. Ma, va, and nānāvidharūpa;
2. Kha, ga, ga, ta, tha, and samañcatyau;
3. Jha, ta, tha, na, ma, va, and yasyāmeḥ.
O Son of Strength, O Child of Power, being upheld and nourished by all, you, assuming radiant and impetuous forms—your brilliant flames—shine forth.
When Agni, the bull, has grown strong through the poetic hymn of the sacrificer, then the streams of honey-sweet ghee—that is, water—flow down.
The meaning is that when the sacrificer is inspired by his hymn, then rain occurs.
Even from his father’s birthplace, he discerned [the truth] and, casting aside [obstacles], released the streams of speech;
though moving in secret with his auspicious friends, the great ones of heaven, he was not hidden away.

By his very birth, he discovered the father’s udder; he released its streams and its milky flows. Though moving in secret with his auspicious friends, he was not hidden from the great ones of heaven. 9.

By his very birth, Agni himself has discovered the udder of the father, the intermediate region— that is, the watery expanse situated like an udder. Furthermore, this Agni has released the streams belonging to that udder—
the streams of milk— and he also releases the *dhenās*, the voices of the intermediate region.

With his auspicious, benevolent friends—the winds—or with the waters that are the offspring of the great atmosphere from heaven, Agni moves within the secret cave; yet, even while he dwells in that secret cave, there was no one at all capable of reaching him.
He bore the embryo of the father and the progenitor; alone he sucked at many swelling breasts. O two wives of the same kin, belonging to the pure bull—protect both for him among men.

He bore the embryo of both his father and his progenitor; alone he sucked at the many swelling udders. O two co-wives, who are united with the pure one, the bull, and share a common kinship—protect both of them for this mortal man. 10.

This Agni bears the embryo of the father, the intermediate space—becoming an embryo by means of rain—and also the world of the progenitor, the Brahman, which consists of plants and other things. Agni alone consumes—the word *adhayat* meaning he eats or devours—the many plants that have swollen, that is, attained growth.

The sun is your common husband, shared equally by you two co-wives; both Heaven and Earth, who are beneficial to men, are kinsmen to this pure, showering Agni—the meaning is that they are his kin, like fire is their own.
O Agni, do thou protect those two, Heaven and Earth, thoroughly.
1. There is no *jha*, *jha-1*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *tha*, *na*, *ma*, *va*, or *sa*.

2. *ka*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *tha*, *na*, *ma*, and *brāhmaṇa*; *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *1*, and *ca* belong to the *brāhmaṇa*; *va* belongs to the *brāhmaṇa*. 3. *ga*, *ṇa*, and *eka* are indeed fire (*agni*).
In the wide, great, and unobstructed space, the glorious waters have indeed increased Agni;
he has lain in the womb of *Ṛta*, the source of the sisters, in the lap of his own siblings.

In the wide, great, and unobstructed space, the glorious waters have nourished Agni together; for he lay within the womb of the eternal Law (ṛta), the root-shaker, in the work of his sisters who are kin.
This great Agni has grown, indeed, increases, in the unconfined, vast, and wide expanse of the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
He states the cause for his growth:
for, because of that reason, there are many ancient glories (*yaśas*).

The waters increase Agni, who is born from glory. Thus having attained growth, Agni, stationed in the womb— the place— of the waters (*vṛta*), namely in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), lies down, self-controlled in mind, within the milk of the sisters (*jāmīnām*) who flow by themselves, acting as the cause [of his existence].

Like a horse bearing its load in the encounter of the great waters, he is eager to give sight; seeking to bestow light upon his son, he is the progenitor who brought forth the kine. He is Agni, the most manly germ, the mighty one who has been born.

Like a pillar supporting the assembly of the great ones, he is eager to shine; he who is adorned with light for his son, the progenitor who brought forth the kine. Agni is the most heroic germ, the mighty one who has been born. 12.

The progenitor of all, the father of the world, the embryo of the waters, the most truthful, the supreme leader, the greatest protector of men, the great one, that Agni who is crooked [in his path], yet invincible by others—
or "na" is used here as a filler for the meter.

In the encounter of battle, the bearer of the great armies of the earth—the one who desires to be seen by all, shining with his own radiance—that Agni generated, for the sake of the sacrificer who offers oblations, the food of the cow.
Regarding "sūnave": the suffix *nup* is added to the root *ap*, meaning "to impel," according to the *ṇādi* group.
The waters have brought forth the lovely germ of the plants; the blessed forest has given birth to him of diverse forms.
Even the gods, having come together in spirit, honored him at his birth—the most praiseworthy and powerful one.

The embryo of the waters, the visible one among the plants—him the blessed forest has brought forth in manifold forms. Even the gods, with their minds, have come together; they have honored him at his birth, the most praiseworthy and powerful one. 13.
The forest (araṇī) produced Agni—the most fortunate, the blessed, the one to be honored by all, the beautiful to behold, and the one of manifold forms—as the embryo of the woods and the plants.
Even all the gods approached that Agni with their minds through hymns of praise as soon as he was born—him who is most secret, worthy of laudation, powerful, and grown strong.
The particle "hi" serves as a filler.
They themselves, desiring to honor him, attended upon him.
1. *Jña* is for the purpose of filling the metrical foot.
2. The forms *ka, kha, ga, ca, ja, jha, ṇa, ṇa, la, ta, tha, na, pha, ma, ba* constitute the *garbha*.

Indeed, the great rays, brilliant like lightning, accompany Agni whose luster is straight and pure; milking the nectar in the boundless ocean, they attend upon him who has grown great within his own secret abode, shining with light like lightning in the sky. The great rays, indeed, brilliant like lightning, accompany Agni whose luster is straight and pure; milking the nectar—water—in the midst of the boundless, deep ocean, they attend upon him who has grown great within his own secret abode, shining with light like lightning in the sky. They, the great rays, like brilliant, shining flashes of lightning, resort to and take refuge in Agni, who is radiant with splendor, who has increased within his own dwelling-place in the atmosphere, as if in a secret cave, while they themselves pour forth the immortal water in the fathomless, vast sea.

The sacrificer praises you with oblations; desiring your friendship and favor, he praises you. Together with the gods, bestow protection upon the singer, and guard us with your domestic powers. The sacrificer praises you with oblations as his means; I praise you for the sake of cattle and other wealth. Desiring your excellent wisdom—that is, a mind directed toward dharma—I praise you for the sake of our friendship. Together with the gods, measure out—that is, provide—protection consisting of cattle and other boons for me, the singer who offers hymns, for our sake. With your "domestic" (damya) powers—by which is meant that they are to be restrained and controlled, implying the absence of unrestrained license—and with your splendors (anīka), protect us. 15. O Agni, well-guided one, may we, as your followers, performing all deeds that bring wealth, impelled by glorious renown born of noble seed, overcome the godless who seek to attack us. O Agni, O well-guided one! We, your followers—here the root *kṣi* is used in the sense of "going"—approaching you; performing all deeds that bring wealth, which are the causes for obtaining cattle and other riches; and offering oblations while being impelled by glorious renown consisting of the food prepared by ourselves; may we overcome the godless ones who come against us in battle. He, O well-guided one, O Agni! Your followers; here the root *kṣi* means "to go. All, every; deeds that bring wealth, acts that serve as the cause for attaining cattle and other riches; performing, carrying out; impelled, presenting the sacrificial offerings; we, by glorious renown—that is, by the food produced by our own efforts—possessing noble vigor; may we overcome the godless ones who seek to attack us.
1. In manuscripts ka, jha, jha, ṇa, tha, na, ma, and va, the phrase "mahāntaḥ sūryā eva" is absent.
2. In manuscripts kha, ga, and ca, the word "stotre" is absent; in manuscript ma, it is "stotraih". 3. In manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ṇa, ṇa, ta, tha, na, va, and dha, the word "dhanāni" is present.
4. [The letters] kha, ga, ca, jha, ṇa, ga, ta, tha, na, va—[these] are not employed;
[the word] "adevān" means other than the gods. By the rule of "negation joined with *iva*," only the *rākṣasas* are understood.
May we overcome those who obstruct the sacrifice, those who seek battle, and those enemies who cause affliction to the body;
or rather, it should be understood as "those enemies who worship the gods."
O God, you are the banner of the gods at their head, the delightful one who knows all poetic wisdom;
as the domestic lord, you come to mortals with help. You go straight to the gods, O charioteer, accomplishing your purpose.

O Agni, you became the banner of the gods at the beginning; as the delightful one, knowing all poetic wisdoms, you, the friend of the house, have come to the aid of mortals. O charioteer, you go straight to the gods, accomplishing your purpose. 17.

O Agni, you, the delightful one, worthy of praise, the banner and the illuminator of the gods at the sacrifices, have become manifest; that is, you exist everywhere, being all-pervasive. Furthermore, knowing all the poetic hymns composed by the sacrificers and others, and having made the mortals—the worshippers—delighted by the accomplishment of their desired objects, you cause them to dwell securely in their homes.
A skillful charioteer, accomplishing the beneficial deeds of the gods, you go after and follow the gods.
The immortal king among mortals has sat down in the dwelling, perfecting the sacrificial assemblies;
Agni, whose face is anointed with ghee, has shone forth widely, knowing all poetic wisdoms.
In the dwelling of mortals, the immortal King has taken his seat, accomplishing the sacred rites. With his face anointed with ghee, Agni has shone forth widely, he who knows all secret wisdom. 18.

The immortal and eternal King, Agni, who shines resplendently, the wise one who perfects and accomplishes the sacrifices within the home (*duroṇe*)—the dwelling—of mortals who maintain the *agnihotra*, sits down firmly.
Knowing all poetic insights (*kāvyāni*), his face anointed with clarified butter (*ghṛtapratīkaḥ*), his limbs drenched in *ghṛta*, our Agni shines forth widely and extensively.
Come to us with your auspicious friendships, O Great One, hastening with your mighty protections. Bestow upon us abundant wealth, enduring and well-spoken, and grant us a glorious portion.

Come to us with your auspicious friendships, O Great One, with your mighty aids, hastening toward us. Bestow upon us abundant, ever-present wealth; make our portion glorious and accompanied by fair renown. 19.

Desiring to go everywhere for refuge, O Great One, come toward us with your auspicious, benevolent friendships—friendships consisting of friendly deeds—and with your vast protections. Come! (Asme) [Note:
The variants ka-kha-ga-gha-ṅa-ca-na-ma-va read "rathīḥ"].

2. O Agnihotra, [you who possess] the syllables *ka-jha-jha-ga-ta-tha-na-ma-va*, grant us wealth—vast, extensive, and continuous; a wealth that carries us across all calamities, possesses beautiful speech, is a portion to be shared by all, and is endowed with glory and renown. Bestow this wealth upon us!
The repetition of the word "to us" (*asmabhyam*) is for the sake of expressing excessive respect.

These ancient births of yours, O Agni, and these new ones, I have proclaimed to you, the full one. For the great bull, these libations have been prepared; at every birth, Jātavedas has been established.

These, O Agni, are your ancient births; I shall proclaim these new ones for you who are full of vigor. These great deeds have been performed for the Bull. At every birth, Jātavedas has been established. 20.

O Agni, for you—ancient and eternal—I have proclaimed these births, deeds, or hymns: whether they be old, worthy of being honored by the great; or new, not found among others; or even those of today. O Jātavedas—one whose wisdom is born, or whose wealth is born—in birth after birth.
"Births" (*janmānaḥ*) refers to those things that are born.
When all of them have arisen, [the soma] has been placed for the sake of sacrifice;
for that Agni, the showerer (*vṛṣṇe*) of riches, these—these very—libations (*savanā*) have been prepared again and again.
Born again and again, Jātavedas is established and kindled by the Viśvāmitras with pure [fuel].
May we abide in the favor and the auspicious goodwill of that one worthy of sacrifice.
Born in every birth, Jātavedas is established; he is kindled by the Viśvāmitras. May we abide in the benevolence and auspicious goodwill of that holy one worthy of sacrifice. 21.
In birth after birth, among all human beings, Jātavedas has been established by the Viśvāmitras—
the plural being used for honor.
That Jātavedas who is kindled and made to blaze incessantly and without interruption by the great seer Viśvāmitra.
Remaining in the good-will of that Agni, who is worthy of sacrifice and deserving of worship, may we also abide in his auspicious and venerable benevolence—that is, in his disposition of favor.

Indeed (hi), for this reason, let no one (na) ever defile (dūduṣat) the eternal (sanatā) laws (dharmāṇi), that is, the sacrifices. *Note on the word *pājaḥ*: Its meanings are derived from its root, not merely from its phonetic form.* **Vocabulary:** *vaiśvānarāya*: to Vaiśvānara (the fire common to all men). *pṛthupārjase*: to him of vast strength or wide-reaching power. *vipaḥ*: the wise ones; the singers. *ratnā*: precious things; delightful offerings. *vidhanta*: they offer; they perform. *dhuruṇeṣu*: in the stations; in the sacrificial duties. *gātave*: in order to go; to attain the right path. *agniḥ*: Agni. *devān*: the gods. *amṛtaḥ*: the immortal. *duvasyati*: he honors; he serves with offerings. *atha*: therefore; now. *dharmāṇi*: the laws; the sacrificial ordinances. *sanatā*: eternal; ancient. *na*: not. *dūduṣat*: let him not defile; let him corrupt. **Translation:** The wise singers offer precious gifts to Vaiśvānara, who possesses vast strength, so that he may proceed to his established stations. Agni, the immortal, indeed honors the gods through the presentation of oblations; therefore, let no one ever defile the eternal laws. **Grammatical Notes:** * *Vaiśvānarāya*: Dative singular masculine. * *Pṛthupārjase*: Dative singular masculine, compound of *pṛthu* (vast) and *pārjas* (strength/power). * *Vipaḥ*: Nominative plural feminine. * *Ratnā*: Accusative plural neuter. * *Vidhanta*: Present indicative middle, third person plural. * *Dhuruṇeṣu*: Locative plural neuter. * *Gātave*: Infinitive used adverbially. * *Duvasyati*: Present indicative active, third person singular. * *Sanatā*: Instrumental singular neuter, used adverbially. * *Dūduṣat*: Aorist injunctive, third person singular. **Contextual Insight:** This verse emphasizes the role of the wise (*vipaḥ*) in maintaining the cosmic order (*dharma*). By offering hymns to the universal fire (*vaiśvānara*), they ensure the continuity of the sacrifice, which sustains both the gods and the world. The "eternal laws" (*sanatā dharmāṇi*) refer specifically to the sacrificial rites, which must remain uncorrupted to preserve the harmony of the universe. The term *amṛta* (immortal) applied to Agni underscores his perpetual presence as the mediator between the divine and the human realms. The Forum was also the site of many important events, such as the election of emperors and the celebration of public holidays. The Forum was also a place of commerce. Merchants would come to the Forum to sell their goods. The Forum was also a place of learning. Schools were located in the Forum, and students would come to study there. The Pantheon: The Pantheon was built by Emperor Hadrian in the second century AD. It was a circular temple dedicated to all the gods of ancient Rome. The wondrous messenger moves between the two worlds, heaven and earth; seated as the Hotṛ-priest, the appointed representative of Manu, Agni—impelled by the gods, rich in wisdom through prayer—adorns the vast dwelling with his rays of light. The wondrous (*dasma*) Agni, acting as the messenger (*dūtaḥ*) of the gods, moves (*īyate*) between the two worlds, heaven and earth (*rodasī*). Seated (*niṣattaḥ*) as the priest of Manu, established (*purohitaḥ*) in front of him in the form of the Āhavanīya fire and others, Agni, having taken his place, adorns (*pari bhūṣati*) the great dwelling—the sacrificial hall—with his rays (*yubhiḥ*). Impelled (*iṣitaḥ*) by the gods and possessing wealth through wisdom (*dhiyāvasuḥ*), he shines forth. These two are epithets of Agni.

The inspired poets magnify with their thoughts Agni, the banner of sacrifices, the accomplisher of the assembly; in him the singers have placed their works and their songs, and for him the sacrificer desires blessings. The banner of sacrifices, the accomplisher of the assembly (the means of attaining it), the unique cause—him, Agni, the inspired poets magnify with their thoughts through their own ritual acts. Furthermore, the singers, in whom they have placed their works—the rites to be performed by themselves—and their songs, for that Agni the sacrificer desires blessings or joys.

That Agni, through his manifold forms such as the terrestrial and the lightning, has entered or pervades both heaven and earth (*dyāvāpṛthivī*).
Purupriyaḥ means he who is exceedingly dear among men; or alternatively, Purupriyaḥ means he who is dear to the *puru*, that is, the most excellent ones.

The wise (*vipra*) one, the intelligent (*medhāvī*), who is conscious (*cekitāna*) of the dawn (*uṣas*), and who, knowing the paths (*padavīḥ*) of the seers (*kavīnām*)—those of lovely vision—Agni, who is awakened (*praty abodhi*), whose strength is broad (*pṛthupājāḥ*), whose splendor is vast (*pṛthutejāḥ*), who performs the work of the gods (*devayajñaḥ*), and who is well-kindled (*samiddhaḥ*), he, the bearer (*vahnī*), has opened up (*apāvaḥ*) the doors of darkness (*tamasaḥ*)—the gateways for the arrival of ignorance.
He has grown great through the praises and songs of the worshippers, he who is worthy of homage with hymns;

Agni has grown great through the hymns and songs of his praisers; he, worthy of homage, has been magnified by their recitations. Desiring the many manifestations of the Eternal Order (Ṛta), the messenger has shone forth at the dawning of the dawn. 2.
He who is Agni is to be saluted and worshipped; he is praised with hymns, with songs, and with words as being "thus much.
He praises Agni by way of his being the universal self:
when Agni is kindled, then he becomes Mitra, and he becomes Sūrya.
Being Mitra himself, he becomes the Hotṛ;
he becomes Varuṇa, the Jātavedas, whose wisdom is born.
As Mitra, he becomes the Adhvaryu—one who is gentle, whose mind is inclined toward giving, or whose mind is self-controlled.
He alone becomes the swift impeller, the wind;
and furthermore, he becomes the friend and ally of the rivers, the streams, and the mountains.

Agni guards the beloved foot of the bird at the forefront of the enemy; he guards the head of the mighty refuge. Agni guards the seven-headed one in the navel; he guards the exhilaration of the gods from the distance.

He protects the beloved summit of the earth, the station of the bird; the mighty one protects the course of the sun. At the navel, Agni protects the seven-headed one; the lofty one protects the exhilaration of the gods.
Lofty and beautiful to behold, Agni protects the beloved summit—the first station—of the earth, the pervasive one who possesses fragrance.
Great and mighty, he follows the path of the sun; "caraṇapra" means he goes along the path.
Desiring, Agni takes his stand upon the womb—the place, the abode—which is like a man, radiant, wide-striding, far-reaching, and yearning.

Shining brightly, pure, beautiful to behold, or indeed purified, the great purifier, Agni who cleanses others, makes the two parents, Heaven and Earth, ever new again and again. Who does this? It is he.
Born at once, he grew by means of the plants when they nourished him with flowing ghee;
like waters gliding down a slope, Agni shone brightly as he was protected in the lap of his parents.

Born at once, he has grown by means of the plants, if they increase him with flowing streams of ghee; like waters gliding down a slope, Agni, being purified, has expanded in the lap of his parents. 8.

When Agni, as soon as he is born, grows by means of the plants—that is, when he is carried along—then those plants, shining brightly like waters flowing down a steep slope, release their fruits and cause him to grow with clarified butter.
May Agni, growing in the lap—the intermediate space—of his parents, Heaven and Earth, protect us from this [danger].
The mighty one has been kindled with fuel at the navel of heaven and upon the earth;
Agni, Mitra, and Mātariśvan are to be praised; may he, as the messenger, carry the gods here for the sacrifice.

Ut! Ūm! Praised with kindling-sticks, the mighty one has extended himself from the sky, upon the navel of the earth. Agni, worthy of praise as Mitra and Mātariśvan, let him, the messenger, bring the gods hither for the sacrifice. 9.

Being situated at the *nābhā*, the navel—the central region—of the *pṛthivyāḥ*, the high altar (*uttaravedi*), he shines forth, *udyaut*, in the *varman*, the form or armor, of the *divaḥ*, the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
*Mitraḥ*: the friend of all; *īḍyaḥ*: worthy of praise; *Mātariśvā*.
He breathes within the mother, the intermediate space (*mātariśvan*); he moves by means of the form of the sun, thus he is *Mātariśvan*.

when Mātariśvan kindled the oblation-bearer who was hidden from the Bhṛgus.

Carrying the sacrificial oblation, the butter-dripping ladle goes eastward, bearing the gift for Agni.

O singers, being urged by Manu, lead her who is directed toward the gods, you seekers of the divine. Carrying the oblation for Agni, the swift, butter-smeared ladle goes forward, bearing the gift to the right.

O performers, you who are doers, desiring the gods, being urged by the mind—that is, by the mantra—lead forth, bring forward, and present the ladle that goes toward the gods. Carrying the oblation for Agni, flowing with ghee, rich in food, directed eastward with its tip pointing forward, and moving as it goes, the ladle, anointed with ghee, proceeds toward the Āhavanīya fire from the south. It goes well.
1. [The letters] ma and śobhamānānām.
2. [The letters] ka, jha, ña, na, and ma are in the cave of the sun; [the letters] jha, ta, tha, ṇa, and dha are in the cave within the cave of the sun.
3. ka-a (ā) comes; jha-ma comes.
At your birth, you filled the two worlds, O you who are worthy of sacrifice; indeed, you have now spread yourself far and wide.
Even beyond heaven and earth, O Agni, your flames, reaching out with their common tongue, surge upward through your greatness.

At your birth, you filled the two worlds, O Heaven and Earth; indeed, you surpassed them, O Agni, you who are worthy of sacrifice. Now, by your greatness, even beyond heaven and earth, let your flames, with their united tongues, rise upward.
O Agni, being born, you filled and pervaded both *rodasī*, heaven and earth.
Furthermore, O *prayajya*—worthy of sacrifice—you have surpassed even heaven, the intermediate space, and the earth by your greatness; indeed, you are preeminent.
By this, the excellence of the bearer (*vahni*) has been expressed.
For you who are of such a nature, let the fires—the sacrificial fires such as the Āhavanīya and others, which have fire as their primary element—be kindled. For what purpose?
For the sake of that state whose essence consists of unified tongues.
Now Pūraṇa:
"And Heaven and Earth, the worshipful ones, establish you as the Hotṛ-priest for the house.
Ya...

The great one, the preeminent one, Agni—who is being desired or longed for by the sacrificers and others, or who desires wealth for the sacrificer—having settled down firmly and immovably in his own place, the *sadhastha*, which is endowed with greatness (*māhina*) between heaven and earth, he sits down. O two wives (*sapatnī*), whose common husband is the sun, who are unaging (*ajara*), unharmed by another, and who yield the nectar-like water (*sabandhu*)—O Agni, [you sit] upon them. (Note: *sabandhu* refers to the nectar-like water; *sabarī* is a variant or related term for that same essence.)

For him, Heaven and Earth are the two milch-cows; Agni is the wide-striding one, possessing a broad gait or, alternatively, a large udder; and these two become the nourishing cows that provide satisfaction.
Truly, O Agni, great are thy greatnesses; by thy wisdom thou hast extended the two worlds, heaven and earth.
At thy birth thou becamest the messenger; thou, O bull, art the leader of the peoples.

Truly, O Agni, great are thy greatnesses; by thy wisdom thou hast extended the two worlds, heaven and earth. As soon as thou wast born, thou becamest the messenger; thou, O bull, art the leader of the peoples. 5.
O Agni, your *vratā*—your great, sublime deeds pertaining to you—become truly vast.
By your *kratvā*, by your power of illumination, you have extended across both *rodasī*, heaven and earth.
You have become the messenger.
O Vṛṣabha, you who are by nature a showerer [of benefits], being born, you are the leader of the *carṣaṇīs*—the sacrificers—and the one who brings them the attainment of their fruits.
Or rather, yoke to the pole with the ritual formulas the two long-maned, ruddy steeds that drip with ghee, belonging to the Cosmic Order (*ṛta*).
Then, O God, bring hither all the gods; O Jātavedas, make our sacrifices successful.

With the two long-maned steeds of Truth, yoked with effort, dripping with ghee, the two ruddy ones—place them at the pole; then, O God, bring hither all the gods, and perform the sacrifice well, O Jātavedas! 6.

O God, [yoke] the two tawny ones (rohita), possessing beautiful manes, endowed with long hair, harnessed with suitable thongs that serve as the means of drawing, dripping with ghee, the two red steeds of the *ṛta*—that is, of the sacrifice.
The word "vā" has the sense of "and" (ca).
And place [the horse] at the pole; that is to say, yoke him. Then, immediately thereafter, having mounted all the gods upon the chariot, bring them hither.
O Jātavedas, make them—those who perform excellent sacrifices—possessors of well-conducted rites.
Even from heaven, the lights have shone forth for you; O Agni, you shine after the many dawns as they break.
When you, O Agni, burn with desire in the forests, the gods praise the joyous invoker.
Even from heaven thy radiant beams have shone forth; thou shinest after many dawns as they break. When thou, O Agni, burnest eagerly in the woods, the gods praise the joyous invoker.
1. You have spread through the sky; you have spread through the earth.

2. You are joined with the rays of light. O Agni, when you dwell among the forests in the woods, burning and desiring the waters, then your lights—your own brilliant flashes—shine forth, illuminating even from the sky, even more than the sun.
Shining forth with special brilliance, you illuminate the ancient Dawns that have shone before;
the gods, as your praisers, celebrate and extol the lights of you, the delightful and hymned Hotṛ-priest.

Whether they are the gods who rejoice in the wide mid-air, or those who dwell in the luminous realm of heaven; or whether they are the worshipful ones, swift to hear, who have extended themselves like horses yoked to chariots, O Agni—8. Whether they are the gods who rejoice in the wide mid-air, or those who dwell in the luminous realm of heaven; or whether they are the worshipful ones, swift to hear, who have extended themselves like horses yoked to chariots, O Agni.

He alone becomes the Hotṛ priest, even for the two vast and wide worlds, heaven and earth, who at the beginning of his sacrifice praise and extol him for the increase and expansion of the entire rite.
For this Hotṛ born of the Eternal Order (Ṛta), the two well-established, beautiful, truth-abiding, water-bearing, and true-natured worlds stand favorably inclined toward him.
How so?
Like two sacrifices, like two rites, like two oblations—O Agni, first bestow nourishment upon the one of many deeds for the sake of the one who invokes you most constantly;
may there be for us a son, a Munu, a progenitor. May that benevolence of yours be with us at the beginning.

First, bestow *iḷā* upon the sage who has many wonders, for the one who constantly invokes you; grant it to him who calls most frequently. May there be for us a son, a progeny, a winner of cattle. Let that benevolence of yours be established first for this man. ||11||
"O Agni, come to the sacrificial food (iḷā)"—this [verse] has been explained previously.
May the illumination of the meaning of the Vedas, dispelling the darkness [of ignorance],
bestow the four aims of human life— Om!
I bow to that elephant-faced one, by saluting whom Vāgīśa and the other wise ones become successful in all their undertakings.
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose breath is the Vedas and who created the entire universe from the Vedas.
In the section beginning with "somasya," there are twelve hymns.
Among them, the seventh hymn, consisting of eleven verses, begins with "praya āḥ.
Its seer is Viśvāmitra, the visionary of the *maṇḍala*.
Because it is in the *anuṣṭubh* meter, it is [classified as] a *triṣṭubh*.
According to the technical conventions regarding the *maṇḍala* and so forth, Agni is the deity.
The application (*viniyoga*) of these three hymns in the *prātaranuvāka* and the *āśvina-śastra* has been stated as: "Agni is present at every approach."
In this regard, here is the third hymn.
Those who have come from the draught of the one with the sharpened back have entered the two mothers; the seven voices are well-adorned.
The two parents move together; he of long life moves forward toward the two who have been milked for his direct perception.

Those who have come from the drink of the white-backed one have entered the two parents and the seven voices. The two parents, well-adorned, move together; they flow forth for the sake of long life, seeking to reach it.
The rays of the *śitippṛṣṭha*—the one with the dark-blue back—the *dhāsi*, the all-sustaining Agni, which rise up pre-eminently, have entered the two parents, heaven and earth, on all sides.
The seven *vāṇīs*—the flowing rivers whose nature is to glide—have also entered them. The two parents, heaven and earth, moving about him, interact perfectly with that Agni who dwells around them.
Likewise, "in the presence" (*pratyakṣe*) they "extend" (*prasrāte*) "long life"—that is, the long-lived movement of Agni or abundant food—by means of "sacrificing eminently" (*prayakṣe*).
The meaning is that they bring it about.
Alternatively, Heaven and Earth, being present, constantly and eminently sacrifice for the sacrificer and thereby bring about his long life.
Being a particle (*nipāta*), it is udātta on its first syllable.
In the Vedic language (*chandas*), according to the rule "even when separated," it is connected with the word *āharati*.
He said: [the root] *ṛ* means "to go";
this is the form in the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*) with the suffix *usi*.
Because it is joined with something else, there is no elision [of the augment].
It has the accent of a suffix. Of Śitipṛṣṭha.
The word *pṛṣṭha*, having the suffix *kta*, is oxytone (*antodātta*).
By the rule *‘śinirniryābahujabahuvrīhābhavasat’* (Pāṇini 6.2.138), there is the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the final member.
[This applies to] *dhāseḥ*.
The root *dhūñ* means "to support" or "to nourish," or alternatively, *dhēṭ* means "to drink.
From these, the suffix *si* is applied in the sense of the agent according to the *āṇādika* [list].
The accent is that of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
In *mātārā*,
it is acutely accented on the final syllable because it is a form ending in the suffix *-tṛ*, as established by the rule *na-sneṣṭṛ-vaṣṭṛ-kṣatṛ-hotṛ-potṛ-mātṛ-pitṛ-jāmātṛ-duhitṛ* (Uṇādi Sūtra 2.153).
By the rule *ṛto ṅo* (Pāṇini 7.3.110), there is *guṇa* substitution.
By the rule *supāṃ suluk* (Pāṇini 7.1.39), the case-ending (*sup*) is replaced by *ṅ*. Thus, *viviśuḥ*.
The root *viś* means "to enter.

In the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*), because it is treated as having the *kit* designation by the rule "the *liṭ* [affixes] following a non-conjunct consonant are *kit*," there is an absence of *guṇa*. There is also the *nighāta* (elision of accent).

The word *masa* [is derived as follows]: from the root *sap*, meaning "to go," the suffix *kanin* and the augment *tuṭ*— which are prescribed by the rule *savyaṣbhyāṃ tud ca* (Uṇādi-sūtra 1.155)— apply to the end of the root as well due to its being a *bahulaka* (irregular) formation.

Furthermore, these two verses are not present; the first verse is missing. 1. In the *sa* manuscript, the first chapter of the third *aṣṭaka* begins with "somasya. 2. In the *ma*, *sa*, and *pratyāmihapasa* manuscripts, there are three [verses]. 3. In the *ja*, *ṇa*, and *matrāśvabhāvāḥ* manuscripts, [the reading is as such]. 4. In the *la* manuscript, [it is] "in the sense of excellence" (*prakarṣeṇa*). 5. In the *la* manuscript, there is the suffix *sip*. 6. In the *kha*, *ga*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *bha*, and *sa* manuscripts, it is "from *sapi* and *asṛ*" (*sapyasṛbhyām*); in the *na* manuscript, "from seven [words]" (*saptamṛbhyām*); in the *la* manuscript, "from *nṛpa* and *saubhya*" (*nṛpa saubhyām*).

The vowel *a* is substituted for the letter *r*. Even though the suffix is *nic*, there is an acute accent (*udātta*) on the final syllable due to "transposition" (*vyatyaya*). *Parikṣiptā*: from the root *kṣi* meaning "dwelling" and "going," with the suffix *kvip* according to the rule *kvip ca*; because the suffix is *pit*, the augment *nuk* is added; this is a *prādi* compound; it retains the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the second member; the case-ending *sup* is replaced by *ḍā* according to the rule *supāṃ suluk...* They move (*carante*): from the root *car* meaning "motion" and "eating"; with the prefix *sam*, the Ātmanepada is used according to the rule *samastṛtīyāyuktāt* (Pāṇini 1.3.14). *Nivāta*: from the root *mṛ* meaning "motion"; this root has the causative sense (*antarbhāvitaṇyartha*) inherent in it; the letter *r* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). In the word *īdṛśena*, there is the designation *pragṛhya*; it receives the grave accent (*nighāta*). *Prayakṣe*: from the root *yaj* meaning "worship of the gods," "forming an alliance," and "giving"; the suffix *sen* is added in the sense of the infinitive marker *tumun*; this is a *prādi* compound; it retains the original accent of the second member; [the suffix] *kṛnmejanta*... [is applied].

When the single substitute for those two [the suffix *kyac* and the preceding vowel] is made, that single substitute is acute according to the rule "an acute replaces [the place of] an acute. The case-ending *am* is unaccented (*anudātta*). By the rule "of an unaccented [syllable] following an acute," the *am* becomes circumflex (*svarita*). *Ekā*: from the root *iṇ* in the sense of "going" (*gatau*), the suffix *kan* is applied by the rule "after *iṇ*, *bhī*, *kai*, *pai*, etc. (*iṇ-bhī-kā-pā-ādi*). From that which ends in *kan*, the feminine suffix *āp* is added. It is without accent (*nis-svara*). *Vartanam*: from the root *vṛt* in the sense of "turning" (*vartane*). The causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) is implied. The suffix *ani* is applied by the rule "and after *vṛt*" (*vṛteś-ca*; Uṇādi Sūtra 2.263). There is *guṇa* substitution. The final acute (*antodāttatva*) occurs by metrical transposition (*vyatyaya*). *Gauḥ*: from the root *gam* in the sense of "going" (*gatau*), the suffix *ḍo* is applied by the rule "after *gam*, the suffix *ḍo*" (*gameḥ-ḍoḥ*; Uṇādi Sūtra 2.225). Due to the *ḍit*-marker, there is elision of the suffix. By the rule "after *go*, the suffix is *ṇit*" (*goto-ṇit*), the case-ending *sup* is *ṇit*, and thus there is *vṛddhi*. This is the accent of the suffix (*pratyaya-svara*).
The wise Lord, the finder of wealth for those who offer praise, caused them to grow up together until they reached maturity;
he whose back is dark blue and who has many faces made them dwell apart from the nourishment of the brushwood.

The well-guided rivers, becoming submissive, carry him up; the wise lord, the winner of riches among all treasures, [ascends]. Strengthening the weak and making them strong, the flowing rivers carry him—the great son of Tvaṣṭṛ, the ageless one worthy of being aged, the supporter who desires to sustain the worlds—thus they bear and uphold him.
In the common dwelling-place near the waters, Agni, shining with his limbs— that is, his constituent parts— has entered heaven and earth in various ways;
he has entered within the two worlds as if they were one.
Just as a man enters a single woman, so too [is it with] Tvāṣṭra. The suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "the offspring of Tvaṣṭṛ" according to the rule *tasyāpatyam*.
The vowel of the suffix;
that which is being obstructed; *stabhu* means obstruction, [referring to] one who desires that.
By the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac*, the suffix *kyac* is added after a nominal stem (*sup*) when expressing one's own desire.
By the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ*, there is lengthening of the vowel;
from that form ending in *kyac*, the suffix *śānac* is applied by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
Because there is no difference in the vowel *a*, [the augment] *muk* is applied before *āna*; [and] *śānac* is substituted for *la*.

The sixth case ending is elided by *aluk*. The accent of the final member remains as in its original form (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvaratvam*) because it is a *kṛt*-derived word. Regarding *surucaḥ*: in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the final syllable of the second member is udātta according to the rule "anambubhyām. Regarding *iḍā*: from the root *īḍ* (in the sense of "praise"), the short vowel is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) anomaly; just as the word *vāk* ends in the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, so it is here. Since the suffix is marked with *p*, it is anudātta, and thus the accent of the verbal root remains. Regarding *gaṇyā*: from the root *gaṇ* (in the sense of "counting"), the suffix *yat* is added in the sense of the word itself (*svārthe*). By the rule "yato nāvah," etc., the first syllable is udātta. Regarding *māhinā*: the suffix *inaṇ* is added to the root *mahi* according to the rule "maheinaṇ ca"; due to the *ṇit* nature of the suffix, there is vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel. The initial syllable is udātta by transposition (*vyatyaya*). Regarding *gīḥ*: from the root *gṛ* (in the sense of "sound"), the suffix *kvip* is applied. By the rule "ṛta iddhātoḥ," the *ṛ* is changed to *i*; then by "voḥ pūrvayoḥ" (or "vohapadhāyāḥ"), the vowel is lengthened. This is the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadikasvara*). || 1 ||

And so, from their two great parents, they have brought forth a far-reaching cry and great nourishment; where the bull, at the end of night, shall carry the singer to his own station across the enclosure.

And so, from the two great parents, they have led forth the great sound with full knowledge; they have brought the nourishment following their own domain, where the bull, at the turning of the night, has carried the singer toward his own abode. 6.

And moreover: from the great, for the two great ones, from the great, for the two great ones—for the two parents, Heaven and Earth—with piercing, with penetration, following the sound, being sounded after, [they brought] the ladle, the well. "Ladle" (*śūpa*) and "well" (*suvam*): because of the reading in the list of names for happiness (*sukha-nāman*) as "the ladle is auspicious" (*śūpaṃ śunam*, Nighaṇṭu 3.6.10). That happiness, the sacrificers brought Agni, they caused him to reach. That Agni, where among the sacrificers—the bull (*ukṣā*), the sprinkler of water by producing rain—at night (*aktoḥ*). The word *akuḥ* denotes night; because of its being read in that list of names as "the dark one is *akuḥ*" (Nighaṇṭu 1.7.4); and because of the etymology: "in which the world is anointed (*ajyate*) and sprinkled (*sicyate*) with mist. Of that night, the surrounding support (*pari-dhānam*), the supporter on all sides, his own (*svam*), belonging to himself, the abode (*dhāma*), the splendor—toward the singer, the praiser, for the sake of hearing the praise—he indeed carries (*vva-kṣa*) near; he brings it close. This is the meaning. *Uto*: the designation *pragṛhya* applies by Pāṇini 1.1.15; thus, etc., ending in an acute accent. *Ghoṣam*: from the root *ghuṣir* in the sense of "sound"; the suffix *ghañ* in the passive sense; the *guṇa* of the light penultimate vowel; the accent of the *ñit* suffix. *Mahaḥ*: the elision of the vowels *a* and *kāra* and the semi-vowel *y* is Vedic; the acute accent of the case-ending by the rule "addition for *brahman* and *mahaḥ*. *Anayanta*: the form of the root *ṇīj* in the sense of "leading" in the *laṅ* tense; the *nighāta* (suppressed accent). *Ukṣā*: from the root *ukṣa* in the sense of "sprinkling"; the word *ukṣan* is established as ending in the suffix *kanin*; by transposition, it has the acute accent at the end. *Ha*: unaccented because it belongs to the *cādi* group. *Yatra*: the syllable preceding the suffix is acute by the rule "when *lit* follows. *Aktoḥ*: from the root *añjū* in the senses of "manifesting, moving, protecting"; the suffix *ku* by the rule "after *vyā*, *añj*, and *ati*"; because it is *kit*, there is the elision of *n* by the rule "of those not having *it* as an indicatory letter"; the accent of the suffix. *Vvakṣa*: from the root *vaha* in the sense of "carrying"; the *liṅ* suffix in the present tense according to the rule "in the Veda, the *luṅ*, *laṅ*, and *liṭ* may be used"; the *sakāra* is Vedic; the substitution of *ṇal* for *tip*; the syllable preceding the suffix is acute by the rule "when *lit* follows."
1. [The suffix] *svārtha* occurs after *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, and *la*.
2. [The suffix] *udātta* occurs after *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, and *sa*.
3. [The suffix] is observed after *gha* when [the word] *agni* is characterized by *dyāvāpṛthivī*.
4. Referring to the hymn being chanted repeatedly; 5. Happiness [is found] in the letters kha, ga, ca, ja, ṇa, bha, la, and sa;
6. One who sprinkles [is found] in the letters ga, ca, ja, ṇa, and sa.
7. Gha is to be retained. 8. A word ending in *ta* has its final syllable acute-accented (*udātta*). 9. *Ghu* consists of *kha, ga, ca, ja, ṇa, na, bha*; *sa* and *śuṣ*.

10. [The suffix *kvi* occurs] after *kha*, *ga*, and *ca* in the sense of pervading (*vyāpti*) and disappearance (*bhrakṣa*); after *ja* and *ṇa* in the sense of manifestation (*vyakti*) and disappearance (*bhrakṣaṇa*); and after *la* in the sense of manifestation (*vyakti*) and throwing (*kṣepaṇa*). 11. [The suffix *kvip* occurs] after *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *bha*, and *vyāja* with the prefix *ati*; after *la* with *vyāja* and *ati*; and after *na* with *vyāja* and *jñāti*.
By means of the Adhvaryus and the sacrificial animals, the seven sages guard the beloved, hidden footstep of the Bird.
The wise bulls rejoice; the ageless gods have indeed followed the ordinances of the gods.

With the Adhvaryus, with the cattle—the seven sages guard the beloved, hidden footstep of the Bird; thus [saying], "of the Bird," the wise ones rejoice; the bulls are ageless; for the gods have followed the laws of the gods; thus they have gone. 7.
There are twelve officiating priests (ṛtvij) excluding the group of Udgātṛs;
among them, seven are the utterers of the vaṣaṭ-call,
while five others conduct the sacrifice.

Together with those five Adhvaryu priests, seven wise and intelligent Hotṛ-priests protect— that is, they preserve— the beloved, established station called Āhavanīya of Agni, whose nature is to move (veḥ).

Moving eastward for the purpose of drinking Soma, the wise ones— those who do not decay (ajūryāḥ), being impossible to age— and who are sprinklers (ukṣaṇaḥ) of the Soma juice, the gods and chanters, rejoice and exult.

Furthermore, those gods, acting as officiating priests (ṛtvijas), followed—that is, understood—the vows (vratā), meaning the sacrifices, belonging to the gods. The particle *hi* indicates a well-known fact;
the meaning is that by the grace of Agni, the gods, possessing oblations as their characteristic, obtained the sacrifices.
They protect. [The root] *rakṣ* means "to protect.
The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs by way of transposition (vyatyaya).
Nighāta (the past passive participle). Nihitam.
From the root *ḍudhāñ* in the sense of "holding and nourishing," with the suffix *kta*, there is the substitution of *hi* for the root by the rule "dhāter hiḥ" [Pāṇini 7.4.42].
In the expression "gatiranantaraḥ," the term *gati* receives its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*).
[The same applies to] *viḥ*.
In the *dī* [section], it is mentioned among the *aṅgirasaḥ* and others.
From this [suffix],
by the rule "sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.84), there is guṇa;
and by the rule "ḍasiḍasośca," there is the formation of the single preceding form (pūrvarūpatva).
*Prājñaḥ*:
By the rule "aniganto'ñjatau," there is the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member.
*Madanti*.
The root *mad* is used in the sense of "joy";
it receives the *nighāta* accent;
it is a *guṇa* vowel.
This is the form derived from the root *iṇ* in the sense of "going" (*gatau*) in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense.
By the rule *iṇo gā luṅi*, there is the substitution of *gā*. By the rule *ātaḥ*, there is the substitution of *jus* for *jhi*.
The absence of the augment *aṭ* [in *hi*] is due to the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi" (Pāṇini 6.4.75);
however, because of its connection with the word *hi*, the *anudātta* accent is not suppressed here.
I invoke the two divine Hotṛ-priests first; the seven nourishers rejoice according to their own nature.
Praising the *ṛta*, they proclaim the *ṛta*; as guardians of the sacred law (*vratapā*), they meditate upon the law.

I draw near to the two divine Hotṛ-priests, the first; the seven nourishers rejoice according to their own nature. Praising the *ṛta*, they speak only of the *ṛta*; as guardians of the sacred law, they meditate upon the law.

5. Divine (daivyā); 6. divine (daivyāḥ); 7. the two divine Hotṛs, the performers of the oblation; 8. the first, the foremost, the principal ones; 9. I, Viśvāmitra, the seer of the mantra, direct toward this world and the other world;

10. I, Viśvāmitra, the seer of the mantra, 11. prepare [them]. Regarding the word *ṛñjati*, Yāska says: "The root *ṛñj* signifies the act of adorning or preparing. I, the seer of the mantra, prepare [them].
The seven *pṛkṣas* (the seven priests), the seven *hotṛkas*, rejoice and exult through *svadhā* and Soma.

Praising the *ṛta*—the hymn of praise—they are the guardians of the vow (*vratapās*), the protectors of the sacrificial rite (*vrata*). Radiant and shining, those *hotṛkas*, according to the vow during the performance of the sacrifice, speak of and proclaim Agni as the very truth, the *ṛta*.
The root *ṛñje*—
from *ṛji* and *bhṛjī*, meaning "to roast"—
this verbal root, preceded by the prefix *ni*, is used in the sense of "adornment."
The *nighāta* (elision).
By means of the *svadhā*,
he places— that is, he bestows— the [victim] in its own world for the sacrificer.

The first member of the compound retains its original accent (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvaratvam*).
They say:

regarding the root *brūñ* in the sense of "distinct speech," in the present tense (*laṭ*), by the rule "for *bruvaḥ*, there is the substitution of the five [endings] beginning with the first, and for *bruvaḥ* there is the substitute *āha*," the ending *jhi* is replaced by *āha* and *bruvaḥ* is replaced by *āha*.
The elision [of the *s*] occurs.
Regarding *dīdhyānāḥ*:
this is derived from the root *dīdhīṅ* in the sense of "shining" or "playing," with the suffix *śānac*.
Since that [suffix] is a *cit* suffix, although the final syllable would have been udātta by default, the initial syllable becomes udātta by the rule "the beginning of reduplicated (abhyasta) forms."
For the great steed who desires to be like a bull, for the many, for the bull, for the wondrous one—may the reins be easy to guide.
O divine Hotṛ, most exhilarating, being mindful, bring hither the great gods and the two worlds, heaven and earth.

For the great steed whose driver is Vṛṣan, for the many, for the bull, for the wondrous one—O divine Hotṛ, most delightful and wise, bring hither the reins that are easy to guide, and the great gods and the two worlds, Rodasī. 9.

O shining one, O Hotṛ, the invoker of the gods— O Agni, for you, the great (mahate), the surpassing one (atyāya) who exists transcending all, the wondrous one (citrāya) of manifold colors— or rather, the wondrous one worthy of being sought after and honored by the gods; for you, the showerer (vṛṣṇe) of desires, the many (pūrvīḥ), abundant, well-guided, and exceedingly extensive rays, pervading everywhere, act like bulls (vṛṣāyante).
They are like sprinklers.
Seeing the kindled fire with its flames, the Hāṇaras throw oblations such as Soma, clarified butter, and milk into it; thus the flames possess the nature of bulls.
Alternatively, the genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental.
And so, from this great, variegated, and virile fire, many rays act like bulls;
that is to say, by means of their virile power, they act like Parjanya (the rain-god).

Furthermore, being most exhilarating—that is, most intoxicating for the sacrificer—and being wise, endowed with knowledge, you bring hither, O Mighty One, the great gods worthy of worship and sacrifice, as well as Rodasī, Heaven and Earth, to this Vedic ritual.
They act like bulls (*vṛṣāyante*).
Following the recurrence of the rule *upamānāt*, the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied by the rule *kartuḥ kyaṅ salopaśca*.
The lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ*.
The elision of the final vowel of the first member [of a compound] when followed by *pāda* and so forth;
the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*);
and *mahe*.
The elision of the *takāra* following the vowel *a* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
The acute accent (*udātta*) on the case ending is due to the rule "of *bṛhat* and *mahat*" (*bṛhanmahatoḥ*). [The word is] *pūrvīḥ*.

From the root *pṛ* in the sense of "protecting" (*pālan*) and "filling" (*pūraṇa*), with the suffix *kuḥ* being carried over, the suffix *kupratyaya* is applied by the rule *pṛbhidividyadhigṛdhī* etc. Due to its *kittva* (indicatory *k*), the prohibition of *guṇa* applies; then, by the rule *udoṣṭhyapūrvasya*, the substitution of *u* occurs. Finally, by the rule *uraṇ raparaḥ*, the substitute *ṛ* is followed by the letter *r*.
Therefore, by the rule "voto guṇavacanāt," the suffix ṅīp is applied.
When the substitution of yaṇ has been made, the lengthening occurs by the rule "hali ca.
Then, by the rule "vā chandasi," the homogeneous long vowel (savarṇadīrgha) is substituted.

*Raśmayaḥ*. [The root] *aś* is used in the sense of "pervading" (*vyāptau*). Because it pervades the entire world, the suffix *mi* is applied—following the recurrence of the rule for *mi*—and by the rule *aśnote raś ca* (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.486), the suffix *mi* is added and the root *aś* is replaced by *raś*. Thus, *raśmayaḥ* (rays).
The accent is that of the suffix (pratyayasvara).
*Suyāmāḥ*:
"yāma" means the act of restraining (*yamana*).
The suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*).
In the *bahuvrīhi* compound, by the rule "nañ-subhyām," the final syllable of the latter member bears the udātta accent.
O King!
Because of the exclusion [expressed by] "not at the beginning of a word" (*apādādau*), there is no optional initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*).
*Hotar*:
the suffix *tṛn* is used here in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlika*) derived from the root *hu*.

The semivowel substitution (*saṃprasāraṇa*) occurs by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi. There is no *tri-ghāta* (tripartite accentuation) because it is not at the beginning of a *pāda* and is not an uninvoked vocative (*amantrita*). It is in the lowest pitch (*mandratara*).
The root *mad* is used in the sense of praising and so forth.
By the rule "sphāyitañcivañci... and others, the suffix *rak* is applied; because it has the marker *iṭ*, the augment *suṭ* is added.
In *tarapaḥ*, because the suffix *pittva* is anudātta, the accent belongs to the suffix *rap*.
In *vakṣi*,
there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix by the rule "in the Veda, [suffixes are] frequently elided."
The states of being *ḍha* and *ka*.
The elision of accent (*nighāta*).

1. The suffix *ta* is replaced by the suffix *la*; the suffix *la* is replaced by *kap*. 2. The letters *kha*, *ta*, *bha*, and *la* are substitutes for *sevakāḥ*. 3. In the case of *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, and *vā*... [the vowel] becomes long; [in other cases], it does not exist. 4. [The rule applies] to *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, and *aśoreśa*.

The dawns, easy to worship, rich in wealth, eloquent, and bright with fair rays, have shone forth with riches. And even at the beginning, by the greatness of the earth, forgive whatever sin has been committed; grant us great favor. pukṣaprayajaḥ | draviṇaḥ | suvācaḥ | suketa-vaḥ | uṣasaḥ | revat | ūṣuḥ | uto iti | cit | agre | mahinā | pṛthivyāḥ | kṛtam | cit | enaḥ | sam | mahe | daśasya || 10 ||
1. *Draviṇaḥ*. Because it moves (*dravati*) and goes constantly, the word *draviṇaḥ* denotes Agni.
O Agni, you whose nature is constant movement, *draviṇaḥ*. 2. *Pukṣaprayajaḥ*.
1. *Pukṣaprayajaḥ*: Those waters in which one begins to sacrifice excellently with oblations characterized as food.

2. *Suvācaḥ*: Those whose words are beautiful, such as the *prātaranuvāka* (morning litany) and other such recitations. 3. *Suketavaḥ*: Those that provide excellent perception through the sounds of birds and humans.

Such Dawns as these have shone forth for us, making us wealthy—that is, endowed with riches. And furthermore, O Agni, whatever sin—characterized by injury or harm—has been committed through the greatness (mahimnā) of the vast flame of the earth, diminish that [sin] for the sake of the great sacrificer, for my own benefit.
*Puṣṭiprajāḥ*.
It has been stated that by the rule "they are seen after other [roots] as well," the suffix *vic* is authorized after the root *dṛś*, and thus it becomes applicable here.
Because it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the accentuation of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) applies. [The word is] *draviṇaḥ*.
From the root *du* in the sense of "going," the suffix *inan* is applied according to the rule *dudakṣabhyāminan*. There is the substitution of *guṇa* and *avādeśa*.
In the vocative, the non-elision of the case-ending *su* is due to Vedic usage.
The *nighāta* (elision of accent) occurs because of its being addressed (*āmantritatvāt*).
In the word *suvācaḥ*, the final syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*) is acute (*udātta*) according to the rule *naṃsubhyām*.
*Revat*: "Possessing wealth" (*rayi*); the suffix *matup* is applied because wealth (*dhana*) is found in this [person].
The accent of *matup* is acute according to the rule *hrasvanuḍbhyām*.
The substitution of *v* [for *m*] occurs by the rule "chandasīraḥ.
The *saṃprasāraṇa* [of *i* to *y*] occurs by the rule "rayimaṃtau bahulaṃ chandasi.
When the preceding [vowel] takes the place of the subsequent, there is *guṇa*.
*u.puḥ* | [The root] *upa-dāha* | Although this verbal root has the meaning of "burning," here it functions in the sense of "illuminating."
While the rule "luṅ in the Veda" (chandasi luṅ) is in force, [the suffix] liṭ [is used];
the form is [from] usi;
there is the nighāta [accent].
Regarding *pṛthivī*: from the root *prath* in the sense of "becoming manifest" (*prakhyāne*), the suffix *pivan* is applied according to the rule *pratheḥ pivan saṃprasāraṇaṃ ca*;
by that conjunction, the vowel substitution (*saṃprasāraṇa*) occurs for the root.
The suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *pitṛgādibhyaśca*. It is oxytone (*antodātta*) due to the accent of the suffix.
The acute accent of the case-ending is then applied by the rule *udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt*.
[The word] *daśasya* [is subject to] the *nighāta* (elision of accent).

O Agni, first grant to the one who invokes you the most constant gift of food, which is rich in wondrous deeds and consists of cattle. May there be for us a son, a prolific offspring; O Agni, let that benevolent favor of yours be ours. *īḷām agre purudaṃsaṃ saniṃ goḥ śaśvattamaṃ havamānāya sādha | syān naḥ sūnus tanayo vijāvāgne sā te sumatirbhūtvasme || 11 ||* Grant to the one who invokes you, first of all, food that is rich in wondrous deeds and the gift of cattle, most constant. May there be for us a son, a prolific offspring. O Agni, let that benevolent favor of yours be ours.

In the passage "O Agni, [the goddess] with many *daṃsas*," the word *daṃsaḥ* denotes action because it is listed among the names for ritual acts (*karman*) in Nirukta 2.1.3, where it is glossed as "wonderful act" (*amaḥ daṃsaḥ vepaḥ*).
Thus, she is the one who possesses *purūṇi daṃsāṃsi*, that is, many actions.

To that deity named *Iḷā*, who is in the form of a cow, who possesses manifold activities, and who bestows cattle and other livestock—[we offer praise] for the sake of the sacrificer who invokes her most constantly and uninterruptedly.

1. By the word *draviṇa* [in the manuscripts] *ja*, *ṇa*, and *la*; 2. *pravra* [is read] in *sa* and *gha*; 3. *yāsu* [is read] in *ja* and *ṇa*; 4. *vistīrṇījvālāyāḥ* [is read] in *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, and *bha*; *vistīrṇījvālāyāḥ* [is read] in *sa* and *ga*; 5. The phrase "revat...vatvam" does not exist in *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, and *ṇa*; 6. The word "daṃsāṃsi" does not exist in *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, and *bha*; 7. The phrase "bahukarmāṇam" does not exist in *gha* and *pa*; 8. "paśūnām" [is read] in *gha*, *ta*, *pa*, and *la*; 9. "pradātrīm" [is read] in *ta* and *la*.

O Agni, may your auspicious wisdom (*sumati*)—which is prolific (*vijāvā*, never barren)—be ours; may it be so. Furthermore, may there be for us a son (*sūnu*), a grandson (*tanaya*), and a great-grandson (*pautra*). *Śaśvattam*: The final syllable is udātta because of its inclusion in the *uṇhādi* list. *Sādha*: From the root *rādha/sādha* meaning "to accomplish" (*saṃsiddhau*). This form has an internal causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*). In the imperative (*loṭ*), the *śap* suffix is applied by transposition (*vyatyaya*). By the rule *serhyapicca*, *si* is replaced by *hi*. By *ano haḥ*, the *hi* is elided. It receives the *nighāta* accent. *Vijāvā*: From the root *janī* meaning "to be born" (*prādurbhāve*). From this, the suffix *vanip* is added according to the rule *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyante*. By *vidvanorunāsikasyāt*, the vowel becomes *ā*. The accent is that of the original form of the second member of the compound (*kṛduttarapada-prakṛtisvaratva*). The suffix is *liṅ*. *Bhūtū*: From the root *bhū* meaning "to exist" (*sattāyām*). By the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, the *śap* suffix is elided. By *bhūsuvosṭiṅi*, the prohibition of *guṇa* applies. 2. Translation complete.
Regarding the eighth hymn, *Añjanti*, belonging to Viśvāmitra, consisting of eleven verses and dedicated to Agni:

"The seekers of the gods anoint thee, O Lord of the Forest, with honey and with length. This "honey and length" is indeed the clarified butter (*ājya*). "If thou shalt stand upright, bestow wealth here; whether thou art in the lap of this mother or dwelling there"—by saying this, he means: "Whether thou art standing or whether thou art lying down, bestow wealth upon us. (AiB 2.2)

And thus it is also stated in the Nirukta: "O Vanaspati, desiring the gods at the sacrifice, they bring you with honey and with abundant clarified butter; when you stand upright, you will bestow wealth upon us, or when your dwelling is prepared in the lap, that is, in the womb of this mother" (Nirukta 8.18).
They say: "The root *aj* [is used] in the senses of moving apart, going, and protecting.
Because it belongs to the *rudh*-class, there is the suffix *śnam*.

In its *laṭ* [present tense] form, because of the doubling of the *śī* suffix, there is elision of the penultimate vowel according to the rule "aniditām..."; then, by the rule "bhasoralopaḥ," there is elision of the *a*. By the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), it is middle-accented (*madhyodātta*).
Regarding *tvām*:

in the case of the second person pronoun *yuṣmad* and the first person pronoun *asmad*, the substitution *tvam* and *mām* occurs in the singular according to the rule "tvamāvekavacane. Furthermore, the vowel *ā* is substituted [for the final *d*] by the rule "dvitīyāyāṃ ca" (Pāṇini 7.2.87).

"By the rule *ekādeśa udāttenodāttaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.5], the resulting single substitute is acute. *Samaṣṭam* means "well-provided"; *suvīram* means "endowed with excellent offspring. *Brahma* refers to food (*anna*). *Vanvānaḥ* means "bestowing" or "granting. *Asmadamatim* refers to our hunger that has become an enemy. For it is heard in the *Aitareya Brāhmaṇa* (2.2): "Hunger, indeed, is evil-mindedness (*pāpmāmatiḥ*)."
Driving away—that is, repelling—such an enemy whether near or far, rise up for great good fortune, that is, for the sake of attaining wealth and other prosperities.

Regarding the meaning stated, the *Brāhmaṇa* says: "'He who, being kindled, is kindled from the front'—for he is indeed kindled from the front at this time. 'Winning the Brahman, ageless, and rich in heroes'—he thus invokes a blessing. 'Driving away from us lack of thought'—lack of thought is indeed hunger; he thus drives that away. 'Arise for great good fortune from the sacrifice and from the sacrificer'—he thus invokes a blessing" (*AiB* 2.2). [The word] *samiddhasya*: [from the root] *jiindhī*, "to shine."

Regarding the formation of the word *samyagdṛś* in the sense of the past participle (*niṣṭhā*), there is a prohibition of the *dvirvacana* (doubling) by the rule "in the case of the past participle, [the doubling] of *śri*, *di*, and *ni* is prohibited.
As for *samyagdṛś*,
the acute accent (*prakṛtisvara*) falls on the first member of the compound according to the rule "a preceding [member] that is immediately followed [by a suffix causing doubling]."
Regarding the form *śrayamāṇaḥ*: this is the present participle (*laṭ*) of the root *śriñ* in the sense of "service" or "resorting to," with the suffix *śānac*.
Once the suffix has been rendered unaccented by the rule for the accent of *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes, the accent of the verbal root remains.
Regarding "purastāt": from the word *pūrva*, the suffix *am-tāti* is applied according to Pāṇini Sūtra 5.3.27 (*dikśabdebhyaḥ saptamīpañcamī...*),
and by Pāṇini Sūtra 5.3.40 (*am-tāti ca*), the substitution of *pura-* for *pūrva-* occurs.
The accent is that of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). *Brahma* is accented on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*) by the rule "of *nañ*, *cit*, *vap*, *ya*, and non-*ani* suffixes."
*Vanvānaḥ*. The root *vanu* means "to beg" (*yācane*);
here, however, this root functions in the sense of "giving" (*dānārthe*).
The suffix *śānac* is substituted for the present participle marker (*laṭ*). It is accented on the final syllable because it is marked with the indicatory letter *c*. [The word] *ajara*.
In *naño jaramaramitrasmṛtāḥ*, the first syllable of the final member is acute by rule; thus, *suvīram*.
In *vīravīryāṃ ca*, the first syllable of the final member is acute by rule.
In words such as *āre*, the udātta accent falls on the final syllable;
[the same applies to] *asmat*.
The suffix *mad* is applied by the rule "yupyasibhyāmidik";
there is elision (*luk*) of the case endings (*sup*) by the rule "supāṃ suluk";
[the word bears] the accent of the *mad* suffix.
*Amatim*:
By the rule "in a *tatpuruṣa* compound," the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member is applied. *Ut*.
As a particle (*nipāta*), it is udātta-accented on the first syllable.

Regarding *śrayasva*: this is from the root *śriñ* in the sense of "service" (*sevā*), with the substitution of *thās* for the second person singular middle voice (*madhyama-puruṣa-ekavacana*) in the loṭ (imperative) mood.
The substitution of *thās* for *se* occurs;
by the rule "svābhyāṃ vāmau," the letter *v* replaces the *e*;
[finally,] the *nighāta* accent is applied.
In *mahate*, because of the irregular formation (*nipātana*) "when *vartamāna* follows, [the word] *mahan* becomes *mahān*," it has an udātta accent on the final syllable.
By the rule "there is a substitution of form for *bṛhat* and *mahat*," the case ending is udātta.
For the sake of good fortune; in this context [of the rule] "prāṇabhṛjjātivayovacana," there is vowel lengthening (vṛddhi) according to the rule "hṛd-adasoḥ syante pūrvapadasya ca."
Because all case endings are optional in the Vedic language (*chandas*), the *vṛddhi* strengthening occurs for the final syllable of the second member [of the compound],
as in *jismbaraḥ*.
Rise up, O Lord of the Forest, upon the height of the earth;
being measured with perfect skill, bestow splendor upon the bearer of the sacrifice.
Rise up, O Lord of the Forest; take your place upon the height of the earth. Being well-measured, bestow splendor upon us for the sake of the sacrifice. 3.

O Lord of the Forest (*vanaspate*), rise up—be uplifted—upon the earth, at the highest point of the earth, in that place called the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*). Being measured with a beautiful mind (*sumitī*) or being determined by a beautiful measurement (*mīyamānaḥ*) in its dimensions, bestow splendor (*varcas*)—that is, food (*anna*)—upon the sacrificer who performs the sacrifice (*yajñavāhas*).
This very meaning is shown in the Brāhmaṇa: "With the words *'Rise up, O Lord of the Forest'*, [the verse] is for the one being raised; whatever is appropriate for the sacrifice is successful."

"Upon the height of the earth, O two heights of the earth, where they erect the sacrificial post—being measured with a good measurement, bestow splendor upon us, O carriers of the sacrifice!"—thus he invokes a blessing (AiB 2.2).
O Lord of the Forest! [The word *vanaspate*] has its initial syllable accented because it belongs to the class beginning with *apāt*. [The word *pṛthivyāḥ*...]
The acute accent (*udāttatva*) of the case-ending is due to the rule *udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt*. [In the word] *sumitī*:
from the root *māṅ* in the sense of "measuring," with the suffix *ktin*, [the form is derived] after *dyati-*...
1. *Ta-āre bādhamānaḥ dūre apanudans-tvam*. 2. *Kha-ga-ca-ja-ṇa-bha-uktārthyam*; *na-uktārthe’pi*. 3. *Ta-la-vvacanodgātrādibhyaḥ*.

In *syāt*, there is the substitution of *ī* by the rule *ghumāsthā°*. In *miti*, [there is the substitution of *ī*] by the rule *tādau ca niti kṛtyatau*, whereby the original accent (*prakṛtisvaratvam*) applies. In *mīyamānaḥ*, from the root *māṅ* (to measure), the suffix *yak* is applied in the passive sense; the substitution of *ī* occurs by *ghumāsthā°*, and the accent is that of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). In *dhāḥ*: from the root *dhāj* (to place), the *luṅ* (aorist) is used in the sense of the imperative (*loṭ*) according to the rule *chandasi luṅlaṅliṭaḥ*. By *itaśca*, the *ī* of the suffix *sip* is elided. By *gatisthā°*, there is the elision of *sic*. By *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is the absence of the augment *aṭ*; [finally] there is the *nighāta* (elision of accent). In *yajñavāhase*: it means "that which carries or attains the sacrifice. From the root *vah* (to carry/attain), the suffix *asun* is applied according to *vahidhāñbhyaśchandasi*. Because of the recurrence of the term *jit*, there is *vṛddhi* of the penultimate vowel. Furthermore, by the rule *gatikārakayoḥ*, there is the original accent for the preceding member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvaratvam*); thus, it has the original accent of the first member.
