I invoke here Dadhikrā, Agni, and Upas, the goddess; Bṛhaspati and the god Savitṛ; the two Aśvins, Mitra and Varuṇa, and Bhaga; the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas. || 5 ||

Indeed, I, the Hotṛ priest, invoke here—in this rite of ours—all these gods who partake of the oblation: Dadhikrā and the others; Dadhikrāvan; Agni; Upas, the presiding deity; Bṛhaspati, the radiant god; Savitṛ, the god who impels the entire world; the two Aśvins; Mitra and Varuṇa; Bhaga; Sūrya; the eight Vasus; the eleven Rudras; and the twelve Ādityas. I call upon you all for the purpose of accepting the sacrificial offering.
*Dadhikrā*: [The word] *dadhi* is derived from the root *dhā* (to place), with the suffix *kvip* applied according to the rule beginning with "ādyama-han" (*Pāṇini* 3.2.171).
With "dadhi" as the upapada, the suffix *vi* is applied to the root *kram* by the rule "jana-sana-... etc.;
by the rule "vid-vanoḥ," there is *ātva* (the substitution of ā for i).

The singer prays:

And you, enjoy these oblations (*havyā*) being offered by us.

The genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative.

O Purifier (*pāvaka*), O Agni who cleanses evil, O you whose own nature is self-dependent (*svadharman*)! At this sacrifice, for your consumption and for the enjoyment of the gods (*devavītaye*)—that is, for the consumption of the deities worthy of worship—the drops (*stokāḥ*) or droplets of the oblation consisting of fat (*medasaḥ*) mixed with clarified butter (*ghṛtavantaḥ*) flow forth and drip down.
Alternatively, it should be construed as "for the enjoyment of the gods" (*devavītaye*) and "for thy enjoyment" (*devasya tava vītaye*).
Therefore, bestow (*dhehi*) upon us (*naḥ*) that which is most desirable (*vāryam*), worthy of being chosen and honored—the most excellent (*śreṣṭham*) and supreme (*uttamam*) wealth (*dhanam*).
They flow; this is the present tense form (*laṭ*) of the root *śru*, meaning "to flow.

*Devavīti*: that in which there is *vīti*, meaning delight, of the gods (*devānām*) is *devavīti*. In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) is retained. It means "the most excellent."

From the word *praśasya* (praiseworthy), the suffix *iṣṭhan* is applied in the sense of excellence. By the rule “*praśasyasya śraḥ*,” there is the substitution [of *śra* for *praśasya*]. 1. The suffix *guṇa*. The accent of the single substitute (*ekādeśasvara*). "ghehi": this is the imperative (*loṭ*) of the root *dhā* (to place). You, the seer who perceives objects beyond the senses and therefore the most excellent, surpassing all—by these drops of fat mixed with clarified butter, you are being properly kindled. As such, become the preeminent protector (*prāvitr̥*) of our sacrifice, the animal sacrifice being performed by us.

O Agni, whose nature is to go toward the non-oblation (the enemy) and whose nature is constant movement, therefore, O powerful one, for your own sake, drops of *ghṛta*— that is, drops of the oblation consisting of fat (*medas*)—
flow forth for you. Thus, being praised by the sages (*kavi*), those skilled in ritual such as the *hotṛ* priests, come with great and abundant luster (*bhānu*) and splendor to our animal sacrifice.
And having come, O wise one, accept and enjoy the oblations such as clarified butter and the like, which are being offered by us through our service.

They flow; [the root] *śru* means "to flow.

In the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*), during the bringing forward of the bricks, this verse beginning with "purīṣyāsaḥ" is to be recited as the *anuvacana*.

Having begun with the rule, "Being impelled, he recites for the piling of the soil," the *sūtra* states: "'purīṣyāso agnayaḥ'—these three verses, softly, together with the *praṇava*" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.8).

7. *ta-gāthī purīṣyāsaḥ* is the beginning of this [hymn].

"This is that Agni in whom Indra, longing, has placed the pressed soma within his belly.
Having won a thousandfold prize like a swift steed crossing the flood, O Jātavedas, you are praised as a victor."
This is that Agni, in whose belly Indra, longing for it, has placed the pressed Soma; having won the thousandfold prize like a swift steed, you are praised as the victorious one, O Jātavedas. 1.
The Gāthī says:

This Agni, who is seen here upon the *uttaravedi* as the *āhavanīya* fire—the locus for the invocation—is indeed that very one, "vāvaśānaḥ," desiring Soma; he is Indra, in whose belly (*jaṭhare*) he held (*dadhe*), that is, sustained, the pressed Soma endowed with the refinements of extraction and other rites.
Therefore, this Agni is possessed of such greatness—this is the connection with the preceding statement.
Furthermore, O Jātavedas, having obtained (sasavān) the thousandfold—

meaning that which possesses a thousand various forms in battle— and having partaken of the food characterized by oblations, such as clarified butter, herbs, and Soma, in many ways like a swift horse (sarmiṇam aśvam iva), you are being praised; being thus lauded, you abide.

In the case of the root *dadhāti* in the *liṭ* (perfect) tense, by the rule *liṭas tajhayoreśirec*, the suffix *tap* is replaced by *eś*. Because it is connected with *yad-vṛtta* (the relative pronoun *yad*), there is no *anighāta* (lack of accentuation); rather, it takes the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
*vāvaśānaḥ*:

This is derived from the root *vaś* (to desire) with the suffix *yaṅluk*; the lengthening of the reduplicated syllable is according to the rule *dīrgho’kitaḥ*, and the substitution of *jñānac* occurs by way of metrical transposition (*vyatyaya*).
Citsvara;
Sasavān; Paṇa and Saṃbhata.
The state of having *kasāyī* as its suffix; the elision of *n*; the accent of the suffix.
You are praised. [The root] *ṣṭuñ* means "to praise.
The suffix *yak* is applied in the passive voice (*karmaṇi*).
The vowel lengthening occurs by the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ*;
[the final syllable] receives the *nighāta* accent.
That splendor of yours which is foremost in heaven, that which is on earth, and that which is in the plants and waters, O worshipful one—
by which you have pervaded the wide mid-air, that is your brilliant, surging light, the beholder of men.

O Agni, that splendor of yours which is in heaven, on earth, in the plants, and in the waters—O worshipful one, by which you have overspread the wide mid-air—that light of yours is brilliant, surging, and beholding men. 2.
O worshipful one, O Agni worthy of sacrifice: that splendor of the Sun which is in heaven, and that light which is there—that is indeed your own light.
That brilliance which exists on earth in the form of the Āhavanīya fire and so forth is yours alone.
Having thus declared his well-known [manifest] brilliance, he now declares his hidden light.
"In the plants, in the waters": that splendor which is in the plants, such as the fire-sticks (*araṇi*) and other pieces of wood;
or rather, that splendor known as Soma which is in the plants, such as the trees (*vanaspati*).
That splendor known as Aurva which exists within the waters—that entire radiance, existing everywhere, is yours alone.
Furthermore, by that splendor in the form of wind, you have stretched out and expanded the vast atmosphere;
it is brilliant, luminous, shining, the beholder of men as their witness, and great like the ocean.
"He stretched out such a sky for himself"—this connects with what precedes.
Regarding this stated meaning, the Vājasaneyaka says:

1. *gha*—he bestows (*dadhati*); *ta*—he sustains (*dhārayati*). 2. *ta*—the connection is with the preceding [verse]. Now, that which is produced by direct perception (*pratyakṣakṛtaḥ*). 3. *ja*—*ṇa*—*taṃ sahasriṇam*. 4. *ta*—like a horse (*aśvamiva*). Or rather, "possessing a thousand" (*sahasrin*) is an epithet of the prize (*vāja*), meaning numbering one thousand. 5. *ca*—having many forms such as clarified butter (*ājya*), herbs (*oṣadhi*), Soma, and so forth; *ta*—of various kinds such as clarified butter, herbs, Soma, and so forth. 6. *ta*—existing as the agent of burning, cooking, and so on. 7. *ja*—*ṇa*—*na*—*pa*—[the word] *oṣadhīṣu* (in the herbs). 8. *ta*—that is yours alone (*tāvakam eva tat*). 9. *ta*—furthermore, you (*kiṃca tvam*). 10. *pa*—wide (*uru*). 11. *kha*—*ca*—*ja*—*ṇa*—*pha*—*ma*—*la*—"you have made" (*kṛtavān asi*) does not exist [in these versions]; *pa*—stretched out (*ātatam*).

Regarding *Ṛgveda* 2.15: “O Agni, that splendor of yours which is in heaven,” etc.—the splendor of this [Agni] is indeed in heaven; “on earth” refers to this [terrestrial] Agni; “that which is in the plants and in the waters, O worshipful one”—this he says of that very Agni who is in the plants and in the waters; “by whom the atmosphere was overspread”—that is Vāyu; “he who is brilliant, radiant, subtle, and beholding men”—this means “great, radiant, subtle, and beholding men” (*Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* 7.1.23).
In *pṛthivyām*,
the acute accent (*udātta*) of the case-ending is due to the rule “*udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt*. In *oṣadhīṣu*.
In *oṣadheḥ*, there is lengthening by the rule "and in the case of a stem ending in *oṣadhi* when followed by a case-ending other than the first. In *apsu*,
the acute accent of the case-ending is due to the rule "the [first] vowel of a monosyllabic stem ending in *sā-* [or *ā-*] is acute."

*Ātatantha*: This is from the root *tanu* (meaning "to expand") in the perfect tense (*liṭ*) with the suffix *thāl*. By the rule *liti*, the syllable preceding the suffix is acute-accented (*udātta*).

"O Agni, you go toward the ocean of the sky— that is, you reach it by means of smoke, directed toward the waters existing in the celestial realm.
Furthermore, the *dhiṣṇyās*—
those who nourish (*uṣ*) the body endowed with intelligence (*dhi*), thus they are called *dhiṣṇyās*— are the deities presiding over the vital breaths (*prāṇas*)."

You have called upon those deities known as the *prāṇas* in succession; you cause them to assemble—that is to say, you have spoken so that they become assembled. [This occurs] in the radiant realm (*rocana*) above, in front of, or beyond the world of the Sun (*sūryasya*).
This world where the fiery light shines is called *rocanā*.

While that world named *rocanā* is shining, you impel both those waters which exist below the solar world—in the intermediate region (*antarikṣa*) beneath the sun—and those waters which stand present [there].

The meaning has been clearly stated by the Vājasaneyins: “The waters, indeed, are the flood of this heaven; he reaches them with his smoke, saying, ‘Thou hast spoken to the gods who are worthy of praise. The gods who are worthy of praise are the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), for they impel all thoughts (*dhiyas*). And: “The waters which are in the luminous realm (*rocana*) before the sun, and those which stand below it—the luminous realm is indeed the world where that [sun] shines; thus he speaks of the waters both beyond and below that. Thus, you impel both kinds of waters.
*Arṇam*:

The elision of the letter *sa* is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*).

The verbal root *gai*, meaning "to praise," when used in the Vedic language (*chandasi*), belongs to the *juhoty-ādi* class and takes the Ātmanepada endings due to the particle *ca*.

*Ūciṣe*: This is the perfect (*liṭ*) form of the root *brū*, meaning "to speak clearly. Because the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix [of the perfect] applies, the substitution of *vac* for *brū* occurs according to Pāṇini Sūtra 2.4.53: *bruvo vaciḥ*.
Furthermore, because the suffix is not preceded by a conjunct consonant, it is marked with the *kit* designation according to Pāṇini Sūtra 1.2.5: *asaṃyogālliṭ kit*.

[Grammatical notes: *Daśa*: From the root *daṃś* "to bite. For that purpose, I set you down completely.
It indicates the supreme locations:

By the rule *jhayaḥ*, the *m* of *matup* is replaced by *v*. Since the paribhāṣā "in a rule concerning vowels, a consonant is as if non-existent" is not applied here, the *matup* does not bear an udātta accent.

O Agni, overcome the hostile armies; casting away those who plot against us, difficult to surpass, cross over our enemies. Bestow splendor upon the one who upholds the sacrifice. O Agni, overcome the hostile armies; casting away those who plot against us, difficult to surpass, cross over our enemies. Bestow splendor upon the one who upholds the sacrifice.

Viśvāmitra praises [Agni]: "O Agni, *sahasva*—overcome—the *apṛtanāḥ*, the attacking armies; *apa*—drive away—the *abhimātīḥ*, the arrogant enemies who cause obstacles to ritual action. Furthermore, being *duṣṭaraḥ*—difficult to cross, impossible for anyone to overcome—you, while *tarann arātīḥ*—crossing over, i.e., casting out the enemies by your own splendor—*dhāḥ varcaḥ*—bestow vigor, that is, food, upon the *yajñavāhase*—the sacrificer who carries out the sacrifice. Perform this; bestow it; overcome it. *Sahasva* is the form of the root *sah* (to endure/overcome) in the imperative (*loṭ*). Because the vocative is treated as non-existent [for the purposes of accentuation], there is no *nighāta* (elision of the accent) because it begins the *pāda*. *Abhimātīḥ*: from the root *māṅ* (to measure). *Mātiḥ* is a noun formed with the suffix *ktin* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). Since this root belongs to the *lug-vikaraṇa* class, the vowel lengthening (*ītva*) and the augment (*guṇa*) do not occur. In the *bahuvrīhi* compound "those whose measurement is on all sides" (*abhito mānaṃ yeṣām*), the original accent of the first member is retained. *Asya*: from the root *asu* (to throw); this is the form in the imperative (*loṭ*) of the *div-ādi* class. *Duṣṭaraḥ*: from the root *tṛ* (to cross/flood); the suffix *khal* is added in the sense of difficulty. By the rule *supāmādi-*, the visarga is replaced by *s*, which then undergoes *ṣatva* (change to *ṣ*). It bears the accent of the *liṭ* (perfect) formation. *Taran*: the present participle (*śatṛ*) of the root *tṛ*. Since the root is taught with a short *u* (*adupadeśa*), the suffix *śatṛ* becomes *anudātta* by the accent rule for *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes; thus, the accent of the verbal root remains. *Dhāḥ*: the form of the root *dhā* (to place) in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense in Vedic usage. It bears the *nighāta* (elided) accent."

24. The Chapter on the Noble Ones (Ariyavagga) [Chapter Twenty-Four] of the *Dhammapada* Commentary. At that time, the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. At that time, there was a certain monk who had committed an offense. He went to another monk and said: "Venerable sir, please grant me rehabilitation from this offense. The other monk replied: "Friend, do not speak thus; it is not possible for you to be rehabilitated. Having spoken thus, he did not grant him rehabilitation. Then that monk, being unable to obtain rehabilitation from that monk, went to yet another monk and said: "Venerable sir, please grant me rehabilitation from this offense. The other monk replied: "Friend, do not speak thus; it is not possible for you to be rehabilitated. Having spoken thus, he too did not grant him rehabilitation. Thus, as he wandered from one monk to another, seeking rehabilitation, he eventually reached the Blessed One. He approached the Blessed One and said: "Venerable sir, please grant me rehabilitation from this offense. The Blessed One replied: "Monk, do not speak thus; it is not possible for you to be rehabilitated. Having spoken thus, the Blessed One did not grant him rehabilitation. Then that monk, being unable to obtain rehabilitation even from the Blessed One, went to the monks and said: "Venerable sirs, please grant me rehabilitation from this offense. To Indra and the other gods, the person offers *vāja*—food characterized by the oblation. O Agni, you who are possessed of many kinds of offerings such as the *puroḍāśa* cake and so forth, being such as you are, bring (*bhā vaha*)—that is, summon—the gods worthy of worship to us at this sacrifice, for the attainment of wealth. Regarding the word *manoti*: from the root *maṇ* (variant of *pan*) meaning "to give," the suffix *dha* is added according to the *tanādi* class; it bears the accent of the suffix. Because it begins a quarter-verse (*pāda*), there is no *anudātta* (low) accent. Regarding *bhūṣan*: from the root *bhūṣ* meaning "to adorn," with the causative sense implied (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*). Since the *śatṛ* suffix is unaccented by the rule of *sārvadhātuka* accents, the accent of the verbal root remains. Regarding *jñiṣyate*: [this is a variant reading]. Regarding *vaha*: this is the form of the root *vah* in the *loṭ* (imperative) mood. Regarding *puruṣaḥ*: one who restrains (*yam*) many (*puru*) hunger-related afflictions (*kṣudho'jñāni*) is a *puruṣa*. The elision of the final syllable is Vedic (*cāndasa*). The *guṇa* substitution occurs by the rule "and in the vocative" (*saṃbuddhau ca*).
Agni, the unerring god, shines upon Heaven and Earth, the two goddesses who encompass all people;
he dwells among them with strengths, most radiant through our adorations.
Agni, Heaven and Earth, those who give birth to all—these two goddesses shine forth, immortal and unerring. He dwells among us with strengths, most resplendent through our adorations. 3.

*Amūraḥ*: unerring, undeluded, the omniscient one; *kṣayan*: ruling as the lord (*īśāna*) of the entire world; for that very reason, *puruścandraḥ*: possessing much splendor, or endowed with abundant gold;
or rather, having the nature of manifold radiance;
*vājaiḥ*: by means of powers or strengths.

Accompanied by obeisances and offerings, that Agni shines forth upon *dyāvāpṛthivī*, heaven and earth—the two who give birth to all (*viśvajanye*), or rather, those from whom everything born (*janyam*) has arisen; they are the two goddesses (*devī*), radiant (*dyotamāne*), and immortal (*amṛte*), free from the nature of death. He illuminates them completely on every side.
*dyāvāpṛthivī*.
Regarding the word *div*, by the rule "divo dyāvā," there is the substitution *dyāvā*, which is udātta on its first syllable.
The word *pṛthivī* is udātta on its final syllable because it ends in a long vowel (*dīrghanta*).
In the compound *devatā-dvandve ca*, both members retain their original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). In *viśvajanye*,
the final syllable of the first member is udātta according to the rule *bahuvrīhau viśvaṃ saṃjñāyām*.
In the case of a *tatpuruṣa* compound, however, the accentuation must be considered.
[The root] *bhā* means "to shine"; [it is derived from] *bhā* in the sense of "illumination."
The causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) is implied. *Kṣayan* [is derived from] the root *kṣi*, meaning "to possess sovereignty" (*aiśvarya*).
Since the suffix *śatṛ* is unaccented by virtue of the accent of the *sārvadhātuka*, the accent of the verbal root remains.
Thus, *puruścandraḥ*.
The augment *suṭ* is applied here because of the rule: "In a mantra, the augment *suṭ* is added after a short vowel when *candra* follows as the second member of a compound."
Regarding *śakāraḥ*:

by the rule “*tricakrādīnāṃ chandasyupasaṃkhyānam*” within the section concerning the acute accent on the final syllable of the second member of a compound, there is an acute accent on the final syllable of the second member;
or else, there is an acute accent on the final syllable by the rule “*mamāsya*”.
O Agni and Indra, come to the sacrifice in the house of the donor who has pressed the Soma;
O Gods, come as those who do not fail, for the drinking of the Soma.
O Agni and Indra, come here to the sacrifice in the house of the donor who has pressed the Soma; O Gods, come for the drinking of the Soma, never failing. 4.

O Agni and you, Indra—both of you gods, being unharmed (*amardhantā*) by the non-arrival [of the sacrifice] and thus not causing injury to the rite—come hither for the drinking of Soma (*somapeyāya*), approaching this sacrifice performed in the dwelling-house (*duroṇe*) of the *dāśvāṃs*, the sacrificer who presses the Soma and offers oblations. Come close to us!
The word *yātam* [is used].

1. [In the case of] *kha-ta-na-bha-sa-tatpuruṣa*; *ga-tatpuruṣeṣu*; *ja-ṇa-la-tatpuruṣa*. 2. [In the case of] *kha-ga-ca-ja-ṇa-na-pha-ma*, there is acute accent (*udātta*) on the final syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*).

3. [The word] *na* is near [to *mṛdhaḥ*]. 4. *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *pha*, and *ma* do not have the form *yātam*. This is the form of the root *yā* (in the sense of "attaining") in the imperative (*loṭ*). It is subject to the *nighāta* accent. It does not end in *madh*. This is the form of the root *mṛdh* (in the sense of "hurting") in the present participle (*śatṛ*). There is a compound with the negative particle (*nañ*). The case-ending (*sup*) is replaced by *ḍā*. In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, there is the accent of the negative particle (*nam-svara*). [Regarding] *somapeyāya*: from the root *pā* (in the sense of "drinking"), the suffix *yat* is applied according to the rule *aco yat*. The vowel *i* is substituted for the final vowel according to the rule *īyati*. The *guṇa* strengthening occurs as a characteristic of the semi-vowel substitute (*ādhyātukalaksana*). The original accent of the final member of the *kṛt*-derived compound remains.
O Agni, son of strength, Jātavedas, you who are eternal, are kindled in the home by the waters; exalting with your aid, you honor the places of assembly.
O Agni, son of strength, Jātavedas, you are kindled in the dwelling as one who is eternal; magnifying your seats with your aid. 5.

O son of strength (*sahasaḥ sūno*), O son of power, O Jātavedas—whose wisdom is born—O Agni, eternal and indestructible, do thou honor and serve the dwelling places (*sadhasthāni*), the worlds that are the abodes of living beings, through thy rising protection (*ūtī*). Thou art kindled and perfectly illumined within the house of the waters (*apāṃ duroṇe*), in the intermediate space.
In *duroṇe*:
the suffix *na* is added [to the root *dur*] according to the *uṇādi* rules;
by the rule beginning with *jvarasvara*, the vowel *u* is substituted.
The suffix is *guṇa*.
Regarding the word *duroṇa*, Yāska states: “*Duroṇa* is a name for the house; they are difficult to reach” (Nirukta 4.5).
It has the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
"Mahayamānaḥ" [is derived from] the root "maha" in the sense of "worship"; the present middle participle suffix (śānac) is used by way of transposition.
Since the *śānac* suffix is unaccented by the accent rule for *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes, the accent of the *ṇic* affix remains.
[The form] *ūtī* [is derived from the root] *ava*, which signifies protection and so forth.
The word is udātta on the final syllable due to its being an irregular formation (nipātana) according to the rule beginning with *ūtiyūtijūti*.
The third case ending undergoes a long vowel by samprasāraṇa (savarṇadīrgha) according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
The fourteenth hymn, consisting of nine verses, begins with “vaiśvānaraṃ manasā.

Regarding this, the Anukramaṇikā states: “Vaiśvānaraṃ nava; two triplets [of three verses each] are addressed to Vaiśvānara and the Maruts, being in the Jāgata meter; the two [remaining] verses are either a self-praise or, according to some, a praise of the teacher; the first is unchanted, while the last praises the teacher.
Thus, the two initial triplets beginning with “vaiśvānaraṃ manasā” are in the Jāgata meter.
The deity of the first [verse] is Vaiśvānara Agni; that of the second is the Maruts.
The three beginning with the seventh are Triṣṭubhs.
For the pair beginning with "agnir asi," the deity is either Agni or the Supreme Brahman.
Because the ninth [verse] is a praise of the Viśvāmitra chapter, its deity is that very one.
For the hymn excluding the seventh [verse], Viśvāmitra is the seer (*ṛṣi*).
Because the seventh [verse] consists of the words of Brahmā, according to the principle that "the seer is the one whose words [it is]," Brahmā is the seer.
The triplet beginning with *vaiśvānaraṃ manasā* is prescribed for the Āgnimāruta Śastra at the Vaiśvānarīya Nivid on the fourth day of the Abhiplava sacrifice;
this is stated in the section titled “Of the third” as: *vaiśvānaraṃ manaseti tisraḥ* (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.7).
This same triplet is also used at the Bṛhaspatisava, serving as the Vaiśvānarīya Nivid insertion in the Āgnimāruta Śastra.
The second triplet, beginning with *pra yantu vājāḥ*, is used for the Māruti Nivid at the Bṛhaspatisava.
Both are prescribed in the section on the *Uśanas-stoma* in the Sūtra: “Having mentally perceived Agni Vaiśvānara, [one recites] *pra yantu vājās taviṣībhir agrayaḥ*” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 9.5).
At the Agnicayana, during the recitation following the piling of the altar, the verse *agnir asmi* is used.

Having begun with the words, "Then one should recite the *anugīta* following the piled fire (*agni-saṃcita*)," it is formulated in the Sūtra: "With the verse 'I am Agni, Jātavedas by birth,' [he recites] three times in a medium voice" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.8).
1. The vowel [of the root] is long.
2. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, Ja, Ṇa, Bha, and La, the phrase "of the second *marata*" does not exist.
3. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, Ja, Ṇa, Na, and Sa, it is because it is a praise of the teacher (*upādhyāya*); in manuscript La, it is because it is a praise of the teacher (*upādhyāya*).

4. Endowed with *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *bha*, and *sa*: Having perceived with our minds Vaiśvānara Agni, who is worthy of praise, the finder of heaven, the bounteous god, the charioteer—O Kuśikas, seeking wealth, we invoke the swift one with our songs. Vaiśvānara; with the mind; Agni; having perceived; possessing oblations; according to truth; the finder of light; the bounteous; the god; the charioteer; seeking wealth; with songs; the swift one; O Kuśikas; we invoke. 1.
Viśvāmitra praises:

O Agni, we Kuśikas—born of the Kuśika lineage, possessing oblations (*haviṣmant*), having prepared the offerings, and desiring wealth for ourselves—[praise] Vaiśvānara. He is called *viśvānara* because all men (*viśve naraḥ*) are the leaders (*netāraḥ*) in rites such as the leading forth of the fire. We praise that Agni.
Vaiśvānara is his relative— that is to say, his offspring—
or alternatively, Vaiśvānara is simply Viśvānara himself.
In another sense, it is a derivative (taddhita) formation, as in the cases of "rākṣasa" and "vāyasa."

Having discerned with our mind that this Agni—who is prone to bestow boons, who follows the truth, who grants fruits in accordance with actions, who is true to his promise, who knows the heavenly realm (svarvit) as the knower of fruits characterized by heaven and the like, and for that very reason is a generous giver (sudānu), who possesses a chariot (rathin), and for that very reason goes to the sacrifices (agvin), and who is radiant (deva)—having recognized him through our inner organ as being distinguished by such qualities, we invoke you here at this ritual with words consisting of hymns of praise.
Regarding *vaiśvānara*:
by the rule “*nare saṃjñāyām*,” there is lengthening of the first member [of the compound].
In the sense of “this belongs to Viśvānara,” the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule “*tasyedam*.”
The accent is that of a suffix (*pratyayasvara*). *Nicāyya* is also a form of the root *cāyu*, meaning "to worship" or "to perceive."
The sound of the bed;
that which has followed truth; that which is accompanied by truth.

The compound is formed according to the rule "the third case ending is used with words such as *ava* when they have the sense of censure (*kutsā*) and so forth. The substitution of *p* for *m* occurs because it belongs to the *supām* group. Due to its inclusion in the *nirudaka*-type list, the word is oxytone (accented on the final syllable).
*Sudānum*:
[The root] *sudāñ* means "to give.
The suffix *nu* is applied in the sense of the agent according to the rule *dābhābhyāṃ nuḥ*.
The acute accent on the first syllable of the second member [of the compound] is due to the rule *parādiś chandasi bahulam*. [Regarding the form] *rathin*:
after the word *ratha*, the suffix *irac* is applied in the sense of the possessive suffix *matup*, according to the rule *medhārathyābhyām iranniracau vaktavyau*.
Citsvara; the Vasus. [The term *vasu* is derived from the root *vas* with the suffix *kyac*: "those who desire wealth for themselves," according to the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac*.

The lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule "akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.25). The suffix *u* is added by the rule "kyācchandasī" (Pāṇini 3.2.170), and then there is the elision of the final *a* by the rule "ato lopaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.48).
The accent of the suffix:
*ragvam*, *rvigarthyathaḥ*.
*Ragvaḥ* [is derived from the root] *raj* meaning "he goes to sacrifices";
it ends in the suffix *ac* according to the *pacādi* group;
it has the *citsvara* accent.
*Kuśikāsaḥ*:
From the word *kuśika*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "lineage" (*gotra*) according to the rule beginning with *vidādibhyaḥ*.
When this [patronymic] occurs in the plural, there is elision (*luk*) by the rule *yañañośca* (Pāṇini 2.4.64).
We invoke.
There is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) due to the rule "it occurs abundantly in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*) [applied] to the root *hve*.
There is the *nighāta* accent.

We invoke that bright Agni for worship—the Vaiśvānara, Mātariśvan, the one worthy of praise; Bṛhaspati for the divine service of men, the inspired sage, the listener, the guest who hastens swiftly. 2. We invoke that bright Agni for worship—the Vaiśvānara, Mātariśvan, the one worthy of praise; Bṛhaspati for the divine service of men, the inspired sage, the listener, the guest who hastens swiftly. 2.
That Agni who was described in the preceding mantra—him, the bright and shining Vaiśvānara, belonging to Viśvānara;
Mātariśvan—that is, Agni, who "breathes" (movers) or pervades in the mother (the intermediate space), in the form of lightning and so forth;
him, the one worthy of praise, with hymns of praise.

1. *kha-ga-ca-ja-ṇa-na-bha-kuśikāḥ*; *pa-kuśikāsaḥ* [read *kuśikāḥ*]. 2. *kha-ga-ca-ja-ṇa-na-bha-la-sa-kaścit*; *pha-abhiḥ* [read *abhiḥ*] *kaścit*. 3. *kha-ga-ca-ja-ṇa-na-bha-la-yadā*. 4. *pa-pha-karmaphalapradāne*. 5. *kha-ga-ca-ja-ṇa-na-yajñam*. 6. *ta-āgacchatīti*.
[Maṇḍala 3, Anuvāka 2, Sūkta 26] The Third Aṣṭaka, [Adhyāya] 285.

[I praise] Bṛhaspati, who is to be extolled with hymns (*śastra*), the lord of the great sacrifice (*yajña*) as its protector, the master, the wise one (*vipa*), the listener who hears the words of the mantras such as the *stotra* and *śastra*, the guest (*atithi*) who has arrived by chance and is worthy of hospitality,
the descendant of Raghu— meaning one whose *syada* (speed) is like that of a chariot, i.e., a swift traveler; or else, by the word *syada*, the path is indicated.

The meaning is that the descendant of Raghu is one who goes swiftly. We, born of the Kuśika lineage, invoke—that is, we call upon—that very Agni, endowed with such qualities, for our protection (*avase*).
Furthermore, for the sake of the sacrifice (*devatātaye*) of a human being (*manuṣaḥ*), we invoke you.
The root *śubhra* is derived from the root *śubh* in the sense of "shining" (*dīptau*).
From this, the suffix *rak* is applied according to the rule *sphāyitañci*, etc., in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).
Due to its *kit* status, there is an absence of *guṇa*.
The accent of the derivative suffix (*pratyayasvara*): *mātariśvānam*. Because it is the cause of creation, the mother (*mātṛ*) is the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
In this context, *mātariśvan* refers to Agni, for he "breathes" (*śvasiti*) within the mother (*mātari*).

The word *mātariśvan* has its acute accent on the final syllable of the first member because it is a conventional form (*nipātana*) ending in the suffix *kap*, as seen in the rule beginning with *śṛṇukṣan*.
[The word] *uktham*.

He is to be praised with the *uktha*, that is, with the hymn of praise (*stotra*). In this sense, the suffix *yat* is applied according to the rule *bhave chandasi*. It is *svarita* (circumflex) because of the rule *tisrvaritam*.
For the sake of the deity (*devatātaye*). *Devatāti* is simply *deva*;
the suffix *tāti* is used here in its own sense (*svārthika*).

By the word "deity" (devatā), sacrifice (yajña) is indicated, because sacrifice has that [deity] as its recipient; this is a case of indirect indication (lakṣaṇā). The vowel *i* is the accent. [This is] the *raghuyadam*.

From the root *syandū* in the sense of "flowing," the word *syada* is formed with the suffix *ghran*. By the rule "syado jave," there is the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika*) due to its being a *nipāta*.
The accentuation follows the rule for the original accent of the second member of a compound when preceded by a *krut* suffix.
Like a neighing horse, Vaiśvānara is kindled by the Kuśikas with sacrificial fuel, age after age.
May that Agni, ever-watchful among the immortals, bestow upon us great heroism, abundance of horses, and precious treasure.

Like a neighing horse, Vaiśvānara is kindled together with the kindling-sticks by the Kuśikas, age after age. May that Agni, ever-watchful among the immortals, bestow upon us abundance of heroes, abundance of horses, and treasure. 3.

That Vaiśvānara Agni, who is kindled day by day—meaning he is properly ignited through the offering of clarified butter libations—by the Kuśikas, namely the Hotṛ priests and others, as they perform their hymns of praise;
in this regard, there is an illustration:
"like a horse."

Just as a newborn horse, neighing and making the sound "haṃ," is properly nourished day by day by its mothers—the mares—through the provision of milk; even so, may that Agni, who is ever-watchful (*jāgṛvi*) and shining with his flame among the immortals, the gods who are free from the law of death, bestow upon us excellent offspring (*suvīrya*), excellent horses and cattle (*svaśvya*), and supreme wealth (*ratna*). May he grant it to us.
In each and every age (*yuge-yuge*). The doubling [of the word] occurs according to the rule *nityavīpsayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.4).
Since it is preceded by another word, it becomes unaccented (*anudātta*), and thus the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member remains.
*Svaśvyam*:
The word *aśva*, ending in the suffix *kan*, is udātta on its first syllable.

In the *bahuvrīhi* compound, by the rule "in the Veda, a two-syllabled [word] has the udātta on the first syllable of the second member," the final member (*aśva*) takes the udātta accent on its initial syllable.
The addition of the letter *ya* is for metrical reasons (*chāndasa*).
Alternatively,
"aśvāḥ" means those who are excellent among horses.
In this case, the suffix *yat* is applied by the rule "sādhuḥ" (Pāṇini 4.4.98).
By the rule "yato 'nāvaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.213), the acute accent (*udātta*) falls on the first syllable.
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the aforementioned accentuation applies.
May he bestow.
This is the form of the root *dadhāti* in the imperative mood.
Jewel.
From the root *ram* in the sense of "to play" (*krīḍāyām*),

the suffix *na* is applied in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇe*) according to the rule *ramesta ca*, and there is a substitution of the letter *t* for the final letter [of the root]. Thus, that in which they delight (*ramante*) is called a *ratna*.
With the word "nit" understood [from the previous rule], [the suffix] is udātta on the first syllable.
*jāgṛviḥ* ends in the *kip* suffix.
By virtue of being a *nittva* [suffix], it is udātta on its first syllable.

1. [The reading] *kha-ga-ca-ja-ṇa-bha* is with the word *syadaḥ*. 2. *ta*: *tadvān*. 3. *kha-ga-ca-ja-ṇa-na-pha-bha*: "In this manner, it is appropriate. 4. *ta*: "From this [word]. 5. *kha-ga-ja-ṇa-bha-sa*: From the word *mātariśvacchadāt*, [the variant] *na-la-mātariśvacchandaḥ*. 6. *kha-ga-ja-ṇa-na-bha-sa*: [The reading] *tisvaritaḥ*. 7. *ta*: *ājyāhuti*. 8. *pa*: *jātyaśvaḥ*. "Let the Vājas go forth, foremost with their powers; mingled for glory, they have yoked the spotted deer.
The Maruts, the all-knowing, the great bulls, the invincible ones, cause the mountains to tremble."

Let the Vājas go forth with their powers as leaders; for the sake of splendor, they have harnessed the spotted deer, mingled together. The Maruts, the great bulls, possessors of all wealth, cause the mountains to tremble; they are invincible. 4.
Let the swift, foremost steeds proceed toward the water;
having gone there, let those foremost ones, joined with the powerful Maruts and mingling in the auspicious waters, have united with one another and have produced droplets—
creating drops in the water.
Or rather, let the *vājās*—the swift ones—proceed toward the water with their vigorous powers (*viṣībhiḥ*) joined by the Maruts who possess strength.

And those Maruts, having mingled with the auspicious waters and having come together with the clouds (*abhribhiḥ*), have yoked the dappled mares (*pṛṣatīḥ*), the multi-colored female horses that serve as their vehicles;
they have yoked them to the chariot for the purpose of piercing the clouds.

Mounted upon their chariots, those Maruts—the all-knowing ones who possess knowledge of the deeds performed by living beings, who are invincible and cannot be overcome by anyone—these winds of such a nature cause the great-seeding mountains, that is, the clouds, to tremble;
they shake the clouds so that there may be abundant rain.
Regarding *taviṣībhiḥ*: the root *tav* meaning "to go" is a Vedic (sautra) root. From this, by the rule *taverṇid vā*, the suffix *ṭipac* is applied, and it is also *nic*.
They move through the sky swiftly; thus they are *tavipas*, the winds.
The suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to the rule *ṭṭidāṇj*; there is a change of gender.
The word *nighāda* has its first syllable accented (*ādyudātta*).
The word *pṛṣatīḥ* [is derived from] either the root *pṛṣu* meaning "to sprinkle" or the root *pṛ* meaning "to protect" or "to fill."
From this [root], by the rule "apṛṣad-ahan-mahat" being a nipātana (irregular formation), the suffix *ati* is applied.
It becomes like *śatru*.
By the rule "ugitaśca," the suffix *ṅīp* is applied.
They are called *pṛṣavyas* because they flow around (*pari-vyanti*). They are *śīkarās*.
They are *pṛṣavyas* mares because they hear (*śṛṇanti*) and protect (*pālayanti*).
*ayukṣata*: this is the form of the root *yujir* (meaning "to yoke") in the *luṅ* tense with the suffix *sic*;
there is a *nighāta* (elision of accent).
*bṛhadukṣaḥ*: [This is formed] from the root *ukṣ* ‘to sprinkle’ with the suffix *kvip*;
it bears the original accent of the final member of the compound (kṛd-uttarapada-prakṛti-svara).
They cause trembling. [The root] *vi-veṣṭ* means "trembling.
It is unaccented (*nighāta*).

Regarding *parvatān*: from the root *parva* in the sense of "filling" (*pūraṇe*), the suffix *atac* is applied according to the rule beginning with *bhṛ-mṛ-dṛ-śi*. That which fills the earth with water is a mountain (*parvata*), namely a cloud.
The udātta accent occurs by way of transposition.
We implore the Maruts, who possess the splendor of fire and belong to all peoples, for their fierce and terrible onset.
They are the roaring sons of Rudra, clothed in rain-garments, like lions in their impetuous intent, and bounteous givers.

The Maruts, possessing the splendor of fire, belonging to all people—we implore their fierce and mighty speed. They are the resounding sons of Rudra, clothed in rain-garments; like lions, they possess roaring power and are bounteous givers. 5.

Resorting to the lightning-fire, the Maruts, who belong to all people— those from whom the "drawing forth" of everything, such as trees and so on, characterized by bending and rising, proceeds— we, the Kuśikas, seek from those great ones their brilliant, fierce, and wool-like protection; we pray for it from every side.

1. Those Maruts, having observed that strength; 2. [The phrase] "endowed with power" is absent in manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ja, ṇa, and bha; 3. [The phrase] "by the Maruts" is absent in manuscripts kha, pa, pha, and bha; 4. [The word] "mutually" is absent in manuscripts kha, pa, pha, and bha; 5. [The reading] "for the purpose of piercing the clouds" is found in manuscript ta; 6. [The reading] "abundant sprinklers" is found in manuscript ta; 7. [The note] "here there is a change of gender" is found in manuscripts ha and ta; 8. [The reading] "in the joining of the flowers" is found in manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ja, ṇa, pha, and bha, while "in the joining of the blossoms" is found in manuscript na; 9. [The reading] "from this" is found in manuscript ta.

"Rudriyāḥ" means "sons of Rudra. "Varṇanirṇijaḥ": the word *nirṇij* denotes form (*rūpa*), as seen from its inclusion among the synonyms for water in the list beginning with "nirṇij vamiḥ. Those whose form or nature (*svabhāva*) is rain are "those who possess rain-forms," that is, the rain-givers (*varṣakāḥ*). "Hepakratavaḥ": those whose performance (*ṛtaḥ karaṇam*) consists of the sound *hepā* are "those who have made the sound *hepā*"; they are like lions (*siṃhā na siṃhā iva*), being "roaring" (*svāninaḥ*), that is, making sounds. Such are those Maruts, the "givers of good gifts" (*sudānavaḥ*), who are excellent bestowers of water. Regarding "agnipriyaḥ": the root *śriñ* is used in the sense of service. By the rule "vacipraccha... etc., there is the suffix *kip*, an absence of vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*), and lengthening of the root vowel. In the nominative plural (*jasi*), the substitution of *iyaṅ* occurs; this is the accent of the affix (*kṛtsvara*). Regarding "ugram": from the root *gamlū* (to go), preceded by *ut*. By the rule "ṛjendrapra... etc., there is the suffix *ra*, elision of the letter *m*, and elision of the final part of the prefix. That which goes upward is "ugraḥ"; this is the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). Regarding "īmahe": the root *ī* is used in the sense of desire, motion, etc. The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs by transposition (*vyatyaya*). There is elision of the *śap* suffix because it belongs to the *ad*-class. This is subject to the *nighāta* (anudātta) accent. Regarding "svāninaḥ": *svānaḥ* means roaring. It ends in that [suffix]. By the rule "ata iniṭhanau," the suffix *ini* is added. This is the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). Regarding "rudriyāḥ": from the word *rudra*, the Vedic suffix *gha* is applied. There is the substitution of *tṛci* (the *ya* of the suffix). This is the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). || 26 ||
We implore with excellent praises each troop of Maruts, wind by wind, for their fury and their might;
they whose horses are spotted, whose gifts are inexhaustible, who go to the sacrifice as wise ones at the assemblies.

We implore the wind after wind, troop after troop, with beautiful hymns—the splendor of Agni and the might of the Maruts. They whose horses are speckled, whose gifts are inexhaustible, the wise ones who go to the sacrifice at the assemblies. 6.

We, the descendants of Kuśika, invoke that radiant splendor of the Maruts, their vital energy. With every breath, with every gathering, in every great assembly, we pray with well-spoken hymns—those mantras by which excellent praises (*suśasti*) are performed—to seek such Marut-like power. They have spotted horses; those whose steeds are of the color of spotted deer are thus described. Their wealth is unfailing; that which does not fall away is "unfailing" (*anavabhra*); those whose riches are unfailing are "possessors of unfailing wealth," meaning they possess full abundance. They are wise; these Maruts, skilled in ritual action, go to the sacrifices—the worshipful oblations—at the *vidathas*, that is, the sacrificial assemblies. *Gaṇaṃgaṇam*: from the root *gaṇ* (to assemble), with the suffix *ac*; the reduplication is according to the rule for "constant repetition" (*nityavīpsayoḥ*). Because the subsequent member is repeated, the accent falls on the first word. *Suśastibhiḥ*: in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the final syllable of the second member is accented according to the rule *nañsubhyām*. *Bhāmam*: from the root *bhā* (to shine); the suffix *man* is added according to the rule *artistusu*, etc.; it has the *nisvara* (low) accent. *Ojaḥ*: from the root *ubja* (in the sense of straightness); the suffix *asun* is added with the elision of *b* according to the rule *ujjerbale balopaśca*; the *guṇa* substitution occurs as an *ārdhadhātuka* characteristic; it has the *nisvara* accent. *Īmahe*: from the root *ī* (in the sense of longing, etc.); it receives the *nighāta* (elided) accent. *Anavabhrarādhasaḥ*: *anavabhram* is accented on the final syllable of the second member according to *nañsubhyām*; in the *bahuvrīhi*, the accent falls on the first member. *Gantāraḥ*: the suffix *tṛn* denotes habitual action. *Vidatheṣu*: from the root *vid* (to know); the suffix *athan* is added with the *kit* marker according to the rule *rudi vidibhyāṃ kit*; because of the *kit* marker, there is no *guṇa* substitution. A *vidatha* is a sacrifice, so called because the Adhvaryus and others know the rites therein; it bears the accent of the suffix.

1. *kha*, *ga*, *na*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, *sa*—these are the sons of Rudra, the Maruts. 2. *pa*, *te*, *he*, *pa*, *kratavaḥ*. 3. *la*, *janasya*. 4. *ta*, *kiñcid vipraccha*. 5. *ta*, *gatyādiṣu*. 6. *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *na*, *ṇa*, *na*, *pha*, *bha*, *sa*—the vowel of the suffix (*pratyaya-svara*) is not elided (*nāśita*). 7. *ta*, *pa*, *samūhe samūhe*. 8. *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *ya*, *janīya-haviḥ*. 9. *ta*, *dāmām* from this [root]. 10. *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *bha*, *la*, *sa*—in a subsequent Bahuvrīhi compound. "I am Agni, Jātavedas by birth; clarified butter is my eye, and immortality is in my mouth."
I am the sun, the threefold, the measurer of the dust, the unceasing heat; my name is the oblation.
I am Agni; by birth, I am Jātavedas. Clarified butter is my eye; nectar is in my mouth. I am the threefold hymn, the measurer of the mid-world, the imperishable heat; "oblation" is my name. 7.
"Having realized the nature of the supreme reality, Agni manifests his own experience of being the self of all through his state as the elemental fire. O Kuśikas!
This entire world is twofold, consisting of the enjoyer and the enjoyed."

According to the Śruti: "All this is indeed food and the eater of food; Soma alone is I, the food, and Agni, the eater of food" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.6). In that context, Agni is the consumer in the form of the entire class of enjoyers.
And he, having become threefold through his non-difference from the deities designated by the words Agni and so forth, presides over the worlds of earth, the intermediate space, and heaven.
This is stated in the Vājasaneyaka: "He divided himself threefold:
the sun as one third, and the wind as one third" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad).

Thus says the Śruti (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1). The word *nāma* (name) signifies that which is well-known. By this demonstration of the name’s being the self of all, its status as the Supreme Brahman is stated. *Cakṣuḥ*: [The root] *cakṣ* is used in the sense of "distinct speech. Following the rule *usiṇ*, by the rule *cakṣeḥ śicca*, the suffix *usiṇ* is applied. Because of the presence of the marker *śit*, there is no substitution of *ru* for the final vowel. It is unaccented (*nisvara*). *Āsan*: For the word *āsya*, the substitute *āsan* is prescribed by rules such as *padomās*. By the rule *supāṃ suluk*, the locative case ending is elided. *Vimānaḥ*: [The root] *māṅ* means "measuring. By the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*, the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of the agent. The accent falls on the *lit* suffix. *Ajanmaḥ*: [The root] *jamu* means "to release. With the negative particle *nañ* preceding it, the suffix *ra* is applied in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlika*) by the rule *namikampisyajasakamahisaṃhasīpāṃ raḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.167). The root *jas* with the prefix *nañ* refers to "not moving" or "remaining still. The accent falls on the negative particle (*namsvara*). Alternatively, *jas* may mean "decay."

Having purified the *ūrg* with three purifiers, and understanding through his heart the thought that follows the light, he fashioned the most excellent treasure by means of the *svadhā* offerings; then he beheld heaven and earth all around.

With three purifiers he has purified the song, for with his heart he discerned the thought and the light. Recognizing [the way], he has fashioned the most excellent treasure by means of his inherent powers; then indeed he beheld heaven and earth all around. 8.

Agni, who is the self of all, [is known] by the heart—that is, by the function of the internal organ—for the sake of reflection; [he is] the light, the self-luminous splendor known as the Supreme Brahman. Perceiving him thoroughly through the sequence of hearing, reflection, and so forth—meaning knowing him with excellence by dispelling doubt, error, and mental impressions through delight in one's own Self—he indeed purified himself by means of the three purifiers, the sanctifying agents: Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya. He distinguished his own Self as the object of worship (arka), which is more pure and purifying than even those three.

Just as one purifies the Soma with the ten-fold filter (*daśapavitra*), so it is here. Knowing this, Agni—by means of the *svadhās* (his own powers)—establishes his own most exalted self, the supreme, and his worlds; thus they are called *svadhās*.
By means of those [powers], namely Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya, he has fashioned (*akṛta*) the delightful treasure (*ratna*).

By means of the *pavitra*s. From the root *pūṅ* in the sense of "purifying" (*pavane*), the suffix *dv* is applied in the active sense (*kartari*) when the deity is the object to be expressed, according to Pāṇini Sūtra 3.2.186: *kartari carṣidevatayoḥ*. Thus, it denotes the deity.
They purify, thus they are *pavitra*—namely Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya. This is a suffix-accent. *Apupot*.
This is a form of the root *pū* (*pūṅ pavane*) in its *yaṅ*-luṅ (*intensive without suffix*) state.
Due to the non-universality (*anityatva*) of rules conditioned by technical names (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*), there is an absence of *guṇa* in the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).
Furthermore, there is no *nighāta* (anudātta accent) because of the rule *yadvituparaṃ chandasi* (Pāṇini 8.1.56).
*Arkam*. [The root] *arc*, meaning "to worship.
The suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule: "The suffix *ka* is added after roots ending in *ṛ*, as well as after *ādhāra*, *ci*, and *kali*."
By the word *hṛdā*; for the word *havya*, there is the substitution of *hṛd* by [Pāṇini 6.1.63], as in *padmopās* and so forth;
[the form is] *matim*.

25. In the case of *manas* and *jñāna*, [the suffix *kvip* is applied]. 26. In the case of *mantra*, *vṛṣa*, *edha*, *pac*, and so forth, the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*), and it is udātta. *akṛta*.

In the case of a compound of two deities (*devatā-dvandva*), there is the original accent (*prakṛti-svara*) of both members.

The hundred-streamed, inexhaustible fountain, the wise father of all that is spoken,
rejoicing in the lap of the nourishing food— O Heaven and Earth, protect him whose word is truth.

The fountain with a hundred streams, inexhaustible, the wise one, the father of words to be spoken, rejoicing as the gathering-place—him, whose word is truth, do you two, O Heaven and Earth, nourish in the lap of his parents. 9.
Because Viśvāmitra obtained the supreme Brahman from his teacher Vaiśvānara, he praises that teacher with this verse:

"O two worlds, Heaven and Earth! [I praise] the fountain (utsam) which possesses a hundred streams—that is, an immeasurable flow of water—and which is inexhaustible, its stream never interrupted at any time.
This is an elliptical simile.

Like a fountain endowed with a constant flow, like a stream possessed of an uninterrupted course, he is a wise and intelligent man, a master of all the scriptures, a protector of his disciples through the instruction of knowledge, and a speaker who synthesizes the collection of Vedic statements—both those already spoken and those yet to be spoken—by unifying the words found in various recensions into a single meaning. He rejoices in the lap, that is, in the presence, of his parents, Heaven and Earth, exulting through the excellence of his knowledge; for this reason, he is one whose speech is truth, speaking truly because there is no unknown object [to be mistaken] and no motive for deceiving others.
Fulfill this preceptor by granting him the desired fruit,
or rather, protect him.
Regarding *utsam*: from the root *und* in the sense of "to moisten," the suffix *map* is applied according to the rule *unyāmigudhikṛpibhyaḥ kit* (Uṇādisūtra 3.348).

*Meḷim*. *Mili* is a verbal root (dhātu) having the sense of "joining together."

The hymns beginning with "pra vo vājāḥ" consist of fifteen verses each.

Viśvāmitra is the seer (ṛṣi).
The Gāyatrī is the metre;
Agni is the deity;
or alternatively, the first [verse] has the Seasons as its deity.
This hymn is to be employed in the *gāyatrī* meter for both the *prātaranuvāka* and the *āśvina-śastra*, according to the rule:
"Having approached with *pra vo vājāḥ*" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 4.13).
Among the verses designated as *ābhilāvika*, the triplet beginning with "pra vo vājāḥ" serves as an optional *stotriya*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "pra vo vājā abhiyavo'bhi prayāṃsi vāhasā" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.8). This is the first *sāmidhenī* verse of the hymn.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "pra vo vājā abhiyavaḥ, ā yāhi vītaye" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 1.2).
Among the *sāmidhenī* verses, there is one beginning with "being kindled" (*samidhyamānaḥ*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The two [verses] 'being kindled at the sacrifice' (*samidhyamāno adhvare*) and 'O Agni, being kindled' (*samiddho agne āhutaḥ')" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 1.2).
At the third offering of the fire-laying (*ādhāna*), between the two *sāmidhenīs* beginning with "being kindled," the two verses beginning with "broad-flamed" (*pṛthupājāḥ*) are to be maintained.

And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The two verses beginning with *pṛthupājā amartyaḥ* [are recited] before the penultimate verse" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.1). In this same way, it should be understood that wherever there is a similar [set of] *sāmidhenī* verses, these two [verses] are to be maintained there as well.
The twenty-one *sāmidhenīs* are recited in reverse order.
In that context, the six verses beginning with "pṛthupājā amartyaḥ" are to be maintained as *sāmidhenī* verses;

this is prescribed in the Sūtra: "The six *sāmidhenī* verses beginning with 'pṛthupājā amartyaḥ' are to be maintained" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.6). At the Mahāvrata sacrifice as well, there are twenty-five [such verses].

"Ha! The seasons are the *vājās*.
They go, they move—thus they are the *vājās*, the months.
They are directed toward heaven (*abhidyavaḥ*)."
The days on both sides are those "on which there is barley," thus they are *abhidyavaḥ*, as are the half-months.
"Possessing oblations" refers to the gods who partake of the oblation.

"By Ghṛtācī. A cow is called *ghṛtācī* because she produces clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Thus it is said in the Taittirīyaka: "The gods, possessing the oblation; the cow, the producer of clarified butter" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.5.7.4).
Alternatively, "possessing oblations" (*haviṣmantaḥ*) refers to the sacrificial animals who are the givers of oblations such as milk;
"ghṛtācyā" means that by which clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is sprinkled or reaches, thus it is a *suk* (a sacrificial ladle).
Accordingly, it is said in the Vājasaneyaka: "The sacrificial animals are possessed of oblations and well-sprinkled with clarified butter."
Accompanied by that Ghṛtācī, the gods, the sacrificial offerings, the months, and the half-months— all these are capable of providing protection for your sake,
for the purpose of sacrificing to you. While those [offerings], such as *vāja* and the rest, are thus efficacious, [the sacrificer] becomes one who desires your favor (*sumnayuḥ*).

Desiring happiness for himself, the sacrificer "goes to the gods" (*devāñ jigāti*), meaning he attains the gods by means of the sacrifice. Regarding this stated meaning, the *Taittirīya-brāhmaṇa* says: "He recites the hymn 'pra vo vājāḥ'. The *vājās* are indeed the months; the *abhidyavas* are the half-months. The gods are possessed of the oblation; the cow is the butter-vessel. The sacrifice goes to the gods, the sacrificer seeking favor" (*Tai. Saṃ. 2.5.7.4*).
Without malice.

*Īḍya*: [This is derived] from the root *īḍ* (meaning "to praise") with the suffix *ṇyat*. Although the rule "*tisvaritam*" would have resulted in a circumflex (*svarita*) accent for this word, the rule "*īḍavanda*" etc. prescribes that it has an acute (*udātta*) accent on its first syllable.
We entreat (*īmahe*). The root *ī* is used in the sense of longing and so forth; here, the meaning of the verbal root is that of requesting.

Those possessing the sacrifice (*yajñavantaḥ*), provided with the oblations suitable for the sacrifice; *yatasrucaḥ*:

Thus: from the word *idam*, in the sense of "manner" (*prakāra*), the suffix *thamu* is added by the rule *idamasthamuḥ*.

The elision of the accent.

The immortal divine Hotṛ goes before by means of his creative power, impelling the sacrificial assemblies. 7. Hotṛ. Divine. Immortal. Before. Goes. By means of his creative power. The sacrificial assemblies. Impelling. 7.

The Hotṛ—the performer of the oblation, the immortal one who is free from the nature of death, the radiant deity—impelling and powerfully urging forward the *vidathas*, the rites that are to be known; that Agni, endowed with *māyā*—the specialized knowledge regarding ritual action—comes toward us even from the front, at the very moment the rite begins.

By *māyā*. From the root *māṅ*, meaning "to measure" (*māna*) and "to sound" (*śabda*), the suffix *ya* is applied according to the rule "after *mā*, *śās*, *sasi*, and *sabhi*, [the suffix] *ya*" to denote either the agent or the object. Thus, *māyā* is that by which one measures—that is, knows—the object, or that by which the object is measured; it is knowledge regarding the object of action.
The accent is *pratyayasvara* (the accent of the suffix).
In the word *vidathāni*,

He is worthy of praise, worthy of homage, visible even through the darkness. The bull is kindled by the fuel. 13.
Worthy of praise, worthy of homage, visible even through the darkness—the bull Agni is kindled together. 13.

"Worthy of praise by those who laud him, wise, and for that very reason 'to be honored' (namasyaḥ)—meaning he is to be saluted with reverence by all—he drives away the darknesses, the glooms, with his own splendors; he is 'lovely to behold,' visible to all because of his beauty.
Such is Agni, the bull, the showerer of the desires of the sacrificer, who is 'kindled'—that is, set ablaze by the casting of oblations.
Regarding this meaning, the Vājasaneyaka states: "For he is worthy of praise, for he is worthy of honor; kindled, he has become visible even through the darknesses."

*Īḍenyaḥ*: [derived from] the root *īḍ* in the sense of "to praise. The suffix *kenya* is applied according to the rule: "The suffixes *natra*, *kenya*, *yan*, and *tvan* are used in the sense of the kṛtya suffixes."
The accent is that of the suffix.
[The word] *namasyaḥ* [is derived from] *namasyati*; the suffix *yat* is applied by the rule "after a vowel, *yat*."
There is elision of *at* and elision of *ya*. By the rule "the [first syllable] is svarita," it is svarita. *Darśataḥ*.

The root *darśir* is used in the sense of "seeing. From this root, by the rule beginning with *bhṛ-mṛ-dṛś-ṛśi*, the suffix *atac* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*). It has the accent of a *cit* suffix.
*Vṛṣā*: From the root *vṛṣū* "to sprinkle," the suffix *kanin* is applied according to the rule *kaninyu vṛṣi* etc.; due to its being a *kit*, there is no *guṇa* strengthening.
[The word *agni*] is accented on the first syllable because it is a *nittva* [derivative].
"Agni is kindled like a horse that carries the gods; him the offerers of oblations praise. (RV 8.43.14)
He is called the Bull; Agni is kindled like a horse that carries the gods. Those possessing oblations praise him. 14.
"Vṛṣo vṛṣeva" means he is the showerer of desires like a bull. "Devavāhanaḥ":
he is called Devavāhana because he carries—that is, conveys—the oblations to the gods.
In this regard, there is an illustration.
"A horse is not [the rider].
Just as a horse carries a king, bringing him to his own city,
so it is with one situated upon a vehicle.

In the same way, that "Agni" who serves as the vehicle and is "kindled"—that is, perfectly inflamed by the offering of clarified butter oblations—such an Agni as he is [approached] by those possessing oblations. (Note: The variants *kha-ga-ca-ja-ṇa-na-bha* do not include the word "agneḥ";
the variants *ca-na-pha* read *yajjñāta*; the variant *ja-ṇa* reads *ajñātat*.)
3. The *ta*-kit suffixes. 4. The *kha*, *ga*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, *sa*, and *ḍu* suffixes; and the *ca* and *ṅa* suffixes. 5.
The *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, *sa*, and *tiṅ* suffixes are unaccented (*anudātta*).
6. *ta-la-īḍe*: from the root *īḍ*, meaning "to praise. 7. *ja-ṇa-ājyāhuti*: oblation of clarified butter (*ājya*).
8. The suffix *ta* has the sense of another causal agent (*tatkartṛpratyaya*).
9. [The suffixes] *ga*, *ca*, *na*, *bha*, and *sa* have the acute accent (*tisvara*).
10. [The suffix *ta* occurs] after this [root] *i*.

11. [The words] *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha* contain the root *vṛṣ*; *la* contains *vṛṣa*; *sa* contains *vṛṣā*. 12. In *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *bha*, the form *avṛṣeva* does not exist. 13. In *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *na*, *pha*: *aśva* means "not a horse," yet he is like a horse (*aśva iva*) as a vehicle for the gods (*devavāhanaḥ*), being possessed of the gods (*devavān*); [in *ja* and *ṇa*] he is the one who carries the oblations (*havīṃṣi vāhanaḥ*) of the gods (*devānām*); [in *ja* and *ṇa*] he is the possessor of that vehicle (*tadvataḥ*). In *bha*: *devavāhanaḥ* means he is the one who carries the oblations of the gods (*devānām havīṃṣi vāhanaḥ*), being the possessor of that (*tadvataḥ*). In *sa*: *devavāhanaḥ* means he is possessed of the gods (*devavān*), being the possessor of that thought (*matvataḥ*).

Just as a horse, having found its vehicle, [proceeds], so too that Agni who is grasped—that fire which is kindled and properly inflamed by the offering of oblations (*āhuti*)—by him [the sacrifice is performed].

(14) *ta-na-la-sa* refers to the oblation (*āhuti*). The sacrificers, having prepared the sacrificial offerings (*saṃbhṛtahaviskāḥ*), "invoke" (*īḷate*) him for the sake of their ritual power; they remember him. He is the bull (*vṛṣan*). This is a secondary derivative (*guṇa*). The designation is "pragṛhya" because it consists of the best among the middle vowels. He is the "vehicle of the gods" (*devavāhanaḥ*). From the root *vah* in the sense of "carrying" (*prāpaṇe*), with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) and the agentive suffix *lyu*, [we derive *vāhana*]. It has the accent on the final syllable (*lipsvaraḥ*). In the compound, the accent falls on the final member of the *kṛt*-derivative (*kṛduttarapadasvaraḥ*).
O Bull, we, the bulls, kindle you, the bull; O Agni, shine forth mightily. 15.
Thee, the bull, O bull, we bulls shall kindle together; O Agni, may thy light shine forth loftily. 15.
"O *vṛṣan* (bull), showerer of desires; O *agne*, bull of the bulls, the pourers of the offerings of clarified butter—[you are] the bull, the showerer of water by means of the oblation.
Thus says the *Smṛti*: "An oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun;
from the sun rain is born, from rain food, and from that, living beings" (Manu Smṛti 3.76).

"O Agni, who art vast (*bṛhat*) and therefore great (*mahān*), we kindle thee (*tvā*) thoroughly; we enkindle thee (*indhīmahi*). [The root] *ji-indhī* means 'to shine'; here the *liṅ* (optative) is used in the sense of a prayer, and the elision of the nasal *n* is Vedic."
Nighātaḥ;
dīryātam; dīdetiḥ is a verb meaning "to shine."
Its form in the *śatṛ* [present participle] suffix is [as follows]:
by the rule "the first syllable of reduplicated (*abhyasta*) stems is acute," it receives the acute accent on the initial syllable.
The group of six verses beginning with "agne juṣasva" constitutes the sixteenth hymn; it belongs to Viśvāmitra and is addressed to Agni.
Regarding this, the Anukramaṇikā states: "agne juṣasva—six verses; the third is in Uṣṇih, [the fourth] in Triṣṭubh, and [the fifth] in Jagatī.
Since the preceding hymn was described as being "in Gāyatrī," this one is also in Gāyatrī.
The third [verse] is *tuṣṇih*, the fourth is *triṣṭubh*, and the fifth is *jagatī*.
"O Agni, accept [it]" (*agne juṣasva*) is the invitatory verse (*anu-vākyā*) for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering of the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) of the *savanīya-puroḍāśa*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Now, for the *sviṣṭakṛt*: 'O Agni, accept our oblation' (*agne juṣasva no haviḥ*)" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.4).

In the Atirātra sacrifice, once the Āśvina-śastra has been concluded, the two-kapāla cake for the Aśvins must be offered as a *sarvahuta* (an offering consumed entirely) together with the groups of camasa-vessels.
If one were to leave a remnant of the cake and perform the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, the invitatory verse (*yājyā*) for that *sviṣṭakṛt* is "puroḷā agne.
It is prescribed in the Sūtra: "If they should perform the *sviṣṭakṛt* for this cake, [the verse] 'puroḷā agne pacataḥ' [is used]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 6.5).

At the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*), for the *savanīya-puroḍāśa*, the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) is "At the midday pressing... (*mādhyaṃdine savane*). And it is stated in the Sūtra: "O Agni Jātavedas, enjoy our oblation at the midday pressing" (*āśva. śrau. 5. 4*). At the third pressing (*tṛtīya-savana*), for the *sviṣṭakṛt* of the *savanīya-puroḍāśa*, the invitatory verse is "O Agni, at the third pressing... (*agne tṛtīye savane*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "At the third pressing, *agne tṛtīye savane hi kānīpāḥ* is the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the recitation" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 5.4).
The offering verse (*yājyā*) for the *sviṣṭakṛt* of the *āśvina-puroḍāśa* is this one: *agne vṛdhānaḥ*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "*agne vṛdhāna āhutiṃ* [is] the pair of concluding verses (*saṃyājye*)" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.5).
O Agni, Jātavedas, accept our oblation, the *puroḍāśa*, at the morning pressing, O you who are enriched by prayer! 1.
O Agni, accept our oblation, the *puroḍāśa*, O Jātavedas, at the morning pressing, O thou who art enriched by prayer! 1.
Viśvāmitra says:
"O Jātavedas, whose wisdom is born; O Dhiyāvasu!
He is called Dhiyāvasu because from him, through *dhī*—that is, through hymn (*stotra*)—wealth (*vasu*) arises."

This is its grammatical analysis: O Agni, bestower of wealth in accordance with [one's] karma; at the morning pressing (prātaḥsāva) of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice, during the morning libation (prātaḥsavana).

[Note: In the *ta*, *la* recensions, there is the term "padasvaraḥ. To you who are being praised (*īḷane*). [The root] *īḍ* means "to praise. [Note 2: In the *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *bha*, *la* recensions, the word "vṛṣaṇaḥ" does not appear. [Note 3: In the *ta* recension, it is "ghṛtāhutīnām. [Note 4: In the *ca* and *pha* recensions, it is "by way of rain" (*vṛṣṭidvārā*). [Note 5: In the *ta* recension, it says "then he says" (*tadāha*); in the *na* and *sa* recensions, "this" (*imam*); in the *la* recension, "this very one" (*tam iyam*). [Note 6: In the *ca* and *pha* recensions, the root is "dīyatiḥ."]

"Naḥ" means "our," relating to us. "Puroḍāśam" refers to the sacrificial cake; [the word] "haviḥ" means the oblation. "Juṣasva" means "enjoy" or "accept. This is the form in the imperative (*loṭ*) derived from the root *juṣ* in the sense of "to please" or "to serve. Because the vocative is treated as non-existent (for the purposes of accentuation), there is no *nighāta* (suppression of the accent) since it begins the quarter-verse (*pāda*). "Prātaḥsāve": [from the root] *su* with the prefix *abhi* in the sense of "pressing. "Sāvaḥ" means "pressing"; the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*). The final syllable is udātta according to the rule "thāthaghañktājabitrakāṇām. "Priyāvasum": the absence of the case-ending is Vedic (*chāndasa*). It is *anighāta* because it is a vocative. 3.
O Agni, this *puroḍāśa* has been cooked for you, well-prepared;
accept it, O youngest one.
O Agni, [this] sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), cooked by you, has been adorned; enjoy it, O most youthful one! 2.
O Agni, youngest and most youthful one,
you who are the *puroḍāś*— the *puroḍāś* being so called because it is placed (*adhvar*) before (*puras*) the sacrificial oblation (*dāś*), or because it is offered first (*puro dāśati*)—
I am cooked in two baking pans.
And this [sacrificial cake], which has indeed been prepared for you— that is, adorned for your sake by means of the *paryagnikaraṇa* and other rites—
this very *puroḍāśa*, do you graciously accept and enjoy.

*Puroḍāśa*: From the root *daś*, meaning "to give," preceded by *puras*, the suffix *ṇv* is applied in the sense of the object according to Pāṇini Sūtra 3.2.71 (*mantre śvavahokthaśaspuroḍāśo ṇvin*). Then, by the rule *śvetavāhādīnām iṣadasya* (Vārttika on Pāṇini Sūtra 3.2.71), the suffix *ḍa* is applied. Finally, by the irregular formation (*nipātana*) in Pāṇini Sūtra 8.2.67 (*avayāḥ śvetavāḥ puroḍāśca*), the letter *a* is changed to *ḍ*.
Thus, because he crushes (*daśati*) him, he is called *puroḍāḥ*; [and since he is] a *puroḍāḥ*, he is a *puroḍāśa*.
The substitution of *l* for *ḍ* occurs predominantly in the plural forms of the agentive case (*kartari bahuvacane*).
It takes the accent of the final member of the compound (*kṛduttarapada-svara*). Example: *pacataḥ*.

From the root *ḍupacaṣ* in the sense of "cooking," the suffix *anac* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*) by the rule *bhṛsṛdṛśi*, etc., resulting in *pacataḥ*. It is called *pacataḥ* because it is cooked (*pacyate*). [The accent is determined] by the *cit-svara* rule.
Ghā. By the rule "ṛci tunugha" and so forth, there is a long vowel in the *saṃhitā*.
[The word becomes] *pariṣkṛtaḥ*.
In the word *yaviṣṭhaya*, the augment *suṭ* is applied after the root *kṛ* by the rule *mapyuryebhyaḥ karotau bhṛṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.137).
The preceding member *gati* retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvaratva*) according to the rule *gatiranantaraḥ*.
[The suffix *cha* is added] for the sake of the patronymic *yaviṣṭhaya*.
*yaviṣṭha* itself is *yaviṣṭhaya*.

In the rule *pādādyāṃ ca*, the word *ca* (and) includes the suffix *yan* after words such as *vamra* in its own sense (*svārthe*). Therefore, in *yaviṣṭhaya*, the suffix *yan* is used in its own sense (Pāṇini 5.3.25).
Because it is an *āmantrita* (vocative), there is no *nighāta* (elision of the accent).
O Agni, partake of the sacrificial cake offered at this rite beyond the day;
you are the son of strength, established at the sacrifice.
O Agni, enjoy the offered sacrificial cake; you are the son of strength, established at the sacrifice throughout the day. 3.

"O Agni, when the day has passed and the day is gone, eat—that is, consume—the *puroḍāśa*, the oblation of the *puroḍāśa*, which has been offered (*āhuta*) on all sides. O son of strength (*sahasaḥ sūnu*), you are placed by us in these locations such as the Āhavanīya fire;
therefore, eat—this is the sense."
*vīhi*. The root *vī* is used in the sense of desire, motion, and so forth;
this is the form in the imperative (*loṭ*).
Because it ends in a short vowel, it has an udātta accent on the final syllable.
*Āhutam*:
the suffix *kta* is applied to the root *juhoti* in the sense of the object.

In the rule "gatiranantaraḥ," the *prakṛtisvara* (original accent) applies to the prefix *gati*. *Tiroahnayam*: [derived from] *ahar*, that which occurs on the day (*ahani bhavam*) is *āhna*. *Tiras* + *āhna* = *tiroahnayam*.
The suffix *yat* is applied [to *tiro-ahna*] by the rule "in the Vedic language (*chandasi*)"; thus,
the time when the day has disappeared is *tiroahnayaḥ*,
meaning the time of night.
The accusative case ending is applied by the rule "kālādhvanoratyantasaṃyoge" (Pāṇini 2.3.5).
The preservation of the original form of the vowel "e" is due to the rule "prakṛtāntaḥpādam" (Pāṇini 6.1.115).
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the accent falls on the first member.

1. *ta-'na:* does not exist. 2. *ta-* refers to this [word]. 3. In the versions *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, and *sa*, the phrase “*āmantritatvātrighātaḥ*” (non-tripartite division due to being a vocative) does not exist. 4. In the versions *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, and *sa*, the phrase “*puroḍāśante'dhvaryvādyaḥ*” does not exist. 5. In the versions *na*, *bha*, and *sa*, the phrase “*enamiti puroḍāḥ*” does not exist. 6. *ta-*: *tumyam* or *gha* means indeed for your sake alone. 7. In the version *ta-*, the word “*vā gha*” does not exist. 8. [The rule] “the accent of the base form of the word” applies.
(Ṛgveda 2.38) O Jātavedas, O Sage, enjoy the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśam*) here at the midday libation (*mādhyaṃdine savane*).
O Agni, the wise do not diminish your portion in the sacrificial assemblies, you who are ever-youthful.
O Jātavedas, O Sage Agni, at the midday libation, enjoy the sacrificial cake here; the wise do not diminish your portion, O Mighty One, in the assemblies of sacrifice. 4.
"O wise one, O Jātavedas, in this rite called Agniṣṭoma, and there at the midday pressing (mādhyaṃdina-savana), enjoy—that is, partake of—the *puroḍāśa* intended for the midday pressing.
O Agni, in the sacrificial assemblies (*vidathā*), the wise ones—the Adhvaryus and others skilled in ritual—attain [thee];
for by means of thee, the great one, the gods go to or reach the oblations; thus thou art the great Agni."
They do not diminish—that is, they do not harm—this *puroḍāśa* cake which has been assigned as your portion for you, the mighty and great one;
rather, they offer it to you. "Accept it," is the implied sense.

In the word *mādhyaṃdina*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "belonging to this" (*madhyaṃdinasyedam*), because it belongs to the *utsādi* group; due to its being marked with *j*, there is vṛddhi of the first vowel.
The initial acute accent (*udātta*) is due to its being a word denoting wealth (*vittavat*).
Regarding *yahvasya*: from the root *yā* in the sense of "to reach," the suffix *van* is applied in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*), according to the rule *śevayahvajihva*.
The augment *ḍu* is added to the root, and the vowel is shortened.
That by which they go is "yahva," meaning fire;
it has an udātta accent on the final syllable due to metrical transposition (*vyatyaya*).

*Bhāgadheya*. From the word *bhāga*, the suffix *dheya* is applied in the sense of the word itself according to Pāṇini Sūtra 5.4.36.2 (*abhāgarūpanāmabhyo dheyapratyayo vaktavyaḥ*). It bears the accent of the suffix.
They say:
because the root *mī* in the sense of "to injure" belongs to the *krayādi* class, it takes the suffix *śnā*;
in that context, by the rule *mīnāter nigame*, there is shortening [of the vowel].
The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] does not occur by the rule "hinu mīnā" (Pāṇini Sūtra 8.4.15), because all grammatical rules are optional in the Vedic language (*chandas*).
O Agni, at the third libation, you who are the lord of the house, accept the sacrificial cake offered with oblations, O son of strength.
Then, through our inspired prayer, establish among the gods the sacrifice, rich in jewels and watchful among the immortals.

O Agni, at the third libation, O Son of Strength, you indeed desire the offered sacrificial cake; therefore, among the gods, establish the sacrifice with a successful conclusion—rich in jewels and watchful among the immortals. 5.
"O Agni, son of strength, you desire the *purōḷāśa*—that which is offered at the third libation (*savana*).

Immediately thereafter, [you desire] the sacrifice (*adhvara*), which is indestructible and rich in jewels; by the word 'jewel' (*ratna*), the supreme fruit characterized by heaven and so forth is denoted—that which bestows such a fruit, and which is watchful (*jāgṛvi*), causing one to remain alert."
"In the morning, Soma becomes watchful, warding off sleep.
You, O Soma, having been praised with this speech characterized by hymns, place us—'among the immortals,' those gods such as Indra who are free from the nature of death.
The particle *hi* is a filler.
Regarding the third [case]: from the word *tri*, the suffix *tīya* is applied in the sense of ordinal number by Pāṇini Sūtra 5.2.55, "atreḥ saṃprasāraṇam" (there is vocalization for the root *atri*);
by the force of that [sūtra], there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*).

The long vowel [substitution] does not apply by the rule "halaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.2). Because the word "aṇaḥ" (from Pāṇini 6.3.111) is carried over there, the accent is that of the suffix (pratyayasvara). Thus: *kāniṣaḥ*.

In *kanī* and similar forms, the suffix *sip* occurs in the *leṭ* mood according to the rule "the suffixes are manifold. Because that [suffix] is not marked with *ñ* or *k*, there is the elision of the initial [augment].

This is the desired expression: 1. O wise one, O Jātavedas, O knower of all that has been born, O Agni, here in this [place]. 2. Pha—here. 3. Kha, Ga, Ca, Ja, Ṇa, Pha, Bha—the word "attain" (prāpnuvanti) is not present. 4. Ta—the suffix -dheya. 5. Ta—that which bestows its fruit. 6. Ta—the form of the root *i* in the *leṭ* mood.

The vowel *ā* for the [root] *akṛ* occurs by metathesis (*vyatyaya*). Because it is joined with the particle *hi*, it does not receive the *anighāta* (non-suppression) accent; rather, it bears the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*). In the word *vipannayā*: the root *pana* means "to praise. The suffix *kvip* is added in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*). The suffix *ka* is added because it "goes beyond" (*virantayāti*). It bears the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). In the word *dhāḥ*: this is a form derived from the root *dadhāti* after its elision (*luk*) according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). The first syllable (*pāda*) receives the *trivāda-anighāta* accent. In the word *jāgṛvim*: the word *jāgṛvi* ends in the suffix *kim*. It bears the accent of the *nit* suffix.
O Agni, increasing one, O Jātavedas, graciously accept this oblation and the *puroḍāśa* cake offered across the night.
O Agni, growing strong, accept the oblation and the sacrificial cake, O Jātavedas, even across the day. 6.
O Jātavedas— O Agni whose wisdom is born— growing, increasing through the oblations,
you have purchased for me the day beyond [the night], that is, the day which has transcended the night; the time when it has become transcendent is "tiroahyaḥ," namely the period of the night.
At that time, accept and enjoy the oblation of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa).
*Āhuti*:
[This is derived] from the root *hu* (to sacrifice) with the suffix *kvin* in the sense of the object (*karman*).
According to the rule “*tātrāṃ ca niti krayatāṃ*,” the verbal prefix (*gati*) retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*).
The sixteenth [sūkta] beginning with "asti idam" is attributed to Vaiśvāmitra.
