"O leader, come together with the swift horses for our well-being; as you approach the many great nourishments."
May we be winners of great wealth; may Indra grant us progeny and fortune.

For well-being, O leader, with the prize-winning steeds; when you have gathered together great and manifold nourishments, may we be winners of vast wealth. May fortune, accompanied by progeny, be ours, O Indra! 18.
O Indra, leader who sustains the world with excellence, make us accompanied by *vājins*—by horses—for our well-being and for our non-destruction.

Whenever you are present near us for the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice, then may we, being great, possess abundant food and vast riches; being the winners and sharers of those, may we become truly great. Furthermore, may there be within us progeny, wealth, and fortune in abundance.
The root *ās* [is used] in the sense of proximity (*āsatti*) and so forth; *paḷ* [is used] in the sense of destruction (*viśaraṇa*) and so forth.
By the rule "In the Veda, [the suffix] *śap* is frequently elided," there is the elision of *śap*.
And [there is] *yaccogādanighātaḥ*;
and the two words *iṣo* and *rāyaḥ* are in the accusative case with the sense of the genitive;
[and the word] *vantāraḥ*.

In the form *syām*, there is the absence of the augment *iṭ* because the rule for the introduction of augments (*āgamānuśāsana*) is not mandatory (*anitya*) after the suffix *tṛc* applied to the root *van* (meaning "to gather" or "to enjoy").
It has the acute accent (*udātta*) on the final syllable.
*Syām*.
The form *asa* is the locative singular of *idam*.
In *asme*,
the word *asmad* takes the substitution *śe* for the seventh case ending according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
O Indra, bring us resplendent fortune; may we take possession of a portion of thy bounty.
Like two wide pastures on a distant path, fulfill our desires, O Lord of Wealth, Master of riches!

O Indra, bring us fortune endowed with power; may we take possession of a portion of thy bounty. Like a wide expanse on a distant path, our desire extends toward thee; O Lord of Wealth, fulfill that wish for us among all treasures.

O Indra, bring to us for our sake brilliant wealth, full of splendor; gather it together from all sides! In the abundance—the giving—of that wealth belonging to you, who are by nature a giver (*deṣṇa*), may we be established as worthy recipients. Why is this so? He says: within us, our desire, like the submarine fire (*ūrva*) whose longing is never satiated, has been set forth upon the great path. O Lord of Wealth (*vasūnām vasupate*), O Indra, Lord of the highest riches among all treasures, fulfill that great desire by bestowing abundant wealth. *Bhara*: This is the form of the root *bhṛñ* (to support) in the imperative (*loṭ*). *Deṣṇasya*: From the root *ḍudāñ* (to give). By the rule *gādābhyāmiṇṇuṇ*, the suffix *iṇṇuṇ* is applied. One who gives exceedingly is *deṣṇaḥ*. It has the accent on the middle syllable (*citsvara*). *Dhīmahi*: From the root *dadhāti* (to place), in the optative (*liṅ*). By the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is elision of the *śap* suffix. By the rule *chandasyubhayathā*, because the *mahiṅ* ending is treated as a *sārvadhātuka*, there is elision of the *sīyuṭ* augment. Because it is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka*, there is elision of the final *ā*. There is the *nighāta* (suppression of accent). *Ūrvaiva*: The accent is on the first member of the compound (*pūrvapadasvara*). *Prapathe*: This is the form of the root *pratha* (to spread/fame) in the perfect (*liṭ*). *Pṛṇa*: From the root *pṛṇa* (to satisfy/please), in the imperative (*loṭ*) with the ending *si* changed to *hi*. It belongs to the *tudādi* class. By the rule *ato heḥ*, there is elision of the *hi*. *Vasūnām*: Being a *nistva* (a word formed with the suffix *tva*), it is accented on the first syllable.
1. *na*, *la*, *sa*, and *ay* are not [included]. 2. *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *pha*, *bha*, and *repha* (r) are for elision (*recana*).
3. *tra*, *ga*, *gha*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, *la*, *sa*, and *sīyuṭ*.

Fulfill this desire with exhilaration, with cattle, with horses, and with radiant wealth; and cause it to spread. Seeking the light, the wise Kuśikas have fashioned hymns for you, O Indra, as vehicles for your praise. 20. This desire. With exhilaration. With cattle. With horses. With radiant wealth. And cause it to spread. Seeking the light. With hymns. For you. The wise ones. For Indra. As vehicles. The Kuśikas. Have fashioned. 20.

O Indra, fulfill this desire of ours regarding wealth—our longing—with cattle such as cows and other means for performing the Agnihotra and other rites, with horses that are the instruments of transport, and with *rādhas*, wealth endowed with splendor (*candratvatā*);
having bestowed these, satisfy this aspiration.
Furthermore:
By these [hymns], spread us abroad and make us renowned.

Afterwards, the *vipras*—the Kuśikas, skilled in ritual action, desiring for themselves the bliss of heaven and other realms—have fashioned this hymn of praise for you, O Indra, with their thoughts, that is, with meditable mantras.
Mandya: This is the form of the second person plural imperative (loṭ) of the root *mad*, meaning "to praise" and so forth.
[The word] *gobhiḥ*.

When the acute accent on the case-ending would have been required by the rule *sāvekācaḥ*, there is a prohibition by the rule *na gośvansāvavarṇe* and so forth. Thus, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) remains.
[The form is] *paprathaḥ*.
In the case of *prath* with the suffix *śyan*, [the root becomes *prathya*].
By the rule *chandasy ubhayathā*, because that [suffix] is treated as a *sārvadhātuka*, there is the addition of *śap*.
In this case, by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi," there is elision (ślu);
the accent is that of the verbal root (dhātusvara); [the form is] akran.
In the *luṅ* (aorist) tense of the root *kṛ*, there is elision (*luk*) by the rule "in a mantra, [there is elision] of *ghas*" and so forth;
[the result is] the *nighāta* (elision of accent).

O Lord of Cows, burst open the cow-pens for us; let well-guided strengths come to us together. You are the dweller in heaven, O Bull of true vigor; O Maghavan, be well-disposed toward us as a giver of cattle. 21. Open up the cow-stalls for us, O Lord of Cows, and let the cows come to us. May noble riches and strengths flow toward us. You are the one who dwells in heaven, O Bull of true power; O Bounteous One, be gracious to us as a bestower of cattle. 21.

O Indra, Lord of Heaven, for our sake (*naḥ*), strike open (*ā dardahi*) the enclosures (*gotrā*); that is, the protective barriers, the waters (*gāḥ*). The meaning is: having burst open the enclosures, bring forth the waters. Then, let the desirable (*sanayaḥ*) strengths (*vājāḥ*), the foods, come together (*saṃ yantu*) for us. O Indra, showerer of desires (*vṛṣabha*), you are one who dwells in heaven (*divakṣāḥ*), existing by pervading the sky; therefore, O Maghavan, possessor of wealth, you whose power is true (*satyaśuṣma*), understand well (*su bodhi*) this: "May I become a giver of cattle (*godāḥ*) to us. *Dardahi*: from the root *dṛhū* (to be firm/strong). This is the form in the imperative (*loṭ*) with the *yaṅ*-luṅ (intensive) elided. By Pāṇini 7.4.92, the augment *ruk* is added to the reduplication. There is the *nighāta* (suppression of accent). *Gāḥ*: by Pāṇini 6.1.93, the *o* of *go* becomes *ā* before the case-ending *amsas*. This is a single-substitute accent (*ekādeśasvara*). *Asmabhyam*: by the rule "bhyaso bhyam," the fourth-case plural ending *bhyas* is replaced by *bhyam*. *Yantu*: from the root *iṇ* (to go); this is the form in the imperative. *Divakṣāḥ*: from the root *aś* (to pervade), with the suffix *asun*. One who pervades the sky is *divakṣāḥ*. This takes the accent on the final syllable of the compound (*kuduttarapadasvaraḥ*). *Godāḥ*: from the root *dāñ* (to give), with the suffix *vic*. This also takes the accent on the final syllable of the compound.

1. The letter ‘ca’ is absent in manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, and Ta. 2. In manuscript Ta, it reads *gopate* (O Lord of cows), whereas in others it is *gavāṃ pate*. 3. The word *vidārya* is present in manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, Ja, Ṇa, Pa, Pha, Bha, La, and Sa. 4. In manuscript Pha, it reads *varṣaka he*. 5. In manuscript Ja, Ṇa, and Bha, it reads *bhavasi*. 6. In manuscript La, it reads *ityasmāt*. 7. In manuscript Ta, there is the rule: *kuduttarapadaprakṛtisvaraḥ* (the original accent of the final member of a compound beginning with *ku* is retained).

For prosperity, let us invoke the bountiful Indra, the most heroic in this battle for the acquisition of booty—him who hears us, the fierce one for our protection in the assemblies, the slayer of Vṛtras, and the winner of riches. 22. śunam | huvema | maghavānam | indram | asmin | bhare | nṛtamam | vāja-sātau | śṛṇvantam | ugram | ūtaye | sumatsu | hantam | vṛtrāṇi | saṃjitam | dhanānām || 22 ||
"O Indra, in the winning of booty"—
the winning (*sāti*) of booty (*vāja*), which is food; that in which this occurs is "the winning of booty," in that [winning], "in the battle."

The word *bharaḥ* refers to battle (*saṃgrāmaḥ*), because by means of this [chariot], warriors bear the fortune of victory (*jayalakṣmīm*). In that battle, *aśunam* means "exceedingly" (*utsāhena prahṛṣṭam*); or else, *aśunam* is a name for happiness (*sukha*).

O you who bring happiness, the possessor of wealth, and therefore Indra, endowed with unsurpassed sovereignty—the most excellent leader of the entire world—we Kuśikas shall invoke you for the sake of sacrifice.

Likewise, we would invoke you for protection—to you who hear the praise being performed by us; who are fierce and terrifying to enemies; who slay all Vṛtras, that is, all demons typified by Vṛtra, in battles; who destroy the wealth of the enemy; and who are the perfect conqueror. We call upon you for our preservation.

*Śunam*: This is derived from the root *śvi* (meaning "to go" or "to increase") in its past passive participle form (*niṣṭhā*). The elision of the semivowel is prohibited by the rule "yasya vibhāṣā. Subsequently, the semivowel is replaced by a vowel (*saṃprasāraṇa*) because the root belongs to the *yajādi* group.
The absence of the long vowel is Vedic;
it bears the accent of the suffix.
[The word is] *huvema*.

The form [hvayet] is derived from the root *hve* (to call) by applying *saṃprasāraṇa* according to the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi," followed by the elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix; it is the form in the *liṅ* (optative) mood.
There is *nighāta* (elision of accent).
[The word] *bhare*.
The root *bhṛ* is used in the sense of "supporting.
The suffix *gha* is applied in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*).
It is accented on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*) because it belongs to the *vṛṣādi* group.
In the word *vājasātau*:
[the root] *paṇu* means "to give";
the suffix *kin* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*).
By the rule beginning with "janasana," there is the substitution of *ā* for the nasal vowel (*anunāsika*).
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the accent falls on the first member. [The word is] *samatsu*.

The root *ad* means "to eat. From the prefix *sam-* combined with this root and the suffix *kvip*, we derive *samadaḥ*. Thus, *samadaḥ* refers to battles (*saṃgrāmāḥ*) in which they consume the lives of the warriors.

The word *hantam* has the accent on the final syllable. It is derived from the root *han* (meaning "to kill" or "to go") with the suffix *śatṛ*; by the rule *gamahana*, etc., there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*).
By the rule "ho hanteḥ," there is the substitution of *k* (kutva). [The form] *mañjitam* [is derived from] the root *ji* in the sense of "to conquer."
The *kvip* suffix is followed by *tuk*.
The second hymn, consisting of twenty-two verses, begins with "śāsad dhi.

Regarding this, the Anukramaṇikā states: "śāsat; Kuśika or indeed Viśvāmitra himself is the seer (ṛṣi) of the [verse] beginning with śṛteḥ. Thus, the seer is either Kuśika, the son of Iṭa, or Viśvāmitra himself.
Indra is the deity;
Triṣṭubh is the meter.
On the day of the fourth consecration, during the midday pressing (mādhyaṃdina-savana), this hymn—known as the Ahīnasūkta—is to be recited by the Acchāvāka priest following the Ārambhaṇīyā verse.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "To him indeed you pray, O Āśāda, who has driven away the waters in the *ahīna-sūkta*" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.4).
In the *pṛṣṭhya* and *abhiplava* six-day periods, on the first day at the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*), there are three *saṃpāta-sūktas* in place of the *ahīna-sūkta* of the Acchāvāka.
In this regard, this is the third *saṃpāta-sūkta*:
"They seek thee with this [hymn], 'The earth instructs thee'—these are the *saṃpātas*" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.5).

Commanding, the knowing one went toward the daughter of the fire-priest, seeking the noble path; he served the meditation of *ṛta*, where the father, releasing the flow for his daughter, moved with a favorable mind. śāsat | vahneḥ | duhituḥ | naryam | gāt | vidvān | ṛtasya | dīdhitim | saparyana | pitā | yatra | duhituḥ | sekam | ṛjhan | sam | śagmyena | manasā | dadhanve || 1 ||

1. *ca-pha* [are] for conjunction (*saṃbhajana*). 2. *gha-ja-ṇa* [occur] in this [context]. 3. In *kha-ga-ja-ṇa-bha*, the word *'aśunam'* is absent. 4. In *kha-ga-ca-ja-ṇa-ta-na-bha-la-sa*, the phrase *'yadvā... sukhakaram'* is absent. 5. *la* [indicates] the state of being heavy (*ghatva*). 6. In *la*, *'tuk'* is absent. 7. In *kha-ga-ja-ṇa-ta-bha-sa*, [it occurs] at the midday libation (*mādhyaṃdinasavana*). Regarding *Kuśika*, in connection with the context, he states a certain point of the treatise: "The daughter of a father who has no son is an heir; being an appointed daughter (*putrikā*), because she effects the continuation of the lineage, her son is called [the father's] son by this [rule]."
A father who, being childless, sends his daughter to another family is called *avahni*.
That father commanded:
"I shall give you this sisterless maiden, adorned with ornaments."

While giving instructions in accordance with the Smṛti statement, "The son who is born of her shall be my son" (Vasiṣṭha-smṛti 17.17), he goes to his daughters—who are appointed daughters (*putrikā*)—to ensure that the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and other rites, which would otherwise cease for him, must be performed by them.
What is he doing?

Knowing, "A son born of my noble daughter will be one who performs the ancestral rites (*svadhākara*"), the father— honoring (*saparyan*) with garments, ornaments, and the like that son-in-law (*jāmātṛ*), the husband of his daughter, who is the "upholder of the *dīdhiti*" (the intention) of the "truth" (*ṛta*), that is, of the seed capable of producing offspring— "goes to the state of being a grandson. The meaning is that at that point, the father, as the protector of the daughter, bestows upon him the "flowing" (*seka*), namely, the discharge of seed through her.
"Unconsecrated [siblings] are to be consecrated by brothers who have already been consecrated;
and sisters shall receive a fourth part from their own share," according to the Smṛti of Yājñavalkya (2.124).

Having raised the objection as to what distinction exists for a male offspring when there is no difference in the fact that offspring—whether female or male—is equally a condition [for inheritance], he demonstrates the distinction.
"Even if [it is said], 'the mothers' refers to both mother and father; for a woman is not a *vahni* (bearer), while a man is a *vahni* because he is the bearer of his own wife;
thus, [the term] refers to one who is both a non-*vahni* and a *vahni*."
They produce such offspring possessing the characteristics of both female and male;

nevertheless, between those two, one who possesses the characteristics of a male becomes the performer of meritorious deeds (*sukṛta*), such as the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and other rites,
while the other, possessing the characteristics of a female, merely prospers (*ṛdhan*) through clothing, ornaments, and the like.

Because he performs the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and other rites, the son is the heir (*dāyāda*); the daughter is not so, for she is not entitled to the inheritance, but is given away solely to another.

Thus it is explained in the *Nirukta*: "Not to the *jāmī*, that is, the sister. She is called *jāmī* because others produce offspring (*apatya*) in her; or it may derive from the root *jam*, meaning "to consume," as she becomes the means of departure [from the family].

"His own son, the offspring, inherited the inheritance from his father; he made this [woman] pregnant for the sake of a son who would take her hand in marriage. Here, the mothers have brought forth a son as a carrier and a woman as a non-carrier; one becomes the continuer of the lineage, while the other, being male, is the heir. Having exhausted [the other], the sister is given away to another. (Nirukta 3.6).
*Tānvaḥ*:

Because the body (*tanu*) is presided over by the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the body is possessed of breath. The suffix *añ* is applied in the sense of "made of that" according to the rule *aprāṇirajatādibhyo 'ñ*.
Because the root *vih* preceded by a nominal stem (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*) is irregular, there is an absence of *guṇa*.
[The form] is *riktham*;
[the root] *ricir* is used in the sense of "purging."
The suffix accent applies to *pātatu*, *diva*, *ciricimya*, and *syak*. [The word] *araika* [is formed with a suffix accent].
In the case of the root *ric* in the sense of "purging," when the *luṅ* (aorist) suffix *sic* is applied, there is a *vṛddhi* strengthening according to the rule "avadavraja... etc.
By the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi," there is an absence of the augment *iṭ*. Then, the elision of the initial consonant (*hal*) and the final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) apply.
Nighātaḥ. Sanirtuḥ: this is the form of the root *paṇ* (in the sense of "sharing" or "bestowing") with the suffix *tṛc*.
*Nidhānam* is a form derived from the root *dhā* before a consonant-initial suffix; it bears the accent of the suffix (*lisvara*).
The mothers:
although, by the rule "the father [remains] with the mother" (Pāṇini 1.2.70), the retention of the father's name would have been expected, the retention of the mother's name is Vedic.
The use of the plural for the dual is for the sake of honor.
"janayanta" is a form derived from the root *jan* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*). "Vahvim."
The word *puṃsaḥ* is the remainder (*śeṣaḥ*) [of the compound] according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 1.2.67, *pumān striyā*. [The form] *sukṛtoḥ* [is derived as follows]:
the suffix *ku* is added to the root *kṛ* by means of an Uṇādi suffix.
‘Ṛndhan. The root ‘ṛdh’ means ‘to increase.
The suffix ‘śan’ is applied by way of transposition (vyatyaya).
Agni was born, trembling with the sacrificial ladle, as the sons of Greatness for the manifestation of the Red-hued One;
great is their embryo, great is their kinship, and great is his growth through sacrifices.

Agni was born, trembling with his tongue; for the manifestation of the great son of Aruṣa, the great embryo has been greatly recognized among them. Great is the downward slope of the one drawn by tawny horses, through sacrifices. 3.
O Indra, for the sake of sacrifice, Agni—trembling with the flames of the ladle (*juhū*) before you, the formless and radiant one—generated great sons, that is, the abundant rays.
There was a great embracing by these rays through their essence as water. Furthermore, the coming together of these rays, born everywhere in the form of plants, became vast and great.

Furthermore, the great (mahī) activity of these rays—proceeding in this manner (pravat)—becomes vast (mahatī) through the sacrifices (yajñaiḥ), that is, through the offerings of Soma and clarified butter worthy of worship, belonging to Indra, who possesses bay horses (haryaśvasya).
*jajñe* is the perfect (*liṭ*) form of the root *janī* in the sense of "manifestation" (*prādurbhāva*),
with the causative meaning (*ṇyartha*) implied within.
Regarding *juhvā*: by the rule "after the root *hu*, there is *kvip* and lengthening," the suffix *kvip* is applied, resulting in reduplication and lengthening of the root vowel.
By the rule "of the udātta and svarita [vowels]," the [subsequent vowel] becomes svarita.
Regarding *haryaśva*: in the *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose horses are bay" (*harī aśvau yasya*), there is the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*).

1. Because of the non-arising of *na* and *pha*. 2. In *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, and *pha*, "external fire" (*avahisva*) is absent; in *la*, *rā*, and *vahnih*, it is "fire" (*vahniḥ*). 3. Even though *ta*, *na*, and *duhituḥ* are likewise [absent]. 4. In *kha*, *ga*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *sa*, "descendants of them" (*tānvaḥ*) is absent. 5. In *kha*, *ga*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *la*, and *sa*, there is the *ku*-suffix (*kupratyayaḥ*). 6. In *la*, "of the shining one" (*ārocamānasya*). 7. In *ca* and *pha*, "by means of the powerful self" (*balātmanā*). 8. In *kha*, *ga*, and *pha*, "fit for sacrifice" (*yajanaīḥ*); in *ta* and *rā*, "by sacrifices fit for those who sacrifice" (*yajñairjamānāhaiḥ*). 9. In *sa*, "with soma, clarified butter, and other such things" (*somājyādibhiḥ prabhṛtibhiḥ*). They honored the victorious one with offerings; they recognized the great light emerging from the darkness.
Knowing him, they gave him back; Indra alone became the lord of the cattle.
Victorious songs attended him in his struggle; they recognized the great light emerging from the darkness. Knowing him, the Dawns rose up with their rays; Indra became the sole lord of the cattle. 4.
The victorious, conquering Maruts attended upon Indra as he contended and strove against Vṛtra; they came together from all sides.

And those Maruts perceived the great, expansive light—the splendor of Sūrya—emerging from the darkness, from Vṛtra who is of the nature of gloom. Knowing him, the Dawns, once risen, moved toward him, reaching him with full awareness.
Then, of the rays of light that had arisen there, Indra alone became the sole, peerless lord.
*Jaitrīḥ*:
This is the form [of the root] *ji* with the suffix *tun*;
in place of the *guṇa*, there is *vṛddhi* by way of substitution.
*nistara-varaḥ* | *asacanta* is the form of the root *√pac* in the sense of "to assemble" (*samavāye*) in the *laṅ* tense.
*spṛdham* | [The root] *spṛdh* [is used] in the sense of "strife. In Vedic usage, there is the substitution of the suffix *kānac*.
In the Vedic language (*chandasi*), because the dual number is subject to modification, there is an absence of the dual; [this is] the accent of *ci*. [The form is] *ajānan*.
This is the form of the root *jñā* in the sense of "cognizing" (*avabodhane*) in the *laṅ* tense;
it is subject to *nighāta* (elision of accent);
[the form is] *āyan*.
This is the form of the root *i*, meaning "to go," in the *laṅ* (imperfect) tense.
In the firm rock, the wise and tireless seven sages, impelled by their minds, directed their thoughts toward the east;
they found the all-encompassing light of immortality upon the earth and entered it through wisdom with reverence.

Upon the firm rock, the wise ones exerted themselves; the seven sages, with forward-striving minds, sent forth their hymns. They discovered every path of cosmic order (*ṛta*); knowing them, he indeed entered into them with reverence. ||5||
In ancient times, it is said that the cows of the Aṅgirases were seized by demons named Paṇis and placed in concealment on a certain mountain. To recover them, those Aṅgirases praised Indra.
Being thus lauded, Indra dispatched his divine hound to search for the cows.
And she, being intent on searching for the cows, did not find their location.
Indra, having been petitioned by her, brought those cows back and gave them to the Aṅgirases; such is the traditional narrative. And thus is the meaning of this Ṛgvedic verse.

The "wise" (*dhīrāḥ*), the "intelligent" (*dhīmantaḥ*), the "seven sages" (*sapta viprāḥ*)—the seven in number, the Aṅgirases—exerted themselves (*atandan*) toward the cows that were hidden, dwelling within the "firm mountain" (*vīḷau dṛḍhe parvate*). Having determined with their minds that the cows were in a mountain cave, those Aṅgirases drove them out (*ahinvan*) by the same eastern path (*prācā*) by which they had entered. Or rather, [it means] "by the eastern [path]."
He approaches Indra with excellence.
1. [The variants] kha, ga, gha, ca, ja, ṇa, ta, na, pa, pha, bha do not contain "saha".
2. [The variants] kha, ga, gha, ca, ja, ṇa, ta, na, pha, bha, sa read "agacchan"; ta reads "āgacchan".
3. Not [applicable] when preceded by *na* or *va*;

4. not [applicable] when preceded by *la*, nor when *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *bha*, or *jaitrī*... *vṛddhiḥ* occurs; [and] not [applicable] when followed by *na*, *la*, *sa*, or the suffix *tṛc*.
5. In the manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ja, ṇa, ta, na, bha, la, and sa, the word ‘asaḥ’ is not present.
6. In the manuscripts kha, ga, gha, ca, ja, ṇa, bha, and sa, it reads ‘gavāmanveṣaṇāya’.
7. In the manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ja, ṇa, ta, na, pha, bha, and sa, the word ‘gavām’ is not present.
8. In *ta*, *'gāḥ* does not exist. 9. In *ga*, *ca*, and *pha*, they are hidden (*nigṛḍhāḥ*); in *ta* and *sa*, they are concealed (*nigūḍhāḥ*); in *la*, they are obstructed (*niruddhāḥ*).
10. In *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *pha*, and *bha*, they did not find (*avindan*) or obtain (*alabhanta*).
It was stated previously that [the sacrificer] attains [it].
By means of that mind which has Indra as its object—
[it is called] "mind" (*manaḥ*) because it thinks (*manute*)— there is the hymn of praise (*stotra*).
With that hymn, they urged Indra forward, strengthened him, and offered praise.
Having praised him, they found and recovered the entire stolen cattle, which had been well-established upon the path of *ṛta*, the way of sacrifice.
Then Indra, fully cognizant of those various deeds of the Aṅgirases, honoring the Aṅgirases with reverence (*namas*), entered the mountain presided over by them.

*anundan*: This is the form of the root *und*, meaning "to injure" or "to disregard," in the *laṅ* (imperfect) tense; because it belongs to the *rudhādi* class, there is *bha*-saṃjñā [of the suffix], and by the rule *tasya asoḥ*, there is the elision (*lopa*) of the *i* vowel.
There is a *nighāta* (elision of accent). By the rule "prācām," and by the rule "agneśchandasyasarvanāmasthānam," the case ending (*vibhakti*) is acute (*udātta*).
*ahinvan*: this is the form of the root *hi*, meaning "to go" or "to increase," in the *laṅ* (imperfect) tense. *Avindan*.

In the word *vid*, from the root √vid in the sense of "obtaining," the augment *num* is applied due to its inclusion in the *muc-ādi* group when in the *laṅ* tense; there is also the *nighāta* (anudātta) accent. [The form] *panthām*.

In the word *pathi*, [the suffix] *yat* is applied according to the rule *tatra sādhuḥ*. When the designation *bha* is established by the rule *yaci bham*, the elision of the final *ṭi* occurs by the rule *naṣṭaddhite*.
Because the vowel *a* in *yataḥ* (from the rule *yato ’nāvaḥ*) is not *udātta*, the *svarita* accent is applied by the rule *tisvaritaḥ*.
He entered.
This is the form of the root *viś* (meaning "to enter") in the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
Saramā found the broken path of the mountain; the great Pārtha, the ancient one, was gathered together.
O Agni, he led her, the well-footed one, toward the syllables of the verses; the first-born [speech], knowing, went toward the sound.

When Saramā found the cleft of the mountain, the great son of Pṛthā made it accessible for all to reach together. With well-placed feet, she led the way at the head of the syllables; knowing the path, she went first toward the roar. 6.

When Saramā—the divine dog named Saramā—was sent by Indra for the purpose of searching for the cattle and found (vidat) the broken (rugṇam) or shattered door of the mountain, then Indra made for her a great (mahi) and ancient (pūrya) path (pāthaḥ)—meaning food characterized by cattle and other such things—in conjunction (sadhryak) with other edible provisions, fulfilling his previous promise at the time of her dispatch that he would make her offspring eaters (aṅgādinī). Who (kaḥ) made this? He, Indra, gave it to her.
Then Saramā, possessing beautiful feet (supadī) and being imperishable (akṣarāṇām) among those who do not decay, reached the limit (amam) of the cows.
Why? To this he says:
because, being the first (prathamā) to recognize their lowing sound (ravam), she went toward it (accha) with her voice directed towards them.
*vidat*: [This is] the *luṅ* (aorist) form of the root *vid* in the sense of "finding" (*lābhe*). Because it belongs to the *ladita* class, there is the substitution of *aṅ* for *clī*.
Its accent is [as follows].
*Saramā*:
[derived from] the root *sṛ* "to go";
the suffix *am* is added according to the *uṇādi* rules.
She is called Saramā because she moves; Yāska states, "Saramā [is so named] from the root *sṛ* (to move)" (Nirukta 11.24). This is the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).

*rugṇam*: This is the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) of the root *ruj* in the sense of "breaking. By the rule *oditaśca*, the substitution of *n* for *t* occurs. It bears the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
The root is *pā*,
meaning "to protect. By the rule *acca ca* (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.644), the suffix *asun* is applied.
The *Thuḍāgama*: "pā" means past; "tha" means food (anna);
"nihasvara."
*Sadhryak*. [The root] *añc* [is used] in the senses of "going" and "worship.
By the rule beginning with *ṛtvik*, the suffix *kin* is applied.
Regarding the term *sahāñcati*: by the rule *sahasya sadhiḥ*, there is the substitution of *sadhi* for *saha*; furthermore, there is the *kutva* (palatalization) of the *kin* suffix.

The specific prescription that the word *sadhr̥* is oxytone (has its final syllable accented) is for the purpose of preventing the accentuation of the whole word (*kṛtsvara*). Thus, *sadhi* and so forth are oxytone.

When the substitution of *yaṇ* has been made, the *yaṇ* becomes circumflex (*svarita*) according to the rule "the *yaṇ* substitute for an acute or a circumflex vowel is circumflex. What [is the result]?
In the *luṅ* tense, after the root *kṛ*, when *sip* follows: by the rule "in mantras, there is elision (*luk*) of *ghas*" and so forth, [the suffix] is elided.
When the *guṇa* substitution has been applied, the *sip* is dropped by the rule beginning with "after *hvi* etc.
The *visarjanīya* [is then substituted].
The elision (nighāta).
*Nayat* is the form of the root *nī* in the *laṅ* tense.
Supadī:
the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule "pādo'nyatarasyām" (Pāṇini 4.1.8). She sang.
This is the form [of the root] *iṇ* in the *luṅ* tense.

1. While performing the praise of Indra (*indrastuti*), [the variants] *ca*, *pha* [are used]. 2. [The word] produced on the path of sacrifice (*yajñamārga*) in *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ja*, *ta*, *na*, *pa*, *pha*, and *bha*; [or] produced by the path of sacrifice (*sa-yajñamārgeṇa*). 3. In *kha*, *ga*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, *la*, and *sa*, there is the "third" (*tṛdi*). 4. In *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *pha*, *bha*, and *ma*, one obtains [the reading]. 5. In *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, and *ṇa*, the word "first" (*prathamā*) does not exist. 6. By way of being face-to-face (*abhimukhyena*), [the variant] *ca* [is used]. 7. In *la*, the word "Saramā" (*saramā*) does not exist. 8. In *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, *la*, and *sa*, it is "Saraṇi. "The most wise one went; the mountain, seeking his friend, destroyed the embryo for the sake of the well-done deed."
The mortal man, seeking to win through sacrifice, has become a path-finder for you, O youthful ones; Aṅgiras immediately became a singer of praise.

He came; "Ūm"—thus [he spoke]. He struck down thrice. "O friend," he said, "destroy it. For the sake of the well-performed deed, the mountain won the embryo. The young man, eager for battle, strove with his companions. Then Aṅgiras immediately became a singer of praise. 7.

The wisest one, exceedingly intelligent, desiring to perform the sacrifice along with his friends, the Aṅgirases, Indra went forth. He approached the mountain inhabited by the cows, just as [the gods] had come.
That mountain, desiring to perform the sacrifice, brought forth—that is, caused to emerge—the embryo consisting of the cows for Indra, the well-performer of the rite, the excellent warrior.
Desiring the wealth of cattle belonging to the Aṅgirases, Indra— the youth, the slayer of the Asuras— wishing to sacrifice together with the great and eternally vigorous ones,

won back those cows that had been carried off by the Asuras and took possession of them. Immediately thereafter, the seer Aṅgiras, the most excellent among the seven Aṅgirases, having obtained those cows from Indra, became one who was at once praising and worshipping Indra.
They were going.
This is the form of the root *gam* with the suffix *laṅ*.
[The word] *sakhīyan*.
The suffix *kyac* is added after a verbal root when expressing "desire for oneself.
*Asūdayata* is the form of the root *pūda*, meaning "to cast out," in its causative (*ṇyanta*) form, in the imperfect (*laṅ*).
*Sasāna* is the form of the root *√ṣaṇ* (in the sense of "to honor" or "to worship") in the perfect tense (*liṭ*) with the suffix *ṇal*;
it bears the accent of the *liṭ*.
Regarding *makhasyan*:

by the rule "in the Veda, [the suffix] *kyac* is used even for the desire of another," *kyac* is applied here despite expressing the desire of another. Furthermore, by the rule "the augment *suk* should be stated after all nominal stems (*prātipadika*) when expressing intense longing (*lālasā*)," the augment *suk* is added.
A single substitute vowel (*ekādeśasvara*).
*Aṅgirāḥ*. [The root] *sa-gatau* ("to go").

When the word *aṅgāra* is used as an upapada, the suffix *sun* is added to the root *sṛ*. By the rule "aṅgirāḥ," this is a nipātana (irregular formation) whereby the vowel following the letter *ga* in the upapada is elided, the final letter of the root is dropped, and the form *aṅgirāḥ* is established. Thus, because he was born from the embers (*aṅgārebhyaḥ*) in the past, the sage is called *Aṅgiras*.
"Aṅgiras is [derived from] aṅgāra" (Nirukta 3.17), says Yāska.
It is without accent (nisvara).
The Son of the Truthful Ones, the foremost, the standard of comparison, knows all births; he slays Śuṣṇa.
The path-finder from heaven, the impeller, the friend has released his friend; he struck him down.

The Son of the Truthful Ones, the counterpart, the leader before whom all things stand—he knows all births; he slays Śuṣṇa. May he, the path-finder from heaven, come to us with his song; as a friend, he has released his friends and struck down the obstructors. 8.
This Indra is the counterpart (*pratimāna*) of the highest mind;
that is, he is the measure (*pratimāna*), meaning that by him everything is measured or compared.
Alternatively, he is the counterpart of all that is thought, exists, or has been born; the meaning is that by his own greatness he measures out and defines everything through his own proportion.
Purobhūḥ: he who goes before in battle, attaining the enemies in front; he knows all births, that is, he knows all created things;
he slays Śuṣṇa, the Asura named Śuṣṇa; he is the path-finder, the most wise, the one who seeks the wealth of cattle.

1. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Gha, Ja, Ṅa, Bha, and Sa, the word ‘tāḥ’ is absent. 2. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Gha, Ja, and Ṅa, it is read as *sūda* in the sense of "to destroy" (*kṣaraṇe*); in manuscript Sa, it is *ṣūda* in the sense of "to impel" (*preraṇe*). 3. In manuscript La, it is *vana* instead of *ṣaṇa*. 4. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Gha, Ja, Ṅa, Ta, Bha, and Sa, the term ‘liṅgavaraḥ’ is absent. 5. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Gha, Ja, Ṅa, Na, Bha, and Sa, the phrase ‘parecchāyām iti’ is absent. 6. In manuscript La, there is the substitution of *para* for *parasya*. 7. In manuscript La, it is *vastunaḥ*. 8. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Gha, Ja, Ṅa, Ta, Na, Bha, La, and Sa, the word ‘pratinidhiḥ’ is absent. 9. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Gha, Ja, Ṅa, and Bha, the passage beginning with ‘yadvā... and ending with ‘chinattītyarthaḥ’ is absent. 10. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Gha, Ja, and Ṅa, it is ‘yuddheṣu’. 11. In manuscript Ca, it is ‘tannāmānam’. 12. In manuscript Gha, it is ‘asuraṃ ca’ instead of ‘ta-sa’.

Desiring our lineage of the Aṅgirases, may Indra, our friend, coming from the sky—the world of heaven—honoring us pre-eminently, release us completely from blame, that is, from the faults consisting of the oppression by Vṛtra. *Pratimānam*: That which is measured is *mānam*; the suffix *nan* is added according to the Uṇādi rules. Alternatively, the suffix *nyuṭ* is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*). *Purobhūḥ*: From the root *bhṛ* (to reach/attain), with the suffix *kvip*. *Ved*: This is the form of the present tense (*laṭ*) of the root *vid* (to know). *Janitam*: From the root *jan* (to be born/appear); the suffix *imanin* is added according to the rule "from *jan* and *han*, *imanin*. It means "those born in the past" (*bhūtakāle jātāni*). The case-ending (*sup*) is elided according to the rule "supāṃ suluk... *Nisvaraḥ*: This is the form of the present tense (*laṭ*) of the root *han* (to strike). Due to the division of the sentence (*vākyabheda*), there is no *anighāta* (lack of suppression of accent). *Śuṣṇam*: He who dries up is *śuṣṇaḥ*. *Pra ṇaḥ*: The change to *ṇ* in the *saṃhitā* occurs according to the rule "after a prefix (*upasarga*), [the *n* of] *dhula*" (referring to a specific grammatical context). *Padavīḥ*: From the root *vī* (to shine, etc.), with the suffix *kvip*. He who knows the steps (*padāni*) and brings them together is *padavīḥ*, the Seer (*kaviḥ*). *Gadhyuḥ*: From the word *go* (cow/earth), the suffix *ka* is added according to the rule "for the desire of another, in the Vedic language (*chandasi*)."

Beholding it, they rejoiced, milking the milk of their own ancient seed; their roar heated heaven and earth, and at its birth, they established their firm foundation among the cattle and the heroes. 10. Beholding it; they rejoiced; toward; their own; milk; of the ancient; seed; milking; across; heaven and earth; heated; their roar; at its birth; they established; the firm foundation; among the cattle; the heroes. 10.

Beholding their own respective herds of cattle and recognizing them as their own, thinking "these cows are mine," those Aṅgirases—milking out milk for the sake of sustaining the "ancient seed" (retas), that is, the son characterized by that [seed]—rejoiced; being thus milking the milk from those cows, they became glad. The roar of these Aṅgirases, a great sound produced by joy or born of praise, heated through and pervaded both *rodasī*, heaven and earth.
Just as the Aṅgirases formerly established their firm foundation upon the world of moving and unmoving beings— which had arisen and come to be regarded as their own—
so too, when the cows were seized, they stationed heroic men, those superior individuals, for the task of protection.

*saṃpaśyamānāḥ*. The ātmanepada ending is applied to the root *dṛś* (to see) when preceded by *sam*, according to the rule "it should be stated that [the ātmanepada occurs] after *dṛś* with *ne*" (*dṛśeneti vaktavyam*). Once the anudātta accent has been assigned to the *śānac* affix by the accent of the *lasārvadhātuka*, the accent of the verbal root remains.
*amadan*:
This is the form of the root *mad*, meaning "to rejoice," in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense;
it is subject to *nighāta* (anudātta accent).
*duhānāḥ*: [This is formed] from the root *duh* in the sense of "filling," with the suffix *śānac*; due to its inclusion in the *adādi* (second) class, there is elision of the *śap* augment.
The suffix -tva is Vedic;
it is ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable) because it belongs to the *vṛṣan* group.
He scorched.
Because the root *tap* preceded by the prefix *vi-* is transitive here, there is no middle voice (*ātmanepada*).
This is the form in the *laṅ* tense.
[The word is] *ghoṣaḥ*.
The root *ghuṣ* means "to call out" (*saṃśabdane*). It ends in the suffix *ghañ*, and its accent is on the first syllable (*jitsvara*).
*niḥṣṭhām*. [The root] *chā* [is used] in the sense of "cessation of motion.
[The suffix] *kvip* is applied by the rule *ṛḥ ka ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.77).
The accent of a *kṛt* suffix is that of the subsequent member.
[In the form] *adadhuḥ*, the *jus* substitute is applied for the *jhi* ending of the root *dhā* in the *laṅ* tense, according to the rule "sijabhyasta...".
Due to the split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*), there is an absence of the *nighāta* (anudātta accent).

In the word *goṣu*, although the case-ending would have been udātta according to the rule *māvekācaḥ*, it is prohibited by the rule *na goścana*; therefore, the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*) prevails.

He, the slayer of Vṛtra, with his progeny and with oblations, indeed, by means of hymns, released the cows. For him, the far-reaching, noble cow, bearing ghee, yielded sweet and delicious honey. He, the slayer of Vṛtra, with his progeny and with oblations, indeed, by means of hymns, released the cows. For him, the far-reaching, noble cow, bearing ghee, yielded sweet and delicious honey. 11.
That Indra, being joined by the Aṅgirases who are endowed with assistance through their offspring, becomes the slayer of Vṛtra, the destroyer of the Asura Vṛtra.

That very same Indra, accompanied by the Aṅgirases, through the *arkas*—which are worthy of praise—and likewise through the *havyas*—which are to be offered—causes the *ustriyās* to rise; the *ustriyās* are cows whose milk and other products serve as the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) within them.
Alternatively, it means that he causes the milk, curd, butter, and so forth, to abide in them sequentially from below upwards.
Regarding the word *ustrī*, Yāska [states in Nirukta 4.19]: "It is a name for a cow; her enjoyments are directed upward.

He released those cows, that is, he properly produced them for the sake of sacrifice. Because it is so, she bears the oblation—such as milk and other offerings—endowed with *ghṛta* (clarified butter).

1. [The words] *ca*, *pha*, and *pa* are observed [as examples]. 2. [The words] preceded by *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *pa*, *pha*, *bha*, and *sa*. 3. [The word] *śrutijātaḥ* [is used] with *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ca*, and *pha*. 4. [The word] *āvartitaḥ* [is used] with *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *na*, *bha*, *la*, and *sa*; [the word] *avartata* [is used] with *ja* and *ṇa*. 5. [The word] *ghuṣaraviśabde* [is used] with *ca* and *pha*. 6. [The rule regarding] the accent of the final member of a compound (*kṛduttarapadasvaraḥ*) applies to *la*. 7. [The word] *kṣīrādi* [is used] with *kha*, *ga*, *na*, *ja*, *ṇa*, and *ma*.

Bearing [milk], she is therefore *vūrucī*—she who eats (*aśnāti*) the vast (*uru*), abundant sacrificial food such as the *agnihotra* and other offerings, and thus reaches them to receive the oblation; hence she is *urucī*. She is *vjemyā*, meaning she is to be conquered (*jetavyā*) or praised (*praśastā*). The *gauḥ* (cow) has yielded (*aduduhe*) for this sacrificer (*vasmai*) her own limbs (*svāṅga*), that is, sweeter milk and so forth; she was milked. Regarding *ustriyāḥ*: from the root *vas* "to dwell," the suffix *rap* is applied according to the rule "raphāyatiñca" and so on. From the word *u*, the suffix *gha* is added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*) because it belongs to the *pṛṣodarādi* class. The accent is that of the suffix. Alternatively, from the root *sṛ* "to go," preceded by *uṣ*, the suffix *kam* is applied. The elision of the final syllable of the first member is Vedic (*chāndasa*). Here too, the suffix *gha* is used in the sense of the base itself. *asujat* is the form of the root *sṛj* "to emit" in the *laṅ* tense. Regarding *ūrucī*: she eats (*aśnāti*) the vast (*uru*), hence the suffix *kin*. The feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added according to the rule "añteścopasaṃkhyānam. By the rule concerning the removal of the acute accent (*udāttanivṛttisvara*), it is oxytone (*antodātta*). *duduhe* is the form of the root *duh* "to milk" in the *liṭ* tense. *jemyā*: from the root *ji*, the suffix *kenya* is applied in the sense of a gerundive (*kṛtyārthe*). The elision of the vowel *i* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). The accent is that of the suffix.
The fathers fashioned him with a seat; for him, the well-doers have indeed resounded with great, mighty power.
Supporting the two parents with a pillar, they sat and established the impetuous one above.

For him, the well-doers have fashioned a seat upon the father’s [altar]; they have gathered for him great, brilliant splendor. For the three supports, having established themselves with a firm pillar, sitting upon the two parents, they have erected the impetuous height aloft.
While performing a sacrificial session (*sattra*), the Aṅgirases prepared for that Indra—a protector (*pālaka*)—a great, lofty dwelling-place (*sadana*) full of splendor and brilliance.
How so? It is said:
because those Aṅgirases, having accumulated meritorious deeds (*sukṛta*), indeed beheld (*vyaty-an*) and entered that place which was appropriate for Indra.
Why is this so? To this he says:

"The Aṅgirases, while performing the sacrificial session (sattra), [established] heaven and earth—the progenitors of the world—as the support, using the *skambhana* (the means of propping) as the instrument of stabilization; thus they made them firmly fixed so that the two worlds would not fall down. While doing so, they placed that impetuous and swift Indra upward in the heavenly world (*ūdhar*), specifically establishing him for the purpose of accepting the oblation."
They made.
This is the form of the root *kṛ* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*) with the suffix *us*.
There is elision of the accent (*nighāta*).

The root is *sthā* in the sense of "manifesting. In its *luṅ* (aorist) tense, after the *cli*, there is the substitution of *aṅ* by the rule: "After the roots *as*, *vac*, and *khyā*, [the *cli* is replaced by] *aṅ*."
There is elision of the vowel *ā* by the rule "āto lopa iṭi";
because of its connection with the particle *hi*, there is no loss of accent (*anighāta*).
[The word is] *viṣkabhantaḥ*.
The root *skambh* in the sense of "obstructing" is a Vedic (sautra) root; from it,
this form is derived in the present participle (*śatṛ*).
The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] is applied by Pāṇini’s rule 8.3.77, *veḥ skambhrāter nityam*.
The accent is that of the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*).
[The word is] *janitrī*.
The suffix *ṅīp* is applied after words ending in *ṛñj*.

By the rule "the suffix *ṇi* is elided in the *mantra* [when followed by *tṛc*]," there is the elision of *ṇi*. Then, by the rule "optionally in the Veda," the long vowel of the same class (*savarṇadīrgha*) is substituted.
"Seated" (*āsīnāḥ*): this is derived from the root *āsa* in the sense of "sitting," with the suffix *śānac*;
the vowel *i* is substituted according to Pāṇini Sūtra 7.2.83 (*īdāsaḥ*).
When the accent of the *śānac* suffix has been applied, the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*) remains.
*Minvan* is the form of the root *√miñ* (meaning "to cast") in the *laṅ* tense.
The elision of the accent.
If the great earth, the supporting vessel, has shone forth for you, you have established the expansive form between heaven and earth;
in whom the united songs are placed, and all invincible powers belong to Indra.

If the great earth, the creative power, and the waters have moistened him, may he bestow that which increases the two worlds; in whom all songs are firmly established together, and in whom all powers for Indra are unyielding.

1. From *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *na*, *bha*, *la*, *sa*, and *savati*. 2. *La* is the highest. 3. Those who have fully accumulated karma through *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *na*, *bha*, *sa*, and *sam*. 4. Those who practice through *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ja*, *ṇa*, and *anu*. 5. The Aṅgirasas are [denoted by] *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, and *aṅ*. 6. By means of the stabilization (*stambha*) of *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *pha*, *bha*, and *sta*. 7. *Sa*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, and *rodasī*. 8. In the upper world (*ūrdhvaloka*), [denoted by] *ta*.

7. *Mahī* means great. 7. *Dhiṣaṇā* refers to the praise directed toward Indra being performed by us. 7. *Rodasyoḥ* [is used] for the sake of the separation of the two worlds, heaven and earth. 7. *Mayobhuvaṃ* means that which is increasing at that very moment. 7. *Viśvaṃ vibhuṃ* refers to the all-pervading means capable of supporting those two. 7. *Yadi* (if). 7. *Dhāt* means he made it manifest in this continuous flow. 7. *Yasmin* (in which) *dvandve* (pair). 7. *Anavadyāḥ* means faultless, free from defects. 7. *Giraḥ* means words characterized as praise. 7. *Samīcīḥ* means they become united. *Indrāya* is an instance of the transposition of case endings (*vibhaktivyatyaya*).
For such an Indra, all powers—every strength—are unyielding, unrestrained, and indeed established by his very nature.
*Dhiṣaṇā*:

[The root] *dhiṣ* is used in the sense of boldness (*prāgalbhya*). Regarding the form, the suffix *kyu* is applied according to the rule: “*dhiṣ* and [others take *kyu*] when a name (*saṃjñā*) is intended.”
There is the substitution of *dhi* for the root [dhṛṣ].
That by which one is emboldened (*dhṛṣṇoti*) is *dhiṣaṇā*, meaning praise. It takes the accent of the suffix.
I instruct. Now, [the root] *hiṃs* has the meaning "to injure.
From this [root], the suffix *kip* [is applied].
Because of the rule *chandasyubhayathā*, that [suffix] is treated as a sārvadhātuka; therefore, the suffix *śap* is applied.
By the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is the substitution of *plu* (i.e., *guṇa*).
By the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is the substitution of *it* for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).
The word *dhātu-svaraḥ* [is explained as follows]:
*dhāt* is a form derived from the root *dadhāti* (to place) in the Vedic *luṅ* tense.
Because of its connection with that, there is no striking; it is the universe.
[The word] *viśva* is derived from the root *bhū* with the suffix *kvip*.

In the Vedic language, the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs according to the rule “chandasyubhayathā. Furthermore, the circumflex (*svarita*) accent applies by the rule “udāttasvaritayoryaṇaḥ...,” resulting in the form *anuttāḥ*.

In the case of the root *nam* (meaning "to bend" or "to bow") preceded by *ni*, when the suffix *niṣṭhā* is applied, there is an absence of the substitution of *n* for the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix due to the specific grammatical rule (*nipātana*) beginning with "namannanipattānutta. [This results in the form] *nataḥ*. The accent is that of the first member of the compound.

Great are your wondrous deeds; your powers come forth for the slayer of Vṛtra; many teams of horses attend you. To the great hymn of praise we have come for protection; O Maghavan, be well aware of us as our guardian. Great are your wondrous deeds; your powers come forth for the slayer of Vṛtra; many teams of horses attend you. To the great hymn of praise we have come for protection; O Maghavan, be well aware of us as our guardian. 14.

O Indra, I desire your great and true increase; I desire your powers and the gifts associated with them. To you, the slayer of Vṛtra, the many, numerous, and constant ones come for the purpose of carrying [the oblations]. We have brought to you, the wise one, your great hymn of praise, protection, and food characterized by the oblation. O bountiful Indra, be mindful that you may become our excellent protector. *Satyam*: from the root *sṛ* with the suffix *ya* in the sense of abstract state (*bhāvārtha*), according to the rule *satyuryaḥ*; the accent falls on the suffix. *Vardim*: from the root *vaś* (to desire); this is the form in the present tense (*laṭ*). *Niyataḥ*: from the root *yu* (to mix); the suffix *kip*. Those who constantly mix themselves [with the chariots] are the mares (*niyato vaḍavāḥ*). *Aganma*: from the root *gam* in the imperfect (*laṅ*) first person plural; the suffix *śap* is elided by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*; *mrośva* changes the *m* to *n*. There is a *nighāta* accent. *Bodhi*: from the root *budh* in the imperative (*loṭ*); the form of *hi* becomes *dhi*. There is a *nighāta* accent. *Gopāḥ*: from the root *gup* (to protect); the suffix *āya* is added by the rule *gupūdhūpa* etc.; from that stem, the suffix *kip* is applied; there is the elision of the vowel *a* and the elision of *y*. The accent falls on the suffix.

Having found the great, widely-shining domain, he, the wise one, brought forth a path for his friends; Indra, shining with the heroes, brought forth together the sun, the dawn, the way, and Agni. 15. Great, vast, and brightly shining—having found this, he then established a path for his companions. Indra, blazing with the men, brought forth at once the sun, the dawn, the way, and Agni. 15.

1. Due to the optional application of the augment *nuṭ* before a root beginning with *ca*, *pha*, or a negative particle (*nañ*), there is an absence of the change of the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix to *n*.
2. [The change to *n* occurs] after *ca*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, *la*, *sa*, or a negative particle (*nañ*) when followed by a vowel.
3. [The change to *n* occurs] also after *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, and *brahma*.
4. Kha, ga, ca, ja, ṇa, pha, ma, yācāmahe.
5. Kha, ga, ca, ja, ṇa, bha; ‘su’ is not present.

This Indra, who, knowing [the way], bestowed upon us—the liberal ones—a great field such as a cultivated plot, much gold, and silver; and immediately thereafter, he properly impelled (or gave) the moving wealth consisting of cattle and the like. Shining brightly, this very Indra, together with men who are his companions in ritual action, produced the Sun, the sustainer of time, at the dawn; he produced Gātu—the earth, so called because the gods Indra and others sing praises therein—and Agni, characterized as the Āhavanīya fire and the means for performing rites such as the Agnihotra. *Gurum*: "candram" (in the Saṃhitā) takes the augment *suṭ* according to the rule "hasvāccandrotpade mantre"; by the change of *śru*, it becomes *śru*. At the time of the *pada* recitation, there is no *suṭ* augment. The accent is that of the suffix *ku*. *Candram*: the accent is that of the suffix *rak*. *Caratham*: the root *car* means "to move"; from this, the suffix *athap* is added in the sense of a derivative (*drauṇādika*). The accent is that of the suffix. *Irata*: from the root *ir* meaning "to go," in the present tense (*laṭ*), the augment *āṭ* is added according to the rule "āḍajādīnām. It bears the *nighāta* (anudātta) accent. *Ajanat*: this is the form of the root *jan* in the causative (*yaṇt*) in the present tense; the *ṇi* suffix is elided according to the rule "bahulamanyatrāpi saṃjñācchandasoḥ. *Gātum*: from the root *gai* meaning "to sound"; the suffix *nu* is added according to the rule "gāpāyāhibhyaḥ. The accent is that of the suffix. 7. Translation complete.

The mindless one, devoid of sight, has released the all-glittering waters that flow together; being purified by the sages through the filters, the sweet, swift-moving streams are urged forward by the days and nights.

Even this one, the all-pervading, with his far-reaching power, has sent forth the converging streams that are radiant on all sides. Being purified by the sages through the filters, they flow onward; urged by the rays of light, they speed along like swift racers.
*Damūnāḥ*:
he whose mind is subdued is *damūnāḥ*, meaning one of subdued mind;
or alternatively, he is *damūnāḥ* because he causes [the senses] to run forth (*drāvayati*).

The meaning is "approached. He is this very Indra, the all-pervading one (*vibhvaḥ*), who has entered into the *dhyāsa*s—those which are *sadhrīcīḥ*, meaning mutually joined together; *viśvacandrāḥ*, meaning those that delight the universe, or alternatively, those by whom the delight of the universe is produced.
Being thus, they "purified" (pra amṛjan) the "waters," that is, they released them.

And those waters, being purified by the "seers"—the purifiers such as Agni and Vāyu—and becoming sweet with "honey," that is, endowed with sweetness; and being "gladdening," that is, delighting the entire world, they "impel" (hinvaṃti) immediately by means of "days" (aktubhiḥ) and even by "nights" (aktubhiḥ).
The meaning is that day and night they cause the entire world to be intent upon its respective activities.
*Damūnāḥ*: [derived from] the root *damu*, meaning "to pacify. The suffix *nasi* is applied according to the rule "imehanasiḥ."
He is called *damūnāḥ* because he tames (*dāmyati*).
Alternatively, from the word *dānta*, the letter *da* is substituted for *da*, and the vowel *u* replaces the *a* following the *m* of *manas*; this is a Vedic usage.
He created.
"Create" (*sṛja*) [is used] in the sense of emission;
"they impel" (*hinvanti*); "go" (*hi*) [is used] in the sense of motion.
Nighāta (the accentual suppression). Dhanutrīḥ.
From the root *dhan* in the sense of "wealth," the suffix *utrac* is applied according to the rule beginning with *aśiñādi*.
In the *śārṅgarava* and other such groups, the feminine suffix *ṅīn* is to be understood;
it is unaccented (*nisvara*).

1. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, Ja, Pha, and Sa, it is "ayam"; in Ta, it is "ayam". 2. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Gha, Ca, Ja, Ṇa, Na, Pha, Ma, and Sa, the word "ca" is absent. 3. In the manuscripts Kha, Ca, Pha, and Bha, it is "nivāsam". 4. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, Ja, Ṇa, Pha, and Bha, the phrase "dāntamanāḥ" is absent. 5. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ya, Ja, Ṇa, Na, Bha, and Ma, it is "devendraḥ". 6. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, Ja, Ṇa, Ta, Na, and Bha, they are "parasparaṃ saṃgatāḥ". 7. In the manuscripts Ca and Ta, the word "somān" is absent. 8. In the manuscripts Ta, Na, and Sa, the word "satyaḥ" is absent. 9. In the manuscripts Na, La, and Ga, it is "aktubhī rātribhiḥ". 10. In Ga and Sa, it is "rātridivam"; in Ca, Na, La, and Ga, it is "gātridivasam".

The two dark treasuries of wealth, both worthy of sacrifice, follow after the greatness of the Sun. O Indra, when your greatness is encompassed, your desirable and impetuous friends [the Maruts] gather around you. anu kṛṣṇe vasudhītī jihāte ubhe sūryasya maṃhanā yajatre | pari yat te mahimānaṃ vṛñjanty ā sakhāya indra kāmyā ṛjipyāḥ || 17 ||

O Indra, by your greatness (*maṃhanā*)—your power as the excellent impeller of the sun and of the world—those two, the dark ones, day and night, which are the repositories of things to be inhabited (*vasudhitī*) and worthy of sacrifice (*yajatre*), follow you again and again in their recurring cycle. Furthermore, your straight-moving (*ṛjipyāḥ*) friends, the desirable Maruts, who act as allies, prevail all around (*pari prabhavanti*) in order to exclude (*vṛjadhyai*)—that is, for the purpose of overcoming—the Asuras who cause obstacles to ritual action, following after your own majesty and power. *Jihāte*: from the root *ohāṅ* (to go), belonging to the *juhotyādi* class; the *it* vowel of the reduplication is applied according to the rule "bhrāmita"; there is the *nighāta* accent. *Maṃhanā*: from the root *maha* (to grow/great); the suffix *lyuṭ*; the accent falls on the suffix-initial (*litsvara*). *Vṛjadhyai*: from the root *vṛjī* (to exclude/avoid); the suffix *kadhyaipratyaya* is used in the sense of the infinitive (*tumun*); there is no application of *kip* or similar suffixes; the accent falls on the suffix. *Kāmyāḥ*: from the desiderative of the root *kam*; the suffix *yat* is applied according to the rule "aco yat"; the initial vowel is acute according to the rule "yato ’nāvaḥ". *Ṛjipyāḥ*: from the root *opyāyī* (to increase); the suffix *kip*; the *y* is elided according to the rule "lopo vyor vali"; the vowel *i* replaces the *a* of the preceding member by metrical transposition (*vyatyaya*); the singular ending is used for the plural, which is Vedic (*chāndasa*); the accent is that of the original form of the second member (*ṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*).

Become the lord of pleasant truths, O slayer of Vṛtra; you who are the life of all, the bull, the bestower of strength. Come to us with your auspicious aids, you who are great, coming with your mighty protections. 18. Lord, become the lord of pleasant truths, O slayer of Vṛtra; you who are the life of all, the bull, the bestower of strength. Come to us with your auspicious aids, you who are great, coming with your mighty protections. 18.

O Vṛtra-slayer Indra, you who possess all life—that is, whose lifespan is entirely complete and undecaying—O bull, showerer of desires, bestower of vigor, and giver of food: as such, become the lord and master of our *sūnṛtā*s, our most beloved words being uttered by us.

O Marut, desiring to go to the forest for the sake of sacrifice, you—the Great One—come toward us with great aids, that is, with mighty protections, and with auspicious, beneficial friendships characterized by the assistance of bestowing fruits; come to us for the sake of the sacrifice.
Regarding *sūnṛtānām*: the root *ūn* means "to diminish. That which excessively diminishes (*sutarām ūnayati*) what is unpleasant is called *sūn*, meaning "the pleasant."
And that which is both *ṛtam* (right) and *satyam* (true) is *sūnṛtam*.
[The accentuation of the first syllable of the second member is due to the rule] "In the Chandas, [the first syllable of] the following word is often acute.
[He is] *vayodhāḥ* (the bestower of vital strength).
When *vayas* is the upapada, the suffix *vic* is added after the root *dhā*.
[In the word] *gahi*,
there is the elision (*luk*) of *śap* after the root *gam* in the imperative (*loṭ*), according to the rule "there is diversely [elision] in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).
This is the rule for the *saṃhitā* reading.
Furthermore,
because that [suffix] is doubled, there is the elision of the *m* by the rule beginning with "anudāttaupadeśa."
Because that [condition] is unestablished, the elision of the *h* by the rule "ato heḥ" does not occur. There is the *nighāta* (anudātta accent). [The form is] *sarayan*.
The suffix *kyac* is applied after the word *saraṇa*;
the accent belongs to the single substitute (*ekādeśasvara*).
1. [The suffix] *ya* is applied after the word *yajña*.
2. According to the variants *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *sa*, [the suffix] *tarha* is also applied.
3. According to the variants *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, there is udātta accent on the final syllable of the compound.
Like Aṅgiras, I honor with my mind that ancient-born one for the sake of winning;
drive away the many godless ones who are malicious, and grant us, O Maghavan, our own wealth for our gain.

Worshipping him with reverence as [I did] for Aṅgiras, I fashion a new hymn for you, O Ancient One. Drive away the many godless oppressors who have existed from of old. And, O Maghavan, bestow upon us the light of heaven so that we may win it! 19.

O Indra, like the Aṅgirases, I, Viśvāmitra, worshipping and honoring you with reverence and praise, make you—who possess such greatness—new again for the sake of your enjoyment; that is, I make you fresh by means of this hymn of praise. O Maghavan Indra, go forth and utterly destroy the many, godless, and long-lasting enemies who are Rākṣasas, appearing as darkness. Bestow upon us our own wealth, O Lord, for the sake of its acquisition and enjoyment. *Commentary:* * *Aṅgirasvat*: "Like the Aṅgirases. The suffix *-vat* is used here in the sense of "equal to that" (*tena tulyam*). According to the rule *nabho'ṅgiromanuṣāṃ vatyupasaṃkhyānam*, there is no change of *s* to *r* in both cases. * *Saparyan*: The root *sapara* belongs to the *kaṇvādi* group. * *Navyam*: From the root *ṇu* (to praise), the suffix *yat* is applied (*aco yat*). There is a substitution of *vānta* (the sound *au*) for the final vowel of the root, and the word is accented on the first syllable because of the suffix *yat*. * *Kṛṇomi*: This is the form of the root *kṛ* in the present indicative (*laṭ*). * *Sanyase*: The suffix *san* forms an abstract noun (*bhāve*), followed by *kip*. From the root *yasu* (effort), *kip* is added: *sanaḥ* (of enjoyment) *yase* (for the effort). Thus, it means "for the sake of enjoyment. * *Purājām*: From the root *jan* with the suffix *viṭ*, resulting in the form *purājām* (ancient). * *Yāhi*: The form of the root *yā* in the imperative (*loṭ*). * *Svaḥ*: Being an indeclinable by the rule *svarādinipātamavyayam*, the case endings (*sup*) are elided after it by the rule *avyayādāpsupaḥ*. * *Sātaye*: From the root *paṇ* (to enjoy/share), the suffix *kin* is added in the sense of an abstract noun (*bhāve*). By the rule *janasana*, there is the substitution of *ā*. It is accented on the first syllable because it is a particle according to the rule *ūtiyuti*.
The purifying flames have spread far and wide; carry us safely to the further shore of these.
O Indra, you who are our charioteer, protect us from harm; quickly, very quickly, make us winners of cattle.
The flames have spread forth, purifying. Carry us safely to the further shore of these; O Indra, you who are the charioteer, protect us from harm. Swiftly, swiftly, make us winners of cattle.

O Indra, those purifying waters of yours, which are the means for pouring down the rains that cleanse the wicked, have become spread far and wide throughout the world. For our sake, carry us across to their auspicious, undecaying further shore;
that is to say, make the water reach from this bank to the other.
O charioteer, you who possess the chariot, protect us from the enemy, the one who seeks to harm;
thereafter, make us very swiftly winners of cattle and other livestock.
The sense is: by providing rain, fill the reservoirs such as tanks and lakes, and thus make us possessed of wealth such as cattle.
*abhūvan* is the form of the root *bhū* in the sense of "existence" (*sattāyām*) after the elision [of the suffix];
it is subject to the *nighāta* (elision of accent).
Fulfill! [The root] *pṛ* is used in the senses of "protecting" and "filling.
1. kha-ga-ca-ja-ṇa-na-bha-sa-svadhanam.
2. *kha*, *ga*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, and *sa* followed by *pa*; *ca* followed by *sa* in the sense of worship (*pūjā*). 3. *sa* followed by *ba* becomes *ṣa*. 4.
*kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *na*, and *sa* [followed by *ma*] become *makṣu* (quickly); *bha* [followed by *ma*] becomes *makṣumakṣu* (very quickly).

*anta* and so forth. By the rule *atipippyauśca*, there is the substitution of *t* for the reduplicated syllable. By the rule *herhrasvādguṇaḥ*, there is guṇa [substitution]. There is the *nighāta* (anudātta accent). *Rathiḥ*. In the sense of the suffix *makha*, by the rule *medhārathābhyāmirñiracau*, there is the suffix *iraC*. *Ripaḥ*. From the root *rip* in the sense of "injury," with the suffix *kvip*. By the rule *sāvekācaḥ*, the case-ending has the udātta accent. *makṣabhakṣa*. By the rule *niravīpsayoḥ*, there is reduplication. In the *saṃhitā*, by the rule *ṛcitanughamaśrutak*, there is lengthening.

The slayer of Vṛtra, the lord of cattle, has assigned the cows; he has gone between the dark ones with his ruddy abodes. Bestowing pleasant gifts according to the cosmic order (ṛta), he has thrown open all his own doors. adediṣṭa | vṛtrahā | gopatiḥ | gāḥ | antaḥ | iti | kṛṣṇān | aruṣaiḥ | dhāmabhiḥ | gāt | pra | sūnṛtāḥ | diśamānaḥ | ṛtena | duraḥ | ca | viśvāḥ | avṛṇot | apa | svāḥ || 21 ||

"May Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, the destroyer of Vṛtra, the lord of cattle, the master of cows, grant us the cows. Likewise, [grant us] the black ones... [Gopatha Brāhmaṇa 3.1.3.32], Third Aṣṭaka, 337.
"‘Indra somam’ and ‘indraḥ pūrbhit’ constitute the midday [pressing]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 9.8).
Even for the Ujjhitalabhidhs, this is the Mahāvatī;
and it is stated in the Sūtra: "‘Indra somam’ and ‘indraḥ pūrbhit’ constitute the midday [pressing]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 9.8).

O Indra, Lord of Soma, drink this Soma, the midday draught—every part of it that is dear to you. O Maghavan, wielder of the bolt, with joyful countenance, loosen your jaws; unyoke your two bay steeds and rejoice here. indra | somam | somapate | piba | imam | mādhyaṃdinam | sarvam | cāru | yat | te | pramudhya | śipre | maghavan | ṛjīṣin | vimucya | harī | iha | mādayasva || 1 ||
Viśvāmitra says:

O Lord of Soma, O Sovereign of Soma, O Indra, drink this Soma, this juice of Soma, being prepared by us at the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*). For that midday pressing connected to the midday, which is being performed for your sake, and the *niṣkevalya* recitation (*śastra*), are beautiful and delightful.
O Maghavan, possessor of wealth, O Ṛjīṣin—
the word *ṛjīṣa* refers to the Soma substance from which the essence has been extracted—

O Indra, having unyoked the two bay horses (*harī*) from the chariot, having opened wide your jaws (*śipre*, i.e., the cheeks), and having filled them with food by means of your protruding snout, rejoice here in this region of the gods and gladden those two horses.
‘Pramudhya’ is the form of the root *protha* with the suffix *lyap*;
the short vowel is a Vedic (Chāndasa) irregularity.
*Litsvara*.
*Ṛjīpin*: from the roots *arja*, *parja*, and *arjema*, the suffix *iṣan* is applied according to *Uṇādi Sūtra* 4.468: "After *arj*, the suffix *iṣan* is added and *ṛji* [is substituted]."
And there is the substitution of *ṛji* for the verbal root; thus, from *arjetha*, [we derive] *ajīṣam*. The suffix *ini* is applied in the sense of "that which belongs to this."
Because he has been addressed, there is no offense.
"Be exhilarated" (*mādayasva*);
the root *mad* is used in three senses, including praise.
The causative suffix *ṇic* is applied because of the causal sense;
there is elision [of the accent].

O Indra, drink the Soma mixed with milk, the stirred offering, the bright juice; we have given it to you for exhilaration. Being in harmony with the Maruts who perform sacred prayer, and being of one accord with the Rudras, drink your fill and pour it down [upon us]. gavāśiram | manthinam | indra | śukram | piba | somam | rarimā | te | madāya | brahmakṛtā | mārutena | guṇena | sajoṣāḥ | rudraiḥ | tṛpat | ā | vṛṣasva || 2 ||

O Indra, drink this Soma which is mixed with milk— blent with the milk of cows— and which is prepared as a mixture; moreover, drink this Soma which is "manthin" (mixed with a mash), "śukra" (pure or fresh), or otherwise present in the Śukra and Manthin cups, existing thus throughout the three pressings.
We offer that Soma for your exhilaration, for your joy;
by means of the Māruta—
the host of the Maruts.
And he is the maker of the *brahman*.
He is called the "maker of the *brahman*" because he performs the *brahman*-hymn.

Being in harmony (*sajoṣaḥ*) with the host of Maruts who perform the Indra-hymn, and with the Rudras—the eleven Rudras—you, being satisfied (*tṛpat*) by the drinking of Soma, pour down [your bounty] (*āvṛṣasva*).
O Siddha, hold this very one within your belly on all sides.

*gavāśiram*: from the root *śrī* (to mix) with the prefix *ā*, followed by the suffix *kvip*; the substitution of *āśīr* for the root occurs according to rules such as "apastṛdhethāmānucuḥ" and others, which apply to irregular forms (*nipātana*). In the *bahuvrīhi* compound, the accent remains on the original form of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*).
"Drink! (pibā). 5.
In the *saṃhitā*, there is a long vowel [vowel lengthening] according to the rule "acyo'tastiṅaḥ.

1. [The suffix] *ṇic* is applied in the sense of the causal agent (*hetumat*). 2. [Variants: kha, ga, ca, ja, ṇa, ta, na, bha, sa read "brahmakṛtā. 3. [Variants: kha, ga, ca, ja, ṇa, ta, na, bha, sa read "ṛṇāteḥ. 4. [The substitution of] *śir* for *la*. 5. [Variants: kha, ga, ca, ja, ṇa, ta, na, bha, sa read "piba. (ka. 1–43)

*rarima*: This is the form of the root *rā* (to give) in the *liṭ* (perfect) tense used in a Vedic (*chāndasa*) sense; because it does not belong to the same syntactical unit (*asamānavākyatva*), there is an absence of the *nighāta* (anudātta accent). Since the augment (*āgama*) is anudātta according to the rule "āgamā anudāttāḥ," the accent of the suffix does not apply here. *nṛpat*: from the root *tṛp* (to satisfy), belonging to the *tudādi* class. Because the teaching regarding augments is not universally obligatory (*anityatva*), the *num* augment is absent. *vṛṣasva*: from the root *vṛṣu* (to sprinkle/secrete); the suffix *śa* is applied by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
O Indra, those Maruts who increased your breath, your power, and your might— at the midday libation, O wielder of the thunderbolt, drink with the Rudras in your company, O fair-cheeked one.

O Indra, those Maruts who increased your vigor and your strength while praising your power—at the midday libation, O wielder of the thunderbolt, drink with the Rudras, you who are accompanied by your host and possess beautiful jaws. 3.

O Indra, those Maruts who increased your *śuṣma*—your energy that withers enemies—and those Maruts who increased your *taviṣī*—your strength—by acting as allies in battle; those Maruts, while praising you (*arcantaḥ*), increased your *ojas*—your prowess in combat. O Vajrahasta, whose hand is joined with the thunderbolt, O Suśipra, whose jaws (or nostrils) are beautiful;
thus says Yāska: "The word *śiprā* means jaws or nostrils."
O Indra, together with the Rudras—
the Maruts are called Rudras because they cause their enemies to weep—
being accompanied by that host, drink the Soma at the midday libation.
They caused to increase; from the root *vṛṣu* in the sense of "increasing," with the causative meaning (*ṇyartha*) inherent within it.
Because of its connection with the *yadvṛtta*, there is no suppression (*anighāta*).
In the *mādhyaṃdina* [recension],
it is so because of its being an *utsādi*.
Because it ends in a suffix marked with *j*, the first syllable is udātta.
O inspired singer, those Maruts were indeed his sweet and powerful host, Indra's own;
by them, when impelled, he found the vital spot of Vṛtra, who, though rushing on, considered himself invulnerable.

They have indeed come; they have now proclaimed his honeyed [draught]. The Maruts, who were the bold host of Indra—by them, when impelled, he found the vital spot of Vṛtra, even though he deemed himself invulnerable. 4.
Those Maruts who were the *śardhaḥ*—the strength—of Indra, they indeed are these very Maruts of him;
the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative.
[They accompany] this Indra, who is full of sweetness (*madhumat*).
There, urging him on quickly with words full of sweetness, saying, "We shall be your companions;
you must go to battle," Indra—impelled by those Maruts who were his allies in war—discovered the vital spot (*marman*) of Vṛtra, the Asura.

[Vṛtra was] one whose vital spots were unknown (*amarmanaḥ*), and thus he was one who thought, "No one can kill me" while he was overestimating himself. Indra found that very place where, if a blow were struck, he would die.
In *vivipre*:
from the root *vi-pṛ* in the sense of "scattering," the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*) in the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
Regarding *ircaḥ*, there is the substitution of *iy* for *ri* according to the rule *iryo re*.
Nighāta (elision). Āsan: this is the form of the root *as* (meaning "to be") in the *laṅ* (imperfect) tense.
The absence of elision (anighātābhāva) results from its occurrence after a word ending in *vṛt*. *Viveda* is the form of the root *vid* (meaning "to know") in the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
*Litsvaraḥ* [is derived from] *marma*. [The word *marman* is formed] from the root *mṛḍ*, meaning "to abandon life," with the suffix *manin* according to the Bāṇādi group.
The sound of a louse.

1. *ca-ja-ṇa-bha* [are used] in the Vedic language (*chandasi*). 2. In *kha-ga-gha-ca-ja-ṇa-pa-pha-bha-sa*, the phrase "the dryer of enemies" (*śatrūṇāṃ śoṣakaṃ*) does not exist. 3. In *kha-ga-gha-ca-ja-ṇa-pha-bha*, [the text reads] "they increased" (*avardhan*), [meaning] they caused to increase (*avardhayan*). 4. In *ca-pha*, [there is] "various power" (*vividhasāmarthyam*). 5. In *sa*, "hands joined with the vajra" (*vajrayukto hastau*). 6. In *ca*, "impelling toward" (*abhiprerayan*). 7. In *pha*, "possessing knowledge" (*jñānavān*).
O Indra, like a man, enjoying everything, drink the Soma for eternal heroic power.
O Lord of tawny horses (*haryaśva*), turn hither through our sacrifices; with the swift ones, you cause the flood of waters to flow forth.

Like Manu, O Indra, enjoying it all, drink the Soma for eternal heroic power. Do thou turn hither, O Lord of the Bay Steeds, through our sacrifices; with the swift-moving [Maruts], thou hast set the waters and the flood flowing. 5.

O Indra! Enjoying—that is, partaking of—the *savana*, the sacrifice, like that of Manu, you should drink this Soma for the sake of eternal, perpetual heroism characterized by the subjugation of enemies. O Haryashva, you who are endowed with green-colored horses! Being such as you are, turn toward us through these great sacrifices worthy of worship; come hither.

Furthermore, together with the *saraṇyu*s— those who desire to hear the mantras recited in unison— or alternatively, together with the *saraṇyu*s, the Maruts who are subject to death, you cause the waters— the waters situated in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) and the flood (*arṇas*) of terrestrial waters—
to flow forth. Or rather, "the waters" (*apaḥ*) is a word in the ablative case.
From the intermediate space, from the sky, cause the waters to flow forth.
*vavṛtsva* [is derived from] the root *vṛt* in the sense of "turning. By way of transposition (*vyatyaya*), there is the elision (*ślu*) of the *śap* suffix.
The form is *loṭ*. [In the word] *saraṇyubhiḥ*, the root *raṇ* has the meaning of "sound."
Kṛpī:
Those whose sounds are similar in battle are *saraṇa* mantras;
they desire those.
The suffix *kyac* is applied after a verbal root ending in *su*. Alternatively, it is the suffix *kyat*, as in the case of the root *sṛ* meaning "to go."
The suffix *anyuc* is applied by the rule *'myuvacibhyāṃ nyujāgṛñkacaḥ'* (Uṇādi Sūtra 3.361). The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs by the rule *'rapābhyām'* (Pāṇini Sūtra 8.4.1).
Due to its *cit*-designation, the word is udātta-accented on the first syllable.
*Āpaḥ*. [Derived from] the root *āp* in the sense of "pervasion" (*vyāptau*).
According to the rule "from *āp* comes *krip* and the vowel is shortened," the suffix *krip* is applied and the root vowel is shortened.
In the word *sārvakācaḥ*, the case ending (*vibhakti*) is udātta.
[The root] *mis* [is derived from] *ṛṣi*.
