O Indra, those Maruts whom you assigned to the Soma, who strengthened you and became your host—with them, being well-pleased and longing for it, drink this Soma with the tongue of Agni, O Indra. 9. yān | ā | abhajaḥ | marutaḥ | indra | some | ye | tvām | avardhan | abhavan | gaṇaḥ | taiḥ | tebhiḥ | etam | sa'joṣāḥ | vāvaśānaḥ | agreḥ | piba | jihvayā | somam | indra || 9 ||

O Indra, those Maruts whom you, O Soma-drinker, have made sharers in the drinking of Soma— those Maruts who strengthened you in battle by inspiring you with enthusiasm, and those Maruts who became your host, meaning they became your allies—

being in harmony with (*sajoṣāḥ*) and united with such Maruts as these, and desiring (*vāvaśānaḥ*) this pressed Soma, drink it, O Indra, with the tongue in the form of the flame of the Āhavanīya fire, which is the locus for the oblation of Agni.
*abhajaḥ*:
this is the form of the root *bhaj* (meaning "to serve") in the *laṅ* tense;
its lack of *nighāta* (unaccented status) is due to its connection with *yad-vṛtta*.

*avardhana*: This is the form of the root *vṛdh* in the sense of "to increase" (*vardhane*) when conjugated with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), in the imperfect tense (*laṅ*). Because of the rule "in Vedic usage [the suffixes] are optionally [treated as either sārvadhātuka or ārdhadhātuka]," the *jhi* ending is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka*; consequently, by the rule "the *ṇi* is elided before an *aniṭ* [suffix]," there is the elision of the *ṇi*.
Here too, there is no loss of accent (*anighāta*) because of the connection [of the words]. It did not exist; there is no loss of accent due to the difference in sentences (*vākyabheda*).
*vāvaśānaḥ*:
this is the form of the root *vaś* (meaning "to desire") in the *yaṅluk* (intensive without *yaṅ*) with the suffix *cānaś*;
it bears the *citsvara* accent.
Drink. [The root] *pā* [is used] in the sense of "drinking. [The suffix receives] the *nighāta* (elision of accent).

O Indra, drink by your own power of the pressed juice; or, O worshipful one, drink with the tongue of Agni. O Śakra, enjoy the offering extended from the hand of the Adhvaryu, or the sacrifice and oblation from the Hotṛ. 10. O Indra, drink! By your own inherent power (*svadhayā*), indeed, [drink] of the pressed [juice]. Or, O worshipful one (*yajatra*), drink with the tongue of Agni. Or, O Śakra, [enjoy] what is offered from the hand of the Adhvaryu, or the sacrifice and the oblation from the Hotṛ. 10.

2. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ṅa, Bha, and Sa, it is ‘vā’; in Ca and Pha, it is ‘ete’. 3.

O Indra, by your *svadhā*—that is, by your own power (*svadhā*) through which you sustain yourself—you, O worshipful (*yajatra*) Indra, drink the pressed juice (*sutasya suta*), that which has been poured out or offered. O Indra, with the tongue of Agni in the form of its flame, drink the Soma that has been offered. O capable (*śakra*) Indra, drink the Soma extended from the hand of the *adhvaryu*, that which is given without limit. Or else, enjoy (*juṣasva*) the sacrifice of the *hotṛ*, the portion of the oblation accompanied by the *vaṣaṭ* call. The sense is: in every way, come here and drink the Soma being offered by us. [Grammatical notes: *Piba*: Because the vocative is treated as non-existent (*avidyamānavat*), there is no *anudātta* accent on the first syllable of the word-group. *Adhvaryoḥ*: From the root *dhvar* with the suffix *kyac* (meaning "one who desires the sacrifice," *adhvaram kāmayate*). There is elision of the visible *k* in *kyadhvara*. The accent is that of the suffix; then follows the accent of the single substitute (*ekādeśasvara*). *Prayatnam*: From the root *yam* meaning "to cease" (*uparame*), used in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*) with the *niṣṭhā* suffix. *Śaka*: From the root *śak* meaning "to be able. The suffix *rak* is added according to the rule beginning with *sphāyitantri*. *Hastāt*: The suffix *tan* is added according to the rule beginning with *asihasi*. It has the *nisvara* (low) accent. *Hotuḥ*: From the root *hu* with the suffix *tan* in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlika*). It has the *nisvara* accent. *Juṣasva*: From the root *jup* meaning "pleasure" and "service" (*prītisevanayoḥ*). This is the form in the imperative (*loṭ*). It has the *nighāta* accent.

The seventh hymn, consisting of eleven verses beginning with "imām pu," is in the Triṣṭubh meter and is dedicated to Indra. Regarding this, the Anukramaṇikā states: "Ghora saw this [hymn] against diseases; it is heard that he was told, 'May Śamyā not burn you. The seer of the tenth verse is Ghora Āṅgirasa.
For the learned, it is the *vidhāmitra*.
In the Agniṣṭoma, at the midday pressing (*mādhyandinasavana*), during the recitation of the Acchāvāka, the hymn "imām pūrvyām" is used, excluding the tenth verse.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "In all cases, one should omit the penultimate verse of 'imām piba'. (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.16).
In the Mādhyandina-savana of both the Pṛṣṭhya and Abhiplava ṣaḍahas, in the Acchāvāka-śastra, there are three *saṃpāta* hymns in place of the *ahīna-sūkta* extended from the Caturviṃśa day.
Among these, this first hymn is recited with the exception of the introductory verse (*upapra*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "‘imām piba’, ‘cchanti tvā’" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.5).

Establish this our offering for the sake of gain, O you who are ever and ever being strengthened by your aids! At every libation you have grown great through your increases; you have become renowned through your mighty deeds. imām | ūm iti | su | ṣaḍbhṛtim | sātaye | dhāḥ | śaśvat-śaśvat | ūtibhiḥ | yārdamānaḥ | sute-sute | vavṛdhe | vardhanebhiḥ | yaḥ | karmabhiḥ | mahadbhiḥ | suśrutaḥ | bhūta || 1 ||
Viśvāmitra praises Indra:
"O Indra, with your aids (*ūtibhiḥ*)— the Maruts, who protect and guard all beings."
By them, constantly, perpetually, and at all times, seeking union—that is, begging for association—you are *prabhṛti*:
you are preeminently maintained (*pra-śrīyate*) and supported for the sake of sacrifice.

"From the beginning, O Soma, or rather, O Indra, [as] the one who bestows gifts (*prabhṛtiḥ*); [grant] this Soma, or this praise, for our gain—that is, for the acquisition of wealth—[you] have well established it (*sudhāḥ*), meaning you have perfectly accomplished it. Likewise, that Indra has grown (*vāvṛdhe*) with the strengthening offerings such as Soma and others at every pressing of the Soma when it is pressed. That Indra, who has become well-known in the world through great deeds characterized by the slaying of Asuras, the cleaving of clouds, and so forth—he is Indra; thus the connection is with what precedes. Grammatical notes: * *prabhṛtim*: By the rule "tādau ca niti kyatau," the root accent remains. * *dhāḥ*: A form of the root *dhā* (to place) in the Vedic *luṅ* tense; it takes the *nighāta* (anudātta) accent. * *śaśvacchaśvat*: Reduplication according to the rule "nityavīpsayoḥ. * *yādamānaḥ*: From the root *duyācṛ* (to beg); a form in the *śānac* suffix. The change of *c* to *d* is Vedic. * *vāvṛdhe*: From the root *vṛdh* (to grow) in the *liṭ* tense; the lengthening of the reduplicated syllable is due to its inclusion in the *tujādi* group. The *nighāta* accent applies. * *vardhanebhiḥ*: From *vardhana* with the suffix *lyuṭ* (added after roots like *nandi*); the accent is on the *lit* suffix. * *suśrutaḥ*: From the root *śru* (to hear) with the *kta* suffix in the passive sense; the accent is on the *gati* (preverb) because it immediately precedes. * *bhūta*: A form of the root *bhū* (to be) in the *luṅ* tense.
At the midday pressing, this verse, "For Indra the Soma juices from of old," serves as the *prasthitayājyā* for the *acchāvāka*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "'For Indra the Soma juices from of old, knowing [them], [the priest] who does not weary' (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.5)."
For Indra, the Soma juices have been known since ancient times, by which he became the far-reaching R̥bhu with bull-like joints.
O Indra, seize these as they are being offered; drink of the bull-strong juice shaken by the bull-strong ones.

For Indra, the Soma juices have been known from of old, by which he became the skillful one with strong-jointed limbs and vast extent. O Indra, take well these being offered; drink of the bullish juice shaken by the strong ones. 2.
O Indra! For you, Indra, the Soma juices have been offered by us from time immemorial, known [as such] through previous days.
"Vṛṣaparvan":
one whose joints (parvāṇi)—the divisions of time—are the showers (varṣāḥ) of fruit; he is thus described. "Tṛpāṇaḥ": one who is satiated.

The meaning is that he is of the nature of time (*kālātmaka*). For this very reason, [the word] *vihāyāḥ* [is used]: because it is derived from the roots *vi*, *hā*, *as*, and *ṛ* with the suffix *yat*, *vihāyāḥ* means "the Great One" (*mahān*).
Such is Indra, by means of those offered Soma juices with which he exists as the radiant *Ṛbhu*.
O Indra, do thou well press these Soma juices being excellently presented in the form of mantras; do thou accept them.
Having accepted them, drink this Soma, which is shaken by the bull [or purified by the necks of bulls] and is the showerer (*vṛṣan*) of fruits such as heaven.
*pradiv-*; [the root] *div-* in the sense of playing and so forth;
[the suffix] *kip*.
The accusative case ending is applied by the rule *kālādhvanoratyantasaṃyoge*.
The word *div* denotes heaven (*divam*).
It bears the accent of the final member of a compound formed with a *kṛt* suffix.

*vidānāḥ*: [This is] the present middle participle (*śānac*) of the root *vid* in the sense of "to obtain," by means of a grammatical anomaly (*vyatyaya*). The elision (*luk*) of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*) occurs according to the rule "in the Veda (*chandas*), [the suffix is] frequently [elided]."
*Vihāyaḥ*:
[derived from] the root *ohāk* in the sense of "abandoning" (*tyāge*),
with the suffix *asun* according to the rule *vahilādhābhyaśchandasi*.

Because of the recurrence of the word "phin," the augment *yuk* is applied by the rule "āno yuk ciṇkṛtoḥ. By the rule "gatikārakayoḥ," the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member is maintained.

*gṛbhāya*: This is from the root *grah* in the sense of "taking up" (*upādāne*), in the imperative (*loṭ*) second person singular (*hi*). For the suffix *śnā*, there is the substitution of *śāyac* by the rule *chandasi śāyaj api*; and for the *bhū* [of the root], there is the change [to *bh*] by the rule *hyahrāṃ bheḥ*.
By the rule "ato heḥ," there is elision of the suffix *hi*;
[the verb] is subject to the *nighāta* (anudātta) accent.
At the midday pressing, the *yājyā* for the Acchāvāka is this verse: "Drink, grow strong...
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "'Drink, grow strong; [the soma] pressed ninefold' is the *yājyā*" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.16).

1. Or it is a praise (stuti) by name. 2. In the manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ja, ṇa, bha, the phrase "this praise" (imāṃ stutiṃ vā) is absent. 3. In kha, ga, ca, [the text] has *vavṛdhe*. 4. In ja, ṇa, there is a connection with what precedes; *u* is a filler (*pūraṇa*). 5. In kha, ga, ca, pha, bha, [the reading is] *ṛṣaṇāḥ*. 6. In kha, ga, ja, ṇa, ta, na, bha, sa, [it is] "or thus" (*iti vā*). 7. In ta, there is an insertion (*prakṣepeṇa*). 8. In kha, ga, ca, ja, ṇa, na, pha, bha, [it is] "of that which is pressed" (*abhiputasya*). 9. In ta, the word "and" (*ca*) is absent. Drink and grow strong through this pressed [juice], O Indra; these Soma juices are both the first ones and these [present ones].
Just as you drank the ancient Soma juices, O Indra, so drink now this newer one today, O Wondrous One.

Drink! Increase! Truly, O Indra, these pressed Soma juices are for you—the first ones as well as these. Just as you drank the ancient Somas, O Indra, so drink them today, O Praised One, as one who is newer [in merit]. 3.

O Indra, drink this Soma! Thereby increase; become nourished in body. For you—for your sake—these Somas, both the ancient ones of old and these new ones, are indeed pressed by the stones. O Indra, just as you drank the ancient Somas of old, even so today, being praiseworthy and therefore newer—that is, exceedingly fresh—you should drink these new Somas. Drink! Drink! [The form *pāhi* is the imperative (*loṭ*) of the root *pā*; the *śap* suffix is elided by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi," and it receives the *nighāta* accent. Increase! [The lack of *nighāta* on *vardhasva* is due to its following another verb-form. You drank! [The lack of *nighāta* on *apibaḥ* is according to the requirements of the context. Drink! [In the imperative *pāhi*, the *śap* is elided by "bahulaṃ chandasi" and it is accented with *nighāta*. Praiseworthy! [From the root *pan* meaning "to praise," the suffix *yat* is applied because it belongs to the *anyādi* group; it is acute-accented on the first syllable by the rule "yato 'nāvaḥ. Newer! [This is the form from the word *nava* with the suffix *īyasun*; it has the *nitsvara* accent.]
Great and measureless, bellowing in the enclosure, he possesses fierce and daring vigor.
Neither the heaven nor the earth can contain him when the Soma juices have exhilarated the Lord of the Bay Horses.

Great, impetuous, and overflowing with strength in the assembly, he wields fierce power and bold vigor. Neither the earth nor I can encompass him when the Soma juices have exhilarated the Lord of the Bay Steeds.

This Indra—who is great, possessed of exceeding power, *amatráḥ* (invincible) in *vṛjane* (battle, won by strength), the overcomer of enemies, and therefore *virapśī* (one who roars or is praised)—is one whose nature is to roar, calling out to his enemies for battle by clapping his arms; or rather, one whose various *rapaṇa* (utterances) consist of praise, meaning he is worthy of praise by all. Of such an Indra, the fierce, high-rising *śávas* (strength), the bold *ójas* (energy characterized by prowess), spreads everywhere. The vast earth (*pṛthivī*) does not contain him (*na vivyāca*); the word *aha* is used in the sense of "indeed," and *cana* in the sense of "even. Thus, even the sky does not contain him. When the Soma juices, consecrated with *svāhā*, exhilarated (*amandan*) Indra, the lord of bay horses, then heaven and earth were unable to contain him. Grammatical notes: *Amatraḥ*: from the root *am* (to go, etc.); the suffix *atran* is added by the rule *aminakṣiyaji*, etc.; it has the *nitsvara* accent. *Virapśī*: from *rap* or *lap* (to speak clearly); the suffix *śa* is *auṇādika*. Those who roar variously (*virapsāḥ*) are the singers of praise. He possesses them, hence the suffix *ini*. Alternatively, *virapśam* is the various roaring itself; he possesses that, hence the suffix *in*. It has the *prāyasvara* accent. *Patyate*: the suffix *yak* is used for the agent by transposition (*vyatyaya*). It has the *nighāta* accent. *Dhṛṣṇu*: from *dhṛṣ* (boldness); the suffix *ku* is added by the rule *trasigṛdhidhṛṣipeḥ*; the change to *ṇ* occurs by the rule *rabhyām*. It has the accent of the suffix. *Vivyāca*: from the root *vyac* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*), third person singular (*ṇal*). There is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the reduplication by the rule *liṭyabhyāsasyobhayeṣām*. It has the *nighāta* accent. *Caneti*: this collection of particles is used in the sense of "and" (*cārthe*). It has the *udātta* accent on the final syllable. *Amandan*: the form of the root *mad* (to praise, etc. in the imperfect (*laṅ*). Due to its connection with *yat*, it does not have the *nighāta* accent.

1. Not for your sake. 2. Kha, ga, ca, ja, ṇa, ta, ma, bha, and sa read *somāḥ sutāsaḥ*; gha reads *somāsaḥ sutāsaḥ*; la reads *somāsaḥ sutāsaḥ*. 3. Na lacks the word *savaiḥ*; la and sa have *savaiḥ*.
Great and fierce, he has increased for heroic power; the bull has gathered himself through poetic wisdom.
Indra is glory; his cows bestow booty; his sacrificial gifts are born forth in abundance.

Great and fierce, he has grown for heroic power; the bull has exerted himself with poetic wisdom. Indra is splendor itself; his cows bestow strength, and his many sacrificial gifts are born forth. ||5||

Great in the act of battle, powerful, fierce, and terrifying to his enemies, Indra has grown (*vāvṛdhe*)—that is, he increases—for valor (*vīryāya*), for the performance of heroic deeds. He is the bull (*vṛṣabhaḥ*), the showerer of fruit; he is Bhaga, to be honored by all. That Indra, through *kāvyena*—the work of the seers (*kavi*), namely their hymns of praise—unites (*samācake*) with that hymn. From such an Indra, the "cows" (*gāvaḥ*)—those who give strength (*vājadāḥ*), providing food in the form of milk and the like—are born forth. Likewise, his many (*pūrvīḥ*) ancient cows are born as sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇāḥ*). Regarding the words: *vāvṛdhe*: This is a form of the root *vṛdh*. It takes the accent of the *Nighāta* (the unaccented enclitic). *vīryāya*: Derived from *vīra*, meaning "heroic power. The suffix *yat* is applied according to the rule *bhave chandasi*. Since the rule *yato ’nāvaḥ* is known to be non-universal (*anitya*) in the case of *vīra-vīryau*, the vowel is circumflex (*svarita*). *samācake*: A form of the root *kṛ* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*). The preceding word (*sam*) is unaccented according to the rule *gatir gatau*. *kāvyena*: The work of a seer (*kavi*) is *kāvyam*. The suffix *vyañ* is added because it belongs to the *brāhmaṇa*-class. Due to the presence of the augment *it*, there is *vṛddhi* of the penultimate vowel. It bears the accent of the *it*. *vājadāḥ*: From the root *dā* (to give), with the suffix *ka* according to the rule *āto ’nupasarge kaḥ*. *jāyante*: A form of the root *jan* (to be born) in the present tense (*laṭ*). *dakṣiṇāḥ*: From the root *dakṣ* (to increase), the suffix *inan* is added according to the rule *dudakṣabhyāminan*. When the rivers have gone forth like an impulse, as other waters flow toward the ocean like servants,
even from that Indra is more spacious than the seat, when the Soma, the pressed stalk, fills him full.
When the rivers have gone forth toward the ocean like Aryans under a leader, even from that place Indra is more spacious, when the Soma, the pressed stalk, fills him.

Just as rivers flow according to their source— *prasava* being that which is produced with intensity, namely desire (*kāma*)— when they proceed forth (*pra āyan*), moving far away toward the ocean, then the waters go to the great ocean like chariot-drivers (*radhya iva rathinaḥ*), proceeding for the sake of satisfaction.
In the same way, Indra is indeed more extensive— that is, vaster— than this very assembly hall, even than this intermediate space.
For when the small stalk of Soma, consisting of a creeper-fragment, pressed and purified, satisfies him— Indra—
just as small rivers and very little water satisfy the great ocean, so too does the Soma, though existing in a smaller portion, satisfy the more extensive Indra.
*Prasava*:
[The suffix] *ap* is applied to the root *sū* (to bring forth) in the sense of the object;
it takes the accent of the first member of a compound (*thāthādi-svara*).
*Āyan*: this is the form of the root *ayati* in the *laṅ* tense;
according to the rule *yathogāt*, it does not undergo *anighāta*.
It is as if [the word] *radhya* were present;
for these chariots belong to the chariot (*ratha*),
[the suffix] *yat* being applied by the rule "after *ratha*, *yat*."
By the rule "supāṃ suluk," there is the substitution of *ḍā* for the case-ending (*sup*). It has an udātta accent.
By the rule "ivena vibhaktyalopaḥ," there is no elision of the case-ending, and the first member retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*).
They went.
This is the form of the root *gam* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
[The rule applies: "In place of *gam*, *han*, etc. (Pāṇini 6.4.98).

1. [The augment] *iṭ* is added after the roots *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *bha*. 2. [The reading] "of this" (*asya*) does not exist in the manuscripts *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *na*, *pa*, *pha*, *bha*, and *sa*. 3. [The root] *vṛdh* increases in the manuscript *ja* and *ṇa*. 4. [The rule applies] to that which is preceded by *l*. 5. *t* and *s* are for the purpose of indicating the breath (aspirated sound). 6. [The word] *purutaraḥ* exists in the manuscripts *pa* and *bha*. 7. [The word] *latākhaṇḍajaḥ* exists in the manuscripts *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *pa*, *pha*, and *bha*. 8. [The rule applies] to the root *sū* in the manuscripts *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, and *ṇa*. 9. [The form] *eti* occurs in the *laṅ* tense in the manuscript *pha*. 10. [The term] *suluk* does not exist in the manuscripts *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, and *sa*. 11. [The term] *nisvaraḥ* exists in the manuscripts *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *na*, and *bha*. 12. [The elision] of the case-ending (*vibhaktilopa*) occurs in the manuscripts *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *sa*. 13. [The rule applies] to the roots *gam*, *han*, and *jan* in the manuscript *la*.

By these and other rules, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*). There is *nighāta* (elision of accent). In *varīyān*: from the word *uras*, with the suffix *īyasun*, the substitution of *vara-* occurs by the rule "priyasthira... etc.; it is accented on the first syllable due to the *niṣ* suffix. In *pṛṇati*: from the root *pṛṇ* meaning "to please," belonging to the *tudādi* class; there is no *nighāta* because it follows the *yathāgata* (original) accent. In *dugdhaḥ*: from the root *duh*, the suffix *ka* is added; there is a prohibition of the *it* augment by the rule "ekācaḥ"; the *ha* becomes *gha* by the rule "dāderdhātorghaḥ"; and [the *gha*] becomes *dha* by the rule "jhapastathordho'dhaḥ"; it bears the accent of the suffix.
Like rivers flowing toward the ocean, they bring the well-pressed Soma for Indra;
with their hands, they milk the stalk with pressing-stones and purify the honey-sweet juice in streams through the filters.
The rivers, like the ocean, moving along while bringing well-pressed Soma for Indra, milk the stalk with their hands; they purify the sweetness with a stream through the filters. 7.
The waters flow toward him in the form of rivers and so forth, together with the ocean; thus he is called *samudra*.

Being addressed by him, the rivers (*sindhu*), seeking union with him, surround him. In the same way, the "elephants"—the priests and others who possess hands—bringing the well-pressed Soma for you, O Indra, and preparing it, milk the stalk, that is, they press the creeper-stalk.
Likewise, those Adhvaryus and others purify—that is, cleanse—the sweet Soma juices with the flowing streams of essence through the *pavitra* strainers;
they are called *bharitras* because their arms bear the ritual materials for the performance of the rites.
With those [arms], they purify the Soma juices endowed with sweetness.

*Samudra*: From the root *dravati* preceded by *sam-ut*, the suffix *ḍa* is applied according to the rule “it is also seen in other cases as well. Due to the indicatory letter *ḍ*, there is elision [of the penultimate vowel].
Or alternatively:
from the root *und* in the sense of "moistening," with the suffix *rak* added to the prefix *sam-* according to the rule beginning with *sphāyi-tañci*.
Due to the presence of the suffix *kit*, there is the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*).
In both cases, the accent belongs to the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
When the single substitution (*ekādeśa*) with the case-ending (*sup*) has been made, that single substitute is itself accented acute (*udātta*).
*yādamānāḥ* [is derived from] the root *duyācṛ* in the sense of "begging";
[the suffix] *śānac* [is applied].

By transposition, the letter *d* replaces the letter *c*. In the accentuation of the *śānac* suffix, which is a *lasārvadhātuka*, the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*) prevails. [Thus: *duhanti*.
The form [‘duhanti’] is the present indicative (*laṭ*) of the root *duh* in the sense of “filling.
Regarding *bharitraiḥ*: from the root *ḍubhṛñ* in the sense of “supporting” and “nourishing,” the suffix *itran* is applied according to the rule *aśitrādibhya itrotrau*.
The accent is that of the suffix (pratyayasvara). They purify; this is the form of the root *pūṣ* in the sense of "purifying" (*pavane*) in the present tense (*laṭ*).
Like bellies with hearts, the soma-holding vessels have widely contained all the many foods;
when Indra had consumed the first foods and slain Vṛtra, he chose the soma.
Like lakes are his flanks; he has encompassed all things, the many foods, as the vessels of Soma. When Indra, having slain Vṛtra, first attained [his power], he chose the Soma. ||8||
The bellies (*vakṣayaḥ*) of Indra are his stomachs (*udarāṇi*), which are the repositories of Soma (*somadhānāḥ*); they are called "Soma-repositories" because Soma is deposited within them.
Regarding this, there is an illustration:
"like hearts" (*hṛdā iva*).
Just as reservoirs of water are formed by the heart, so it is here:

this Indra has fully pervaded—that is, he has completely encompassed—the three libations, the many offerings. Since Indra has specifically devoured—that is, eaten—the first, that is, the earliest foods such as Soma and other edibles, therefore Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, [drinks] the Soma at the midday libation for the sake of the gods.
1. [The words] *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *pha*, and *abhiṣuta*.
2. [The words] *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, and *adhvaryu* etc. 3. [The words] *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *pha*, and *pāvana*.
4. With their arms—[those beginning with] *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *pa*, *pha*, *bha*, and *ra*—they purify, that is, cleanse, the *somas* endowed with the sweetness of honey (*madhu*).
5. [The syllables] *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *pha*, and *la* do not exist in the "midday pressing" (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*).

*avṛṇīta samabhajan* (they chose together). *kukṣayaḥ*: [The root] *kup* is used in the sense of "to be agitated. According to Uṇādi Sūtra 3.435 (*lupi-kudi-śupi-bhyaḥ ksiḥ*), the suffix *ksi* is applied. That which is agitated (*kupyati*) is the *kukṣi*. It bears the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). *somadhānāḥ*: [From the root] *dhā* with the suffix *nyuṭ* in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*). It bears the accent of the *liṭ*-suffix (*litsvara*). *vidhyāca*: This is the form of the root *vyac* in the *liṭ* tense. *annā*: [From the root] *ad* in the sense of "eating" (*ada bhakṣaṇe*). They ate the two-fold food (*dvayannam*). *āśa*: [From the root] *aś* in the sense of "eating" (*aśa bhojane*). This is the form of the root in the *liṭ* tense with the suffix *ṇal* for the dual. By the rule *ana ādeḥ*, there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). Due to its connection with *yat* (the relative pronoun), it does not lose its accent (*anighāta*). It bears the accent of the *liṭ*-suffix (*litsvara*). *vṛtram*: There is a prohibition of the *ṣatva* substitution by the rule *na lokāvyaya* (Pāṇini 2.3.69). *jaghanvān*: This is the form of the root *han* with the suffix *ksnu* in the absence of *iṭ*. It bears the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). *avṛṇīta*: This is the form of the root *vṛṅ* in the sense of "choosing" (*saṃbhaktau*) in the *laṅ* tense.
Bring it here; let no one conceal this, for you are the distributor of treasures among the riches.
O Indra, whatever magnificent gift is yours, bestow that upon us and grant it to us.
O Maghavan, possessor of wealth, drinker of the dregs, you who have drunk the Soma whose strength has departed— O Indra, [grant us a share] of that which contains all desirable things.
That which has a selection (*varaṇa*) by all (*viśvaiḥ*), meaning by everyone, due to its being worthy of being honored;
*bhūraiḥ* means "by many"; *bhūri* means "much"; *rāyaḥ* means "wealth" (*dhana*).
The genitive case is used here in the sense of the accusative.
Bestow upon us; grant to us.
Furthermore, for our living—for the sake of our life—grant us a hundred autumns, that is, years.
O Śiprin, you of the beautiful jaws, O Indra, [grant] to us [a life] lasting forever.
"Śaśvat" is a name for "many.
Grant many heroic sons.
*jīvase*: This is the *se* suffix used in the sense of the infinitive (*tumun*) for the root *jīv*, meaning "to live" or "to sustain life. It carries the accent of the suffix.

Śaśvataḥ. From the root *duośvi*, meaning "to move" or "to increase," the form is established as beginning with *śaśvat* by means of the addition of the suffix *ati* according to the rule "saṃśraddehan" and so forth.

We invoke for our welfare the bountiful Indra, the most heroic in this battle for the acquisition of booty; the one who hears us, the fierce one for our protection in conflicts, the slayer of Vṛtras, the winner of riches. 11. We invoke... for our welfare... the bountiful... Indra... in this... battle... the most heroic... in the acquisition of booty... the one who hears... the fierce one... for our protection... in conflicts... the slayer... of Vṛtras... the winner... of riches. 11.
"Śunaṃ huvema" has been explained.

The eighth hymn, consisting of eleven verses beginning with "vātrahatyāya," has the eleventh verse as an *anuṣṭubh* while the remaining verses are *gāyatrīs*. Thus it is stated in the index: "vātrahatyāya; [it is] in the *gāyatrī* meter, with the final verse being an *anuṣṭubh*."
In the first *paryāya* of the *atirātra*, the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin* should recite the hymn beginning with "For the slaying of Vṛtra" (*vātrahatyāya*), omitting the final verse.
Thus it is stated in the Sūtra: "One should exclude the last verses of 'For the slaying of Vṛtra'" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 6.4).
This hymn, omitting the final verse, is also included in the *gāyatrī-cāśīti* of the *mahāvrata*.
It is stated in the Pañcamāraṇyaka: "He recites the last [verse] with the words, 'For the slaying of Vṛtra, for strength' (Ai. Ā. 5.2.5)."
For the slaying of Vṛtra, for strength, and for victory in battle—O Indra, we turn you hither. 1. For the slaying of Vṛtra; for strength; and for victory in battle; O Indra, we turn you hither. 1.
Viśvāmitra praises:

O Indra, for the sake of *vātrahatyā*—that is, for the power (*śavas*) resulting from the slaying of Vṛtra—and also for *pṛtanāṣāhāya*, the overcoming of the enemy's armies, we cause you to turn toward us from all sides; we set you in motion.
For the sake of the slaying of Vṛtra; in the sense of "the act of the slayer of Vṛtra," the suffix *pyañ* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.1.124 (*brāhmaṇādibhyaś ca*),
and the substitution of *t* for *n* occurs according to Pāṇini 7.3.32 (*hanasta ac-ṇaloḥ*).
The word *jīra* is udātta by virtue of the rule *jīrādīnām udāttaḥ*.
[In the compound] *pṛtanāṣāhāya*,
the suffix *yat* is applied according to the rule *śakisahoś ca* after the root *sah* (meaning "to endure") in its causative form (*ṣāhayati*).
In the *Saṃhitā*, the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 8.3.109: *saheḥ pṛtanābhyāṃ ca*.
The lengthening of the vowel is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
[The form is] *vartayāmasi*.
From the root *vṛt* in the sense of "turning," with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the suffix *mas* is replaced by *masi* according to the rule *idanto masiḥ*;
[this form] receives the *nighāta* accent.
1. O Viśvavāra, for you who possess all colors, may there be abundant and manifold riches for us.
2. *Ja* and *ṇa*: explained as before; *la*: "We invoke for well-being"—this has been explained.
3. *Ga*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *sa*: the hymn of supreme strength (*uttamavājasūkta*).
4. [The variants] kha-ga-ca-ja-ṇa-ta-na-bha-sa read "tathā ca sūtritam nāsti" (and thus it is not stated in the Sūtra).

5. [The variants] kha-ga-ca-ja-ṇa-na-bha read: "pṛtanāsāhāya | arvācīnaṃ su te mana uta cakṣuḥ śatakrato | indra kṛṇvantu vāghataḥ || 2 ||" Arvācīnam | su | te | manaḥ | uta | cakṣuḥ | śatakrato | indra | kṛṇvantu | vāghataḥ || 2 || O Indra, O Lord of a hundred powers, may the priests bring thy mind and thy eye hitherward.

O *śatakrato* (O you of a hundred powers)! He who possesses a hundred *ṛtus* (ritual acts) is *śatakratu*. O *indra*, *vāghataḥ*—those who carry the yoke of the sacrifice are called *vāghatas*, meaning the singers (*stotāraḥ*). May they make your *su-manas*—your auspicious mind, which is excellent through the accomplishment of the fruits desired by us—*arvācīna*, that is, directed toward us; may they turn it so. And furthermore (*uta*), may they direct your *cakṣus*—your vision—toward us, that is, may they cast upon us a glance of grace. Regarding *arvācīnam*: the suffix *khap* is applied according to the rule *vibhāṣāñcaredikṣiāyām*; for *kha*, there is the substitution of *in*. Regarding *cakṣus*: the suffix *usi* is applied according to the rule *cakṣeḥ śiśca*; because of the presence of *śit*, there is no substitution of *khyā*. Due to the continued application of the term *nit*, it is *ādyudātta* (accented on the first syllable). Regarding *kṛṇvantu*: this is the form of the root *kṛvi* (meaning "to injure" or "to do") in the imperative (*loṭ*). Because the vocative (*āmantrita*) is treated as non-existent (*avidyamānavat*), it does not lose its accent due to being at the beginning of a *pāda*; rather, it retains the accent of the suffix. Regarding *vāghataḥ*: from the root *vaha* (meaning "to convey"), the suffix *ati* is applied according to the rule *saṃśradhet* etc.; thus, there is *vṛddhi* of the penultimate vowel, and the change of *ha* to *dha*. It retains the accent of the suffix.

We invoke all your names, O Śatakratu, with all our songs—O Indra, you who overcome the assailant. (3) We invoke all your names, O Śatakratu, with all our songs—O Indra, you who overcome the assailant. (3)
O Indra, O performer of a hundred sacrifices, [be] for the overcoming of those who oppose us.
*Mati* means pride or arrogance;
those whose pride extends everywhere are "abhimātayas," the enemies.
Enduring them is indeed what must be endured.

When that battle has arrived for us, we implore those names of yours—such as Śakra, Vajrahasta, and others—or rather, the powers characterized by those names, with all our songs, that is, with all words consisting of praise. We entreat you.
*īmahe*. The root *ī*, meaning "to shine" and so forth,
takes the *ātmanepada* when used with the suffix *dhyamayi*.
Because it belongs to the *adādi* class, there is elision of the *śap* suffix;
[the verb] is subject to the *nighāta* accent.

With a hundred powers of the one praised by many, we magnify Indra, the sustainer of the people. 4. Of the one praised by many; with the powers; with a hundred; we magnify; of Indra; the sustainer of the people. 4.

Of that Indra— who is much-praised (*puruṣṭuta*), who is lauded by many (*purubhiḥ*) numerous worshippers, who is endowed with a hundred (*śatena*) immeasurable powers (*dhāmabhiḥ*) or splendors (*tejobhiḥ*), and who is the sustainer (*carṣaṇīdhṛtaḥ*) of men (*carṣaṇīnām*)— that is, the supporter of those who perform rites among humanity by accomplishing their desired fruits;
or alternatively, *carṣaṇi* refers to strength (*balam*), as all things are drawn forth (*ākṛpanti*) by it.
We magnify you, the bearer of that; we magnify, that is, we offer praise.
In *puruṣṭuta*,
[the root] *pṛñ* means "to praise"; the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).
The vowel *thā* and so forth;
in the *saṃhitā*, by the rule "in the Veda, [the suffix] *parasmaipada* is used for the roots *stu* and *stu*" (Pāṇini 7.1.41),
it becomes *mahayāmasi*.
In the form *mahāpūjāyām*, the suffix *mas* ending in *i* is used in the imperative (*loṭ*),
and there is a *nighāta* (elision of accent).

1. ca-na-pha: "the view of favoring us. 2. kha-ga-ca-ja-ṇa-na-bha-sa: the reading "the substitution of *khasya*" does not exist. 3. la-sa: "accented on the first syllable" (*ādyudātta*). 4. ṇa-la-sa: "by way of non-existence. 5. kha-ga-ca-ja-ṇa-na-pha: "assistance" (*sāhyam*). 6. kha-ga-ca-ja-ṇa-pa-pha-ma: "the names of Śakra and others. 7. ta: "he draws" (*ākṛṣati*). 8. na-la-sa: the reading "we honor" (*mahayāmaḥ*) does not exist.

*Karṣaṇīya*: from the root *kṛṣ* in the sense of "drawing" (*ākarṣaṇe*). By the rule *kṛperādeśca:* (Uṇādi Sūtra 2.261), the suffix *ani* is applied; the letter *k* is replaced by *c*. Alternatively, from the root *kṛp* in the sense of "scratching" (*vilekhane*). Those who draw are called *karṣaṇas*, i.e., humans. [The word *ghṛ* means] "to hold. [The suffix] *chip* is applied. The accent falls on the final syllable of the compound (*kṛduttarapadasvara*).
I invoke Indra, who is invoked by many, for the slaying of Vṛtra and for the winning of booty in battles. || 5 ||
I invoke Indra, the much-invoked, for the slaying of Vṛtra and for the winning of booty in battles. 5.

O Indra, for the sake of slaying Vṛtra—the demon named Vṛtra—in battles, and for the winning of booty characterized by food, I, Viśvāmitra, call upon you, the powerful Indra who is invoked by many, for the purpose of drinking Soma. [Regarding the term] "for Vṛtra":
since it is a goal of action, it takes the dative case according to the rule "the mention of an action must be made [to include its object]."
*hantave*: the suffix *taven* is used in the sense of the infinitive (*tumun*);
it is unaccented (*nisvara*).
*bruve*:
This is the form of the verb *brūñ* (meaning "to speak clearly") in the first person singular of the present tense (*laṭ*), with the augment *iṭ*. There is elision of the accent (*nighāta*).
For the winning of booty (*vājasātaye*). *Sāti* means winning. The winning of booty is *vājasāti*.
In compounds such as *dāsībhāra*, the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada*) prevails.
O Śatakratu, we implore you, the victorious in battles, Indra, for the slaying of Vṛtra. 6.
In the contests for booty, be victorious; we implore you, O Śatakratu, Indra, for the slaying of Vṛtra. 6.

O Indra, O performer of a hundred sacrifices, be victorious in battles; be the overcomer of enemies. We entreat you for the slaying of Vṛtra, that you may kill Vṛtra. Regarding *sāsahivaḥ*: the suffix *kip* is prescribed by the rule “*kikinau vaktavyau*” after roots ending in *yaṅ*, such as *sah*, *vah*, and *lap*. Its accent is acute (*udātta*). Regarding *vṛtrāya*: this is the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) of the action. Regarding *hantave*: the suffix *taven* is used in the sense of the infinitive (*tumun*).
O Indra, be victorious in battles, in the contest for the prize, among those who overcome the foe, and in the struggle for glory; conquer our adversaries! 7.
In battles, in the contest for troops, in the overcoming of armies, and in the pursuit of fame—O Indra, be victorious over those who plot against us. 7.

O Indra, subdue those who are arrogant regarding wealth that is to be won in battles while it is shining forth; those who are arrogant in the *pṛtanājya*—that is, in the battle (*saṃgrāma*) which is the place of going (*gamana*) to the birth (*ajana*) of armies (*pṛtanā*); and those who are arrogant in the *pṛtastūr*—the heroes who have the habit of crossing over (*taraṇaśīla*) in armies (*pṛtanāsu*)—and in their fame (*śravas*) and strength (*bala*). Subdue them all!
Likewise, overcome those who are hostile— men who are everywhere filled with pride— and lead them as a host.
[The word] *pṛtanājye* is derived from the root *aj*, meaning "to go" or "to throw," in its causative form (*ṇyanta*), followed by the suffix *yat* according to the rule *aco yat*.
*Pṛtanānām ājyam* becomes *pṛtanājyam*;
it has the accent of the single substitute (*ekādeśasvara*).
[The word] *pṛtaḥ* occurs in the sense of "swift."
When the word *pṛtanā* is followed by the nominative suffix *su*, the substitution of *pṛt* for *pṛtanā* is applied according to the rule: "The addition of *pṛt* to *māṃs-pṛtanā* is prescribed.
[The root] *kṣitvar* is used in the sense of "agitation";
the suffix *kri* is added to denote habitual action (*tācchīlika*).
The suffix *uṭ* is applied by the rule *jvaratvara-* etc.;

the non-elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending of the first member occurs by the rule *tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam*; and the accent falls on the final syllable of the compound because it is a *kṛd*-derived word with a following member.
*Sākṣva*:

from the root *vah* in the sense of "to endure," in the imperative (*loṭ*), there is elision of the *śap* suffix by the rule "there is frequent elision in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*). [Then] the substitution of *ḍa* for *ta* and the addition of the augment *k*.
The long vowel [in *yudhebhyaḥ*] is an archaic Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).

1. In the *la* recension: *he indra yudhebhyaḥ*. 2. In the *kha*, *ga*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *bha*, and *la* recensions: [the word] *pṛtanātaraṇaśīleṣu*; in the *na* and *sa* recensions: *taraṇaśīleṣu*. 3. In the *na*, *la*, and *sa* recensions: the phrase “*he indra*” is absent. 4. In the *na* and *bha* recensions: *saha*.

On the twenty-fourth day, at the midday pressing (*mādhyandina-savana*), in the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin* litany (*śastra*), the triplet beginning with “*śuṣmintaṃ na ūtaye*” serves as an optional counterpart (*anurūpa*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Like those seeking refuge in the sun, [we approach] the powerful one for our protection" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.4).
"O Indra, Lord of a hundred powers, protect the vigorous, glorious, and watchful Soma for our aid."
For our protection, O Indra, drink the powerful, glorious, and watchful Soma, O Śatakratu! 8.

O you of a hundred powers, O Indra, drink—having come here—for our protection that Soma which belongs to us, which is most powerful among the powerful, most brilliant, or rather, drying up the enemies (*śuṣmintam*) and glorious (*dyumnine*), ever-watchful (*jāgṛvim*); for it is said that "the Soma, when drunk, is watchful and a warder-off of sleep. Regarding *śuṣmintam*: since the suffix *tamaP* is followed by an unaccented vowel, the accent falls on the suffix itself. Regarding *pāhi*: from the root *pā-* in the imperative, there is the elision of *śap* by the rule "in the Veda [it is] manifoldly [so]. There is the *nighāta* (suppression) of the accent. Regarding *jāgṛviḥ*: it ends in the *kin* suffix; because it is formed with *ni*, it is udātta on the first syllable.
O Śatakratu, those senses of yours which are among the five peoples— O Indra, I choose them for you.
O Śatakratu, those powers of yours which exist among the five peoples, O Indra, those I choose for myself. 9.

O Vṛtrahan, O Indra of a hundredfold power, those faculties—namely the capacities for perceiving forms and so forth—which reside among your five classes of beings, namely the Gandharvas, the Pitṛs, the Devas, the Asuras, and the Rakṣases; those faculties belonging to you, I choose and partake of.
Or alternatively: those faculties and capacities which exist among the five peoples—the four classes of men with the Niṣādas as the fifth—those faculties belonging to you, I choose.
[The word *indriyāṇi* is repeated.]

The word *indriya* is accented on the final syllable because it is a *nipāta* (irregular formation) ending in the suffix *dhac*, according to the rule: “*indriya* [is derived] as that which is the mark (*liṅga*) of Indra, seen by Indra, created by Indra, or given by Indra.
The form *vṛṇe* is the present indicative (*laṭ*) of the root *vṛñ* in the sense of “to choose” (*saṃbhakti*).
The elision of the accent: "O Indra, come for great glory; bestow upon us invincible splendor, and we shall increase our strength."
O Indra, bestow upon us great renown and invincible splendor; we cause your vital strength to increase. 10.
O Indra, slayer of Vṛtra, may this great and lofty glory—characterized by Soma, namely the food being offered by us—reach you.
Do you bestow upon us wealth that is difficult for enemies to overcome; grant it to us.
We, for our part, increase your supreme vigor—that strength of yours—by means of Soma, clarified butter, and other offerings.
From the root *gam* with the suffix *liṅ*, there is elision of *śap* according to the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi" (Pāṇini 2.4.73);
then, by the rule "halḍyābbhyo dīrghāt... (Pāṇini 6.1.68), there is elision of the *ti*.
‘mo no dhātoḥ’: the vowel accent of the augment aṭ; [thus] *dadhiṣva*.
In the imperative (loṭ) of the root *dadhāti*:
1. In the manuscripts kha, ga, ca, pha, and bha, the word "saṃbhaje" is absent; 2. In the manuscripts gha and la, the word "vṛtrahan" is absent.

3. *na la sa tarītum* | By the rule *chandasyubhayathā*, the suffix *thās* is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka*, and thus the augment *iṭ* is added. There is *nighāta* (anudātta accent). *dustaram*: from the root *tṛ*, the suffix *khal* is added in the sense of difficulty (*kṛcchra*). In the *saṃhitā*, the *phatva* (change to *pha*) occurs according to *supām sulu...* [Pāṇini 7.1.39]. There is the accent of the *liṅ* (optative). *tirāmasi*: the suffix *masi* ends in *i*. There is *nighāta*.
O Śakra, come to us from nearby, or even from afar;
O wielder of the stone, come here to this world which is yours, O Indra.
Come hither from near at hand; come also from afar, O Śakra. Whatever world of yours there is, O Indra, wielder of the stone, from that place here come to us. 11.

O powerful Śakra, O Indra, come toward us from nearby, from the vicinity (*arvācīnāt*), and also from afar, from a very distant place (*parāvataḥ*). O wielder of the thunderbolt (*adrivaḥ*)—he who eats or destroys his enemies is *adri-vajra*; O Indra, possessor of that—you have a supreme world (*lokaḥ*); from that world also, come here to this place of sacrifice for the drinking of Soma. *Gahi*: This is the form of the root *gam* in the imperative (*loṭ*). *Parāvataḥ*: By the rule "In the Veda, the suffix *vat* is added after a preposition when it has the sense of a verbal root," the suffix *vat* is applied; it bears the accent of the affix (*pratyayasvara*). *Adrivaḥ*: By the rule "After *manu*, *vasu*, etc., *ru* is substituted [for the final vowel]," *ru* is substituted. *Tataḥ*: By the rule "The suffix *tasil* is used after a word in the ablative case," *tasil* is applied; it bears the accent of the affix (*lisvara*). || 22 ||

“Abhi tatraiva” is the ninth hymn, consisting of ten verses. Regarding this, the Anukramaṇikā states: “Abhi tatraiva; ten [verses]; Prajāpati, or Vaiśvāmitra Prajāpati, or Vāc, or both of them, or neither of them.
Thus, the seer (ṛṣi) is either Prajāpati of the Viśvāmitra lineage, or Prajāpati the son of Vāc, or both, or neither.
The second position is that both of them together are the seers (ṛṣis) of this hymn;
or else, the third position is that neither of them is so, but rather Viśvāmitra alone is the seer.
The metre is Triṣṭubh.
Indra is the deity.

On the twenty-fourth day, at the midday pressing (*mādhyandina-savana*), during the *acchāvāka* recitation, there is the hymn named *aharahaḥ-śasya* (to be recited daily), beginning with “*abhi tatraiva*.
This is prescribed in the Sūtra: “*udu brahma* and *abhi tatraiva* are for the *irā* and the *aharahaḥ-śasya*” (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 7.4).
Thus, in all multi-day sacrificial sessions (*ahargaṇa*), on the second day and subsequent days, this hymn is used in the *acchāvāka* recitation at the midday pressing.

Thereupon, let me contemplate with wisdom, like a prize-winning steed leaping forward with a well-yoked chariot; touching upon my dear and most distant goals, I, the wise one, desire to behold the works of the skillful.

There, indeed, he has fixed his inspired thought, like a prize-winning steed leaping forward with a well-yoked chariot. Touching upon his own dear and supreme goals, the wise one desires to behold them. 1.

The sacrificer speaks to the praiser: "O praiser, contemplate—that is, perform thoroughly—the *manīṣā*, the hymn directed toward Indra. In this regard, there is an illustration: just as a carpenter refines wood by means of carving, so it is here. [Note: Regarding *sudhuraḥ*: 1.

The form *masi* ending in *-i* does not exist in the *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, and *sa* recensions. 2. From a nearby place; 3. from a very distant place; 4. the seer (*ṛṣi*). (Ṛgveda 2.48).

Like a swift horse (*vājī*) endowed with a beautiful yoke, moving forward (*jihānaḥ*) like a steed as it engages in its task, you—being highly intelligent (*sumedhāḥ*)—thoroughly touch (*abhi marṣaśata*) the supreme (*parāṇi*), most beloved (*priyāṇi*) deeds of Indra;
or rather, the deeds to be performed on subsequent days. I am the wise one (*kavīn*);
those sages (*kavayaḥ*) who previously performed sacrifices went to the abode of the gods (*devabhūm*).
I wish to see them together at this meeting.

Regarding this matter, the Brāhmaṇa states: “‘I have meditated with my mind as if upon a craftsman’—this is the form of the Acchāvāka’s daily recitation for the sake of speaking toward [the future]. ‘He polishes the dear subsequent days’—those very days that follow are the dear ones; it is toward these that he goes, touching them while taking hold of them. ‘I, the wise one, desire to see the sages’—those who have passed away before are indeed the sages; it is toward them that he speaks. (AiB 6.20). In that same [section]:
In the word *tatkaraṇe*, the form is from the suffix *tṛn*.
It has an acute accent (*udātta*).
[The root is] *dīdhī*.

Regarding the root *dīdhīṅ* in the sense of “to shine” or “to play,” when it carries an implied causative meaning (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*), the *śap* suffix is elided in the *loṭ* mood by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*;
furthermore, the active voice (*parasmaipada*) occurs by way of metrical transposition (*vyatyaya*).
[The form is] *sudhuraḥ*.
The acute accent on the first syllable of the compound is due to the rule *ādyudāttaśchandasi* (Pāṇini 6.2.119).
Regarding *jihānaḥ*:
from the root *ohāṅ* in the sense of "going," with the suffix *śānac*, the vowel of the reduplicated syllable becomes short *i* by the rule *bhṛñām it* (Pāṇini 7.4.76).

Since the root *cit* is heavy, it would have been unaccented were it not for the rule "the first syllable of reduplicated (abhyasta) forms is acute," by which its initial syllable receives the acute accent.
[The form] *marṣṭaśat*:

from the root *mṛś* in the sense of "touching" (*āmarśane*), with the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix, the augment *rug* is added to the reduplicated syllable by the rule "the augments *rug* and *rik* occur when there is elision."
The form [is derived] from that which ends in -śatṛ; by the rule "nābhyastāc chatuḥ," there is an absence of the augment *num*,
and it bears the accent of the reduplicated (abhyasta) stem.

In *saṃdṛśe*: from the root *dṛśir* in the sense of "seeing," the word is derived with the suffix *ken* in the sense of the infinitive (*tumun*), according to the rule *dṛśe vireye ca*; thus, by virtue of this grammatical derivation (*nipātana*), it is ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable).
In the compound, the accent falls on the final syllable of the latter member (*kṛduttarapadasvara*).
*Sumedhāḥ*:
the suffix *as* is applied according to the rule “*nityamasicca prajāmedhayoḥ*” (Pāṇini 5.4.122),
and the accent is that of the *cit* suffix.
Ask of this birth of the sages; they, upholding the mind, fashioned the heaven through their good deeds.
These prayers of yours, increasing and impelled by the mind, have now come according to the sacred law.

Ask also of the births of the sages; they, steadfast in mind and well-performing deeds, fashioned the heavens. These your exalted thoughts, increasing and wind-swift, have now come into their proper course.
Furthermore, *uta* is used here for addressing.

O Indra, ask the *inās*, the lords or teachers, regarding the *janima*, the birth, of the *kavīs*, those of well-performed deeds who have attained the state of gods—by what action did they go to heaven, or from where was their origin? This is the matter you should inquire about.
Those sages, whose minds are held in restraint and who are therefore performers of auspicious deeds, fashioned you as heaven.
Now, at this sacrifice, may these praises being offered for your sake—possessing the speed of thought, increasing, and magnifying you—quickly go to you.
(The particle *u* is used here for the sake of universal renown.)
"Ask. In the imperative (*loṭ*) of the root *pracch* in the sense of "desire to know," the suffix *śa* is applied because it belongs to the *tudādi* class.
Because that [suffix] is marked with *ṅ*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) according to the rule beginning with *grahi-jyā*.
Nighātaḥ | Praṇayaḥ | From the root *ṇīñ* in the sense of "leading" (*prāpaṇe*), the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*) according to the Uṇādi rules.
Since all rules are optional in the Vedic language (*chandasi*), the *yaṇ* substitution takes precedence over the *iyaṅ* replacement.
By the rule “*udāttasvaritayoḥ...*” [Pāṇini 8.2.4], the circumflex (*svarita*) accent is applied. [The form is] *gman*.

The elision of the *śap* suffix occurs by the rule "elision is frequent in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*). Because the root *kṣi* has a *cakāra* (indicatory letter) attached to it, there is elision of the penultimate vowel according to the rule "gamahana... and so forth. There is also the *nighāta* (anudātta accent).

1. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, Ja, Ṇa, Na, Bha, and Ma, the phrase "yadvā parāṇi" is absent; in manuscript Ta, it is "aparāṇi. 2. In the manuscripts Ca and Bha, the reading is "anuṣṭhitayajñodevabhūya°.
3. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, Ja, Ṇa, Pha, and Bha, the reading is "asminnarthe."

4. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, Bha, and Sa, it reads *devabhūyagatānām*; in La, it reads *devarūpaṃ gatānām*. 5. In Kha and Ga, it reads *etamartham*; in Na, it reads *evamartham*. 6. The word *eva* does not exist in Kha, Ga, Ca, Ja, and Ṇa.
7. In the versions kha, ga, ca, ṇa, bha, and sa, the word *tvām* does not occur. 8. According to [Pāṇini 6.1.19] *prahijyetyādinā*:
"We have settled here, establishing ourselves in secret; and we have consecrated the two worlds for sovereign power."
They measured it out with measures; they stretched out the wide, great [spaces], and established them within for nourishment.

Here, having established them in secret within the enclosure, they anointed the two worlds for sovereign power; they measured them out with their proportions and held them wide. The two great ones, meeting together, were placed for the sake of sustenance.

Here, on this earthly world, these sages (*kavayaḥ*), performing secret deeds within the cave (*guhā*)—that is, in the hidden place—and establishing them on every side, have indeed adorned the two worlds, heaven and earth (*rodasī*), for the sake of dominion (*kṣatrāya*), for strength, or for wealth. They made the earth united with plants and the sky with the gods. Furthermore, by means of measures (*mātrābhiḥ*)—*mātrāḥ* being so called because they are measured or they set limits—namely, the mountain masses, they measured them out together; they made those two worlds, heaven and earth, limited and well-defined. Having come together, joined with one another, vast and great, they restrained those two, heaven and earth. Within, by means of the atmosphere as a support, they lifted them up; likewise, for the sake of their maintenance (*dhāyase*), they fixed the atmosphere between them. [Notes on the grammar: *Ida*: used here in the sense of restriction. *Guha*: "in the cave"; derived from *guhā*, with the suffix *yat* added in the sense of "being there" (*bhavārthe*), resulting in an udātta accent on the first syllable. *Dadhānāḥ*: a form of the root *dhā* (to place) in the present participle middle voice (*śānac*). It takes the accent of the reduplicated stem (*abhyastasvaraḥ*). *Añjan*: from the root *añjū* (to manifest, to smear, to move); the *kṣu* suffix causes the elision of the vowel *a*. It is unaccented (*nighātaḥ*). *Mātrābhiḥ*: from the roots *mā* (to measure) or *māṅ* (to measure); the suffix *trap* is applied according to rules such as *huyām-ādi*. It is unaccented. *Mamire*: a form of the root *māṅ* (to measure) in the perfect tense (*liṭ*). It is not unaccented because of the rule *cādilope vibhāṣā*. *Yemuḥ*: a form of the root *yama* (to restrain) in the perfect tense with the suffix *śnu*; it is unaccented due to being followed by a finite verb (*tiṅ*). *Dhāyase*: formed with the suffix *asun* after the roots *vahi*, *hā*, and *dhā* in Vedic usage. It is unaccented. *Dhuḥ*: a form of the root *dhā* (to place) in the aorist (*luṅ*). The final result is: "In this world, these wise ones, performing secret deeds in the cave and establishing them everywhere, have adorned heaven and earth for the sake of power, strength, or wealth; they measured them out by means of the mountain-masses, and having joined them together, they restrained the vast and great pair, supporting them within by the atmosphere and fixing the atmosphere for their sustenance."
All have honored him as he stood firm; clothed in splendors, he moves with self-radiant light.
Bearing the great name of the Asura, he of universal form has taken his stand upon the immortal realms.

As he stood firm, all the gods adorned him on every side. Clothed in splendors, he moves with self-luminous radiance. Great is the name of the Asura; assuming all forms, he has taken his stand upon the immortal realms.
All the seers together adorned Indra as he mounted his chariot;
they made him resplendent,
shining like the sun.
He whose own radiance is his delight is *svarociḥ*;
the meaning is that he shines by his own splendor alone.
Therefore, *vasānaḥ*—clothing himself in, or enveloping, the *śriyaḥ*, which are lights—he, this Indra, *carati*, moves everywhere.
Of the bull (*vṛṣṇaḥ*), the showerer of desires; of the *asura*.
He is called *asura* because he hurls (*asati*) or impels all things through his lack of interior limit.
That is the name of that very Indra, such as it has been experienced before.

It is called *nāma* because by means of it one "bends" (*namayati*) all enemies; or else, it is called *nāma* because it is "bowed to" (*namyate*) and honored by all. Indra’s body or his action exists as "great" (*maha*), endowed with a support.
Likewise, he who possesses "universal form" (*viśvarūpaḥ*), assuming various kinds of forms—that Indra, in the form of Varuṇa, [produces] the immortal waters.

1. [The letters] gha, na, la, sa, and ṅa are not followed by a *śagaram*. 2. The letter *ta* and others possess the acute accent (*udātta*). 3. [The letters] kha, ga, ca, ja, ṇa, na, pha, bha, and sa do not have a *śagaram*. 4. [The word] *vā* does not exist in the *ca*-recension.

*vā* [he] stood; he stands upon. *viśve*: the form *śī* for the nominative plural (*jas*). *abhūṣan*: this is the form of the root *bhūṣ* (meaning "to adorn") in the *laṅ* tense. *vasānaḥ*: this is the form of the root *vas* (meaning "to clothe") with the suffix *śānac*; by the rule regarding the accent of *lasārvadhātuka*, the accent of the verbal root remains. *nāma*: from the root *ṇu* (meaning "to bow"), it is derived as an *ādyudātta* (accented on the first syllable) because it is listed among the group beginning with *nāman-sīman* as ending in the suffix *manin*. *viśvarūpa* is its name; according to the rule *bahuvrīhau viśvaṃ saṃjñāyām*, the final syllable of the first member is accented. *amṛtāni*: the accusative case is used according to the rule *kālādhvanoratyantasaṃyoge*. *tasthau*: this is the form of the root *sthā* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*) with the suffix *ṇal*.
The ancient bull brought forth the elder one; these many powers of his exist in abundance.
O two Kings, sons of Heaven, by the insights of the assembly, you have maintained sovereign power from of old.

The first, the bull, the elder, begot these many strengthening powers (*śurudhas*). The two grandsons of Heaven are clearly mentioned in the *Taittirīyaka*: "O Svāna, Āja, Dvāra, Bambhāra, Hasta, Suhasta, Kṛśānu—these are your *sorukrayaṇas*; guard them, let them not deceive you" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 1.2.7).
*Bhūpathaḥ*: This is the form of the root *bhūpa* (meaning "to adorn") in the present tense (*laṭ*).
I saw.
This is the form of the root *dṛś* (in the sense of "seeing") in the *laṅ* tense;
it lacks the *nighāta* accent because it occurs at the beginning of a *pāda*. [The form] is *jaganvān*.

In the case of *gami* with the suffix *kas*, the absence of the augment *iṭ* is optional according to the rule *avibhāṣā gamahanavidaviśām*. By the rules *mo no dhātoḥ* and *mvośca*, the *m* is replaced by *n*. The accent is that of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
Regarding *gandharvān*: from the root *dhṛ* in the sense of "holding" (*dhāraṇe*), when the word *go* is the upapada, the suffix *vap* is applied according to the rule *gavi gan dhṛjo vaḥ*.
By virtue of that [suffix], the substitution of *gan* for the word *go* occurs.
The accent of the suffix.
Then, by means of the bellies of this bull and the cow,
the two skillful ones, assuming various forms, fashioned a shared likeness within him— the great Asura clothing himself in one form after another.

Then indeed, by means of the hollows of this bull and the cow, they measured out the shared domain of the bull; clothing themselves in various divine powers, the two masters of illusion fashioned their form within him. 7.

Those sacrificers who have quickly milked for the sake of this Indra—the bull who bestows desired fruits—the cow characterized by names such as *viśvāyu* and *viśvavyacā*, [obtaining] the sacrificial offering consisting of her milk and so forth, which is *sakmya*, meaning fit for enjoyment.
(The verb *mimire* is used here because verbal roots possess multiple meanings.)

Having performed the sacrifice with that oblation, those sages attained the state of being gods; "wearing" (*vasānāḥ*) various other, ever-new "non-asuric" (*asuryam*) powers—the strength of the Asuras—they were therefore "magicians" (*māyinaḥ*), assuming whatever forms they desired through their *māyā*.
Alternatively, being "wise" (*māyinaḥ*), they "measured out" (*ni mamire*) their own respective forms within this Indra, determining them by heart and depositing them there.
In *pūraṇaḥ* [the suffix] *khaṃś* is applied;
[in *mamire*],
from the root *māṅ* meaning "to measure."
The form is from the perfect tense (liṭ). There is the nighāta accent.
The word is *sakmyam*.

In the rule *yujirucitijāṃ ku ca* (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.143), because the letter *ca* has the sense of an inclusive conjunction (*anuktasamuccayārtha*), the suffix *man* is applied to the root *sac*, and there is also the substitution of *kṛt*. Thus, *sacana* becomes *sakma*.
In the sense of "existing therein" (*tatra bhavaḥ*), the suffix *yat* is applied according to the rule *bhave chandasi*.
In *yato ’nāvaḥ*, the first member is udātta;
in *goḥ*,
the single-substitute accent (*ekādeśasvara*) applies.
*Asuryam*: in the sense of "belonging to an Asura," the suffix *yat* is applied by Pāṇini’s rule 4.4.123 (*asurasya svam*).
The suffix *tit* is svarita-accented.
Rūpa:
[derived from] the root *rūp* in the sense of "forming" (*rūpakriyā*),
with the causative suffix (*ṇyanta*).

In the rule *‘svapna-śilpa-śapbavāpya-rūpa-parpa-talyāḥ’* (Uṇādi-sūtra 3.308), because of the irregular formation (*nipātana*) with the suffix *pra*, there is the elision of the letter *pa* and the absence of *guṇa*. [The word] *rūpa* is so called because it forms or is formed. It has the accent of the suffix.
Then, as if on the ship of this Savitṛ, he has mounted this golden chariot;
with fair praise, he has drawn toward himself the two world-halves that encompass all things, just as a maiden chooses her kinsmen.

Truly, there is none who can restrain this golden radiance which Savitṛ has extended for me. With fair praise, he has drawn near to the two world-halves that encompass all; like a maiden choosing her kinsmen, he has chosen them both. 8.

1. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, Ja, Ṇa, Ta, Na, Bha, and Sa, the phrase "pratyayasvaraḥ" is absent. 2. In the manuscripts Ta, Na, Bha, and Sa, the word "gośabdasya" is also absent. 3. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ja, Ṇa, Pa, Pha, and Bha, the reading is "svīkṛtakāmarūpāḥ santaḥ. 4. In the manuscripts Gha and Ca, the passage "yadvā... prajñāvantaḥ" is absent. 5. In manuscript Ta, the reading is "svarūpam. 6. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, and La, there is an insertion (pūraṇam). Therefore (*tat tasmāt*), no one at all (*nakiḥ ko vā*) indeed limits (*paricchinatti*) the golden (*hiraṇyayīm*), i.e., the radiant (*dīptim*), wisdom (*amatim*) of this *Indra*, who is the *Savitṛ*—the impeller of the entire world by acting as its inner controller (*antaryāmitayā*)—and of me (*mama*).

He who rests upon—that is, takes refuge in—my radiance, being praised with a beautiful hymn (*suṣṭuti*), chooses for himself the two worlds, Heaven and Earth (*rodasī*), which satisfy all things (*viśvaminve*), encompassing them on all sides as his own.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
like a woman [choosing] her offspring (*janimāni*).
Just as a woman chooses her successive births, so [does she choose] those born later;
*nuḥ* is a filler.
nakiḥ | an indeclinable particle (nipātaḥ) | hiraṇyayīm |

The suffix *mayaṭ* is applied in the sense of a modification of gold according to Pāṇini’s rule 4.3.143, *mayaḍvaitayoḥ*. The elision of the letter *m* in *mayaṭ* occurs due to the Vedic nipātana (irregular formation) stated in the rule: *ṛtvyavāstvyavāstvamādvīhiraṇyayāni chandasi*. Because the suffix is marked with the *ṭi*-indicator, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added according to the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*.
The accent is that of the suffix (pratyayasvara). [The root] *am* is used in the sense of "going" and so forth.
In *ame ratiḥ*, the suffix *-ti* is an *atipratyaya*; it has the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). [Thus: *aśiśret*.

In the case of the root *śri* with the suffix *laṅ*, there is the elision (*bhlu*) of the *śap* by the rule "there is frequent [elision] in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*). Due to its connection with *yadṛtta*, it does not undergo the low-pitched accent (*anighāta*). [The word is] *suṣṭutī*.

In the form *viśvaminve*, there is a long vowel by rule of homogeneous blending (*savarṇadīrgha*) from the third case ending according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*. [The word is derived] from the root *ivi* in the sense of "pervasion" and "pleasing," with the suffix *aṇ* in the passive sense (*karmaṇi*).

The augment *num* is applied because it is a *hr̥di*-stem. There is no elision (*aluk*) of the second case ending due to the rule “*tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam*”. The accent is that of the final member of the compound, as it is a *kṛd*-derived word.

*Yoṣā*: from the root *yu*, meaning "to mix" (*miśraṇa*) or "to separate" (*bhedana*), the suffix *sa* is applied according to the rule *vṛtuvadidhanikamikapiyumucibhyaḥ saḥ*. It is *ādyudātta* (accented on the first syllable) because it belongs to the *grāma* group.
The word *janimāni* [is derived as follows]: from the root *janī* in the sense of "manifestation," the suffix *imanin* is applied according to the rule *hajanibhyām imanin*, denoting past time.
The word *nisvāda* is udātta at its beginning.
*Vave* is the form of the root *vṛṣ* (meaning "to choose") in the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
You two accomplish the ancient, great, and divine well-being; may it encompass us on every side.
All the wise ones behold the manifold deeds of the one who stands firm, whose tongue is the cowherd’s staff.
You two accomplish the great work of the ancient one; may divine well-being encompass us. All the wise ones behold the diverse deeds of the one who stands with tongue as a cowherd. 9.

O Indra and Varuṇa, you two accomplish—that is, you bring about—for the ancient praiser such great excellence. To explain what that is, he says: "that which is divine well-being"—namely, this excellence pertaining to the gods, characterized by self-sovereignty (*svārājya*).
Furthermore, may you two be around us—be our protectors on every side.
All the gods, who are possessed of *māyā*, belong to him whose tongue is a protector;
that is, he whose speech is such that it says, "O tongue, do not fear."
They behold the manifold deeds—such as the slaying of Vṛtra and others—performed by Indra, who is steadfast and most firm while remaining still;
in this way, Indra’s possession of all forms has been described.
*Yuvam*:
In the dual number of the word *yuṣmad*, the substitute *yuva* is applied according to Pāṇini Sūtra 7.2.92, which states, "In the dual, *yuva* and *āva* [are substituted for *yuṣmad* and *asmad*].
Then, by Pāṇini Sūtra 7.1.28, which states, "For the [case endings] *ḍe* and the first five case endings, *am* [is substituted]," the case ending *sup* is replaced by *am*.

*sādhathaḥ* is the form of the root *sādh* in the sense of "accomplishment" (*saṃsiddhi*) when conjugated in the present tense (*laṭ*) with the causative suffix (*ṇic*). The elision of the causative suffix (*ṇiluk*) occurs according to the rule: "The suffix *ṇi* is frequently elided elsewhere as well. (*bahulam anyatrāpi*)
The elision [of the case-ending] occurs.
In the word *daivīm*, the suffix *añ* is applied according to the rule *devād yañ*.
The dual ending *au* is [used]; these two would be the forms of the root *as* in the *liṅ* (optative) mood.
Regarding *gopājihva*:
from the root *gup* (meaning "to protect") with the suffix *āya*, the form *gopā* is derived by eliding the vowel *a* and the *y* after applying the *kvip* suffix.
In the *bahuvrīhi* compound, the accent falls on the first member.

Regarding *tasthuṣaḥ*: from the root *sthā* in the sense of "ceasing to move," when the suffix *kvasu* is applied, the augment *iṭ* is dropped by the rule *vasvekājādāsām*. Then, because the substitution of semivowels (*saṃprasāraṇa*) is stronger than that which depends upon such a substitution, according to the principle *saṃprasāraṇaṃ saṃprasāraṇāśrayaṃ ca balīyaḥ*, the *iṭ* is removed due to the predominance of the *saṃprasāraṇa*.
‘There is vṛddhi substitution for the vowel of *vasu*.
The accent of the suffix [prevails].
They see.
The root *haśira* is used in the sense of "seeing.
It is unaccented (*nighāta*).

1. The suffix *ta* [is used] after the root *prasū*. 2. The suffixes *ta* and *janitāni* [are used]. 3. The suffixes *kha*, *gha*, *pa*, and *nu* are for ordinal numbers (*pūraṇa*); the suffixes *na*, *la*, and *sa* are not for ordinal numbers. 4. The suffix *ca* and *pha* are for the sense of "immortality" (*amara*). 5. The suffixes *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, and *na* are the characteristics of sovereignty (*svarājya*).

May we invoke for our welfare the bountiful Indra, the most heroic among men, in this battle for the acquisition of booty—him who hears us, the fierce one for our protection in the conflicts, the slayer of Vṛtras, and the winner of riches. 10. May we invoke for our welfare the bountiful Indra, the most heroic among men, in this battle for the acquisition of booty—him who hears us, the fierce one for our protection in the conflicts, the slayer of Vṛtras, and the winner of riches. 10.
This has been explained.
Now, in the fourth anuvāka, there are fifteen sūktas.
Among them, the first sūkta, consisting of nine verses beginning with "indraṃ matiḥ," belongs to Viśvāmitra; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter and is addressed to Indra.
This is indicated by the Anukramaṇī: "indraṃ matirnava."
The application of the hymn is to be understood from its indicative mark (liṅga).

The prayer, fashioned from the heart and being uttered aloud, goes toward Indra, the Lord, as it is wrought by hymns of praise. That which is watchful and recited at the assembly—O Indra, know this as it is born for thee. Indra; matiḥ; hṛdaḥ; ā; vacyamānā; accha; patim; stomataṣṭā; jigāti; yā; jāgṛviḥ; vidathe; śasyamānā; indra; yat; te; jāyate; viddhi; tasya. || 1 ||
Viśvāmitra praises:
O Indra, let this hymn—shaped from the heart, fashioned by those who compose the *stoma*, and being uttered—go forth toward you, the Lord and Master of the entire world.
This my hymn, which remains ever-watchful as it awakens you, the object of praise, shall be recited at the sacrificial assembly (*vidatha*).
O Indra, know—that is, take note of—that hymn which arises from me for your sake; "of that" (tasya) is used in the genitive case with the sense of the accusative; it refers to the hymn (mati).
In the mantra "vṛṣa" and so forth, the suffix *ktin* is anudātta.
[The form] "hṛdaḥ" [is derived from] the word *hṛdaya*, which undergoes the substitution of *hṛd* by the rule "pañcamyāmās" (Pāṇini 6.1.63).

In the word *udidam*, the case ending (*vibhakti*) is acute (*udātta*). It is that which is being spoken; from the root *vac* in the sense of "speaking," the suffix *yak* is applied in the passive (karmaṇi).
The absence of *saṃprasāraṇa* is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). It has the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). [The word] is *stomataṣṭā*.
The word [takṣu] is derived from the root *takṣū* (or *tvakṣū*) in the sense of "making thin" (*tanūkaraṇe*), with a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) suffix in the objective sense (*karmaṇi*).
By the rule "the third case [is used] in the sense of the object" (*tṛtīyā karmaṇi*), the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member of the compound is preserved.
[The verb is] *jigāti*.
The root *gā* is used in the sense of "praising" (*stuti*) in the Vedic language (*chandas*), belonging to the *juhoty-ādi* class.
According to the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, the reduplication vowel is shortened.
There is elision of the accent (*nighāta*).

It is born (*jāyate*). This is the form of the root *janī* in the sense of "manifestation" (*prādurbhāve*) in the present tense (*laṭ*). Due to its connection with the word *yat*, there is no loss of accent (*anighāta*).
Know (*viddhi*). This is the imperative second person singular (*loṭ*) of the root *vida* in the sense of "to know. By the rule *hujhalbhyo hedhiḥ*, the substitution of *dhi* for *hi* occurs.
Due to the division of the sentence (*vākyabheda*), there is no loss of accent (*anighāta*).

Born from the very heart of heaven with beauty, wide-awake, being recited at the assembly, wearing auspicious, bright garments—may this ancestral prayer be fully realized for us. From the very heart of heaven, born with splendor, wide-awake, being recited at the sacrificial assembly, wearing auspicious, bright garments—may this ancestral prayer be fully realized for us.
1. *Ja* and *ṇa* have been explained previously; *na* has not been explained. 2.
In the versions *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *pa*, *pha*, and *bha*, it reads "his husband. 3. In the version *ca*, it reads "he goes."

O Indra, that ancient speech (*pūrvyā*) belonging to the time of dawn, which arises even from the shining sun situated in heaven—this very speech, manifesting at the sacrifice (*vidathe*), remains wakeful (*jāgṛtiḥ*), keeping watch over you, the object of praise. Wearing auspicious, bright, and pure-colored rays as her fitting luster, she becomes our ancestral thought (*dhīḥ*), handed down through the lineage of our fathers, and thus she is your eternal hymn of praise.
From *div* [is derived] *diveḥ*; [the suffix] *kip* [is applied].
By the rule "udidam," the case ending (*vibhakti*) is unaccented (*anudātta*).
The suffix *unan* is applied by the rule "arje-ṇilucca" (Uṇādi-sūtra 3.338). It is devoid of accent (*nissvara*).
*Sanajā*:
from the root *jan*, the suffix *ḍa* is applied according to the rule "it is seen after other roots as well";
it bears the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
From *pitṛ*. In the sense of "come from that," the suffix *yat* is applied by the rule *pitṛyacccha*;
then, by the rule *rīṅtaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.27), the substitution of *rī* for the final vowel occurs.
In the word *yasya*, there is elision [of the case-ending];
by the rule *yato ’nāvaḥ*, the first syllable receives the udātta accent.

Even Yama here, the son of Yami, let the tip of his tongue fall from his hand as he was born; the pair of forms, having come together, destroy the darkness—the wise one, being satisfied, perceives this.

The two Yamas have indeed been born here; the mother of Yama has brought them forth. The tip of the tongue has risen up, for it has reached the forms. Once born, the pair move together; the two slayers of darkness have come to the base of the sap-filled plant.

In this context, he praises the time of dawn (*upaḥkāla*). "The mother of twins" (*yamasūḥ*): she is the deity presiding over the form of one who has given birth to twins (*yamau*), the two Aśvins. She "gave birth" (*asūta*) to the twin Aśvins here at this time of dawn. Because the two Aśvins are lying here [in the womb], the tip of my tongue, in order to praise those two Aśvins, has "fallen"—that is, become restless—and indeed "stands still" (*āsthāt*). "Dispelling darkness" (*tamohanā*): the destroyers of darkness. "Of the heating" (*tapuṣaḥ*): that which heats is the sun; thus *tapuḥ* refers to the day. At its "base" (*budhne*), that is, at its root, "these two" (*etā*) have arrived; "the pair" (*mithunā*), joined with each other—those two Aśvins—"were born" (*jātā*), meaning they were produced. "Forms" (*vapūṃṣi*): things are sown or deposited, hence *vapūṃṣi* refers to the rites such as the recitation of hymns (*śastra*) performed at the time of dawn. They "meet together" (*sacete*), they come into contact. Grammatical notes: *yamasūḥ*: from the root *ṣūṅ* (prāṇigarbhavimocane, Dhp. III.1), with the suffix *kvip*. The accent is on the final syllable of the compound. *asūta*: the same root in the *laṅ* (imperfect); due to the *adādi* class, there is elision of *śap*; the *nighāta* (suppression) of accent applies. *patat*: from *patlū* (gatau). The accent of the root remains because it is followed by the *sārvadhātuka* suffix *śatṛ*. *āsthāt*: from *ṣṭhā* (gatinivṛttau). This is the form in the *luṅ* (aorist). Due to the connection with *hi*, there is no *nighāta*. *vapūṃṣi*: from *ḍuvap* (bījasaṃtāne). The suffix *usi* is added according to the rule *artipavapiyajitanidhanitapibhyo nit*. Because it is marked as *nit*, it is udātta on the first syllable. *sacete*: from *pac* (samavāye) in the *laṭ* (present). *tapuṣaḥ*: from *tapa* (saṃtāpe). The suffix *usi* is added according to the rule *atipvapi*. *budhne*: from *bandha* (bandhane). The suffix *na* is added according to the *Uṇādi* rule *bandherdhividhudhī ca* (3.285). The *dhivi* and *dhudhi* are replacements for the root. The accent is that of the suffix. *etā*: from *iṇ* (gatau) in the passive sense with the *niṣṭhā* suffix. The accent of the preceding word (*gati*) applies according to the rule *gatiranantaraḥ*.
Among mortals, there is no one who can revile these who are our fathers, warriors for the sake of cattle.
Their daughter, the mighty one, accompanied by Indra, has released her songs of praise, she who possesses wondrous deeds.

None among mortals has reproached them—those who are our fathers, warriors for the sake of cattle. Indra, the possessor of greatness, the one endowed with wondrous power, has burst open their enclosures for them.

1. Kha, ga, ca, ja, ṇa, na, pha, bha, and la are auspicious. 2. Gha, ja, ṇa, and pitṛ (the father-lineage) have descended from the sequence. 3. That which destroys delusion is named La-tamo-hanā. 4. Ta is the region. 5. Na and la are mutually connected. 6. From this "la":

O Indra, among us who are engaged in the sacrificial session (*sattra*), there is no one at all (*nakiḥ*)—none whatsoever—who is a reviler or defamer (*ninditā*) among these mortals, even regarding those Aṅgirases who were our fathers and who acted as warriors (*yodhāḥ*) when the cattle had been carried off by the Paṇis.
Why is this so? To this he says:
