Indra, possessed of greatness, endowed with wondrous power, and the performer of deeds such as the slaying of Vṛtra, released—that is, bestowed upon those Aṅgirases—the well-hid, that is, the abundant, herds of cattle.
‘Ninditā’ is the form of the root ‘nid’ (meaning to reproach) in the *tṛc* suffix;
[it means] among mortals.
The suffix *yat* is applied in its own sense (*svārthika*) because [the root] begins with *vasu*. By the rule “*yato ’nāvaḥ*,” the acute accent (*udātta*) falls on the first syllable. Thus: *yodhāḥ*.
*Yudha* is the form derived from the root *yudh* with the suffix *ac* (as in *saṃprahāra*).
*Haṃhitā* is the form of the root *ih* (meaning "to grow") in its past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) state.
*Māhināvān*:
the suffix *ina* is applied by the rule *maha-er-inac* (Uṇādi Sūtra 2.214);
then the possessive suffix *matup* is added by the rule *tad asyāsti*.
‘Māhināvān’ is its name;
the lengthening of the vowel occurs in the *saṃhitā* according to Pāṇini’s rule 6.3.119, ‘*mato bahvo’najirādīnām*’.
[It refers to] the mountain ranges (*gotrāṇi*).

In the sense of "a herd of cows," following the rule *akhalagorathāt* (Pāṇini 4.2.50), the suffix *ñ* is applied to the word *go* by the rule *iniñakaccayaśca* (Pāṇini 4.2.51). The accent is that of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). [The form] *sasṛje*.
This is the form of the root *sṛj* (in the sense of "emitting") in the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
In the *daśapeya* sacrifice, during the *niṣkevalya* recitation, this verse beginning with “*sakhā ha yatra*” is placed before the *nividdhānīya* verses.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “‘*sakhā ha yatra sakhibhir narvair*’ is [the first of] the two *nividdhānīya* verses” (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 9.3).

Where the friend, with nine companions— the men, the steeds, and the warriors— went forth to win back the cattle by kindling the fire, there Indra truly, with ten Daśagvas, found the Sun dwelling in the darkness.

Friend! Indeed, where the Navagva companions, with their followers and warriors, pursued the cattle with their flames—that deed Indra truly performed with the ten Daśagvas; he found the sun dwelling in the darkness. 5.
"By the *sakhī* (companions), who share the same station, by the *satvan* (warriors) sitting around Indra, and by the *navagva*s.
Medhātithi and others among the Aṅgirases, as well as certain others, performed a sacrificial session (*sattra*) for nine months and obtained the fruit; some performed it for ten months.
Among them, those who rose after performing the sacrificial session for nine months and obtaining the fruit were the *navagva*s.

With those beings, the Aṅgirases, Indra—their companion and one who shares their station—went to that cave where the cows were confined by the Paṇis; he followed them with his knees bent down to the ground. There in that cave, Indra [acted] with the Daśagvas—those who, having performed the sacrificial session for ten months and obtained its fruit, emerged as the Daśagvas.
Accompanied by the ten seers (ṛṣis), he found—that is, obtained—the Sun, who is the true light according to reality, dwelling in the darkness within the cave;
the sense is that Indra, having thus regained his light, brought back those cows and gave them to the Aṅgirases.
The two words *āha* and *u* are expletives.
*Sakhi*:
[derived from] the root *katha* with the prefix *pra*, meaning "to speak.
The suffix *in* is applied according to the rule: "The suffix *in* is added after the root *katha* preceded by the prefix *samāna*, and the vowel is udātta."
Regarding *ḍicca*: by the rule *samānasya chandasi*, there is the substitution of *sa* for *samāna*.
Since it is stated that [the substitute] is udātta, it is understood by implication that this refers to the *upapada*.
It has the acute accent on the first syllable.
[The form] *navagvaiḥ* [is derived from the root] *gam* with the *ḍu*-suffix prescribed by the *Uṇādi* [sūtras].
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the accent belongs to the first member.
In the word *abhijñu*, the suffix *ju* prescribed by the rule “*prasaṃbhyāṃ jānuno juḥ*” applies to the syllable *dhu* following *abhi* by means of *sthāny-adeśa*.

[The word] *satvabhiḥ* [is derived as follows]: from the root *pad*, meaning "to go," "to perish," or "to sink," the suffix *kanip* is applied according to the rule *pra īrasadyostuṭ ca*; there is also the augment *tuṭ*.
The word *niśvāda* has its first syllable accented (*udātta*).
[In the form] *anugman*,
the suffix *śatṛ* is applied to the root *gam* by the rule "in the Veda, diversely" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).

1. In the *nalasa* recension, the term ‘āhīṃhitā’ does not exist. 2. In the *ca* recension, [the vowels] are ‘saṃbhṛtāni’. 3. In the *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *pa*, *pha*, *bha*, and *da* recensions, [the term] ‘utpūraṇaḥ’ is used. 4. In the *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, and *pha* recensions, [the consonants] are ‘samānasthānaḥ’. 5. In the *na*, *la*, and *sa* recensions, the phrase ‘āhīṃ pūraṇau’ does not exist. 6. In the *kha*, *ga*, *ta*, *na*, and *ḍi* recensions, [the term] ‘tvam’ is used. 7. In the *ja* and *ṇa* recensions, it is stated as ‘ityuktena’. (Ka, 2–49)

When the *śap* affix has been elided (*luki kṛte*), there is the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) according to the rule "agama-hana-" and so forth. This is a *prādi-samāsa* (compound with a prefix). The accent is that of the *śatṛ* suffix. *Viveda*: this is the form of the root *vid* (meaning "to know") in the perfect tense (*liṭ*) with the *nal* suffix. *Kṣiyantam*: this is the form of the root *kṣi* (meaning "to dwell" or "to go") in the present participle (*śatṛ*). || 25 ||

Indra knows the honey gathered within the udder of the cow; he knows the hoofed [milk] of my cow. That which was placed in secret, hidden, and concealed in the waters—he, the possessor of skill, has grasped it with his right hands.
Indra found the honey gathered in the cow, winged and hoofed, within the breast of the earth; hidden, secret, and concealed in the waters, he, the skillful one, took it with his right hands. 6.

Indra discovered—that is, he became aware of—the "honey," such as milk and so forth, which had been gathered and prepared in the "cow" known as Bhogavatī, who was swelling with milk through the sequence of milk, curds, and the like.
Then, for that purpose, he discovered and obtained the "wealth of cows" (godhana) that is "footed"—that is, possessed of feet—and "hoofed"—that is, equipped with hooves.
How he obtained it is now explained.
The word "goḥ" means "of the cow. The genitive case here functions in the sense of the accusative.
He brought back the cow that had been carried off by the demons named Paṇis.

Likewise: "He who possesses the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), who is noble and capable—he, Indra, has taken hold of the Asura, the master of illusion (*māyin*), who was hidden in the secret place (*guhā*), that is, concealed within the cave; for this very reason, he who moves secretly in the waters—that is, in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*)—he held him in his right hand. The meaning is that he seized and took possession of him. Regarding the second verse, in the hymn beginning with "Hear our call" (*śrudhi havam*), the phrase "hidden in the secret place" (*guhā hitam*) is correctly explained [in Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 2.11.5].
Regarding the word *ustriyā*: the derivation (*prakriyā*) has already been correctly explained previously. [The form] *viveda* [is derived as follows].
The forms [of the roots] *vid* in the sense of "knowledge" and *vid* in the sense of "acquisition" in the *liṭ* (perfect) tense are like those of *śaph*.
The suffix *matup* is applied because he possesses hooves (*śapha*).
By the rule "after a short vowel or a word ending in *-ṅ*, *matup* [is acute]," the *matup* is accented.
[This applies to the form] *nama*.
The form *ṇamu* is the perfect tense (*liṭ*) form of the root meaning "in bowing" (*prahvatve*).
Due to the optional nature of reduplication in the Vedic language (*chandasi*), there is no reduplication here.
Because it constitutes a separate sentence, it lacks the low-pitched accent (*anighāta*).
*Guhyam*:

From the root *guhū* in the sense of "concealing" (*saṃvaraṇe*), the suffix *kyap* is applied according to the rule "it should be stated that [the suffix *kyap*] may be added after roots ending in *śam* and *guh*. Due to its *kit* status, there is no *guṇa* strengthening.
Because the affix has the *pittva* designation, it is unaccented (*anudātta*), and thus the accent of the verbal root remains.
*Dadhe* is the form of the root *dhā* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
*Dakṣiṇāvān*.
[The root] *dakṣ* means "to increase.
By the rule "from *du* and *dakṣ*, the suffix *iman*," the suffix *in* is applied.
The suffix *matup* is applied in the sense of "this belongs to him.
In the *saṃhitā*, the lengthening of the preceding vowel occurs according to the rule "it is seen in other cases as well.
It is without accent (*nissvara*).
Discerning the light from the darkness, may we choose it; may we be far from misfortune in the encounter.
O Indra, drinker of Soma, strengthened by Soma, enjoy these songs of the most frequent singer.

Choosing light, discerning it from darkness, may we be far removed from misfortune in the encounter. O Indra, drinker of Soma, increased by Soma, take pleasure in these songs of the most devoted singer. 7.

From out of the darkness of night, Indra—manifesting as the Sun and knowing [the world] with particular clarity—chose light; he distributed the illumination that sustains the worldly activities of the universe. Alternatively, it means manifesting while specifically discerning [the enemy], such as Vṛtra, who consists of darkness (tamas).
1. Kha, ga, ca, ja, ṇa, ta, na, bha, sa—thus.
2. In the manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ja, ṇa, na, bha, and sa, the phrase "the form ending in ... [is] non-existent" does not appear. 3.
In the sequence of kha, ga, gha, ca, ja, ṇa, ta, na, pha, bha, and sa, it occurs in the Ūrdhvasāvinī [recension].
4. The [variant] "bhogavatyām" does not exist in manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ja, ṇa, na, bha, and sa.
5. The [variant] "gūḍham" does not exist in manuscripts kha, ga, ja, ṇa, na, bha, la, and sa.
6. The [variant] "vijānan" does not exist in manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ja, ṇa, na, bha, and sa.
7. There is no [word] "not knowing. Having slain Vṛtra, he chose light.
May we, being free from evil or sin, remain—be—in a place that is *vabhīka*, devoid of fear, far removed (*vāre*) from evil.

O Soma-drinker, you who drink the Soma, therefore O Indra, increased by the drinking of Soma— O Vṛtraghna, you who cause many enemies to wither away (purutamasya)— enjoy, that is, accept, the measured words, the voices characterized as hymns, of the officiating priest who performs the praise for you, the one who acts as a benefactor (kāruḥ).
*vṛṇīta* is the form of the root *vṛṅ* (meaning "to choose" or "to select") in the *laṅ* tense. *Vijānan*.
The root *jñā* means "to know. Specialized knowledge is illumination (*prakāśa*). It takes the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
*Abhīke*:
that in which fear (*bhī*) does not exist.
From this, the suffix *kap* is applied according to Pāṇini Sūtra 5.4.154: *śeṣād vibhāṣā*.

When the rule "nañsubhyām" [Pāṇini 6.2.172] would have resulted in an udātta accent on the final syllable, the rule "akapi pūrvam" [Pāṇini 6.2.173] prescribes that the preceding member takes the udātta accent.

Regarding *purutamasya*: from the root *tam* (meaning "to be weary") with the causative suffix (*ṇi*), followed by the suffix *ac* (as in the *pacādi* class), the initial of the second member receives the udātta accent according to the rule "parādiś chandasi bahulam" [Pāṇini 6.2.199].
May the two worlds, Heaven and Earth, swell with light for our sacrifice; may we be free from abundant distress.
For even the many assaults of a mortal who oppresses us, O Vasus, you bring across safely with your great protection.

Light for the sacrifice, may it be with both heaven and earth; may we be far from abundant evil. For even against the many attacks of a mortal, O Vasus, you who are easy to cross over, protect us with your great support.
O Indra, may that Sun, the light that illuminates the world, distinguish heaven and earth for the performance of rites such as the Agnihotra; let him experience and illuminate them.
May we remain far away from abundant evil or sin.

O Vasus, you who cause all things to dwell [in prosperity], who, through Indra’s gift, are excellent ferrymen—excellent ferrymen meaning those whose crossing is beautiful, and who are capable of being brought face-to-face through praise—you bestow vast wealth, exceedingly abundant and endowed with prosperity; you grant it to the mortal who gives much.
Here, an appropriate verb must be supplied.
It may be so;
it is a form derived from the root *as* in the potential mood (*liṅ*).
In this case, due to the *saṃhitā*, the substitution of *ṣ* for the initial *s* of the following *asti* occurs by the rule "upasargāt prādurbhyāṃ styaścaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.3.77).
Nighātaḥ | Tuñjataḥ | [The root] *tuji*, *piji*, and *laji* [are used] in the senses of injury, giving, and dwelling.
In the word *śatrunamaḥ*, the case ending (*vibhakti*) is udātta. In *bṛhaṇāvat*:
from the root *bṛh* (meaning "to grow" or "increase"), the suffix *yu* is added in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) according to the Uṇādi rules.
The accent of the suffix.
We invoke for our good the bountiful Indra, the most heroic in this battle, the winner of booty;
the one who hears us, the fierce one for our protection in the soma-pressings, who slays the Vṛtras and is the conqueror of riches.

For prosperity, let us invoke the bountiful Indra in this battle, the most heroic in the winning of booty—he who hears us, the fierce one for our protection amidst the hymns, who slays the Vṛtras and is the conqueror of riches. 9.
This has been explained.
By illuminating the meaning of the Vedas, may the Lord— who dispels the darkness within the heart—
bestow the four goals of human life, which transcend the world of duality.

Thus ends the second chapter of the third book (*aṣṭaka*) in the *Ṛgveda-saṃhitā-bhāṣya*, titled *Vedārthaprakāśa*, composed by Sāyaṇācārya, the upholder of the imperial sovereignty of the illustrious King Vīrabukka—the glorious sovereign over kings, supreme lord, and promoter of the Vedic path—under the patronage of Mādhava.
1. In the manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ja, ṇa, na, bha, and sa, the word "bahūn" is absent.
2. In the manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ja, ṇa, and na, the word "sevasva" is absent. 3. In the manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ja, ṇa, and sa, the word "dūre" is absent.
4. *gha*—you give.
*Hi* is *pūraṇa* (a filler).
5. *kha*—thus it has already been explained previously; *ja* and *ṇa* are as before; *na* has not been explained.
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose very breath is the Vedas and who fashioned the entire universe from the Vedas.
Now begins the third chapter of the third Aṣṭaka. The second hymn, consisting of nine verses beginning with “indra tvā,” is addressed to Viśvāmitra; it is in the Gāyatrī meter and dedicated to Indra.
Thus it has been enumerated: “indra tvā, [in] Gāyatrī, indeed.”

This hymn is used in the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin’s śastra during the morning pressing at the Agniṣṭoma. It is stated in the Sūtra: “The three beginning with ‘O Indra, thee the bull, we invoke’” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 5.10). The first [verse] is the Prasthitayājyā for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin at the morning pressing.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "O Indra, [the Maruts] of whom you are the bull... (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.5).
O Indra, we invoke you, the bull, when the Soma is pressed; as such, drink of the sweet food.
O Indra, we invoke you, the bull, when the Soma is pressed; as such, drink of this sweet food. 1.
He is called Indra because he rejoices and plays within the moon, the essence of Soma;
or else, he is Indra because he directly beholds this entire world.
O Indra, praised by many, take delight in the pressed Soma, which knows the sacred seasons.
Drink and pour yourself forth until you are satiated.
O Indra, praised by many, take pleasure in the pressed Soma that knows the seasons; drink it and pour down the satisfying draught! 2.
O Indra, take pleasure in this pressed and purified Soma, which knows the proper season (*ṛtuvid*) and brings about the attainment of wisdom (*kratu*).
O you who are praised by many (*puruṣṭuta*), O Indra, drink this Soma which satisfies and provides nourishment.
Having drunk this Soma, pour it into your belly.
The meaning is that one should hold [the breath] in such a way that it does not fall from the navel.
*harya*: this is the form of the root *harya* (meaning "to move" and "to desire") in the imperative (*loṭ*),
with the *nighāta* accent.
O Puruṣṭuta!
[The change to *p* in *puruṣṭuta* occurs in the Saṃhitā by the rule "stutastomayoś chandasi" (Pāṇini 8.3.105). O Vṛṣan!
This is the form of the verb *vṛṣ* (meaning "to sprinkle") in the imperative (*loṭ*).
Due to its following the prefix *āṅ*, it is subject to the rule of *nighāta* (elision of accent).
[The form] is *tātṛpim*.

From the root *tṛp* in the sense of "to satisfy" (*prīṇana*), the suffix *kin* is applied according to Pāṇini Sūtra 3.2.161.2, which states: "In the Veda (*chandasi*), [the suffix *kin* is seen] after *sad* and others. Because that [suffix *kin*] is a *liṅga* (neuter gender), there is dual number and so forth.
In the *saṃhitā*, the lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) occurs by the rule "anyeṣām api" (Pāṇini 6.3.137).
A word beginning with *nic* is udātta on its first syllable.
O Indra, Lord of All, being praised, further our sacrifice accompanied by prayer along with all the gods.
O Indra, Lord of All, being praised, further our sacrifice accompanied by offerings along with all the gods. 3.

O Lord of all, praised by those who offer hymns, being lauded by the singers, O Indra, Lord of the people, the Maruts—accompanied by all the gods, by all the deities worthy of sacrifice—you, [O Lord] of *dhitāvān* (one who possesses the offering)—*vāna* means that which is gathered or brought together; thus *dhitāvān* refers to one for whom the *dhita* (placed) offering has been prepared; that is to say, one who has the sacrificial oblation ready—extend (*pra tira*) this our sacrifice, cause it to increase greatly. The sense is: "Make it complete by accepting the oblation. *Naḥ*: The substitution of *ṇ* occurs in the *saṃhitā* according to the rule *upasargādbahulam*. *Dhitāvānam*: Derived from the root *dhā* (in the sense of holding or nourishing) with the suffix *niṣṭhā* (*kta*). In the *bahuvrīhi* compound, the accent falls on the first member. *Tira*: From the root *tṛ*, the suffix *śa* is added by the rule *chandasi luṅlaṅliṭaḥ*. The accent is that of the suffix. *Stavāna*: From the root *ṣṭuñ* (to praise). By the rule *saṃmānaca ratuvaḥ*, the suffix *ānac* is added in the sense of the object (*karman*), even in the absence of an accompanying word (*upapada*). It receives the *nighāta* (elision of accent) because it is an *āmantrita* (vocative).
O Indra, lord of the virtuous, these pressed Soma drops, the bright juices, go forth toward your dwelling.
O Indra, these pressed Soma drops of yours, the bright drops, go forth toward your dwelling, O Lord of the True. 4.
O Indra, Lord of the Good, these bright, exhilarating drops—these radiant, pressed, and purified Soma juices given by us—dwell within your abode (*kṣaya*).
"Abode" (*kṣaya*) means that which is inhabited; it refers here to the belly (*jaṭhara*). They go forth, entering into you with great force.
The meaning is: "Hold them fast."

*Kṣaya*: From the root *kṣi* in the sense of "dwelling" (*nivāsa*) and "going" (*gati*), the suffix *gha* is applied in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Although the accent of the suffix would normally result in an udātta on the final syllable, by the rule "the word *kṣaya* [meaning] dwelling" (*kṣayo nivāse*), it takes an udātta on the first syllable.
*Candrāsaḥ*: [The root] *cad* is used in the senses of "to delight" and "to shine. From this, the suffix *ra* is applied according to the rule beginning with *sphāyitañci*, etc.
‘Ājaser amuk’—thus [the suffix] amuk [is applied]. It has the accent of the suffix (pratyayasvara). Indavaḥ.

The suffix *u* is applied by the rule "underdivādeḥ" (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.12). Because the term "nit" is understood as a carry-over [from a previous rule], the word is udātta-accented on its first syllable.

1. [The suffix] -a occurs after *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *bha*, and others. 2. [The suffix] -a occurs with *ja*, *ṇa*, and the deities to be sacrificed to (*yajñīyadevaiḥ*). 3. In *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *na*, *bha*, *la*, and *sa*, the word "tava" does not exist. 4. In *kha*, *ga*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, and *sa*, it has an udātta accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*). 5. In *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *na*, *bha*, *la*, and *sa*, [the root means] "to shine" (*dīptau*); in *ja* and *ṇa*, "in shining" (*dīptau*) does not exist. 6. *La* indicates the addition of the augment *asu*.

**Dadhiṣvā jaṭharai sutaṃ somamindra vareṇyam | tava yukṣāsa indavaḥ || 5 ||** O Indra, place within your belly the pressed Soma, the most excellent. Your juices are ready for you. || 5 || **dadhiṣva** (place), **jaṭharai** (in the belly), **sutam** (pressed), **somam** (Soma), **indra** (O Indra), **vareṇyam** (most excellent), **tava** (your), **yukṣāsaḥ** (ready/fit), **indavaḥ** (juices). || 5 ||

O Indra, hold within your belly and sustain the pressed Soma, which is most excellent (*vareṇya*) and desirable by all. These drops (*indavas*), these Somas, are your *yukṣās*. They dwell or reside in heaven; thus they are called *yukṣās*. Therefore, the sense is: "Sustain those that are your own. *dadhiṣva*: This is the form of the root *dhā* (to place) in the imperative (*loṭ*). Since the augment (*iṭ*) is unaccented according to the rule "augmentals are unaccented" (*āgamā anudāttāḥ*), the accent falls on the suffix. *vareṇyam*: From the root *vṛṅ* (to choose). The suffix *eṇya* is added according to the rule "from *vṛṅ*, *eṇya*" (*vṛṅ eṇyaḥ*). It is acutely accented on the first syllable because it belongs to the *vṛṣādi* group. *yukṣās*: From the root *kṣi* (to dwell). The suffix *ḍa* is added according to the rule "it is seen after other roots as well" (*anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate*). The accent follows the rule for the final member of a compound (*kṛduttarapadasvaraḥ*). 5.

The rule "of that which is addressed" (*āmantritasya*) accounts for the optional acute accent on the first syllable. *Pāhi* is the form derived from the root *pā* (to drink) in the imperative (*loṭ*).

*Vuninaḥ*:

The suffix *ni* is applied by the rule *ata ini-ṭhanau*. Its accent [is udātta]. *Sacante*: this is the form of the root *pac* (meaning ‘to join together’) in the present tense (*laṭ*). *Akṣitā*: this is the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) of the root *kṣi* (meaning ‘to perish’). Here, because it has the sense of the causative (*ṇyad-artha*), there is no lengthening of the vowel; for that very reason, by the rule *kṣiyo dīrghāt*, there is no substitution of *n* for the final *t* of the suffix. In the compound with the negative particle (*nañ*), its accent [is udātta]. *Pīśvī*: from the root *pā* (‘to drink’), the suffix *kaśva* is added, and by the rule *snādhyādayaśca*, the feminine form *strī* is substituted [for the suffix]; the accent is that of the suffix. Therefore, the sense is: "Come for the purpose of drinking the Soma."

*Sattaḥ*: This is derived from the root *pallu* in the sense of "falling apart" (*viśaraṇa*) and so forth, with the suffix *kta* used in the active sense (*kartari*) according to Pāṇini’s sūtra 3.4.72, *gatyarthakarmakaśliṣ...*.
Because all grammatical rules are optional in the Vedic language (*chandas*), there is here an absence of the change of the *niṣṭhā*-suffix vowel to *ṇa*.

Then, by the rule *pratyayottarapadayośca*, the substitution of *tvā* for the stem ending in *m* (i.e., *mad*) occurs before the suffix and in a subsequent member of a compound.

Although *tvayava* would have been expected [by the rule *tvā-au*], the substitution of *ā* occurs even before a consonant-initial case ending (other than those subject to the *anādeśa* restriction) due to the irregularity (*vyatyaya*) prescribed by the rule *yuṣmadasmador anādeśe*. *Asmayuḥ*. In the sense of "desiring us," the suffix *kyac* is applied. Regarding that, he says: "a suffix."
The elision of the final syllable of the preceding word is a Vedic (Chāndasa) phenomenon; it bears the accent of the suffix.

O Indra, come hither to this Soma—pressed by the stones, placed upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), the exhilarating drink (for *mada* means that by which one rejoices, i.e., Soma). Come to this very Soma! And by drinking of this Soma, may you quickly become satiated; indeed, be satisfied as much as possible. Regarding *mada*: from the root *madī* (to rejoice), the suffix *ap* is applied according to the rule *mado 'nupasarge*. Since the suffix is marked with *pittva*, it is unaccented, and thus the accent of the verbal root remains. Regarding *barhiṣṭhām*: from the root *ṣṭhā* (to stand), the suffix *kvip* is applied. In the *saṃhitā* stage, the *s* of the preceding word becomes *ṣ* according to the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ*; then *ṣ* changes to *ṣṭ* [before *th*]. The accent is that of the secondary member of the compound (*kṛduttarapadasvara*). Regarding *tṛṣṇavaḥ*: from the root *tṛp* (to satisfy), the suffix *leṭ* is applied with the augment *yaḍ*. Because of its connection with *kuvit*, it does not lose its accent (*anighāta*). Although the form *nṛmanas tṛṇoti* is listed among the *kṣubh*-class words (which would normally prohibit *ṇatva*), nevertheless, since all rules are optional in the Veda (*chandasi*), the prohibition of *ṇatva* does not apply here. The accent is that of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).

O Indra, drink the Soma of the bull shaken by the hands, pressed out with stones—the bull that pours forth the desired fruit. The falcon, whose flight is praiseworthy, the fair-winged one in the form of the meters, brought that Soma for you, who desire it. When the exhilaration born of the intoxication of that Soma has arisen, you draw toward yourself and bring under control all people (*kṛṣṭīḥ*); "people" (*kṛṣṭayaḥ*) are so called because they are drawn by action; you cause those rival men to fall away. When the intoxication of that Soma has arisen, you have caused the *gotrā* to swell; "clouds" (*gotrāḥ*) are so called because they protect (*gopāyanti*) the water (*go*) enclosed by rays within the rain-givers; you open them up. Regarding *vṛṣadhūtasya*: the root *dhṛñ* means "to shake"; in the past participle (*niṣṭhā*), there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* according to the rule *yasya vibhāṣā*. The accent of the first member is determined by the rule *tṛtīyā karmaṇi*. Regarding *śyenaḥ*: from the root *syaiṅ* "to go," the suffix *iman* is added by the rule *śāstyāhapravibhya imac*, forming *śyena*. It is called *śyena* because it moves swiftly (*śyāyate*). It is accented on the final syllable because of the *cit* suffix. Regarding *jabhāra*: this is the form of the root *hṛ* in the perfect tense with the suffix *ṇal*; the substitution of *bha* for *ha* occurs by the rule *hagrahorbhaśchandasi*. Due to its connection with *yad-vat*, it is not subject to the *anighāta* rule; it bears the accent of the perfect tense. Regarding *made*: from the root *madī* "to rejoice," the suffix *ap* is added by the rule *maḍo'nupasarge*. Because it ends in *pi*, it is unaccented; thus, the root accent remains. Regarding *gotrā*: from the root *gai* "to protect," the suffix *ka* is added by the rule *āto'nupasarge kaḥ*. The case-ending is replaced by *ḍā*; the accent is that of the single substitute. Regarding *vavardha*: from the root *vṛñ* "to choose/cover," in the perfect tense with the suffix *thal*, there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by the rule *ṛto bhāradvājasya*. There is *guṇa* strengthening; it bears the accent of the perfect tense.

This one | be | for thee | pleasing | Soma | hither | by the bay steeds | pressed | rejoicing | O Indra | with the bay steeds | come | mount | the golden chariot || 1 ||
"O Indra, with the bay horses"—for they carry the Soma juices, thus the pressing-stones are called *hari*s.
By them [the stones], this *sutaḥ* (pressed), i.e., poured forth from all sides; *haryataḥ*, i.e., desirable and lovely; *juṣāṇaḥ*, i.e., an object of delight—this *soma* shall be for *te*, for you.
Mount the green, i.e., green-colored, chariot yoked with bay horses;
then come toward us,
O desirable one.
The root *harya* is used in the senses of "going" and "desire."

This very Indra supported the *hariyāyasam*—that [earth] whose *dhāyasaḥ* (sustaining) rays are *haritaḥ* (green-colored). Likewise, he supported the earth, which has a *harivarṣasam* (green appearance) due to its plants. Between those two, heaven and earth, which are green (*haritaḥ*) in color, he found abundant (*bhūri*) food (*bhojanam*)—that is, fodder and such things which are called "food" because they are enjoyed—for his own two horses. And between those two, heaven and earth, Indra, who is green (*hariḥ*), moves about (*carati*). Those two, heaven and earth, Indra supported and supported. Regarding *hariyāyasam*: from the root *ḍudhāñ* (to support and nourish), the suffix *dṛśyasun* is applied according to the rule *vahilādhābhyaśchandasi*. Because *jin* is supplied as a governing suffix, *āto yuk* applies. In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the accent falls on the first member. Regarding *pṛthivīm*: by the rule *pratheḥ pivan saṃprasāraṇaṃ ca*, the suffix *pivan* is added, and by *pitrādibhyaśca*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added. It is oxytone by the accent of the suffix. Regarding *harivarṣasam*: from the roots *vṛṅ* (to enjoy/partake) and *śīb*, the suffix *asun* is added with the augment *puk* by the rule *vṛṅśībhyāṃ rūpasañjñayoḥ*. That which is enjoyed is *varpas* (form/appearance). In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the accent falls on the first member. Regarding *haritaḥ*: from the root *hañ* (to take away), the suffix *iti* is added by the rule *hyuruhiyuṣibhya itiḥ*. It is oxytone by the accent of the suffix. Regarding *bhojanam*: from the root *bhuja* (to protect and to eat), the suffix *lyuṭ* is added in the sense of the object by the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*. It is oxytone by the accent of the *lit* suffix. Regarding *antaḥ*: since it is listed among the *svarādi* group as being oxytone, it is oxytone. Regarding *carat*: the root *car* means "to move. This is a form in the *leṭ* (subjunctive) mood; it does not undergo *anudātta* (low pitch) because of its connection with *yat*.
Born as a tawny bull, he illumines the entire radiant realm;
the tawny-horsed one takes up his tawny weapon, the golden thunderbolt, within his arms.
As soon as he was born, the tawny bull illumines the entire radiant realm. He whose horses are tawny takes up his tawny weapon; he places the tawny thunderbolt within his arms.
The bull, the showerer of desires, Indra—golden-hued and having been born—shines upon the entire radiant world, illuminating it from all sides.
Likewise, Indra, whose horses are bay, holds the golden weapon in his arms;
he likewise holds the golden thunderbolt, which takes away the life-breath of enemies, in his two arms.

*jajñānaḥ*: [This is formed] from the root *jan* in the sense of "manifestation" (*prādurbhāve*), with the suffix *kānac* of the perfect tense (*liṭ*). By the rule beginning with *gamahana*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*).
Because it ends in a *cit* suffix, it has the udātta accent on the final syllable.
*Bhāti*: this is the form of the root *bhā* (in the sense of "shining") in the present tense (*laṭ*), with the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) internalized.
*rocana*: from the root *ruc* in the sense of "shining," the suffix *yuc* is applied according to the rule *anudāttetaśca halādeḥ*;
because it has the marker *c*, it is oxytone (accented on the final syllable).
In the word *bāhvoḥ*,
the case-ending is acute according to the rule "udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt" (Pāṇini 6.1.174).
Indra, with his bay horses, uncovered the desirable, vigorous, and bright thunderbolt enveloped in light;
he drank the pressed juice with his bay steeds and went forth with his bay steeds.
Indra [threw] the longing, bright, white thunderbolt, encased in brilliance; he opened [the way] for the Soma pressed by the tawny stones. With his tawny steeds, he drove forth the cows. ||5||

1. *ca*, *na*, *bha*, and *sa* are of green color (*haritavarṇa*). 2. In *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, and *sa*, the letter ‘ya’ is not present. 3. *na* is not observed [in this context]. 4. In *kha*, *ga*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *sa*, and *ta*, [the same applies]. 5. In *kha* and *bha*, it means "he holds" (*dhārayati*). 6. *Ja*: those two whose form is green-colored (*harita-varṇa-rūpa*). 7. *Na* and *sa* mean "striking" (*prahāraka*); *la* means "life-taking" (*prāṇahāraka*). 8. In *kha*, *ga*, *dha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *la*, and *sa*, it means "or" (*vā*).
This very one is Indra, who [seizes] the desirable (*haryantam*), lovely (*kamanīyam*), and bright (*arjunam*) [object]. He establishes its brightness.

He uncovered—that is, he made free from obstruction—the Soma that had been pressed by means of the white parrots, the milk and other ingredients, Vyāsa, the thunderbolt, and the swift bay horses; for they are called "bay" (*hari*) because they carry the juices of Soma. He [uncovered] it with those waters and the pressing-stones.
And so says a Vedic mantra: “Pūṣan, the glowing one, found the king who was hidden, concealed in a secret cave” (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.23.14).
Likewise, Indra—accompanied by his bay horses (*haribhiḥ*)—drove out the cows that had been carried off by the Paṇis; he brought them forth from the cavern and caused them to emerge.
*Arjuna*:
From the root *arja* in the sense of "to accumulate" (*arjana*), the suffix *un* is applied according to the rule *arjerṇiluk ca*,
resulting in a word that is devoid of accent (*nisvara*).
It is surrounded.
By the rule “the preceding member [of a compound] retains its original accent,” the verbal root *gati* retains its natural accent.
He drove away.
The root *aj* means "to go" and "to throw. In the present tense (*laṭ*), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
There is elision (*nighāta*) [of the verb accent].
8 | “With the delightful [songs]”—
thus [is he praised as] the devourer of Vṛtra, the shatterer of Vala, the destroyer of forts, and the driver-forth of the waters.
Indra, the driver of the chariot with the two bay horses, shatters even the firmest things.

Devourer of Vṛtra; breaker of Vala; shatterer of the fortresses; the driver of the waters; the mounter of the chariot; standing at the call of the two bay steeds—Indra breaks even that which is firm. 2.
This is that Indra, the devourer of Vṛtra—
he is called the devourer of Vṛtra because he devours, that is, destroys, Vṛtra; he is the shatterer of Vala.
Vala is the cloud because it covers the sky;
he is the breaker of that [cloud].
And thus says the mantra-text: "He split Vala" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 3.14.10).
Then, the "driving-away of waters" (apāmajaḥ)—the impeller of waters by means of bursting the clouds; the "shatterer of forts" (purāṃ darmah), the destroyer of the citadels belonging to the enemy;

likewise, when there is the "calling toward" (abhisvare) our two bay horses (haryoḥ), acting as the cause for their being urged toward us; he becomes the "stander upon the chariot" (rathasya sthātā), the one who mounts the chariot;
and thus, the "breaker" (ārujah) who completely shatters even those "firm" (dṛlhā cit)—that is, even the very strong enemies.
*vṛtrakhādaḥ*:

[This is derived] from the root *khād* in the sense of "eating," with the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of the object; the accent falls on the final syllable of the compound according to the rule for the accentuation of the subsequent member of a *kṛt*-derived compound.
*Valarujaḥ*:
[The root] *ruj* means "to break.
When the object (*karman*) is used as an upapada, the suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule for words such as *mūlavibhuja*.
In the compound *ārujaḥ*, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the second case ending according to the rule *tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam*; it takes the accent of the *thā-thādi* group. Thus, *ārujaḥ*.
From the root *ruj* in the sense of "breaking," the suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule for roots ending in *ig* and having a penultimate vowel;
in the compound, the accent is determined by the rule for *thā-thādi* suffixes.
Like a deep well, you nourish our mental power; like cows, O good guardian, they have flowed forth toward the pasture like streams to a pool.
Like wells, you bring forth the deep; like a skillful herdsman, you nourish the cows. Like milch-cows to the pasture, like streams reaching the lake, they have attained [you]. 3.

O Indra, just as you nourish the deep and vast expanses of the oceans with water, so too do you nourish—meaning you cause to thrive by bestowing desired fruits—this sacrificer who performs the sacrifice.
Here is an illustration:
just as a good herdsman (*sugopāḥ*) properly nourishes the cows with pasture grass, even so [do you nourish this sacrificer].
Just as cows reach the pasture—grass and such—you likewise reach the Soma juices.
And those Somas, like artificial rivers (*kulyā*), pervade you, just as they reach a lake, a great reservoir of water; thus they have reached and encompassed you.

Regarding *gambhīrān*: from the root *gādh*, meaning "to seek a firm footing" (*pratiṣṭhā*) or "to desire," and also "in a knot" (*granthe*), the suffix *harac* is applied by the rule *gabhīra-gambhīrau* (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.475).
By this rule, the addition of the augment *num*, the substitution of *s* for the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*), and the change of the vowel to *a* are all prescribed as irregularities (*nipātana*).
Because it ends in the suffix *cvi*, it is accented on the final syllable (*antodātta*).

As in the word *uddhi*: when the word *udaka* is used as an upapada with the root *dhā* in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), the suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule "after a verbal root, [the suffixes] *kvip* and others are added in the sense of an object or a locus."
In the word *udaka*, there is the substitution of *ud* [for *udaka*] by Pāṇini’s rule 6.3.58, *pepavāsavāhanadhiṣu ca*.
It has the accent of a *kṛt*-derivative (*kṛtsvara*).
There is no elision of the case-ending when combined with *iva*.
"puṣyasi" is the form of the verb "puṣa" (meaning "to nourish") in the present tense (*laṭ*), with the causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) implied;
it is subject to *nighāta* (elision of the accent).
"Sugopāḥ" is a form derived from the root *gopāyati* with the suffix *kvip*. For example:
The word *yathā* is unaccented at the end of a foot according to *Phiṭ-sūtra* 85 (*yatheti pādānte*).
[Regarding] *āśata*: from the root *aś* in the sense of "pervasion," the *laṅ* suffix is applied; by the rule *bahulam chandasi*, there is elision (*luk*) of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*).
The elision of the accent.

1. [The variants] kha, ga, ca, ja, ṇa, na, bha, and sa read "connected with enemies. 2. [The variants] kha, ga, ca, ja, ṇa, na, bha, and sa do not have the word "of the ancients" (*purāṇāṃ*). 3. [The variant] gha reads "like wells. 4. [The variants] ja and ṇa read "like oceans. 5. [The variants] na, la, and sa do not have the prefix "pra-.
O Indra, bring us wealth that impels us; recognize our share as one who knows it. Shake down for us, O Indra, the wealth that carries us across, like a tree laden with ripe fruit.
Bring us powerful wealth, as one brings his allotted share; shake it for us like ripe fruit from a tree, O Indra, like a branch—wealth that carries us across to the further shore.
O Indra, bring to us—that is, bestow upon us—*tuja*, wealth characterized by riches that overcomes our enemies, and a son; accomplish this for us.
In this regard, there is an illustration: *aṃśam na*.
Just as a father, when his son has mastered the ways of worldly affairs, grants him a share of his own property, so [should you grant us this].
Furthermore, just as a hook shakes a tree for the sake of ripe fruit, so do you shake—that is, move—our wealth (*vasu*), which is the means of crossing over and the perfect fulfiller of our desires;
that is to say, grant it.
They assert:
this is the form of the root *jñā* (in the sense of "to understand") in the present participle (*śatṛ*),
forming a *prādi-samāsa*.
In the word *śatrunoḥ*, the case ending (*vibhakti*) is udātta.
[The form] *dhunuhi* is the imperative (*loṭ*) form of the root *dhūñ* (meaning "to shake").
*Saṃpāraṇam*:
This is derived from the causative form (*ṇyanta*) of the root *pṛ*, meaning "to protect" or "to fill," with the suffix *lyuṭ* used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*).
In the compound, the accent falls on the final syllable according to the rule for *kṛt* suffixes (*kṛtsvara*).
O Indra, you are self-sustained, the self-ruler, easy to invoke, and most readily praised.
Increasing in might, O much-invoked one, become for us the most glorious of those who hear our call.

Self-moving, O Indra, you are the self-ruling sovereign; you are one whose sacrifices are remembered and who is most highly praised by himself. Increasing in strength, O much-lauded one, become for us the most renowned of those who hear. 5.

O Indra, you are self-sustained (*svayu*) and possessed of wealth; likewise, you are the self-ruling king (*svarāṭ*) of heaven. You are one whose desires are fulfilled, worthy of auspicious praise, and most highly renowned for your own glory. O much-praised Indra, increasing and growing by your might and strength, become for our sake the most excellent possessor of glorious food (*suśravastama*). *svayuḥ*: From the word *sva*, the suffix *yu* is added in the sense of possession. *svarāṭ*: From the root *rāj* (to shine), the suffix *kvip* is applied; the change to *ṣ* occurs by rule [Pāṇini 8.3.61] due to the preceding vowel. *smadiṣṭiḥ*: *Smat* has the meaning of *sumat*. The elision of the vowel *u* is Vedic. In the *bahuvrīhi* compound, the accent falls on the first member. *puruṣṭuta*: In the *saṃhitā* text, the change to *ṣ* occurs by the rule "after *stata* and *stoma* in the Veda" [Pāṇini 8.3.107]. *bhava*: This is the form of the root *bhū* in the imperative (*loṭ*). The lengthening in the *saṃhitā* occurs by the rule "for a word of two syllables ending in *at*, before a non-tiṅ verb" [Pāṇini 6.3.135]. *suśravastamaḥ*: The word *śravaḥ* ends in a case-suffix. In the *bahuvrīhi*, the first syllable of the second member is acute by the rule "in the Veda, a word of two syllables [beginning with a prefix] is acute on the first" [Pāṇini 6.2.119]. To that, the superlative suffix *tamap* is added. Because this suffix is marked with *p*, it does not cause the udātta accent; thus, the accent of the *bahuvrīhi* remains. || 5 ||
The eighth hymn, consisting of five verses, beginning with "yudhamasya te," is dedicated to Indra and composed by Viśvāmitra;
this is indicated by the *Anukramaṇikā* as "yudhamasya.
On the fourth day of the ten-night rite (*daśarātra*), during the *niṣkevalya* litany, the hymn "yudhamasya te" is used for the insertion of the *nivid*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Where has Indra been heard of as his warrior? [This is] the Niṣkevalya" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.11).
In the one-day sacrifice named Ṛṣabha as well, this hymn is the insertion for the Niṣkevalya.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "'Yudhamasya ta' is the midday [service]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 9.7).

1. He who possesses the form of wealth and fame as described before, increasing by vigor and strength—that is, having the nature of increasing again and again—he who is praised by many (puruṣṭuta), [be] for us.
2. He who is a giver of excellent food (ca).
3. [The reading] kha-ga-ca-ja-ṇa-sa belongs to Ṛṣabha.

O Indra, the heroic deeds of you—the warrior, the bull, the self-ruling lord, the fierce one, the youth, the ancient, the impetuous, the undecaying wielder of the thunderbolt, the renowned and the great—are indeed mighty. *Yudhmasya te vṛṣabhasya svarāja ugrasya yūnaḥ sthavirasya ghṛṣvaiḥ | ajūryato vajriṇo vīryāṇi indra śrutasya mahato mahāni || 1 ||* O Indra, yours—of you who are *yudhma* (warlike), *vṛṣabha* (a bull that showers desired fruits), *svarāj* (self-ruling lord of wealth), *ugra* (fierce and capable), *yuvan* (ever-youthful in seizing), *sthavira* (ancient and enduring), *ghṛṣva* (impetuous in crushing enemies), *ajūryat* (undecaying), *vajrin* (wielder of the thunderbolt), *śruta* (renowned throughout the three worlds), and therefore *mahat* (great)—your heroic deeds (*vīryāṇi*) are truly *mahāni* (mighty). Grammatical notes: * *Yudhmasya*: From the root *yudh* (to fight); the suffix *map* is applied according to the rule *iṣuyudhīndhidasi*. * *Yūnaḥ*: From the root *yu*; the suffix *kanin* is applied according to the rule *kaninyuvṛṣi*. The vowel change (*saṃprasāraṇa*) occurs by the rule *śruvamaghonāmataddhite*. It has the accent of the first syllable (*nisvara*). * *Sthavirasya*: Derived from the root *stha*; it is an irregular form (*nipātita*) ending in the suffix *kirac*, according to the rule *ajiraśiśaraśithila*. * *Ghṛṣvaiḥ*: From the root *ghṛṣ* (to rub/struggle); it is an irregular form ending in the suffix *kin*, according to the rule *kṛvigṛdhivacchavi*. Because of the suffix *nic*, it is accented on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*).

O Great One, O Buffalo, by these manly powers you are great; you are the piercer of wealth, the fierce one, overcoming others. You alone are the king of the entire universe; as such, fight for the sake of battle and dwell among the people. O Mahiṣa, worthy of honor, O fierce Indra, you are great. O piercer of wealth—meaning you who lead wealth to its fulfillment through giving, enjoyment, and renunciation—you exist overcoming and subduing other enemies by means of your manly powers (*vṛṣṇyebhiḥ*). Likewise, you are the sole, peerless king of the entire world. As such, "fight" (*yodharyā*) against your rivals and "dwell" (*kṣayaryā*) among the people. The intention is: having slain the oppressors, establish the virtuous in their proper place. *Mahiṣa*: from the root *maha* (to honor). The suffix *ṭiṣvan* is applied according to *avimahoṣṭiṣvan* (Uṇādisūtra 1.45). It is unaccented due to being in the vocative case. *vṛṣṇyebhiḥ*: derived from *vṛṣan*. The suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of "belonging to" (*bhava*) according to *bhave chandasi*. It is acutely accented on the first syllable by the rule *yato ’nāvaḥ*. *yodharyā*: the form of the causative of the root *yudh* (to fight) in the imperative. It is not unaccented because it follows *ca* in the list of particles (*cādiṣu ca*). Its own accent remains. *kṣayaryā*: the form of the causative of the root *kṣi* (to dwell/to go) in the imperative. Here too, as before, there is no elision of the accent.

Shining forth, he has surpassed all measures; unopposed from every side, he has surpassed the gods. By his might, Indra has surpassed heaven and earth; the impetuous one has surpassed the broad and vast mid-air. 3. He has surpassed all measures; shining forth, he has surpassed [them]; unopposed from every side, he has surpassed the gods. By his greatness, Indra has surpassed heaven and earth; the impetuous one has surpassed the broad and mighty mid-air. 3.
1. To be honored by all people.
2. Unassailable by men; unassailable even by the gods.
Shining forth, being given away from all sides—by everyone.
Unfathomable—his capacity being thus undeterminable—Indra, the possessor of Soma, surpassed even the *mātrās*.
"Mātrās" are so called because they are measured (*mīyante*) or delimited; they refer here to gleanings of grain.
Even from those, he excelled (*vyririce*), being preeminent due to his greatness.
Likewise, by his might (*majmanā*), he surpasses even the gods; "might" (*majman*) refers to the ocean of suffering, for he overcomes enemies through it—
he has surpassed them with that power.
Thus he has surpassed both heaven and earth;
thus he has surpassed even the vast and great intermediate space.
Regarding *mātrābhiḥ*:
from the root *māṅ* in the sense of "measuring" (*māne*) and "sound" (*śabde*), the suffix *tṛn* is applied according to the rule *huyāmāśubhasibhyastṛn*.
Due to its being marked with *ṇi* (the *ṇ* of *tṛn*), it is acutely accented on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*).
In the *saṃhitā* [text], there is a long vowel according to the rule “*dvalope pūrvasya dīrgho’ṇaḥ*” (Pāṇini 6.3.111).
The form *rocamānaḥ* is derived from the root *ruca* (to shine) with the suffix *śānac*.
In its case, by the rule regarding the accent of sārvadhātuka suffixes, the accent of the verbal root (dhātusvara) prevails; it is uncontradicted [by other rules]. [The root is] *iṇ* "to go."
The suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).
It forms a *prādi*-compound.
In a compound with the negative particle *nañ*, it bears the accent of that [particle].
*Majmanā*:
[derived from] *dumasjo* in the sense of purification;
the suffix *manic* is added according to the *Auṇādika* rules.
The substitution of *jaś* occurs by the rule "jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi. Because it possesses the *cit* designation, it is udātta-accented on the final syllable. [The form is] *pṛthivyāḥ*.
The acute accent (udātta) of the case-ending is due to the rule "udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt."

The Somas pressed from of old enter into Indra—who is wide, profound, formidable by birth, all-encompassing, and the protector of prayers—just as flowing rivers enter the ocean. 4. Wide. Profound. By birth. Toward. Formidable. All-encompassing. Protector. Of prayers. Indra. The Somas. From of old. Pressed. Like the ocean. As flowing [rivers]. Enter. 4.
The vast, the great, and therefore the deep, the great space; by birth, that is, by his very nature, fierce and terrifying to enemies—the depth itself is being described.

Pervading all, extending everywhere, the protector (*vratam*) of prayers (*matīnām*) or of the singers—such an Indra, from of old, on former days, the pressed Soma juices, purified by the stones, enter him face to face.
In this regard, there is an illustration: "Like the ocean"—just as flowing rivers enter the ocean, so it is.
By birth (*januṣā*): from the root *janī* in the sense of "manifestation," the suffix *usi* is applied according to the rule *janerusiḥ*. [He is] all-encompassing (*viśvavyacasam*).
The word *vyaca* is derived from the root *vyac* in the sense of "making wide" (*vyājīkaraṇe*).

According to the rule "it should be stated that for the root *vyac*, [the suffix] does not take the *ḍi* augment when followed by *kuṭādi* or *amanas*," there is an absence of the *ḍi* augment here because of the exclusion (*paryudāsāt*) regarding the word *anasi*.
Thus, *viśvavyacāḥ* is a name of Indra.
In the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the final syllable of the first member is acute-accented according to the rule "viśvaṃ saṃjñāyām. [The word] *avataṃ* [is derived from] the root *ava*,
meaning "to protect" and so forth.
The suffix *at* is derived from the *auṇādika* [list]; because it is marked with the indicator *c*, it is udātta-accented on the final syllable.

O Indra, that Soma which Earth and Heaven bear for you with longing, as a mother bears her child—that very one they urge forth for you; that very bull the Adhvaryus purify for you to drink. 5. O Indra, that Soma which Earth and Heaven bear for you with longing, as a mother bears her child—that very one they urge forth for you; that very bull the Adhvaryus purify for you to drink. 5.
O Indra, may Heaven and Earth—the two worlds—sustain and hold this Soma for you with their own desire; they maintain it as an internal possession, just as a mother bears her embryo.
In this matter, there is an illustration: "like an embryo.
Just as a mother carries the embryo, so too [do Heaven and Earth].
He is the bull of all desires: 1. with all the gods;
2. [the variants] kha, ga, ca, and cha; [the variants] na, sa, and ya.

3. For those who possess *kha*, *ga*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *na*, or *sa*, [the vowel] *vā*; for those who possess *gha* or *pa*, [the vowel] *u*; for those who possess *ca* or *pha*, [the vowel] *ū*. 4. For those who possess *ja* or *ṇa*, the sound *he* does not exist.

O *adhvaryu*s, desiring the sacrifice for the sacrificer, O Indra, you who rain down blessings, do you prepare that Soma; they impel it, they send it forth. Moreover, they cleanse that Soma for your drinking. Now, Heaven and Earth—[the form] *dyāvā* is a substitute for *divaḥ*, accented on the first syllable. Because of the exclusion [in the rule] "not when the second member begins with an unaccented vowel, except in the case of *pṛthivī*, *rudra*, *pūṣan*, and *manthin*," the rule "in a dual compound of deities" applies, resulting in the original accent of both members. The reversal of the order in the compound is Vedic. Regarding *bibhrataḥ*: from the root *bhr̥* (to bear/sustain), in the present participle (*luṭ*), the substitution of *it* occurs in the reduplicated syllable by the rule "for *bhṛ*, *jr̥*, and *mi*. Due to its connection with *yat* (the relative pronoun), there is no elision of the accent. Since it does not follow a suffix beginning with a vowel, the accent "the first syllable of reduplicated stems" does not apply; rather, it has the accent of the suffix. Regarding *tvāyā*: in the sense of "desiring you," the suffix *kyac* is added after a noun ending in a case-suffix (*supa ātmanaḥ kyac*). The change of the initial *d* of the preceding word to *ā* is Vedic. The suffix *ap* is added in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*) by the rule "after a root. By the rule "of case-endings, *su*, *luk*, etc.," the third case ending takes a long vowel through homogeneous combination; this is the accent of the single substitute. Regarding *adhvaryavaḥ*: "desiring the sacrifice" (*adhvaram icchantah*). The suffix *kyac* is added after a noun ending in a case-suffix. There is the elision of the vowel *a* by the rule "there is elision of the *a* of *kyac*, *adhvara*, and *pṛtanā* before the suffix *ṛc*. The suffix *up* is added in the Veda by the rule "after a stem ending in *kyac* in the Veda. It has the accent of the suffix. Regarding *pātavai*: from the root *pā* (to drink). The suffix *tavai* is used in the sense of the infinitive (*tumun*). By the rule "the final syllable of the root and the suffix are simultaneously acute," both the end of the root and the suffix are acute. The particle *u* is designated as a *pragṛhya*. 10.
The fifth hymn, consisting of nine verses, beginning with "marutvān," is composed by Viśvāmitra, is in the Triṣṭubh metre, and is addressed to Indra.
"Marutvān" is its entry in the Anukramaṇikā.
In the ten-night sacrifice (daśarātra), on the fourth day, this hymn serves as the "Nividdhānīya" in the Marutvatīya Śastra.

And it is stated in the Sūtra: “Hear our call, O Indra, accompanied by the Maruts”—this is the *marutvatīya* [śastra] for the one-day sacrifice named *Ṛṣabha*. And it is stated in the Sūtra: “O Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, fight this [foe]”—this is the midday [service].
O Indra, bull among the Maruts, drink the Soma for the battle; enjoy it for exhilaration.
Pour the wave of sweetness into your belly; you have been the king of the pressed juices from time immemorial.

Accompanied by the Maruts, O Indra, bull-like, drink the Soma for the battle, according to your own nature, for exhilaration. Pour into your belly the wave of the sweet juice; you have been the king of the pressed libations from of old. 1.
O Indra, you who are the bull, the showerer of waters,
accompanied by the Maruts— the divine hosts—

do thou drink that Soma for exhilaration, for the sake of the delightful battle, following after the *anuṣvadham* (the portion of one's own will) which is attended by Agni in the form of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and other offerings.

Furthermore, pour out from all sides—that is, sprinkle—the wave, the mass of many-flavored Soma which intoxicates, into your *jaṭhara* (belly); for that in which swallowed food settles is called the *jaṭhara*, the belly. Pour it into that belly.
Since from of old, through former days, you have been the king—the lord—of the pressed-out Soma juices;
that is to say, not only of those [pressed] now.

On this matter Yāska says: "O Indra accompanied by the Maruts—that bull, the showerer of waters—drink the Soma for the sake of the battle, for the delightful encounter; drink it following after the food, for exhilaration, for intoxication, and for victory. Pour the wave of honey into your belly."
1. "Madhu somam" is a figurative expression (aupamika). 2. "ta-" is used in the sense of the infinitive suffix -tum. 3. "na-" is the index (anukramaṇikā).
On the tenth day, this hymn is recited during the Marutvatīya Śastra.
Accordingly, in the section titled "On the Tenth Day," the Sūtra states: "The Marutvatīya [Śastra] begins with 'Indra accompanied by the Maruts'.
O Great-minded One, this hymn belongs to the Marutvatīya Śastra.
The auspicious narrative of Padmāratha, along with Rāvayasa and Sanīla, is prescribed by the Sūtra: "Marutvān indra vṛṣabho raṇāya" (RV 8.96). 3.
[This occurs] in the third Śastra of the Marutvatīya section in the Ga and Ca recensions; in the Ja and Ṇa recensions, it is in the third Śastra known as the Marutvatīya.
4. In the Kha, Ga, Ca, Ja, Ṇa, and Sa recensions, the word "sūktaṃ" (hymn) does not appear.
5. [The syllables] kha, ga, ca, ja, ṇa, ta, and sa are pierced.
6. Kha and ga are likewise. 7. Ta is to be offered into the fire.
8. For the sake of battle with one who delights in *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *pha*, and *sa*; for battle with one who delights in *ja* and *ṇa*.
(Ṛgveda 2.52)

He prepares [it]. This other honey also [is so called] for this very reason. "Thou art the king of those who are in front on the days" (Nirukta 4.8). *Anusvadham*: existing following its own village (*svagrāma*); the compound is formed according to the rule "words beginning with *ati* take the second case when meaning 'surpassing' and so forth. In the *saṃhitā*, there is the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule "after a preceding word" (Pāṇini 8.3.106). It has an udātta accent on the final syllable because it belongs to the class beginning with *nirudaka*. *Ūrmim*: the suffix *mi* is added by the rule "and *ū* after the root *ṛ*" (Uṇādi Sūtra). For the root, there is the substitute *ū*, followed by *r*; the accent is that of the suffix.
"O Indra, being well-pleased... is the *yājyā* for the *marutvatīya-graha*.

And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Having consumed [the draught] with the mantra, 'O Indra, being well-pleased, together with the troop of Maruts,' one should [consume from] this vessel" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 5.14).
O Indra, rejoicing together with the Maruts as your host, drink the Soma, O wise hero, slayer of Vṛtra!
Slay the enemies, drive away the adversaries, and grant us security from every side.
O Indra, rejoicing together with the Marut host, drink the Soma as the Vṛtra-slayer, O hero and wise one. Slay the enemies, drive away those who assail us, and grant us security from every side. 2.

O hero, O powerful one, O Indra, being well-disposed and united with the gods, the Maruts, and their host—that is, together with the Maruts themselves—you who are the slayer of Vṛtra, the destroyer of Vṛtra, and the knower who is conversant with the sphere of ritual action, drink the Soma.
Then slay our enemies;
drive away the *mṛdhas*, the harmful foes.
Alternatively, *mṛdhaḥ* refers to battle; for living beings are struck (*hiṃsyante*) therein, thus it is called *mṛdhaḥ*, meaning combat.
Drive away the enemies who are present there.
"Then immediately after that, 'make' (kṛṇuhi) 'for us' (naḥ) 'fearlessness' (abhayam) 'on all sides' (viśvataḥ). The meaning is: make us free from fear in every respect."
Vṛtrahā [is formed] from the root han with the suffix kvip according to the rule "brahmabhrūṇavṛtreṣu kvip. Abhayam [means] fearlessness.
From the root *bhī* with the suffix *ac* (Pāṇini 3.3.56), and because it is a negative (*nañ*) compound, it takes its accent [on the final syllable]. *Viśvataḥ*.
The suffix *tasil* is applied after the fifth case-ending; it bears the accent of the *lit* suffix.
And by the seasons, O guardian of the seasons, drink our pressed Soma, O Indra, together with the gods who are your friends.
Those Maruts whom you shared [the sacrifice] with, and those who followed you when you struck Vṛtra—they have bestowed strength upon you.

And also with the seasons, O drinker of the season-juices, drink our pressed soma, O Indra, together with the gods who are your friends—those Maruts whom you assigned to yourself, who followed you when you struck Vṛtra, and who bestowed strength upon you. 3.
Furthermore, O *ṛtupā*: you are a drinker of the seasons because you sustain them; or, you are a drinker of the seasons because you drink the Soma during the seasons;
or else, you are a drinker of the seasons because you drink the Soma together with the *ṛtus*, that is, the Maruts.

O such Indra, together with your friends— the Maruts who share the same renown— and with the gods, drink, that is, consume our pressed Soma. Furthermore, those great ones whom you chose as allies for battle, and those Maruts who followed you as their lord in combat—
you thereby slew Vṛtra.
Those Maruts [said], "For you," that is, for your sake, "strength" (*ojas*)—[in battle against] the enemy.

Ja: *savane* (at the libation); 7. Gha, Ja, Ṇa: *kiṃ ca tvam* (and furthermore, you); 8. Kha, Ga, Ja, Ṇa, Ta, Na: *yudhi* (in battle).

They displayed—that is, they performed—valor in the form of slaying and other such acts. *Abhajaḥ*: this is the form of the root √*bhaj* (in the sense of "to serve") in the *laṅ* tense; because it occurs after *yat*, there is no *nighāta* (lack of accent). *Ahan*: this is the form of the root √*han* (in the senses of "to strike" and "to go") in the *laṅ* tense with the suffix *sip*; its elision is by the rule *halḍyādi*. Because it begins the quarter-verse (*pāda*), there is no *nighāta*. *Adadhuḥ*: from the root √*dhā* in the *laṅ* tense, the suffix *jhi* becomes *jus* by the rule *sijabhyasta*. Due to the division of the sentence (*vākyabheda*), there is no *nighāta*.
In the Mahāvrata sacrifice, the *yājyā* verse is “ye tvāhihasye.
This is also stated in the Sūtra: “The *yājyā* for the *vadhañjanī* [offering] is ‘ye tvāhihasye maghavan’” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.14).
O Maghavan, Lord of the Bay Steeds, those who have laughed at you in battle against Vṛtra, Śambara, or in the quest for cattle—
those wise ones who now rejoice after you, O Indra, drink the Soma together with the Maruts.

O Maghavan, those inspired singers who strengthened you at the slaying of Ahi, who [strengthened] you at the [slaying of] Śambara, O Lord of the Bay Steeds, who [strengthened] you at the quest for cattle—those sages who now indeed rejoice after you: drink the Soma, O Indra, together with your troop of Maruts.

O bountiful Indra, possessor of wealth, those Maruts who strengthened you during the act of slaying Ahi—that is, in the deed of killing Vṛtra—increased you by bestowing strength, saying, "Strike, O Blessed One! Slay! Be heroic!
And, O Indra, possessor of bay horses, they also strengthened you in the battle concerning the slaying of Śambara.

Regarding the meaning "Indra slew Śambara," there is a mantra-text: "He who in the fortieth autumn roared against Śambara dwelling in the mountains—he who struck down the serpent displaying his prowess" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 2.12.11).
Likewise, those Maruts who strengthened you in the battle for cattle, known as *gaviṣṭhau*, against the demons named Paṇis.
O Indra, together with those Maruts who are now indeed the inspired sages (vipras) and the wise ones who rejoice in you, drink this Soma as one accompanied by that host.
In *ahihasya*: the suffix *kyap* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) by the rule *hanaṣtaca*; it takes the accent of the final member of the compound (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*).

*avardhan*. This is the form of the root *vṛdh* (meaning "to grow") in the *laṅ* tense with a transposition (*vyatyaya*). According to the rule *chandasyubhayathā*, because the suffix *śa* is treated as both [sārvadhātuka and ārdhadhātuka], there is the elision of *ṅi*.
Because of its connection with the syllable *yad*, there is no loss of accent (*anighāta*).
In the word *śāmbara*: the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "belonging to this," according to the rule *tasyedam*.
*gaviṣṭhau*:
[derived from] the root *iṣ* in the sense of "desiring" (*icchāyām*); the suffix *kin* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*).
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the accent belongs to the first member.

[The form] *anumadanti* [is derived from] the root *madi* in the sense of "praising" and so forth; in the present tense (*laṭ*), the active voice (*parasmaipada*) occurs by way of irregularity (*vyatyaya*).
Due to the non-eternality (anityatva) of the rule regarding the suffix *āgam*, there is an absence of the augment *num*.
Once the accent of the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix *jhi* has been applied, the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*) prevails.
By the rule "tiṅi codāttavati," the verb (*gati*) receives the *nighāta* (suppressed) accent.

We invoke here for our new protection that Indra, the bull accompanied by the Maruts, who has grown great, who is the consumer of the hymn, the divine ruler, the all-conquering, the fierce, and the giver of victory.

Accompanied by the Maruts, the bull, the one who has grown great, the enemy of the non-praisers, the celestial ruler, Indra, the all-conquering, the fierce one who bestows conquering power—for new prosperity, let us invoke him here. 5.

O Indra, accompanied by the Maruts—that bull who rains waters by means of bursting the clouds, who has grown strong through his enthusiasm in deeds such as the slaying of Vṛtra, and who possesses abundant enemies (or, whose enemies are irreproachable)—as the mantra says: "They strengthened him... (Svarir amantro).
2. "Possessing abundant sounds such as *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *pa*, *pha*, *bha*, and *la*," as in [the verse] "He has grown for battle" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.61.9).
"Divine" means existing in the sky, in the heavenly world (*svargaloka*).

We invoke you, Indra—endowed with such power—for new, most recent protection in this rite; you who rule through instruction that teaches what is beneficial and avoids what is harmful; you who are trustworthy to all; you who are the subduer of every adversary; you who are fierce against enemies; you who bestow strength upon the Maruts, your allies in battle. *Note:* Regarding *nūtanāya*: the word *nava* undergoes the substitution *nū*.
The suffix *tanap* must be stated as a secondary derivative (*pratyaya*); thus, it is the *tanap*-suffix [in *sadyas*].
"Sadyo ha" is the fifteenth hymn; it belongs to Viśvāmitra, is composed in the Triṣṭubh meter, and is addressed to Indra.
The *Anukramaṇikā* states: “*sadyo ha*.
In the Agniṣṭoma, during the midday pressing (*mādhyandina-savana*), this hymn, “*sadyo ha jātaḥ*,” is recited as the Maitrāvaruṇa-śastra.
And it is prescribed in the Sūtra: “*sadyo ha jāta evā svāmindraḥ*” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.16).
On the twenty-fourth day as well, this hymn is designated as the *aharahaḥ-śasya* (daily-recited) within the *maitrāvaruṇa-śastra*.
It is prescribed in the Sūtra: "The *aharahaḥ-śasya* for the Maitrāvaruṇa is 'sadyo ha jātaḥ... (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.4).
In a multi-day sacrificial session (*ahargaṇa*), this hymn is used in this *śastra* during the midday pressing (*mādhyandina-savana*) on the second and subsequent days.
Regarding this, it is stated in the Sūtra: “Every day [the verses] beginning with ‘The grains’ are for the Hotrakas, starting from the second day” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.1).
In the *sādyaska* one-day sacrifice, at the Marutvatīya Śastra, the opening hymn begins with “As soon as born” (*sadyo ha jātaḥ*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “‘As soon as born, the bull...’; ‘As soon as born, O Indra, you drank... (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 9.5).
As soon as he was born, the young bull has turned toward the abundant pressed juice;
drink of the pure soma according to your desire, for it is the first portion of the Soma-mixture mixed with juices for you.

As soon as he was born, the bull, the young one, turned toward the drinking of the pressed juice. Drink according to your desire of the excellent, pressed soma, first of all, of that which is mixed with milk. 1.

The bull—the showerer of waters through rain—Indra, the lovely one, born and manifested at that very moment, has protected (āvāt)—that is, shall protect—the sacrificer who is the excellent supporter and gatherer of the pressed soma, the food characterized by the oblation;
*ha* is used for emphasis.

Furthermore, O such one as you, whenever there is a desire for each and every wish— specifically, when there is a longing to drink Soma— drink first, before all the gods, the essence of Soma consisting of nectar, which is perfectly prepared with its head of nectar and mixed with milk, so that your desire may be fulfilled, O virtuous one.
"Pratikāmam" means toward each and every desire.

In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member [is retained].
In the word *somyasya*: from the word *soma*, the suffix *ya* is applied in the sense of *mayaṭ* by the rule "also before *maya*."

"When you were born, O Ahi, you drank the desire of this [plant], the nectar of the stalk dwelling on the mountain.
Your mother, the youthful woman, the progenitor, poured that [milk] for you first in the house of the great father."

On the day that you were born, you drank the nectar of this Soma-stalk, which dwells upon the mountain; it was poured for you by your mother, the youthful progenitor, at the beginning, in the house of your great father.

O Indra, on that very day when you were born—on the day of your birth—you drank the fresh essence, the newly produced sap, of the *ṛjīṣa*, which is a portion (*aṃśu*) of the Soma plant situated upon the mountain (*giriṣṭhā*), high in the peak; this was done while there existed a longing for this Soma, a desire to drink it.
Thus, he shows the reason for drinking the Soma at the very moment of his birth.
Your mother Aditi, a young woman, poured that Soma around into your mouth—in the house, the birth-chamber, of her great father Kaśyapa—before the giving of the breast-milk.

*jāyathāḥ*: [this is] the *laṅ* (imperfect) of the root *janī* in the sense of "manifestation"; the absence of *ad* is due to the rule "in the Veda [the substitution is] diverse" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).

driving away others, he moved through the two worlds, performing great deeds with his many-formed countenance.
