This very Indra—who is fierce, a source of terror to his enemies, a swift conqueror who overcomes his foes with speed, and thus possesses the power to subdue them, being endowed with the prowess to overcome his enemies—has made his own body (*tanvam*) assume various forms according to his will and desire. Thus says a Vedic mantra: "The Maghavan assumes form after form" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 3.53.8). That Indra...

Praise great Indra, in whom all the people who drink Soma have fulfilled their desire; him, the one of excellent wisdom, fashioned by the two world-halves (Dhiṣaṇās), whom the gods brought forth as the slayer of Vṛtras. śaṃsa | mahām | indram | yasmin | viśvāḥ | ā | kṛṣṭayaḥ | soma-pāḥ | kāmam | avyan | yam | su-kratum | dhiṣaṇe iti | vi-vva-taṣṭam | ghnám | vṛtrāṇām | janayanta | devāḥ ||1||

He is the Hotṛ-priest; [he says: "Praise, extol with recitations (śastra), the great Indra. When that Indra is the protector, all people (viśvāḥ kṛṣṭayaḥ)—all men—becoming drinkers of Soma by performing sacrifices, "attain" (ā avyan) their "desire" (kāma); for desire is that which is desired, such as heaven and so forth. O "Dhiṣaṇe," the two who sustain gods, humans, and others; or rather, the two bold and capable ones, Heaven and Earth, able to protect those dependent on them. And the gods [extol] him of "good will" (sukratum)—*kratu* being action, such as the protection of the world; he whose *kratu* is excellent is *sukratu*. Such [a one], "fashioned by Viśva" (*vibvataṣṭam*)—fashioned by the all-pervading Brahman and established in the sovereignty of the universe—the great "slayer of Vṛtras" (*ghnam*), the destroyer of evils in the form of obstacles, they brought into being (*ajanayan*). "Praise" (*śaṃsa*): this is the form of the root *śansu* (to praise) in the imperative (*loṭ*). It is unaccented because it occurs at the beginning of a quarter-verse (*pāda*). In the *saṃhitā*, there is a long vowel according to the rule *aco 'tastiṅaḥ*. "Attained" (*avyan*): from the root *vī* (in the sense of longing, going, etc. in the imperfect (*laṅ*). It is not unaccented due to its connection with *yat* (in *yasmin*). It has the accent of the particle *adaḥ*. "Sukratum": by the rule *katvādyaśca*, the first syllable of the second member of the compound is acute. "Dhiṣaṇe": from the root *dhiṣ* (in the sense of boldness), the suffix *kyu* is added by the rule *dhr̥ṣer ṣuk ca saṃjñāyām*. There is the substitution of *dhiṣ*. It has the accent of the suffix. "Ghnam": from the root *han*, the suffix *gha* is added by the rule *puṃsi saṃjñāyām*. By the rule *ho hanteḥ*, there is the substitution of *k* (resulting in *ghan*). It has the accent of the suffix. "Ajanayan": this is the form of the root *jan* (with the suffix *i*) in the imperfect. It is not unaccented due to its connection with *yat*.

Indeed, no one at all in the battles overcomes him—the self-ruling, most heroic one who stands upon his bay horses; he who, as the most powerful lord with his splendid warriors, has shortened the life of the Dasyu on his broad course. yaṃ nu nākiḥ pṛtanāsu svarājaṃ dvitā taraṃti nṛtamaṃ hariṣṭhām | inatamaḥ satvabhir yo ha bhūṣaiḥ pṛthujryā aminād āyur dasyoḥ || 2 || Indeed, no one at all in the battles overcomes him—the self-ruling, most heroic one who stands upon his bay horses; he who, as the most powerful lord with his splendid warriors, has shortened the life of the Dasyu on his broad course.
"In the *pṛtanā*s"—here, *pṛtanā*s are battles, so called because warriors engage therein.

Among those, [Indra] who is "self-ruling" (*svarāja*), "standing on the bay horses" (*hariṣṭhā*)—that is, standing upon a chariot yoked with bay horses; "most manly" (*nṛtama*), meaning he who possesses leadership in battle; and who, having encountered the fight "twofold" (*dvitā*), exists having divided the army into two parts—that Indra, "no one" (*nākiḥ*, i.e., no one at all) "overcomes," meaning no one goes beyond him by crossing over.
The meaning is that "there is no one at all [who is his equal].
The particle *nu* is used for emphasis.
That Indra, the most powerful (*inatamaḥ*)—meaning the supreme lord of armies—together with the *satvans*, the Rudras who sit around him on all sides, [is he].
Moving along their broad paths,
they dry up the enemy forces through fear, as if with arrows;
by them, the earth is traversed.
Possessing intense impetus toward battle, he "mined"—that is, he diminished, struck down, or destroyed—the "life," "food," or "vital breath" of the "dasyu," the enemy; he destroys them in combats.
The particle "ha" is used for emphasis.
Regarding this, the Nirukta states:
1. [The reading] "kha-ga-gha-ca-ja-ṇa-pha-bha" contains the word *śobhanakratum*.
2. [The reading] "na-sa" does not contain the word *taṣṭam*.
3. [The reading] "kha-ga-ca-ja-ṇa-na-bha-sa" does not contain the phrase "vī kāntigatyādiṣu".
4. In the case of the *hariyukti* [meter], there is *kha-ga-ca-ja-ṇa*.
5. There is some [meter] consisting of *kha-ga-ca-ja-ṇa-ta-na-pha-bha-la-sa*; in the *gha-pa* [tradition], there is some [other]. 6.
In *kha-ga-gha-ca-ja-ṇa-na-bha-la-sa*, the word "together" (*saha*) does not exist.

7. *kha-ga-na-bha* means "he diminishes" or "he injures"; *gha-amināt* means "he injures in battles"; *ca-la-amināt* means "he injures. Regarding the phrase "pṛthujyāḥ pṛthujavaḥ," [it is explained as]: "pṛthujyā aminādāyurdeśyoḥ | prāmāpayadāyurdeśyoḥ" (Nirukta 5.9). *Tarati* is the form of the root *tṛ* ("to swim" or "to cross") in the present tense (*laṭ*). Due to its connection with the word *yat*, it receives the *nighāta* (elision of the accent). Because the suffix *jhap* is marked with *pi*, it is unaccented (*anudātta*), and thus the accent of the verbal root remains. *Yaḥ*: from the root *yā* ("to go" or "to reach"). The suffix *ka* is added according to the *uṇādi* rules. There is elision of the final *ā*. The accent belongs to the suffix.
A great bull, a victor in battles, pervading both heaven and earth with his greatness;
like Bhaga to be invoked in the act of praise by our hymns, he is as dear as a father, bestowing easy invocation and granting vital strength.

Swift in battle, like a courser crossing over, he has pervaded both worlds with his abundance; like Bhaga, he is to be invoked in the song of hymns; like a father, he is beautiful, swift to hear, and the bestower of vital strength.
Indra, who is "asahāvā," powerful, "taraṇiḥ," victorious in battles,
and "niyuvān," accompanied by allies—
or rather, the particle "na" (not) is also connected with the subsequent clause.

Just as the wind, drawing [the chariot] with yoked horses and mules, possesses such power; even so Indra, accompanied by the Vasus and Maruts as his allies, becomes the distributor who properly apportions the *vāja*—the food consisting of the fruit of ritual action—which is the share to be enjoyed. He does this while covering the night (*akṣapā varatā*), the progenitor of the Sun (*janitā*), the generator of Āditya, the illuminator of the world.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
Like the intellect (*dhiṣaṇā*): just as speech makes a distinction between the beginning and the end, saying "this is it," so too [is this].
Regarding *rajas*: from the root *rañj* in the sense of "coloring" (*rāge*), the suffix *asun* is applied according to *uṇādi-sūtra* 4.656, *bhūrañjibhyāṃ kit*;
due to its being marked with *k*, there is the elision of the *jhal* consonant.
It is called *rajas* because it moves toward light (*prakāśa*); it refers to the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
Due to its being a *niṣṭhā* suffix, it is accented on the first syllable.
It is the "weaver" (*vastṛ*).
The form *vasa* is derived from the root *vas* meaning "to clothe," with the suffix *tṛc*.

The word *janitā* is derived from the root *jan* (to beget) with the suffix *tṛc*; the elision of the *ṇi* augment occurs by virtue of the Vedic rule: "In the *mantra*, [the form] *janitā* is an irregularity (*nipātana*)."
Because it has the suffix *cvi*, it is udātta on the final syllable.
[The word] *vibhaktā* [is derived from] the root *bhaj* in the sense of "service" (*sevā*), with the suffix *tṛn* in the sense of one who performs an action well (*sādhukārī*).
By the rule *ekāca upadeśe*, there is a prohibition of the substitution of *it*;
and by the rule *tādau ca niti kṛtyatau*, the root accent (*prakṛtisvara*) is maintained for the element *gati*.
We invoke the auspicious Indra, the bounteous one, the most heroic in this battle for the acquisition of booty;
the sustainer, the fierce one, for our protection in conflicts, the slayer of Vṛtras, and the winner of riches.

For prosperity, let us invoke the bountiful Indra in this battle, the most heroic in the winning of booty—the fierce one who brings [victory], for our protection in the conflicts; may he slay the Vṛtras and be the conqueror of riches. (5) “For prosperity, let us invoke”—as before. (13)
‘indraḥ svāhā’—this is the twelfth hymn, consisting of five verses; it belongs to Viśvāmitra, is in the Triṣṭubh metre, and is addressed to Indra.
This hymn is used in the *marutvatīya* śastra on the ninth day of the ten-day sacrifice (*daśarātra*).
It is prescribed in the Sūtra: “On the third [day], ‘indraḥ svāhā’, with the Gāyatra Sāman” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.7).
May Indra drink the *svāhā*-offering, he to whose soma the bull Tugra, accompanied by the Maruts, has come;
may the far-reaching one satisfy him with these oblations as food for his body.
May they prosper according to their desire.

Indra—svāhā!—let him drink, he for whom Soma has come, the bull accompanied by the Maruts, the far-reaching one; let him fill himself with these foods, and may the oblation fulfill the desire of his body. 1.
May this Indra drink this Soma offered with the cry of *svāhā*.

May that Indra, for whom this Soma is intended, come to the sacrifice; may he, the *tugra*—the destroyer of those who obstruct the ritual—the *vṛṣabha* who rains down the desired fruits for the sacrificers, accompanied by the *Maruts*, possessing vast pervasiveness, be fully satisfied and gratified on all sides by these foods, namely the oblations such as Soma, given by us.
Then, may the oblation offered by us fulfill—that is, completely satisfy—the desire of this Indra for his own body, namely the longing directed toward objects such as the back and other parts.
Tugra;
Tumi said: "By those who have no protector";
Uruvyacas.

Regarding *vyacer-asuna*: according to the rule “it should be stated that after the root *vyaci*, [the suffix] *asun* takes the augment *kut* when followed by *tādi* and *amana*,” the absence of the *chit* accent occurs here because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the word *anasi*.
The accent is that of the subsequent *kṛt* suffix.
*ṛdhyāḥ* is the form of the verb *ṛdh* in the optative mood (*āśīrliṅ*).
1. Kha—thus it was explained previously; sa—established.
"I yoke for thee the two attendants who have from of old been swift to hear thy call."
May the bay steeds with beautiful jaws bring you here; drink of this well-pressed, delightful soma.
I yoke for you the two attendants to carry you, whose service you have favored since ancient times.
May your bay horses with beautiful jaws place you here; drink then of this well-pressed, delightful draught.
O Indra, for your speed—that is, for your return to the sacrifice—I yoke, that is, I harness, the two bay horses (*harī*) who are your attendants.
Of those two horses, which have existed since of old, I [harness] the *śruṣṭi*, meaning their speed;
for Yāska states, "The word *śruṣṭi* is a name for swiftness."
"Thou followest him;
O Indra of beautiful jaws (*suśipra*), let thy bay horses (*harayaḥ*) harnessed to the chariot bring thee here to this rite;
having arrived, drink quickly this Soma of the skillful one, which has been well-pressed by the praisers and is desirable."
The word *saparyu* belongs to the *kaṇvādi* group;
from that [base], the suffix *ku* is added according to the *uṇādi* rules. [Thus] *āvaḥ*.
The root *ava* is used in the sense of protection and so forth.
This is a form in the Vedic *laṅ* tense.
Due to its connection with *saparaśva*, there is no *anighāta*.
*dheyuḥ*.
From the root *dhā*, in the āśīr-liṅ (optative of benediction), the suffix *yāsuṭ* is applied by the rule "kidāśiṣi.
Then, by the rule "eliṅi" (Pāṇini 6.4.67), the substitution of the vowel *e* occurs.
The *nighāta* (elision of accent) [does not apply].
"Drink" (*piba*)—
there is no *nighāta* because it begins the quarter-verse (*pāda*).
Of one who has fallen into deep sleep.
[The root] *puñ* means "to press"; the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).
The term *gati* receives the *gati-svara* (acute accent) by the rule "gatiranantaraḥ";
furthermore, by rules such as "upasargātsunoti," it acquires the status of being subsequent (*paratva*) within the *saṃhitā*.
They have established Indra, who is eager for the cows and brings a successful crossing, as the preeminent one to be upheld while they sing his praises.
O drinker of the *ṛjīṣa*, rejoicing after drinking the Soma, impel toward us cattle in many ways.
Desiring to mix [the draught] with milk, they have established Indra as the one who brings a good crossing; being praised for his preeminence and for being upheld.
O you who possess the *ṛjīṣa*, having drunk the Soma and being exhilarated, drive forth cattle for us in many ways. 3.

The officiating priests (*ṛtvijaḥ*), chanting praises and performing the hymn of praise, have established—that is, they sustain—Indra with Soma juices mixed with milk (*gobhiḥ*). Indra is one who "desires to rain down" (*mimikṣum*) the desired fruit for his worshippers; he is "easily crossed" (*supāram*), meaning he can be brought face-to-face through hymns of praise. They sustain him for "supremacy" (*jyeṣṭhyāya*), that is, for excellence through the abundance of wealth and other goods, and for "sustenance" (*dhāryase*), that is, for the maintenance of life for a long time.
The remainder [of the verse] is directly perceived:

O *ṛjīṣin*, O Indra who possesses the *soma*-residue, you who are *mandānaḥ* (rejoicing) and *somam papivān* (having drunk the *soma*), being the drinker of *soma*, *sam iṣaṇya*—drive forth properly—the *dhenūḥ* (cows) for us, the worshippers, in many ways (*purudhā*) for the sake of accomplishing the *agnihotra* and other rites.
In *gobhiḥ*,
although the acute accent on the case-ending would have applied by the rule "sāvekācaḥ," there is a prohibition by the rule "na gośvasāvavarṇa.
[The form] *mimikṣum*.

In the case of the root *siñ* (meaning "to sprinkle") with the suffix *san*, the prohibition of *it* by Pāṇini 7.2.10 (*ekācaḥ*) applies; however, by Pāṇini 1.2.1 (*halantācca*), it acquires the status of a *kit*. Then, by Pāṇini 3.2.168 (*sanāśaṃsabhikṣa uḥ*), the suffix *u* is added. This [final syllable] bears the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
For *jyeṣṭhya*:
in the sense of "the state of being the eldest" (*jyeṣṭha*), the suffix *vyañ* is applied because it belongs to the *brāhmaṇa*-class (Pāṇini 5.1.124).
Due to the marker *ñ*, the word is accented on the first syllable.
*gṛṇānāḥ* [is formed from] the root *gṛ* in the sense of "sound"; because it belongs to the *kry-ādi* class, the suffix *śnā* is applied.
Because it has the suffix *cvi*, it is udātta on the final syllable.

[The form] *mandānaḥ* is derived from the root *madi* (in the sense of praising, etc. with the suffix *śānac*; by the rule "there is diversely (*bahulam*) elision of *śap* in the Veda," there is elision of *śap*.
In the word *purudhā*: the word *puru*—1. [In the variants] kha, ga, ca, pha, and sa, it is *saparyvāraka*; in ja and ṇa, it is *saparyvāraka*; and in na, la, and sa, it is *parivāraka*.

2. *ca-pha-tataḥ*. 3. *ta-suputasya*. Here, it is a word denoting number (*saṃkhyāvācin*). The suffix *dhā* is applied according to the rule "after a numeral, the suffix *dhā* is used in the sense of distribution" (*saṃkhyāyā vidhārthe dhā*). *iṣaṇya*: from the root *iṣ* meaning "to go. In the Vedic language, the suffix *kyac* is added in the sense of another's desire (*parecchā*) to express "one who desires *iṣaṇya*. From that form ending in *kyac*, the causative (*ṇic*) is understood within the stem; the form is derived from the imperative (*loṭ*) of that.
With this desire, with cattle and horses, with radiant wealth,
and along the paths, the Kuśikas— seeking heaven, wise, and with their hymns— have fashioned this vehicle for you, O Indra.

This—[we offer] at will—with cattle, with horses, with splendid wealth; and from afar, dwelling in heaven, the wise Kuśikas have fashioned this hymn for you, O Indra, as a vehicle with their prayers. 4.
We invoke for our prosperity Maghavan Indra, the most heroic in this battle for the winning of booty—
the one who hears us, the fierce one for our protection in the midst of conflicts, the slayer of Vṛtras, and the conqueror of riches.

For prosperity, let us invoke Indra, the munificent, the most heroic in this battle for the winning of booty; the one who hears us, the fierce, who grants aid with his favors, who slays the Vritras, and who is the conqueror of riches. (5)
These have been explained.
The thirteenth hymn, consisting of twelve verses beginning with "varṣaṇīṣṭataṃ," is dedicated to Indra and composed by Viśvāmitra.
Regarding this, the Anukramaṇikā states: "varṣaṇīṣṭataṃ; [it has] twelve [verses]; the last two triplets are in the Jāgata and Gāyatra meters.
Thus, the first triplet is in the Jāgata meter, and the other triplet is in the Gāyatra meter.
The remaining *ṛc*s are *triṣṭubh*s.
The application (*viniyoga*) of the hymn is based on its characteristics.
When the sacrifice has been mentioned, the first triplet (*tṛca*), which was previously unsuitable for the *maitrāvaruṇa* recitation, is to be recited immediately thereafter.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The triplet beginning with *varṣaṇīṣṭatama* [is for] the *asura* chant" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 6.1).
At the Viṣuvat day, in the *Niskevalya* Śastra, the triplet beginning with *nṛṇāmu tvā* is used.
In the section titled "Viṣuvān," it is stated in the Sūtra: "'nṛṇāmu tvā nṛtamaṃ gīrbhirṛthaiḥ'—these three [verses]" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 8.6).
This triplet is also to be inserted as the *nivid* in the *nikevalya* [śastra] at the *bṛhaspatisava*.
It is stated in the Sūtra: "The midday [śastra] is 'nṛṇāmu tvā'... (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 9.5).
This triplet is also used in the *nikevalya* at the *mahāvrata*.
On the fourth day of the *daśarātra* sacrifice, there are three verses beginning with "O Indra, accompanied by the Maruts" (*indra marutvaḥ*) for the *marutvatīya* śastra.

On the sixth day, it is prescribed in the section [of the Sūtra] beginning with "of the sixth" (*ṣaṣṭhasya*) as follows: "The *marutvatīya* consists of the three verses beginning with 'O Indra, accompanied by the Maruts'" (*āśvalāyana-śrautasūtra* 8.1).
Furthermore, at the *bṛhaspatisava*, this triplet of verses is to be inserted into the *marutvatīya* śastra.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The midday [service] is 'O Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, here... O you among men... (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 9.5).
This is the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the first *marutvatīya* cup-offering.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "They proceed with the *marutvatīya* cup-offering: 'O Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, drink the Soma here... (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 5.14).
In the third round, at the recitation of the Hotṛ, the triplet serving as the *stotriya* is "idaṃ hyanvojasā" [RV 8.96.13–15].
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "'idaṃ hyanvojasā', 'mahāṃ indro ya ojasā'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 6.4).

1. *kha-ga-ja-ta-na-ma-la-sa-iṣu* | 2. *kha-ga-ja-evāyam*; *ca-cāyam* | 3. *kha-ga-ca-ja-ṇa-na-bha-sa-mādhyandinaḥ* | 4. *ga-ca-ja-ṇa-marutvatīyagṛhasya śastre* | 5. *kha-ga-ca-ja-na-bha-sa-mādhyandinaḥ*:

"The great hymns have sung aloud to Indra Maghavan, the one who wields the plough, worthy of praise at the midday libation—him who grows strong, invoked by many, the immortal one, being celebrated day by day with beautiful hymns."

The lofty songs have resounded toward Indra, the wielder of the plow, the possessor of wealth, the one worthy of praise—him who is magnified by well-fashioned hymns, the much-invoked, the immortal, who is celebrated day after day. 1.
Our vast and abundant songs— our words characterized by praise— support the one who sustains the *karṣaṇis*, that is, those who nourish by bestowing desired fruits upon human beings;
or alternatively, he is the supporter of *karṣaṇi*, which is strength, so called because by it all things are drawn forth (*ākṛṣyate*).

The bountiful one, possessed of wealth; worthy of praise through hymns, to be extolled by recitations; ever-increasing through the attainment of strength, riches, and other blessings; invoked many times by the singers; the immortal one, free from the law of death.

Thus [is formed] *yaṇ*. There is the *nighāta* (elision of accent). Regarding *vājasanim*: [the root] *yaṇ* means "to give. By the rule beginning with *khanika-vyasivasi*, the suffix *ip* is applied. By the rule *parādiś chandasi bahulam*, the acute accent (*udātta*) falls on the first syllable of the subsequent member. Regarding *tūrṇim*: [the root] *jitvarā* means "in agitation. By the rule beginning with *vahidhri*, the suffix *nip* is applied. By the rule beginning with *jvaratvara*, the substitution *ūṭh* occurs. Due to the extension of the designation *nit*, it has the acute accent on the first syllable. Regarding *asuram*: [the root] *tura* means "speeding. The suffix *kip* is applied. It takes the accent of the subsequent member of a *kṛt*-derived compound. Regarding *abhighācam*: [the root] *paca* means "to assemble. The suffix *kip* is applied to its *ṇi*-derivative form.
The one who stirs the world is praised as the one who quickens life; Indra, the supporter of the blameless, honors him.
For he has taken delight in the dwelling of Vivasvat; praise him, the ever-conquering slayer of adversaries.

In the agitation, the singer of the Vasu is praised; Indra, the peerless pillar, honors [the worshiper]. For he has taken pleasure in the dwelling of Vivasvat; praise him who is ever-conquering and the slayer of the arrogant foe. 3.

The *jaritā* is the one who causes the decay of enemies; [this refers to] Indra. In the *ākara*—that is, in the battle (*ākara*), so called because wealth is gathered there for the sake of war—in that [battle], which is the locus of *vasu* (wealth), he is *panasyate*: he is praised by all. Alternatively, *vasoḥ* may be construed as "of the enemy" (*vasuḥ* being one who stands facing [us] with hostility); thus, he is the destroyer of that enemy. That Indra, the *anehasaḥ* (sinless ones)—those free from evil—*stabhaḥ* (praises) he *duvasyati* (honors/attends to). The meaning is that, bestowing the fruit of those praises, he honors them. Furthermore, that Indra *pipriye hi* (is indeed well-pleased) in the *sadane* (dwelling/home) of *vivasvataḥ*—the sacrificer who especially dwells [there] for the sake of the *agnihotra* or possesses oblations—being exceedingly delighted by the drinking of Soma and other rites. O Viśvāmitra, praise Indra, the *satrāsāham* (conqueror of enemies), or rather, the one who overcomes enemies together with the Maruts, and therefore the *abhimātihanaḥ* (slayer of adversaries). Grammatical notes: * *Ākare*: From the root *kṛ* (to scatter/dispense). In the locative sense, the suffix *ap* is added by the rule *ṛdorap*. It is oxytone by the rule regarding the accent of *thāthādi* compounds. * *Jaritā*: A form of the root *jṛp* (to age/decay) with the suffix *tṛc*; it is ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable) due to its being a *cit* suffix. * *Panasyate*: *Panasyati* means "to praise. This is the present indicative (*laṭ*) in the passive/objective sense (*karmaṇi*). There is a *nighāta* (elision of accent) due to the preceding verb. * *Anehasaḥ*: From the root *han* with the negative particle *nañ* as an upapada. By the rule *nañi hana eha ca*, the suffix *asi* is added, and the root *han* is replaced by *eha*. It is oxytone by the rule *nañsubhyām*. * *Stabhaḥ*: The root *stobhati* means "to praise. The suffix *kvip* is applied. * *Duvasyati*: Derived from *duvas* (service/attendance) with the suffix *kyac* in the sense of "desiring service for oneself. There is a *nighāta*. * *Pipriye*: From the root *prīṅ* (to satisfy/delight). This is a form in the perfect tense (*liṭ*). Due to its connection with the particle *hi*, there is no *nighāta*.
With songs and hymns, the men have celebrated you, the most heroic among heroes, the subduer;
he of many wiles yields to his conquering power. Homage to him! From of old, he alone is the Lord.

With songs and hymns, praise aloud the Hero, the most manly among men—Oṃ! To you, the one who is most effective in subduing, the one of many wondrous powers bows down for the sake of conquest. Homage belongs to him; from of old, he alone is the Lord. 4.

O Indra, those who are *sabādhaḥ*— that is, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*)— are so called because they exist together with the suppression of obstacles through the recitation of mantras that destroy the *rakṣas*. With songs (*gībhiḥ*), [we praise] you, the most heroic among men (*nṛṇāṃ nṛtamam*), the leader of humans in their respective duties, the hero endowed with power.

1. From that which ends in *ja*. 2. The agent formed with *ṇa* from *jṛ* is *jaritā* (the one who causes to age). 3. *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *pha*, *bha*, and *ā* are all-encompassing (*āsamantam*). 4. *ta*—truth alone is the subduer of the assembly (*satrāsāham*). 5. The action of praising is denoted by *ṇa*. 6. *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *pha*, *bha*, and *sa* belong to their own respective actions. 7. *sa*, *ga*, *ca*, *na*, *pha*, *ma*, *la*, and *sa* do not exist as [separate entities].
With *ukthas*—sentences that serve as the means of praise—and with words, they "praise forth" (*pra arcata*), meaning they worship intensely and with directness (*abhi*).
Possessing manifold powers and many deeds, such as the slaying of Vṛtra, that Indra exerts himself for the sake of *sahasa*, that is, for the sake of strength; he makes an effort to advance.
Furthermore, ancient from of old, that unique and peerless Indra rules over *namas*—that is, over this oblation characterized by the act of bowing—or alternatively, he rules over this entire world.
Homage to that Indra.
For men;
the acute accent on the case-ending is by the rule *nāmanyatarasyām*. Chant!
In the imperative (*leṭ*), *jhi* is substituted [by *at*], according to the rule "the substitutes for *tiṅ* take the place of *tiṅ*s. [The form is] *sabādhaḥ*.
[The root] *bādh* means "to agitate" (*viloḍana*).
In *kip*,
by the rule "vopasarjanasya," there is the substitution of *s* for *sa-*;
it takes the accent of the final member of a *kṛt*-derived compound.

Regarding the final acute accent (*antodātta*), there is a supplementary rule stating that "the words *tricakra* and others are to be included" in this section; thus, [the word] has the final acute accent.

O Indra, who art our friend (*sakhā*) and have become our companion (*sakhibhūta*), you are a kinsman (*āpiḥ*) and a wide-expander (*vyāsa*). Be mindful (*bodhi*) of the newest (*nūtanasya*) and most recent (*navatama*) food (*avasaḥ*)—that is, the oblation characterized by grain—which is being offered for your sake; recognize it.
Therefore, grant—bestow—vital strength, that is, food, upon us, who are your singers and praisers.
For you;
[the word *tubhyam*] has its initial syllable udātta by the rule “*ḍayi ca*” (Pāṇini 6.1.213).
[The verb] *jupasva*.
This is the form of the verb *juṣ* (meaning "to enjoy" or "to serve") in the imperative mood (*loṭ*).
Due to the division of the sentence (*vākyabheda*), there is no suppression of accent (*anighāta*). [The word is] *bodhi*.

In the case of the root *budh* in the sense of "understanding," when the imperative suffix (*loṭ*) is applied, the substitution of *dhi* for *hi* occurs optionally according to the rule *vā chandasi*. Because [the root] is here *pit*, there is *guṇa* [substitution]. By the rule *humabhyo hedhiḥ*, the substitute *dhi* is applied.
Due to its being *ṅit*, it is accented on the final syllable.
O Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, drink the Soma here, as you did at Śāryāta’s, O ancient one, of the pressed juice.
Under your guidance and in your protection, O Hero, the sages who perform fair sacrifices seek to win [favor].

O Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, drink the Soma here, just as you did at Śāryāta’s, O friend, of the pressed juice. Under your guidance and in your protection, O Hero, the sages who perform fair sacrifices seek to win your favor.
O you who are accompanied by the Maruts, even so, O Indra, having come here to this sacrifice of ours, drink the Soma;
that is, drink it just as you formerly drank the pressed Soma at the sacrifice performed by Śāryāta, the son of Śaryāti, while he was a king—so drink here as well.
That Indra drank the Soma at the sacrifice of Śāryāta is clearly stated in the Kauṣītaki [Brāhmaṇa].
Likewise, there is a Vedic mantra: “O Hero, you stand upon the chariot of Śaryāta, among those who have offered oblations at the soma-pressings” (Ṛgveda 1.51.12).

O Hero Indra, those wise sacrificers (*kavayaḥ*), who have performed excellent sacrifices (*suyajñāḥ*) and are established in your protection (*śarman*)—that is, in a place free from oppression—serve you alone on all sides through your guidance (*praṇītī*), that is, by the bringing forward and offering of their oblations.
The root *vi-vās* has the sense of serving.
In the word *śāryāte*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *tasyedam* (Pāṇini 4.3.120) in the sense of "this belongs to Śaryāti.
[The form] *apibaḥ*.
According to the appropriate [application], there is no elision; the vowel *a* is not elided. *Praṇītī*.

The suffix *ktin* is applied in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) to the root *nī*. By the rule "and when a *kṛt* suffix beginning with *t* follows *ni*, the original accent of the stem remains," the stem-accent of *gati* is preserved. Furthermore, by the rule "the *su* of *sup* [stems]," there is a long vowel of homogeneous quality (*savarṇadīrgha*) for the third case ending.
The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule "upasargādasamāse 'pi" (Pāṇini 8.4.14).
Roaring, O Indra, drink here our pressed Soma with the Maruts as your companions;
for when you were born, O much-invoked one, all the gods adorned you for the great battle.
Longing for it, O Indra, drink here our pressed Soma with the Maruts as your companions, since all the gods, O Much-invoked One, surrounded you at your birth for the great battle. || 8 ||

O Indra, you who are longing for Soma, desiring it—such as you are, together with the Maruts, your friends of equal renown, drink, that is, consume, the pressed Soma belonging to us here at this sacrifice. O Puruhūta, Indra invoked by many, all the gods [seek] you, who have become powerful through the drinking of Soma, for the sake of the great [rite].

For the sake of *bhara*—for *bhara* is battle (*saṃgrāma*), so called because warriors are carried away (*hiyante*) while fighting. For that battle, they *pari-abhūṣan*: they adorned themselves, making themselves ready on all sides. *Vāvaśānaḥ*: this is a form in the *cānaś* suffix with the elision of the *yaṅ*; it is accented on the final syllable as it ends in a vowel like *cit*. *Abhūṣan*: from the root *bhūp* meaning "to adorn," belonging to the *bhū*-class; this is the form in the *laṅ* tense. There is no suppression of accent (*anighāta*) due to its being part of a *yathāgṛhīta* compound. *Bharāya*: from the root *hṛ* (here *han*) meaning "to carry away"; the suffix *gha* is used in the sense of location (*adhikaraṇe*). By the rule *hagrahor bhaś chandasi*, the letter *h* is replaced by *b*. It is accented on the first syllable because it belongs to the *vṛṣādi* group.

Those Maruts who are our kinsmen have exhilarated Indra with this food, like swift steeds with their fodder. Together with them, let the slayer of Vṛtra drink the pressed Soma of the donor in his own dwelling-place. 9. amūrye | marutaḥ | āpiḥ | eṣaḥ | amandann | indram | anu | dātīvārāḥ | tebhīḥ | sākam | pibatu | vṛtrakhādaḥ | sutam | somam | dāśuṣaḥ | sve | sadhasthe || 9 ||

O Maruts, that Indra who—acting as your friend and ally in the impelling of those waters—remains as one who bestows boons (*dātīvāraḥ*; *vāra* meaning desirable strength or wealth; thus, one who has granted strength or wealth)—those Maruts gladdened (*amandan*) and rejoiced after him, Indra, the devourer of Vṛtra (*vṛtrakhādaḥ*), the destroyer of Vṛtra. Together with those Maruts, let him drink the pressed Soma in the *sadhastha* (dwelling-place) of the donor (*dāśuṣaḥ*), the sacrificer who has offered the oblation. [Grammatical notes: *asūrye*: from the root *tūr* (in the sense of speed and non-injury), the suffix *yat* is added by the rule *adyādayaśca*; it is acute-accented by the rule *yato 'nāvaḥ*; in the compound, the accent falls on the final member. *amandan*: from the root *mad* (in the sense of praise, etc.), Parasmaipada; it is not elided because it begins a Pāda. *vṛtrakhādaḥ*: from *khād* (to eat); the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of an object. *dāśuṣaḥ*: from the root *dāś* (to give), with the suffix *kvasu*; the form *dāśvan* is established by the rule *dāśvānsāhvānmīḍhvāṃśca*; there is vocalization of the vowel (*saṃprasāraṇa*); the accent is that of the suffix. *sadhasthe*: by the rule *sadhamādasthayośchandasī*, *saha* is replaced by *sadh*.
