O Indra, that Soma which is for your own sake—having followed after your *svadhā* (food) and being pressed by the stones—let it be; into that pressed Soma, direct (*ni yaccha*) your own body (*tanvam*).
May that Soma, the Soma-like one, exhilarate you, O Soma-drinker.
*asat*: this is the form [resulting] from the addition of the suffix *laṭ* and the augment *aṭ*; because it is joined with a word-form (*vṛtta*), there is no loss of accent (*anighāta*).
When the prefix (āgama) is unaccented, the accent belongs to the verbal root (dhātu).
May your two flanks resound, O Indra; may your head, O Hero, resound for the sake of sacred prayer; may your two arms resound for the bestowing of bounty.
O Indra, let your two bellies be filled; O Hero, let your head and your two arms be directed toward the granting of bounty through our prayer. 12.
O Indra, let that Soma enter into both your *kukṣi*s—both sides of your belly—and pervade them thoroughly.
Likewise, accompanied by the *brahman* (the hymn of praise), let that Soma enter the *śiras*, the body; for by mentioning a part, the whole is indicated.
May his body extend forward;
O heroic Indra, may even your two arms extend forward for the sake of wealth and bounty.
*aśrotu*:

[This is derived] from the root *aśū* in the sense of "pervasion" (*vyāptau*); it is in the imperative (*loṭ*) mood, with the active voice (*parasmaipada*) used by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*), and is subject to the rule of *nighāta* (accentual suppression).
In the two words *kukṣyoḥ*, the accentuation of the case-ending is due to the rule: “The case-ending following a vowel that contains an udātta [vowel] and is preceded by *ha* is udātta.”
The fourteenth hymn, *dhānāvantam*, consists of eight verses; it belongs to Viśvāmitra and is addressed to Indra.
Regarding this, the *Anukramaṇikā* states: “*dhānāvantaḥ*: the first half [of the hymn] is in the Gāyatrī meter, and the sixth verse is a Jagatī.
The first three verses are Gāyatrīs; the sixth, beginning with “*tṛtīye dhānāḥ*,” is a Jagatī; the remaining verses are Triṣṭubhs.
The application of the hymn (*sūkta*) is to be understood from its indicative mark (*liṅga*).
The invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the morning-sacrificial cake (*prātaḥsavanīya-puroḍāśa*) begins with "dhānāvantaṃ" and so forth.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "At the morning pressing, 'dhānāvantaṃ karambhaṇam' is the invitatory verse" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.4).
O Indra, enjoy at dawn our offering accompanied by parched grain, by groats, by cakes, and by hymns of praise.
O Indra, enjoy at dawn our offering consisting of parched grains, mixed with curd, accompanied by cakes, and celebrated with hymns. 1.
O Indra, [bring] that which possesses *dhānās*—
*dhānās* being parched barley—
and that which possesses *karambha*.
Karambha is groats mixed with curds;

enjoy—take pleasure in—at every morning pressing this our Soma, which is accompanied by that [karambha], provided with cakes (apūpavant), endowed with the Savanīya sacrificial cakes, and accompanied by the recitation of hymns (ukthin) and the chanting of the Śastra.
In the morning;
it is udātta on the final syllable because it is listed among the *svarādi* group as being udātta on the final syllable.
Cook the sacrificial cake; O Indra, take pleasure in it and give your approval;
for you the oblations flow forth.
He bakes the sacrificial cake; may you enjoy it, O Indra; give your approval, for the oblations flow toward you. ||2||

O Indra, [accept] the *puroḍāśa*, which is fit for cooking in the vessel; for they offer it before [the other oblations], hence it is called *puroḍāśa*, the sacrificial oblation. Enjoy it! Furthermore, "take heart" (*ā gurasva*); make an effort for the purpose of consuming the *puroḍāśa*. The oblations—such as the *puroḍāśa* and others—which are worthy of being offered, "flow toward you" (*sisrate*), that is, they go toward the place of slaughter for your sake. The sense is: "partake of them. Regarding *pacatyam*: from the word *pacata*, by the rule *tatra sādhuḥ*, there is the suffix *yat*; because this word does not end in a vowel (*ac*), the rule *yato 'nāvaḥ* does not apply here. It has three *svarita* accents. *gurasva*: from the root *gurī* in the sense of "exertion" (*udyame*). It takes the *śap* and *vikaraṇa* suffixes. There is *nighāta* (suppression of accent). *sisrate*: from the root *sṛ* in the sense of "motion. In the Vedic language (*chandasi*), it belongs to the *juhoty-ādi* class. The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).

1. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, Na, Pha, Bha, and La, the word *te* does not exist. 2. In the manuscripts Ca and Āgama, there is no *anudātta* accent. 3. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, Ja, Ṇa, Ta, Na, Bha, La, and Sa, the phrase *ubhau pārśvau* does not exist. 4. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, Ja, Ṇa, Na, Bha, and Te, [the reading is as follows]. 5. In the manuscripts Ja and Ṇa, it occurs among the *ghṛtādi* group. 6. In the manuscript Ta, it reads *puroḍāśam*. 7. In the manuscript Ca, it is because of the absence of *dyut*. Ṛgveda 2.54.3:

*puroḍāśaṃ ca no ghasaḥ joṣyāse giraṃ naḥ | vadhuyuriva yoṣaṇām ||3||* *puroḍāśam | ca | naḥ | ghasaḥ | joṣyāse | giraḥ | ca | naḥ | vadhuyuḥ | iva | yoṣaṇām ||3||* "Eat our sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and enjoy our songs; like a suitor for a young woman. (3) *Sacrificial cake*, *and*, *our*, *eat*, *you shall enjoy*, *our songs*, *and*, *our*, *like a suitor*, *for a young woman*. (3)

O Indra, eat—that is, consume—our *puroḷāśa* (sacrificial cake) which belongs to us. And you shall take pleasure in—that is, enjoy—our songs characterized by praise. Therein lies the illustration: "like one desiring a bride" (*vadhuyur iva yoṣaṇām*). Just as one who desires a wife (*vadhuyuh*) enjoys a desirable young woman (*yoṣaṇām*), so [should you enjoy our songs]. Regarding *ghasaḥ*: this is a form of the root *ghaslu* (to eat) with the suffix *leṭ*. According to the rule *cavāyoge prathamā*, there is no *nighāta* (elision of the accent). Regarding *joṣyāse*: this is a form of the causative of the root *juṣī* (to please/to serve) with the suffix *leṭ*. Since the augment is unaccented, the accent belongs to the causative suffix (*ṇic*). Because it occurs at the beginning of a *pāda*, there is no *nighāta*. Regarding *vadhuyur iva*: [the derivation is] *supa ātmanaḥ kyac*; then, by the rule *kyācchandasī*, the suffix *up* is added. The accent belongs to the suffix. Regarding *yoṣaṇām*: from the root *yuṣ* (to enjoy/to share).

[The word *jitta*] is udātta on the first syllable because of the suffix [NiC]. It has the sense of "swift. [The form] *tūrṇinaḥ*: from the root *ji* (in the sense of "agitation") with the suffix *nip* according to the rule "vahintri... etc., and *niC* is added. [The word] *arthaḥ*: from the root *ṛ* (in the sense of "going"). The suffix *than* is applied according to the rule "uṣik-piṇati-bhyas-than. In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the accent of the prior member prevails. [The word] *vṛṣāyamāṇaḥ*: in the sense of "acting like a bull" (*vṛṣan*), the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied by the rule "kartuḥ kyaṅ salopaśca. [There is] lengthening [of the vowel] by the rule "akṛtsārvadhātukayordīrghaḥ. Because it ends in a *hit* suffix, the *ātmanepada* is used by the rule "anudāttahitaḥ...". [The tense is] *laṭ*; [the suffix is] *śānac*. Its accent is that of the verbal root, as it is a *sārvadhātuka* suffix following a *la* suffix. [The word] *īṃṭe*: this is the form of the root *īḍ* (in the sense of "praise") in the *laṭ* tense. There is no *nighāta* (elision of accent) because it follows a *yathāgāda* (as-ordered) sequence. || 17 ||
At the third pressing, the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the *savanīya* sacrificial cake is "tṛtīye dhānāḥ.
And it is stated in the sūtra: "At the third pressing, 'tṛtīye dhānāḥ savane puruṣṭuta' [is used]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.4).

At the third pressing, O much-praised one, honor our offered cake at the libation. O Sage, may we, possessing nourishing food, serve you—who are accompanied by the *Ṛbhus* and rich in booty—with our inspired prayers.

At the third pressing, O you who are praised by many, at the libation, accept our offered cake. O Sage, may we, possessing horses, serve you—who are accompanied by the R̥bhus and possessed of strength—with our prayers. 6.

O you who are praised by many (*puruṣṭuta*), O Indra, at our third pressing, honor— that is, exalt and acknowledge— our parched grains (*dhānāḥ*) that have been offered along with the sacrificial grass, and the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) that has been presented.
O Sage (*kave*), we, possessing milk and having prepared the oblation,
[invoke] you who are accompanied by the *Ṛbhus*— those gods known as the *Ṛbhus*— and who are accompanied by *Vāja*.
Vāja is the son of Sudhanvan; with our prayers and hymns of praise, may we attend upon you, who possess him, and serve you closely.
*Āhutam*: the suffix *kta* is used in the passive sense (*karmani*) of the root *hu*.
The accent falls on the prefix (*gati*) according to the rule "the immediately preceding prefix [is acute]."
Māmahasva.

This is the imperative (loṭ) of the root *maha* in the sense of "worship" (*pūjā*), in its yaṅ-luk form; the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs by way of irregularity (vyatyaya), and the absence of the suffix *śap* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
"Śikṣema": from the root *śikṣ*, in the āśīrliṅ (benedictive) mood, the suffix *aṅ* is applied by the rule "liḍyāśiṣyaṅ";
there is *nighāta* (elision of the accent).
By means of [the suffix] *dhīti*.
According to the rule “*hivatsaratiśathāntānām*,” there is an udātta accent on the final syllable.

I prepare for you, the possessor of bay horses, the *karambha* mixed with curds; for you, the lord of bay steeds, I offer parched grains. For you have brought forth the host together with the Maruts; O wise hero, slayer of Vṛtra, drink the Soma.

Prepare the groats for him; prepare the porridge for the Lord of Bay Steeds, for the one with bay horses. Eat the parched grains and the cake, O you who are accompanied by your troop, with the Maruts. Drink the Soma, O hero, slayer of Vṛtra, you who are wise. 7.
O Indra,
for you who possess Pūṣan— Pūṣan being a certain toothless deity— we have prepared *karambha*, that is, groats mixed with curd, for you to eat.
And so says the Śruti: “Pūṣan has entered as a sharer, for he is toothless” (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.6.8.5).

O Lord who possesses bay horses (*harivata*), to you, Indra, who are accompanied by the two horses named Hari—that is, to you who are joined with bay-colored steeds (*haryaśvāya*)—we have prepared these parched grains (*dhānāḥ*) for your consumption.

1. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Gha, Ca, Ja, Ṇa, Pa, Bha, and La, the word *asmadīyāḥ* is found. 2. In Kha, Ga, Ca, Bha, and Mahaya-sva; in Gha, Ja, Ṇa, and Mahaya; in Na, Sa, and Mahasva. 3. In Kha, Ga, Ca, and La, *svā*; in Na, Bha, and Sa, *tvām*. 4. In Ta, it is noted as being Vedic (*chāndasaḥ*) and subject to the rule of *nighāta* (elision of accent). 5. In Pa, the reading is *kaścana devaḥ*. 6. In Na, La, and Sa, the word *cakum* is absent.

We perform [the ritual]. And thus says the Vedic mantra: "Let the black ones swallow; let the red ones be released here; day by day, bestow similar riches" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 3.35.3). O you who are accompanied by the host of Maruts, consume the cake with water. O hero, O Indra, who are without companion, the slayer of Vṛtra, the knower—knowing all—you drink the Soma. Regarding *pūṇavate*: the suffix *matup* is added to the word *pūpa*; the augment *nuṭ* is applied according to the rule "ano nuṭ"; the change to *ṇ* occurs according to the rule "rapābhyām". Regarding *cakram*: from the root *kṛ*, in the Vedic present tense (*liṭ*), there is an absence of *iṭ* because it belongs to the *krādigaṇa*; there is the *nighāta* accent. Regarding *harivate*: the substitution of *vat* for *matup* occurs according to the rule "chandasīraḥ".

Bring forth parched grains and the swift offering of *puroḷāśa* for him, the most heroic among men. Day after day, O Indra, may these similar offerings increase for you; O bold one, let them serve for your drinking of Soma. 8. *prati* (toward), *dhānāḥ* (parched grains), *bharata* (bring), *tūryam* (the swift offering), *asmai* (for him), *puroḷāśam* (the *puroḷāśa* cake), *vīratamāya* (to the most heroic), *nṛṇām* (of men), *divedive* (day after day), *sadṛśīḥ* (similar), *indra* (O Indra), *tubhyam* (for you), *vardhantu* (may they increase), *tvā* (you), *somapeyāya* (for the drinking of Soma), *dhṛṣṇo* (O bold one). 8.
The sacrificer speaks to the Adhvaryu and the others:
"O Adhvaryu and others, quickly bring forth—that is, prepare—the parched grains (dhānāḥ) for this Indra;
and prepare the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśam) for this Indra, who is the most heroic among men."

Now, regarding the direct manifestation: O bold Indra, you who are by nature the overcomer of enemies, these similar—that is, uniform—praises are performed for your sake by us day after day. May those praises, for the purpose of drinking the Soma, cause you to increase—that is, make you grow through enthusiasm.
*Sadṛśīḥ*. The suffix *kan* is applied according to the rule "samānānyayośca," and the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to the rule "ṭiḍḍhāṇañ... and so forth.
In the case of "dṛśavatsu," there is the substitution of *sa* for *samāna*.

The hymn beginning with "indrāparvatā" consists of twenty-four verses and is the fifteenth [sūkta]. Regarding this, the Anukramaṇikā states: "The hymn 'indrāparvatā' has twenty-four verses; it belongs to Ādha Indrāpārvata. Two verses from the fifteenth onwards are addressed to Vāk; four are for the chariot-parts; the others are curses. They reached Vasiṣṭha, yet they did not pierce him; the Vasiṣṭhas do not hear them. The tenth and sixteenth verses are Jagatīs; the thirteenth is a Gāyatrī; the twelfth, twentieth, and twenty-second are Anuṣṭubhs; the eighteenth is a Bṛhatī."

The seer is Viśvāmitra. The tenth and sixteenth verses are two *jagatī*s; the thirteenth is a *gāyatrī*; the twelfth, twentieth, and twenty-second are three *anuṣṭubh*s; the eighteenth is a *bṛhatī*; and the remaining verses are *triṣṭubh*s.

The first verse has Indra and Parvata as its deities; the fifteenth and sixteenth have Vāc as their deities; the one following them (the seventeenth) and the hundredth have the chariot-parts (*rathāṅga*) as their deities; and the rest are addressed to Indra.

O Indra and Parvata, bring hither on your great chariot desirable refreshments accompanied by noble heroes. O Gods, enjoy the oblations at the sacrifices; wax strong through our songs and through our praise, rejoicing. 1. O Indra and Parvata, on your great chariot, bring hither desirable refreshments accompanied by noble heroes. O Gods, enjoy the oblations at the sacrifices; wax strong through our songs and through our praise, rejoicing.

"O Indra and Parvata"—that is, Indra and Parvata. O Indra and Parvata, having arrived on your great chariot, bring hither for us, and bestow, those desirable foods accompanied by excellent heroes—that is, endowed with noble sons. (The meaning is: "bring them" and "grant them.")

1. From the word *pūpa* [the rule applies] after *ca*, *ja*. 2. By the restriction [of the rule] for *kr̥t* suffixes beginning with *ṇa* following *ja* and *ṇa*. 3. In the manuscripts *kha*, *ga*, *caṃ*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, and *sa*, the word "not" (*na*) is absent. 4. In *kha*, *ga*, *na*, *bha*, and *sa*, it is *tvām*; in *ca*, *la*, it is *tvā*. Furthermore: O two radiant ones (*devau*), consume (*vītam*) the oblations (*havyāni*)—the sacrificial offerings such as the *puroḍāśa* cake—which are fit to be offered (*havanayogyāni*) in our sacrifices (*adhvareṣu*).
Likewise, being exhilarated (*madantā*) by the food (*iḷayā*) offered by us, may you two, being strengthened (*vardhetām*) by our words (*gīrbhiḥ*) characterized by praise, become prosperous.
*Indrāparvatā*:
because it is a vocative, it possesses the sixth-stage (*pāṣṭhika*) acute accent on the first syllable due to its being treated as the beginning of a *pāda*.
*Suvīrāḥ*.
In the *bahuvrīhi* compound, by the rule “*avīravīryau ca*,” the first syllable of the final member is udātta.
[The form] *vītam* is derived from the root *vī* in the sense of “shining” and so forth, in the imperative (*loṭ*), with the elision of *śap* due to its belonging to the *adādi* class.
The accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
[In the form] *vardhetām*,

from the root *vṛdh* in the sense of "growth" (*vṛdha vṛddhau*), in the *loṭ* mood with the ending *āthām*, the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*) applies by virtue of the rule that the accent of the verbal root prevails over the accent of the *l-sārvadhātuka* suffix.
On days other than the *ahargaṇa* sacrifices, on those days excluding the *anvaya*, the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the *hāriyojana* offering is "tiṣṭhā su kam.
This is also stated in the Sūtra: "tiṣṭhā su kaṃ maghavan mā parāgā ayaṃ yajño devayā ayaṃ miyedhaḥ" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 6.11).
Stay here, O Maghavan; do not depart. Now I shall worship you with the well-prepared Soma.
As a son worships his father, I, O Indra, have sung this to you with a most sweet song, O Lord of Might.

Stay here, O Maghavan; do not go away. Now I shall worship you with well-pressed Soma. Like a son embracing the hem of his father’s garment, I have embraced you, O Indra, with a most sweet song, O Lord of Might.

"O Maghavan, O wealthy Indra, stay well for some time here at this sacrifice with ease (*kam*); do not depart from our sacrifice. He states the reason for this: I shall quickly worship you with the Soma of the well-prepared [libation]. O powerful Indra, I grasp the hem of your garment (*sicam*) with a most sweet song characterized by praise; that is, I take hold of it. Therein lies the illustration: just as a son grasps the hem of his father’s garment with sweet speech. *Su* and *kam* are two particles. For the first, the acute accent (*ādyudātta*) applies according to the rule "particles are acutely accented on the first syllable. For the second, the grave accent (*anudātta*) applies according to the rule "the group beginning with *ca* is gravely accented. *Somasya yakṣi*: the root *yaj* (to worship, to honor the gods, to unite, to give) takes the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) because it begins with a svarita vowel and ends in a consonant. In its aorist form with the suffix *sic*, there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* because it has a single vowel. By the rule "for the sake of clarity," it is treated as if ending in a *parasmaipada* suffix. The change of *pa* and *ṣa* to *ka* occurs by the rule "for *pa* and *ṣa*, *ka* before *si*. There is the substitution of *ṣ* for the *s* of *sic*. The *nighāta* (elision of accent) applies. *Rebhe*: from the root *ḍulabhaṣ* (to obtain). This is the form of the first person singular in the present tense (*laṭ*). There is a distinction between the letters *ra* and *la*. The *nighāta* applies. *SVĀDIṢṬHYĀ*: this is the form of the word *svādu* (sweet) with the superlative suffix *iṣṭhan*. It is acutely accented on the first syllable because it is a *nivāt* (a word formed with a primary suffix).
Recite, O Adhvaryu! Answer me; let us both prepare an acceptable offering for Indra.
Sit upon this sacrificial grass of the sacrificer, and let it be well-prepared as a recitation for Indra.

Praise! O Adhvaryu, respond to me; let us both prepare an acceptable offering for Indra. Sit upon this sacrificial grass (*barhis*) of the sacrificer, and then let there be a hymn recited for Indra. 3.
1. [The reading] by means of the phonetic characteristics of *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *pha*, *bha*, and *sa* is *śruti-lakṣaṇābhiḥ*.
2. In the manuscripts *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, and *sa*, the word ‘*hāriyojanasya*’ is absent.
3. In the manuscripts *kha*, *ga*, *na*, and *bha*, it is *tvām*; in *ca* and *la*, it is *tvā*.
4. *ca-ja-ṇa-cailāñcala* means "with the hem of the garment. *Sa-vastrāñcala* means "with the hem of the cloth.
Intending to recite, the Hotṛ says to the Adhvaryu:
"O Adhvaryu, let us two recite together."
"You yourself praise the office of the Hotṛ priest. How then shall I praise?
To this he says:"
"Sing back to me," he says. "Do you sing back to me.
The response (*pratigara*) beginning with "Othā modaiva" is intended to generate enthusiasm for the Hotṛ priest (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.11).
Give that to him. Likewise, let us both prepare—a "vāha" being a hymn of praise—pleasing and agreeable to Indra.
You, for the sake of the sacrificer, sit down upon this sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
And immediately thereafter, may the *uktha*—the recited hymn being performed by us for Indra, for the sake of Indra—be praised, that is, become highly extolled.
*Śaṃsāva*. This is the form of the root *śaṃs* (to praise) in the first person dual of the imperative (*loṭ*). The augment *āṭ* is added according to the rule *āḍuttamasya*.
Since the *ut* of *uttama* is unaccented (*anudātta*) due to the rule *pidvacanānuttame* (Pāṇini 8.1.29), the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*) remains.
[The word *me*] receives the designation of recipient (*saṃpradāna*) by the rule *anupratigṛṇaśca* (Pāṇini 1.4.41).
*Juṣṭam*:
by the rule "nityaṃ mantre," etc., the first syllable is udātta.
O Maghavan, let that same seat be born; may the harnessed bay steeds carry you there.
Whenever we shall press the Soma, Agni shall speed as your messenger toward you.
The wife is indeed the home, O Maghavan; she is the womb. Let the yoked bay horses carry you thither. Whenever we shall press the Soma, may Agni as our messenger hasten toward you. 4.

O Maghavan, O wealthy Indra, come to our *asta*. *Asta* means "home," because objects are cast (*as*) or thrown there. A wife alone becomes a home; for the Smṛti says, "They do not call a house a home; the mistress of the house is called the home. Thus, she—the wife—is the *yoni*, the place of union for the man. *U* has its well-known meaning. Therefore, let the *harayas*, the bay horses yoked to the chariot, carry you to that very home. But whenever we press the Soma for your sake—that is, perform its extraction—then may Agni, sent by us as a messenger, go toward you (*accha*), moving straight to meet you. *Astam*: from the root *asu* (to throw), with the suffix *tan*; due to the *nic*-accent, it is udātta on the first syllable. *Sunavāma*: the form of the root *sū* (to overcome) in the imperative; it is not subject to the *nighāta* accent because of its connection with *yad-vṛtta*. *Tvā*: in the *saṃhitā* text, it follows the rule *yudhmattatakṣuvantaḥpādam*. *Dhanvāti*: from the root *dhavi* (to move); this is the form with the *leṭ* augment; it is subject to the *nighāta* accent.
In the *ahargaṇa* sacrifice, on the days other than [the first], for the *hāriyojana* offering, there is an optional alternative *anuvākyā*: "aparā yāhi" (Go away).
Or else, the *anuvākyā* is "parā yāhi maghavannā ca yāhi" (Go away, O Maghavan, and come back), as prescribed in the *Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* (6.11).
Depart, O Maghavan, and come back again; Indra, O brother, your purpose lies in both places:
where the great chariot is stationed and where the prize-winning donkey is unyoked.
Depart, O Maghavan; come hither, O Indra. From here, your purpose lies in both places: where the great chariot is stationed and where the swift ass is unyoked. 5.

1. [The reading] beginning with *kha-ga-ca-pha* does not exist. 2. [The reading] *kha-ga-ca-ja-ṇa-vadasva* does not exist. 3. [The reading] *kha-ga-na-bha-sa-akaravāva* does not exist. 4. [The reading] *kha-ga-ja-ṇa-bha-sa-śastam* does not exist. 5. [The reading] *kha-ga-ca-ja-ṇa-na-bha-sa-maghavan dhanavan* [is as follows]. 6. Only *la* [is correct], where your wife stands.

O Maghavan, O wealthy Indra, go away from this place of sacrifice for the gods; turn your face away and go toward your own home. Or else, come back toward the place of sacrifice for the gods. O brother, O nourisher, in both cases it is for your sake—that is, it has come to you; it is the purpose. There, [in going home], there is a wife, food, and Soma. He states another purpose: in the case of going toward the home, the purpose is the placing or resting of the great chariot upon it. In the case of staying here, the purpose is the unyoking of the swift horse—the ass that makes a braying sound—from the chariot. *Artham*: from the root *ṛ* "to go. According to the rule *upikupitārthasya*, the suffix *than* is added. It is unaccented (*nisvara*). *Nidhānam*: from the root *dhā* with the suffix *hyuṭ* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*). By the rule *liti*, the vowel preceding the suffix is acute. *Rāsabhasya*: from the root *rāsu* "to sound. By the rule *rāsivalbhyāṃ ca* (Uṇādi-sūtra 3.405), the suffix *abhac* is added in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). It is acute on the first syllable according to the *prāmādi* group. 19. Translation complete.
On the final days, "apāḥ somaṃ" (you have drunk the Soma) is the invitatory verse for the Hāriyojana cup.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "In the Hāriyojana [rite], 'apāḥ somaṃ astam indra pra yāhi'" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.11).

You have drunk the Soma; O Indra, go forth to your home, where your beautiful wife is, a source of joy in your dwelling—there where the great chariot is laid down, where the unyoking of the prize-winning steed takes place, rich with sacrificial gifts.

You have drunk the Soma; go home, O Indra. Your wife is auspicious, and your home is a place of delight, where there is a place for the setting of the great chariot and the unyoking of the prize-winning steed, accompanied by sacrificial gifts.

O Indra, you have drunk the Soma; stay right here and drink the Soma. Or else, go forth to your home, proceed with haste. In your house dwells a beautiful, auspicious wife, Śacī; there is also pleasant sound, such as the music of singing and the like—or rather, in your house dwells a wife who is most delightful. As for the passage beginning "where," etc., it has already been explained. [The term] *dakṣiṇāvat*: while staying here, the unyoking of the horses (*vājinaḥ*) harnessed to the chariot becomes purposeful, being provided with food and drink like a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); they offer food and drink to the horses once they are released. [Grammatical notes: *Apāḥ*: from the root *pā* (to drink). In the *luṅ* (aorist) tense, by the rule *gātisthā...* there is elision of the suffix *sic*. The accent belongs to the augment *aṭ*. *Kalyāṇīḥ*: "one who possesses beauty" (*kalyāṇam asyā asti*). In the sense of possession (*matvarthe*), the suffix *ī* is applied according to the rule *chandasi vanniṣau*. The accent belongs to the suffix. *Suraṇam*: the root *raṇ* means "sound. From this, the suffix *khal* is added in the sense of "not with difficulty" (*akṛcchre*). The accent belongs to the suffix-initial *liṭ*. Since the suffix is not marked with the *vi* indicator, it is *anudātta*, and thus the accent of the verbal root remains. In the compound, the accent falls on the final member of the *kṛt*-derived word.
These Bhojas, Aṅgirases, Virūpas, sons of Dyaus, heroes of the Asura,
bestowing riches upon Viśvāmitra at the thousandfold pressing, have prolonged his life.
These Bhojas, the Aṅgirases, the Virūpas, the sons of Heaven, the heroes of the Asura—granting riches to Viśvāmitra at the thousandfold pressing, may they prolong our life. 7.

O Indra, these Bhojas, the Saudāsa Kṣatriyas who perform this sacrifice, their variously-formed (virūpāḥ) priests such as Medhātithi and others, and the Aṅgirases— those heroes who are the sons of Rudra, the Asura of heaven who is stronger even than the gods— and the powerful Maruts— all of them [are present] at the great thousand-fold pressing for Viśvāmitra.
The Aśvamedha is called *sahasrasāva* because a thousand [oblations] are pressed therein.
In that Aśvamedha, those who bestow—that is, grant—*maghāni*, which are great riches, extend—that is, increase—the *āyus*, meaning life or food.

In the *saṃhitā* [reading] of *divasputrāsaḥ*, the *visarjanīya* is replaced by *s* according to the rule “*ṣaṣṭhyāḥ patiputra°*”. *Dadataḥ* is the form of the root *ḍudāñ* (to give) in the present participle (*śatṛ*).

The initial vowel [of *abhyastānām*] is udātta according to the rule "abhyastānām ādiḥ. They cross over (*tirante*). The suffix *śa* is applied to the root *tṛ* with the sense of intensity (*atiśayena*).
Maghavan assumes form after form through his creative power, fashioning for himself a body at will.
Like a bird from the sky, he has come in an instant by his own mantras, the guardian of the seasons, true to the cosmic order.

Form after form Maghavan assumes, fashioning his own body through illusion, when thrice from heaven he has come for a moment—guardian of the seasons at the wrong times, yet true to the cosmic order (*ṛta*)—by means of his own mantras. 8.
Maghavan, the wealthy Indra, *rūpaṃ-rūpam*—whatever form he desires, that very form he *bobhavīti*, he intensely attains;
he becomes identical with each of those forms.
The reason for this is stated:
Possessing the power to assume manifold forms, performing his own body—he creates various bodies from his own self;
"from" (pari) is used here in the sense of the ablative case.
He fashions diverse bodies out of his own physical form.
Or rather, he makes his own body (*tanūm*) endowed with various forms;
thus says a Vedic mantra: "Indra, through his creative powers (*māyābhiḥ*), assumes many forms" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 6.47.18).
Since he is invoked by his own mantras—that is, by the sentences characterized as praises belonging to himself.
*Anṛtupāḥ*: He does not drink only during the seasons, but also outside of the seasons;
the meaning is that he drinks Soma many times.

Indra, who is the upholder of *ṛta* and the speaker of truth, comes from heaven—that is, from the celestial world—in a single moment; he arrives at sacrifices situated in various places, and even there, thrice at each of the three daily libations (*savana*).
*bobhavīti*: from the root *bhū* with the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix (*yaṅluk*), followed by the ending *tip*; the augment *iṭ* is applied according to the rule *yaṅo vā*;
[the first member] receives the *nighāta* accent.
"He went" (agāt).
This is the form of the root *iṇ* in the *luṅ* tense.
Due to its connection with *yad*, it does not undergo the *anighāta* (lack of suppression of the accent).
The great seer Devajātāstaṃbhra, the far-seeing one, crossed the oceanic river;
when Viśvāmitra brought Sudās, Indra took pleasure in him along with the Kuśikas.
The great seer, born of the gods, impelled by the gods, the unbending Viśvāmitra, beholding the oceanic flood, when he struck down Arbuda, Indra took pleasure in Suḍāsa along with the Kuśikas. 9.

The great *ṛṣi*—one whose power is surpassed by his asceticism (*tapas*), a seer of objects beyond the senses, the progenitor of radiant splendors (*devajā*), impelled by those splendors (*devajūta*), and the supervisor (*nucakṣas*) of men who lead the ritual acts such as the *adhvaryu* priests—that Viśvāmitra solidified the ocean-like river Sindhu, the confluence of the Vipāś and Śutudrī, and brought its current to a standstill.

Furthermore, when that Viśvāmitra led King Sudās, the son of Pijavana, [to perform a sacrifice], Indra, together with the Kuśikas—the sages born of the Kuśika lineage—acted as if he were a dear friend.
*avahata*. This is the *luṅ* (aorist) form of the root *vaha* in the sense of "to carry" (*prāpaṇe*).
[The suffix] *la* is [applied]. These are the things worthy of being honored (*mahaniyāni*).

2. In the versions kha, ga, gha, ja, ṇa, bha, and sa, the reading *bhṛśaṃ prāpnoti* does not exist. 3. In the versions kha, ga, gha, ja, ṇa, pa, pha, bha, sa, and sa, there is the form *saṃbhedanam*. Due to its connection with this [word], there is no *nighāta* (absence of accent). The form is *apriyāyata*. In the sense of "he acts like one who is dear" (*priya ivācarati*), the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied according to the rule *akartuḥ kyaṅ salopaśca*. From that [stem ending in] *kyaṅ*, the form is derived in the *laṅ* tense. Because it begins with a *pāda*, there is no *nighāta*.
Like swans, produce a hymn with the pressing-stones, rejoicing with songs at the sacrifice when the Soma is pressed;
together with the gods, O wise seers who behold men, drink the Soma-sweetness, O Kuśikas!

Like swans, fashion a hymn with the pressing-stones, crushing [the stalks] with songs at the sacrifice when the Soma is pressed; together with the gods, O wise seers who behold men, drink the Soma-mead, O Kuśikas! 10.

O wise ones, O sages who perceive objects beyond the senses, O you who have special insight into the deeds of men, O sons of Kuśika born of the Kuśika lineage—when the Soma has been pressed with stones at the sacrifice, rejoicing with songs and gladdening the gods with hymns, you [should chant] the *śloka*.
A *śloka* is that by which something is praised or recited; it is a liturgical hymn (*śastra*).
Perform [it] correctly; utter it.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
like swans.
Just as swans utter their proper cry, so do you;
moreover, together with the gods—the deities of the sacrifice—drink the honey-like essence of Soma, which consists of Soma, drinking it mutually with one another.
The word *śloka*: from the root *ślok* in the sense of "sound," with the suffix *ghañ* in the instrumental sense (denoting the instrument).
Because of the *jittva* [designation], the first syllable is udātta. Regarding *madantaḥ*:
from the root *madī* in the sense of "joy," the *śap* affix is applied by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*), with the causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) included within it.
"Drink!
[This is from] the root *pā* in the sense of "drinking. The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used here according to the rule *kartari karmavyatihāre*.
"Somya": from the word *soma*, the suffix *ya* is applied according to the rule "and in the sense of 'made of' (*maya-*)".
Come near, O Kuśikas, and take heed! Release wealth for this Sudās.
May the King slay Vṛtra to the east, to the west, and to the north; then let him sacrifice at the best place upon the earth.

Come hither, O Kuśikas; take heed! Release the stone for the sake of wealth from Sudās. May the King slay Vṛtra in the east, in the west, and in the north; then let him sacrifice at the choice places upon the earth. 11.
O Kuśikas, born of the lineage of Kuśika, O sons, approach the horse; go near it and proceed with diligence. Having gone there, be mindful—that is, remain alert—or else:
O horse-guards, remain vigilant!
Release the horse of King Sudās Paijavana for the sake of wealth—that is, for the acquisition of riches through his world-conquest.
Indra, the sovereign Lord of the gods, has struck down Vṛtra, the asura who obstructs ritual action, violently in the east, west, and north—in the regions of the front, the back, and the left.
Therefore, the sense is: "Release the horse.
Then, immediately thereafter, in the most excellent place upon the earth, the sacrificial ground for the gods, that king shall sacrifice; he should perform the sacrifice.

"Cetayadhvam" is the form of the causative (ṇyanta) of the root *cit* in the sense of "to perceive," in the imperative (loṭ). Due to the treatment of the vocative as non-existent (*avidyamānavat*), there is no suppression of the accent (*nighāta*) for the following finite verb (*tiṅ*).
*Jaṅghanat*:

From the root *han*, meaning "to strike" or "to go," in its *yaṅluk* (intensive without suffix) form, the augment *nuK* is added to the reduplicated syllable according to the rule "the augment *nuK* is added after a reduplicated syllable ending in a nasal.
Following that [form], the suffix *leṭ* is applied with the augment *yaṬ*.
Previously,
the form [is derived] from the root *añc* with the suffix *kin*;
according to the rule "in the case of the suffix *vap*, there is no accent for the prefix when the root is *añjati*," the accent falls on the prefix.
*yajāte*:
the suffix *lyap* is applied to the root *yaj*,
and there is the *nighāta* (anudātta) accentuation.
Regarding *vare*: from the root *vṛñ* in the sense of "choosing" (*varaṇe*), the suffix *ap* is applied according to the rule *grahavṛhaniśrigamaśca*.
Because that suffix is marked with *p*, it is unaccented (*anudātta*), and thus the accent of the verbal root remains.

1. The suffixes gha, ja, and ṇa are applied after the word *pṛthivī*. 2. There is the augment *nu* after the root *jū*; and by the rule "also after the reduplicated syllable," the form *kulam* is derived.
I, who have praised Indra for both these worlds, heaven and earth—
this prayer of Viśvāmitra protects the Bhārata people.
I, who have praised Indra for both these worlds, heaven and earth—may this prayer of Viśvāmitra protect this Bharata people. 12.

O Kuśikas, sons of Kuśika: "I, who am Viśvāmitra, have praised Indra, both the *rodasī*, heaven and earth. The meaning is that the hymn for Indra was caused to be performed by me through heaven and earth;
or alternatively:
"I praise Indra, who stands between both heaven and earth.
This *brahman*—this hymn concerning Indra—of mine, Viśvāmitra, who am performing the praise, protects and sustains the Bharata people, the lineage of Bharata."
*Anuṣṭubh*. [It is derived from] the root *stuñ*, meaning "to praise. It is the form in the locative singular (*ṅi*) of the causative stem with the elision (*luk*) of the causative suffix (*ṇic*).
Because of its connection with the *vṛtta* [meter], there is no *anighāta*.
It is the *Bhārata*;
the word *bharata* has been elided.
Because it ends in a long vowel (jittva), it is udātta on the first syllable.
The Viśvāmitras have fashioned prayers for Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt—
prayers that grant rewards and bestow great wealth.
The Viśvāmitras have offered prayer to Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt; may he indeed make us richly prosperous. 13.
The Viśvāmitras have offered, that is, performed, a *brahman*—a hymn of praise—for Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt who holds the bolt in his hand.
May that Indra, being thus praised, make us "surādhasas," that is, endowed with excellent wealth. May he indeed do so.

*arāsata*. This is from the root *rāsu* (meaning "to sound") in the *laṅ* tense; the *śap* suffix is elided by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi" (in Vedic usage, [suffixes] are frequently omitted). There is a *nighāta* (elision of accent) [on the verb].
*karat*. From the root *kṛ* (to do/make), in the *laṅ* tense, for the *cli* suffix, there is the substitution of *aṭ* according to the rule *kṛmṛdṛhibhyaśchandasi*. [The word] *surādhasaḥ*.
The initial syllable of the second member [of the compound] is acute by virtue of the rule: "In the Veda, a word consisting of two syllables has its first syllable acute."

What do those cows do among the Kīkaṭas? They yield no milk-mixture, nor do they satisfy us with the *gharma* offering. Bring to us the wealth of Pramaganda; O Maghavan, bestow upon us the Naicāśākha, even as you did for Andhas.

What do your cows produce among the Kīkaṭas? They yield no milk-mixture for the Soma, nor do they satisfy the *gharma* oblation. Bring to us the wealth of Pramaganda; O Maghavan, subject Naicāśākha to our will! 14.
O Indra, among the Kīkaṭas—those regions inhabited by non-Aryans;

or rather, those atheists (nāstikas) known as Kīkaṭas who, lacking faith, ask "What fruit will result from actions characterized by giving and sacrifice? and instead say, "Drink and eat! This world alone exists, not the next. Among them.
"What do your cows do?"—that is, what do they perform? The meaning is that none of them provides you any utility.
He demonstrates this lack of utility:

They do not "milk" (na duhe) the *āśira*, the milk fit for mixing with Soma; furthermore, they do not "satisfy" (na tarpanti)—that is, they do not cause to shine—the *gharma*, the Mahāvīra vessel used in the ritual known as the Pravargya, by means of providing it with its own milk.
By this, it is also indicated that they are not employed even for the sake of the *Sāṃnāyya* and other such offerings.
Thus, being engaged in some Vedic rite, he says to those cows: "Bring them to us. (1. kha-ga-ca-ja-ṇa-na-bha: *taumi*; gha: *stavāmi*. 2.
kha-ga-ca-ja-ṇa-na-bha-sa: *antarasthitam*.)
3. Those born of the Bharata lineage have *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *la*, *sa*, and *bha* as their food syllables (*āhāra*). It is not only those [syllables] alone.
Rather, it refers to Pramaganda.
A *maganda* is a usurer who gives to others with the thought, "The object, having reached its full measure for the protection of [my] *haigupya* and so forth, will come back to me alone.
His offspring—son and so on—is *pramaganda*.
The prefix *pra-* indicates the sense of "offspring," as in the case of *Praskaṇva* and others;
bring the wealth—that is, the Veda—of that family of Antaka and Sīdin.
Furthermore, O wealthy Indra, bestow the *Naicāśākha*.

One who has produced branches—meaning a lineage of sons, grandsons, and so forth—from low-born *śūdra* wombs is called "one of low branch" (*nīcāśākha*). [The phrase] "and with the offspring of *śūdras*" refers to those born solely from such unions; [the phrase] "one who marries a *śūdra* woman" (*śūdrāvedī*) refers to one whose status falls low.
And because it is declared to be a cause of falling [from caste] (*pātaka*);
the wealth of one who has fallen is not for the *Naicāśākha*. Therefore, make that wealth ours—make it attainable for us.
The meaning is this: that wealth does not serve you directly; however, since that wealth is under our control, it serves you by means of sacrifices and other such rites. Therefore, give it to us.
Yāska also states this same point: "What do the cows do among the Kīkaṭas?
Kīkaṭa is the name of a country inhabited by those who lack wealth. Why are they called Kīkaṭas? Because they perform no [proper] actions, or because they are seekers of 'what' (kim)."
One does not milk [the cow] upside down, nor do they heat the *gharma* vessel improperly; follow the proper course!
Bring to us the riches of Pramaganda.
A *maganda* is a usurer; thinking "Māgadha will come to me," he gives.
His offspring was Pramaganda, born of an extremely indolent family;
or he was a *pramadaka*, one who desires only this world and not the next;
or he was a *paṇḍaka*—a eunuch, a *paṇḍaga*, or one whose testicles were removed (*prādeko* or *prādeyyāṇḍau*).
It causes shame, like a testicle.
"Tasthaṃ naicāśākham" [means] "nīcāśākha," that is, one whose branches are low.
The word *śākha* is derived from the root *śak* ("to be able"). It is used in the sense of "until the end" (*āniraraṇāt*).
Regarding the phrase "give us that over, O Maghavan," the root *radh* signifies "coming under one's power" (*vaśagamana*), according to Nirukta 6.32.
*Āśiram*: from the root *śrī* preceded by the prefix *ā*, with the suffix *krip*, there is the substitution of *āśira* according to the rule beginning with "apastṛdhethām.
[The word] *duhe*.

In the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*) of the root *duh*, there is the substitution of *re* [for the suffix *aṭ*] according to the rule "in the periphrastic perfect, *irayo re*. Because the reduplication is optional, there is an absence of reduplication.
Due to the rule "there is optionally no suppression [of the accent] when *ca* and so forth are elided," there is no suppression of the accent.
*naicāśākha*: [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *tasyedam*; the accent is that of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
*randhaya*. In *radhyet*, there is the augment *num* by the rule "radhi-jabhor aci."
Those who know the ancient legends say that the *Ṛgveda* hymn known as the "Sasapārī" was uttered by Śakti,
the son of Vasiṣṭha,
when the power and speech of Viśvāmitra were completely overwhelmed by the milk-offering of Saudāsa.

Then, having been overcome by Vasiṣṭha, that son of Gādhi lived in exile; Jamadagni, however, having brought from the abode of the Sun a speech endowed with the power of Brahmā, known by the name Sasa-parī, gave it to him.
"That was the thought of the Kuśikas; that speech was not a thought—he dispelled it. (Anu Bhā 3.53)
Increasing the delight of her husband, the great one given by Jamadagni has grown;
the daughter of the Sun has extended her fame among the gods—immortal and ageless.
The daughter of Sūrya, given by Jamadagni, has lowed loudly; increasing the lack of wisdom, she has spread her fame among the gods—immortal and undecaying. 15.

1. Kha, ga, ca, ja, ṇa, ta, na, bha, and sa read *tasyāpatyaṃ tatkusīdakulasya*. 2. Ta reads *ta-utpāditāḥ śākhāḥ*. 3. Kha, ga, ca, ja, ṇa, ta, na, pha, bha, and sa read *śūdravittaiśca*; in the manuscript Ja, this is written as a marginal note (*ṭippaṇī*): “By means of Śūdra wealth—[that is,] in the accumulation of wealth belonging solely to a Śūdra—one attains the state of a Śūdra.”

"In that case, by approaching her, one becomes a Śūdra, falls low, and becomes an outcast (patita)—this is the sense," this was included as a marginal note in the Ja manuscript. 4. In the Ta, Pha, and Bha manuscripts: "that wealth" (yaddhanam).
5. In the Na manuscript: "desiring this" (itiprepsavaḥ).
6. Kha, ga, ca, ṇa: taking away; ja, sa: palace; ta: sound. 7. Kha, ga, ca, ja, ṇa, na, bha, la: one who is extremely indolent and of noble birth.
8. Kha, ga, ca, ta: serpent.
9. *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-na-bha-la-randhayasva*. 10. *kha-ga-ca-ja-ṇa-na-bha-sa-‘sasaparī’...* [the reading] ‘...tām apānudat’ does not exist; [it reads] *ta-...apāṇudat*.
Kuśika Viśvāmitra urged him on, saying, “Come near! (*upa preta*).
Having regained his speech, he, with a joyful heart, honored Jamadagni while himself uttering another speech consisting of the two verses beginning with "sasapari."

Given by the Jamadagnis, kindled by the Jamadagnis, and given for the sake of prosperity by the Bhṛgus—Sasarparī, the speech that dispels ignorance (*amati*) and whose nature is to pervade everywhere as sound—has measured out the vast expanse, producing sound in the sky.

This very daughter of Sūrya, the goddess of speech, has extended among the gods, such as Indra and others, the imperishable, undecaying, immortal food characterized by immortality; she extends it on all sides through the utterance of *svāhā*.
*Jamadagnidattā*:
In the case of the root *dā* (meaning "to give") in its past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) form, the substitution of *dad* for *dā* occurs according to the rule *do daddoḥ*.
By the rule *tṛtīyā karmaṇi*, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member [of the compound] is retained.
*Ajūryam*.
[The root] *ṛ* [in the sense of] "decay of age" (*vayohānau*). [The suffix] *ṇyat* [is applied] according to the rule *ṛhalorṇyat*.
The rule "bahulam chandasi" provides the broad scope [for the application of the suffix],
while "nassubhyām" prescribes the final acute accent (antodāttatva).
Sasarparī has brought forth this musical instrument for them, a glory among the Pañcajanya peoples;
she, the winged one, bestows new life—she whom Palasti and Jamadagni gave to me.
Sasarparī brought forth renown for these people from among the Pañcajanya tribes. She, bestowing new life upon her wings, is she whom Palasti and Jamadagni gave to me. 16.
May Sarasvatī— the goddess of speech, whose nature is to flow everywhere through both prose and verse—

bring to us, in abundance and with speed, that fame which consists of food found among the *pañcajanāḥ* (the five peoples), namely the four castes with the Niṣādas as the fifth; may she bestow it upon us.

The *palasti-jamadagnis*—the *palastis*, the grey-haired, long-lived Jamadagni sages—who, having extracted this speech from the Sun, gave it to me; may that speech, the daughter of the Sun who carries [the world] like a wing (*pakṣyā*), grant me ever-new life, food, or vitality.
In the word *pāñcajanya*,
the suffix *ṅī* is applied according to the rule "it should be stated that [the suffix applies] after *pañcajana* when preceded by *bahiḥ*";
the acute accent (*udātta*) falls on the syllable *jihvā*.
*Pakṣyā*:
that which exists in the wing (*pakṣa*);
[the suffix] *yat* is applied because it belongs to the class beginning with *diś*.
There are three svaritas.
[The word] *navyam*:
from the word *nava*, the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of the base itself (*svārthika*) because it belongs to the *vasu*-class and so forth.
*Palastijamadagnayaḥ* means "the Palastas who are Jamadagnis.
This is a *karmadhāraya* compound;
it takes the accent of the compound.

May your two oxen be firm, may your sheep be strong and your rams steadfast; let not the yoke break nor the pole split asunder. May Indra grant us protection from the fall of the shafts; O you of uninjured rim, be our companion.

May your two wheels be firm; may your axle be strong. Let not the pole be torn asunder, nor let the yoke be shattered. May Indra protect the pole-strap from injury. O you of unimpaired rim, come to our aid and be with us. 17.

Having performed the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) at King Sudās’s sacrifice and desiring to depart from the sacrificial hall, Viśvāmitra, while yoking the horses and other animals to his chariot, praises the parts of the chariot:
"The two oxen" (*gāvau*); they are called "oxen" (*gāvau*) because they go (*gacchataḥ*). They are the two horses.
May the two [axles] be firm;
may the axle also be strong and solid;
and may the pole and the shaft not be shattered or destroyed.
And let the yoke not be shattered; let it not become broken.
May Indra hold fast the two falling pins before they fall apart.
O chariot of unimpaired felly, O you whose circumference is unhurt, come toward us and be united with us.

The sacrificer prays for his own welfare. O Vanaspati (Lord of the Forest), may this chariot made of forest wood not abandon us—may it not leave us behind—and may it not harm us—may it not destroy us. Furthermore, may there be well-being (*svasti*) for us until we reach our homes; likewise until the cessation of the journey; and until the unyoking of the horses harnessed to the chariot. *Hāḥ*: from the root *ohāk* (to abandon), in the *luṅ* tense, the suffix *sic* is elided by the rule "in mantras, *ghas*" etc.; there is a change of person. Because of the connection with *ca* or *vā*, there is no *nighāta* (anudātta accent) according to the rule "when joined with *ca* or *vā*, the first [verb is unaccented]. *Ririṣat*: from the causative of the root *riṣ* (to injure), in the *luṅ* tense with *caṅ*; the form is due to the doubling of the second syllable and the *ṇilopa* (elision of the causative marker). *Gṛhebhyaḥ*: from the root *grah* (to seize), with the suffix *ka*, meaning "house. The fifth case (*pañcamī*) is used here because of the rule "with *apa*, *āṅ*, or *pari*, the fifth case is employed. *Avase*: from the root *pū* (in the sense of ending/cessation), with the suffix *kvip*. In the singular dative, the absence of the elision of the long *ā* is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). There is *vṛddhi* strengthening, and the accent is that of the single substitute vowel (*ekādeśasvara*). 22.
The four hymns beginning with "indrotibhiḥ" are those hostile to Vasiṣṭha.
Long ago, there was indeed a royal sage named Sudās who was a disciple of Viśvāmitra;
for some reason, he became an enemy of Vasiṣṭha.
Viśvāmitra, however, out of anger for the sake of protecting his disciple, cursed Vasiṣṭha. These [verses] are of the nature of a curse; the Vasiṣṭhas do not hear those Ṛgvedic verses.

O Indra, with your many and most excellent aids, come to us today; O Maghavan, O Hero, quicken us! May he who hates us fall low; may the vital breath abandon him whom we hate. Indra! With your many aids, come to us today; O Maghavan, O Hero, quicken us! He who hates us—may he fall low; him whom we hate—may his vital breath abandon him.
One who intends to cast a curse upon another first provides protection for oneself with the first half-verse.
O Śūra, O heroic one capable of overcoming others; O Maghavan, O wealthy Indra; *adya*, at this time; *yāt*, from the root *yātayati*, which means "to increase" or "to cause to grow.
That which causes to grow is called *yāt*.
The elision of the case-ending *śas* is according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*.

Then he curses: "He who hates us—our enemy who harbors enmity toward us—may he, being base and inferior, fall down."

[He] heats even an axe and cuts even a *śimbala* tree.
Even the cauldron, O Indra, when it was heated and overturned, spat out foam.
He heats even the axe; he hews even the *śimbala* tree. O Indra, even the cauldron, boiling over and overturned, casts up foam.

Just as a tree, having encountered Indra’s axe— that is, his hatchet— is split apart and consumed by heat, becoming utterly deprived of its excellence, so too shall my hater be consumed. Just as the *śimbala*— the flower of the *śalmalī* tree— is severed from its stalk with ease, so shall it be.

Thus, may my hater—his limbs severed and cut asunder—be destroyed. May that hater, struck down and smitten, trembling and leaking like a heated cauldron or a cooking pot, vomit forth foam from his mouth, spitting it out by the power of my mantra.
People do not understand the nature of the arrow; they lead it away, thinking it to be a common beast.
They do not cause a swift horse to run a race with one that is not swift, nor do they place a donkey in front of horses.
O people, you do not perceive the arrow; thinking it to be a mere beast, they lead it away. They do not cause a swift horse to run a race, nor do they lead a donkey before a horse. 23.
Long ago, fearing that his ascetic merit might be exhausted, Viśvāmitra desisted from the curse and remained silent; however, Vasiṣṭha’s men bound him and brought him back.
To them, Viśvāmitra says:
"O people, you do not perceive—that is, you do not know—the power of the collection of mantras belonging to Viśvāmitra, who brings an end to the arrow."

For this very reason, thinking him to be a beast— using *paśu* as a particle with the same meaning as the word "beast"— they lead away, having bound that ṛṣi who remained silent out of greed so that there might be no depletion of his ascetic merit (*tapas*). They lead them to their own country.

Thus, having demonstrated his own capability, he censures Vasiṣṭha, saying that he is unlike [himself] and ought not to compete with me. "Not a horseless one" (nāvājinam) means "one who is not without horses" (avājinam).

The masters of speech, the eloquent ones, do not cause the all-knowing one—who is distinct from that—to laugh; they do not make him an object of ridicule. The meaning is that they do not compete with him.
Likewise, they do not lead a donkey—that is, a rāsabha—before or in front of a horse. In the same way, Vasiṣṭha is so dissimilar that he is not able to rival me; this is the meaning.

These sons of Bharata, O Indra, perceive neither the father’s side nor the grandfather’s side; they urge on their own horse as if it were a stranger, and they lead the bowstring-striving steed around in the race as if it were not their own.
O Indra, these sons of Bharata, the descendants of Bharata, these Viśvāmitras, perceive— that is, they know— the *apapitvam*, the departure from the Vasiṣṭhas;
they do not know the *prapitvam*, the approach toward them.
They have no association with the cultured;
the meaning is that they are indeed outsiders.

they move about, aiming their arrows to slay the Vasiṣṭhas.
In the fifth Anuvāka, there are nine hymns.

Among them, the first hymn, "imaṃ mahe," consisting of twenty-two verses, is in the Triṣṭubh metre and addressed to the Viśvedevas. It is the seerly composition (ārṣam) of Prajāpati, the son of Vāk or the son of Viśvāmitra. Regarding this, the Anukramaṇikā states: "imaṃ mahe; [the seer] Dyutako-gotra Prajāpati [composed] the Vaiśvadeva hymn."

In this hymn, the first verse is addressed to Agni; the following seven verses are addressed to Heaven and Earth (Dyāvāpṛthivī); the next is addressed to various deities (Śudevatā). The tenth is addressed to Heaven and Earth; the eleventh is addressed to Savitṛ. Following that, the verse beginning with "sukan" is addressed to Tvaṣṭṛ and Agni; the verse beginning with "vidyudrāḥ" is addressed to the Maruts and Sarasvatī. After that, there are three verses addressed to Viṣṇu, Indra, and Agni; and the verse beginning with "svadasva" is addressed to Agni. Thus is the Vaiśvadeva hymn.
The application of the hymn (*sūktaviniyoga*) is based on its indicative mark (*laiṅgika*).
Regarding the leading forward of the fire (*agnipraṇayana*) for a Kṣatriya, the verse "imaṃ mahe" serves as the *pratipad*.
This is stated in the Sūtra: "On the fifth full moon: 'imaṃ mahe vidadhyāya bhūpam'" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 2.17).
For this great festival, they have repeatedly brought forth the oblation for him who is worthy of praise;
may he hear us with his domestic fires, and may he, the tireless one, hear us with his celestial ones.

To this great one, for the sake of bestowing wealth, they have repeatedly brought forth the oblation for him who is worthy of praise. May he hear us with his domestic fires; may Agni, the eternal, hear us with his celestial flames. 1.

To Agni— the great one, worthy of being established at the vast sacrificial assembly (*vidatha*), produced by churning, and worthy of praise by all— [the priests] repeatedly, again and again, offer forth and sustain this hymn of praise (*stoma*) which brings happiness. That Agni, endowed with splendors (*anīka*) present in the home (*dame*) or belonging to those skilled in subduing others, may he hear this our hymn.
With divine splendors existing in heaven, he is eternal and uninterrupted.

"Let him hear the hymn measured by Agni when [the sacrifice] is joined, with the words: *śaśvat karava īḍayāya pra jabhruḥ* (AiB 1.28). Regarding *īḍayāya*: the acute accent (*udātta*) is applied by the rule *īḍavanda* etc. Regarding *damyebhiḥ*: the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of 'skilled therein' (*tatra sādhuḥ*). Sing praise to the Great Earth and to the Great Heaven! Desiring my desire and knowing it well, may they grant me no discontent. For at their hymn of praise in the assemblies, the gods, full of reverence, rejoice together with those who are present.

To the great earth, to the great heaven—to the two, sing praise! Desire moves about seeking, discerning, those two at whose hymn of praise in the assemblies the gods, full of reverence, rejoice together. 2.
O singer, knowing well, offer a great hymn of praise to the Great Heaven—the deity of the celestial world—and to the Great Earth.
My desire, seeking all enjoyments, moves everywhere.
In the assemblies and sacrifices of living men, the gods—or the worshippers—desiring honor, rejoice together with these two, Heaven and Earth, in their praise. Indeed, they revel in unison.
To the Earth.

O Heaven and Earth, let that which you have performed be true; be present for our great prosperity and well-being.
This homage first to Heaven and to Earth I offer with oblation; I seek precious treasure.

O Heaven and Earth, may your cosmic order be truth; be present for our great and auspicious welfare. This homage first to Heaven and to Earth I offer with a pleasing oblation; I seek a treasure from you. 3.
O Heaven and Earth (Rodasī), may your *ṛta*—your compassion—and your *satya*—that which is according to reality—prevail.
For our great prosperity and exaltation, for the successful completion of the sacrifice, may you two be fully present and powerful.
O Agni, let this homage be unto Heaven and Earth.

*Chāndasaḥ*: [This is] a Vedic form. *Bhūtam*: This is the form resulting from the elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix after the root *bhū* in the imperative (*loṭ*), according to the rule "in the Veda, [the substitution is] manifold" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*). Alternatively, it is the form of the aorist (*luṅ*) in the Veda, where there is the elision of the *sic* suffix by the rule "after *gā*, *sthā*, etc. (*gātisthā...*). There is the suppression of accent (*nighāta*). *Dive pṛthivyai*: The dative case is used according to the rule "to *namaḥ*, *svasti*, etc. (*namaḥsvasti...* Pāṇini 2.3.16). *Saparyāmi*: The root *pari-car* belongs to the *kaṇvādi* class; it means "to attend upon" or "to serve. It bears the accent of the affix (*pratyayasvaraḥ*). *Yāmi*: This is the form of the root *yā* in the present indicative (*laṭ*). Because of the division of the sentence (*vākyabheda*), there is no suppression of accent (*anighāta*).
For thus have the two world-halves, the observers of cosmic order (*ṛtāvarī*) who speak truth, been made manifest for you through the depth of wisdom;
even men, seeking heroic conquest, have paid homage to you both, O Earth, as they strive to kindle you.
And indeed, O two worlds, observers of cosmic order (ṛtavarī), the broad expanses have manifested themselves for you both.
Men of truthful speech, even in the assembly for the winning of heroes, have extolled you both, O Earth, seeking your favor.
Moreover, O *ṛtāvarī*— that is,

O you two who possess *ṛta*, or truth— O *rodasī*, Heaven and Earth! The ancient, primordial great seers (*maharṣi*), whose speech was true, indeed obtained from you both whatever object they desired.

Likewise, O Earth, in that battle—the encounter where the prize is won by heroes—men of even today, knowing and perceiving the greatness of you both, O Heaven and Earth, have praised and continue to praise you.
The root *vid* is used in the sense of "attainment" (*lābhe*). It belongs to the class of roots ending in a consonant (*abhayapadī*).

Who truly knows? Who here can declare it? Whence did these gods arise? Whence this creation? Whence comes this assembly? Their lowest seats are visible, but they are in the highest, secret ordinances. 5.

Heaven, the progenitor of you, the great one—the father of all, the protector and the generator—[I] remember now that ancient, primordial kinship of ours, inherited from of old;
for since everything is born from one source, Heaven is our sister. I recall such a state of sisterhood even now.

the sense is that the gods stationed there listen to my hymn of praise.
*Purāṇam*:
From the word *purā*, the suffix *ṭa* is applied in the sense of "belonging to" (*īpikārthe*) by the rule "sāyaṃciram...", as in *hiraṇyapāṇiḥ*.
He is so described because gold is in his hand for the purpose of giving;
or alternatively,
in a sacrifice performed by the gods, the Adhvaryus placed the *prāśitra* (the portion for consumption) in the hand of Savitṛ, who had become the sacrificer, for the sake of eating it.
There, he cut off the two hands of Tvaṣṭṛ before the *praśitra* portion was taken.
Then the Adhvaryu priests, having fashioned two golden hands, joined them together;
thus, he became Hiraṇyapāṇi (the Golden-handed).

And thus says the Kauṣītaki: "When they were offering the *prāśitra* portion to Savitṛ, his hand was severed; they gave him two golden [hands] instead; therefore he is Hiraṇyapāṇi. *Sujihvaḥ*: Savitṛ, having beautiful speech, comes from the sky—that is, from the atmosphere—to the *vidatha*, the sacrifice, thrice, at the three *savanas*; "coming" (*āpatyamānaḥ*) is the ellipsis to be supplied.
The latter half-verse is direct address (*pratyakṣa*).
O Savitṛ, you [should grant] among the gods both [prosperity] and the *śloka* existing among those who praise;
for *śloka* is that by which one is praised— namely, a hymn of praise—
and that you should cause us to attain.
Immediately thereafter, O All-pervading One, impel toward us all the desired fruit.
"Hiraṇyapāṇiḥ" (the golden-handed one).

Yāska provides various etymologies for the word *hiraṇya*: "Why 'hiraṇya'? Because it is held (*dhīyate*) when being stretched out, or because it is held from person to person" (Nirukta 2.10), and so forth.
He also explains the word *pāṇi*: "'Pāṇi' is derived from the root *paṇ*, meaning 'to honor'" (Nirukta 2.26).
The root *harya* is used in the senses of "desire" and "movement.
According to the rule *haryateḥ kanyan hira ca*, the suffix *kanyan* is applied; *hira* is the substitute for the verbal root.
Because of its status as a *nit* (having an indicatory *n*), it is accented on the first syllable.
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the accent belongs to the first member. For example: *patyamānaḥ*.
[The root] *pad* means "to go."
The root *div* belongs to the first class and is conjugated in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*).
The substitution of *t* for *d* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
[The form is] *aśreḥ*.

In the case of the root *śri* in the sense of "service" (*sevā*), when the *laṅ* suffix is applied, there is the elision of the *śap* affix according to the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi. There is no *nighāta* (anudātta accent) because of the rule "cavāyoge prathamā. [The word] *suva*.
The root √ṣū, meaning "to impel," belongs to the *tudādi* class. [It forms] *sarvatāti*.
The suffix *āt* in *sarvadevāttātil* is a *svārthika* (adjectival) suffix; it bears the accent of the *lit* suffix.
May the skillful, fair-handed, self-strong, and holy divine Tvaṣṭṛ grant us those things for our protection.
O Rbhus, accompanied by Pūṣan, rejoice; with the pressing-stones raised, you have fashioned the sacrifice.

He of good deeds, of beautiful hands, possessing noble speech, the upholder of Truth, the divine Tvaṣṭṛ—may he grant us those things for our protection. O Ṛbhus, accompanied by Pūṣan, rejoice! With the pressing-stones raised aloft, you have fashioned the sacrifice. 12.

The well-doer, the excellent creator of the world, the fair-handed one whose hands are auspicious, the possessor of wealth, the possessor of power, the observer of Truth whose resolve is infallible—the divine Tvaṣṭṛ—may he grant us those things which we require for our protection and for our aid. O Ṛbhus!
They are called Ṛbhus because they shine widely.
O Ṛbhus, accompanied by Pūṣan and joined with Pūṣan, do you rejoice;
gladden us by the bestowing of wealth.
With the pressing-stones raised for the purpose of extracting Soma, being those who have lifted the stones, O priests, you fashioned this our sacrifice.
Thus, *ataṣṭa*. [The root] *takṣū* (or *tvakṣū*) means "to make thin.
Because it is marked with the letter *u*, there is no reduplication.
The elision of the *s* is by the rule "jhalo jhali";
the elision of the letter *k* is by the rule "skoḥ saṃyogādyoḥ";
and the use of the singular number for the plural is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*).
The Maruts, with their chariots of lightning and spears, the youths of heaven, born of Truth, tireless;
may Sarasvatī and the noble ones hear us—may the swift ones bestow wealth along with heroic sons.

The Maruts, whose chariots are lightning, armed with spears, the youths of heaven, born of Truth, tireless; Sarasvatī, the worshipful ones who hear us; Dhātṛ—may you swift ones bestow wealth along with heroic sons. 13.
1. Ta-gatikānyāḥ. 2. Elision of *ca* and *sic*; elision of *ja*, *ṇa*, and *sal*.
^1Viśudrathāḥ: endowed with shining chariots. ^2Ṛṣmantaḥ: possessing splendor.
*Ṛṣi* is a specific type of weapon; [the word *maryāḥ*] ends with that [suffix].
*Divah*: "shining from heaven. *Maryāḥ*: "slayers of enemies. *Ṛtajātāḥ*: "born from the waters," or manifested from the source of water.
Or else: [an alternative interpretation follows].

"Ṛtajātāḥ" means those from whom *ṛta* (truth) was born as water. "Ayāsaḥ" means those whose nature is constant movement. "Yajñiyāsaḥ" means those worthy of sacrifice. "Marutaḥ" refers to the Maruts. "Sarasvatī":
she is called Sarasvatī because her flow exists in the form of prose and verse (*gadyapadya*).

And the Goddess of Speech—may all these gods hear this hymn of mine, yes, hear it! O Maruts, you who are swift (turāsaḥ), being intent on hastening to bestow fruit upon us, grant us wealth (rayim) consisting of heroic sons (sahavīram) along with riches; bestow it upon us!
*Dhāta*: from the root *dhā*, in the imperative (*loṭ*), there is elision of the suffix *śap* by the rule “*bahulaṃ chandasi*” (Pāṇini 2.4.73);
then, by the rule “*tasantasananathanāśca*,” there is the substitution of *ta* for the suffix.
Because it begins with *pāda*, there is no *anighāta*.
Since *tapaḥ* has the *pittva* designation, it is *anudātta*, and thus the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*) remains.
[The word] *turāsaḥ*.

The root *tur* is used in the sense of "hastening. The suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule for roots ending in *i* or *u*. Because it is in the vocative case (*āmantrita*), there is no elision of the following word.
The hymns and songs of praise have gone forth to Viṣṇu, the one who is renowned in many places, as singers go to the dwelling of Bharga;
he of the wide stride, the one who is sought after, whose many youthful mothers, the progenitors, honor him.

To Viṣṇu, the hymns of praise and the songs of those who perform sacred rites have gone, as if to the path of Bharga—[to him] the wide-striding, the preeminent one, whose many youthful mothers do not fail at the head [of the sacrifice]. 14.

The *stomas* are hymns of praise, so called because they are praised by means of them; the *arkas* are the *śastras* (recited liturgical texts) which are worthy of being praised. Like those who produce wealth—that is, like the makers of riches—they stand as such in this sacrifice (*yāman*) which is continuously extending. [They attend] upon the one of many deeds (*purudasma*).
Alternatively,
he is called *purudasma* because he destroys many *dasyus*;
let them go to that god, Viṣṇu.
The many mothers, the progenitors of all that is born; the young women, mutually mingled;
the *kakubha*s—so called because they "prop up" (*kaṃ skumbhanti*) or expand [space], namely the quarters of the sky.
Or else:
The meaning of the *kakubh* meter is as follows:
for the quarters of space stand as if uplifted, being perceived at the tops of trees.
These quarters do not disregard nor do they harm the command of Viṣṇu.
Maḥ: Viṣṇu; Urukrama:
he whose stride (krama)—that is, his step—is wide (uru) and great (mahān).
In the Trivikrama incarnation, he stood having traversed the entire universe with a single foot.
They went. In the conditional mood (*luṅ*), *caleluka* [is applied] by the rule "in mantras, *ghas* [and other roots take *luk*]" and so forth. *Kakubhaḥ*.
The correctness of the form and accent is established by virtue of its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group.
Indra, ruling through all heroic powers, has filled both world-halves with his greatness.
Purandara, the slayer of Vṛtra, with his bold army, seize and bring to us abundant cattle.
Indra, ruling through all heroic powers, has filled both worlds with his greatness. O breaker of forts, slayer of Vṛtra, leader of bold armies, gather for us and bring much cattle. 15.
He, Indra, being attained through all heroic powers—that is, through all capacities—filled both worlds, heaven and earth, with his own greatness;
the remainder [of the verse] is expressed in the direct [present tense]:
Purandara.
1. *ta-la-dyotamānā*: the sons of the radiant Rudra; or 2.
*ta-mārayitāraḥ*: those who are beneficial to human beings; or 3. *ta-jāyate*.
4. *ta-ṇa-stomaṃ* means "the hymn of praise. 5. In all instances of *kha-ga-gha-ca-ja-ṇa-na-bha-ya*, [the *ya*] is present.
6. In *kha-ga-gha-ca-ja-ṇa-na-bha-sa*, the letter *sa* does not exist.
7. In the manuscripts kha, ga, gha, ca, ja, ṇa, na, bha, and sa, the phrase *uru...kramaḥ* does not exist; in manuscript ja, it reads *uruḥ vistṛtaḥ kramaḥ*.
8. In the manuscripts kha, ga, gha, ca, ja, ṇa, na, bha, and sa, the phrase *śeṣaḥ pratyakṣakṛtaḥ* does not exist.
[He is] the shatterer of the cities of enemies, the slayer of Vṛtra—the destroyer of Vṛtra—endowed with a virile host characterized by the habit of overwhelming others.
As such, having gathered together the cattle of the cattle-herd, bring to us— that is, give to us— an abundance, in such a way that it becomes plentiful;
or rather, grant us the abundance of cattle, meaning many cattle.
Puraṃdara: To the root *dṛ* in the sense of "tearing apart" (*vidāraṇe*), when the word *pur-* is used as an upapada, the suffix *khac* is applied by the rule *pūḥsarvayordārisahoḥ*.
By the rule *vācyamapuraṃdarau ca*, there is the augment *ām* for the first member of the compound due to its being a nipātana (irregular formation).
Because it contains the letter *c*, it is udātta on the penultimate syllable.
In *vṛṣṇena*,
the substitution of *ṣ* occurs in the *saṃhitā* stage by the rule "after a preceding word [ending in a sibilant]."
Alternatively, when there is *pāva*, the substitution of *ṇa* occurs as in *āraṣyām*.
Having combined [the vowels],
even in the case of *praheli*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) due to the status of the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*).
The form *bhavam* is derived from the rule "grahijyāvayivyadhivaṣṭivicativṛścatipṛcchatibhṛjjatīnāṃ ṅiti ca" (Pāṇini 6.1.16).
The acute accent on the vowel preceding the suffix is due to the rule "liti" (Pāṇini 6.1.193).
[The form] *paśvaḥ*.

From the word *paśu*, before the suffix *śas*, there is no substitution of a homogeneous long vowel (*savarṇadīrgha*), according to the rule: "In the Vedic language, there is an option regarding [the application of] *jas* and the following [suffixes]."

The Nāsatyas are my parents, inquiring after their kin; the Aśvins’ name of common descent is beautiful. For you two are the bestowers of wealth upon us; O undeceivable ones, you protect the gift of riches through your tireless deeds. 16. Nāsatyā | me | pitarā | bandhu-pṛcchā | sa-jātyam | aśvinoḥ | cāru | nāma | yuvam | hi | sthaḥ | rayi-dhau | naḥ | rayīṇām | dātram | rakṣethe | akarvaiḥ | adabdhā || 16 ||
O Nāsatyas, Aśvins, you are the inquirers after kinsmen;
because you inquire of us—your kinsmen—as the givers of oblations regarding the matter required, you are the questioners of kinsmen.
May you both be my protectors, O Fathers.
O Aśvins, your kinship is indeed beautiful—a lovely name signifying your common origin and union.
O Aśvins, you two are surely the bestowers of the highest wealth among all riches for us.
Furthermore, you two, who are invincible and cannot be surpassed by anyone, protect me—the giver of oblations—with blameless and excellent deeds.
Nāsatyā:
by the rule *nabhrāṇnapāt* etc., there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) of the negative particle *nañ*.
Bandhupṛcchā.
One should ask. [The suffix] *kvip* [is applied].
By the rule “*supāṃ suluk...*” (*Pāṇini 7.1.39*), there is the substitution of *ḍā* for the case-ending (*sup*).

Sajātya means "belonging to the same class" (sajāti). It is derived by applying the suffix *yat* according to the rule *bhave chandasi* ("the suffix *yat* is used in the sense of 'being' in Vedic usage").
*tirasvaritaḥ* is the form of the root *as-* in the present indicative (*laṭ*).
From the absence of exertion, there is no affliction.

Great is that beautiful name of yours, O sages, since you, O gods, become [manifest] as all the Indras. O much-invoked one, as a friend with the beloved Ṛbhus, fashion this prayer of ours for the winning of wealth. 17. Great is that, O sages, your beautiful name, since you, O gods, become all the Indras. As a friend with the Ṛbhus, O much-invoked one, with those who are dear—fashion this prayer of ours for the winning of wealth. 17.

O wise ones, O gods, that great and abundant name or deed of yours is indeed beautiful and captivating; for by that deed, all of you become gods in Indra—that is, in the world characterized by Indra—and truly attain divinity. O Puruhūta, invoked by many, O Indra, [you were accompanied] by the R̥bhus, who are dear and most beloved.

1. *Ta-*: "Endowed with" means "possessing. 2. *La-sa-*: "The two parents. 3. *La-*: "The Nāsatyas"—this is the name and their beautiful form. 4. *Ja-ṇa-*: The word "he" does not exist. 5. *Ta-*: "That greatness. 6. *Ja-ṇa-*: The word "he" does not exist.
[They] exist by means of *ṛta*, or they shine by means of *ṛta*.
You are a friend with the divine *Ṛbhus*.
O Ṛbhus, accompanied by Indra, fashion—meaning accept—this our prayer, this hymn of praise, for our attainment, that is, for the sake of obtaining wealth and other blessings.
Since [the suffix] *sup* is elided by the rule "supāṃ suluk" and so forth,
[the form] is *bhavatha*.
This is the form [of the verb] *bhavati* in the present tense (*laṭ*).
Due to its connection with *yadvat*, there is no elision of the accent (*anighāta*).
In the compound *sakha ṛbhubhiḥ*, according to the rule “*ṛtyakaḥ*” in the context of *saṃhitā*, there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) and the shortening of the vowel.
May Aryaman and Aditi, who are worthy of sacrifice, [uphold] the undeceivable ordinances of Varuṇa.
Keep away from us childlessness for as long as we live; may our path be rich in offspring and abundant in cattle.
May Aryaman, Aditi, and the worshipful ones—unassailable are the ordinances of Varuṇa—keep us far from childlessness. May our path be rich in progeny and abundant in cattle. 18.

Aryaman: He is called Aryaman because he always goes (ṛcchati) or moves; he is the Sun. Aditi is the Mother of the Gods. The worshipful (yajñiyāsaḥ) gods are those worthy of sacrifice. Varuṇa is he whose ordinances (vratāni)—that is, his actions—are inviolable (adabdhāni), meaning unharmed. May that Varuṇa and these other gods, beginning with Aryaman, protect us—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Therefore, you [are the ones] for us who have performed deeds harmful to our offspring— that is, to our sons—
or rather,
"offspring" (apatyam) refers to that which does not cause one to fall.
Separate—keep apart—from the traveler those other childless deeds that cause one to fall;
the meaning is: act in such a way that those harmful actions do not touch him.
Now, regarding the word *gātuḥ*.
Because they sing and praise Indra and the other gods here, it is called a *gātu*, a house.
May our house—our own home—be rich in cattle, endowed with livestock and the like, and rich in progeny, possessed of offspring. [May] Aryaman [grant this].
The root *ṛ* means "to go.
The formation of the word is established by the rule of irregular derivation (*nipātana*) beginning with "śramukṣan-līhan-kreḍan," etc.
[Thus we have] *aditiḥ*.
From the root *dīṅ* in the sense of "to perish," the suffix *kvip* is applied in the agentive sense;
this forms a compound with the negative particle *nañ*.
Yāska [explains] as "Aditi is not perishing" (*aditir adīnā*, Nirukta 4.22).
The shortening is Vedic.
The accent belongs to the negative particle *nañ*.
[The verb form is] *yuyota*.
From the root *yu*, meaning "to mix," in the *loṭ* (imperative) mood, the suffix *śap* is replaced by *plu* according to the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*.
By the rule *tasanap*, the suffix *tap* is replaced by *tab*.
[The form is] *gantaḥ*.
The root *gam* means "to go.
The suffix *tun* is applied according to the rule *sitanigamimasisacyavidhāṅkuśibhyaḥ*. Because it is [included] among the *nis* group, it is ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable).
*gātuḥ*: the suffix *tu* is applied according to the rule *gāyāhibhyaśca* (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.72).
May the messenger of the gods, sent forth in many ways, proclaim us as sinless in our integrity.
May Earth, Heaven, and the Waters hear us, as well as the Sun with the stars and the wide mid-air.

The messenger of the gods, sent forth in many ways, shall declare us sinless in our completeness. May Earth, Heaven, and the Waters hear us, as well as the Sun with the stars and the wide firmament. 19.
