"Purudha" means produced or appointed in many places for the purpose of the *abhihotra* sacrifice;
or alternatively,
"purubhiḥ" means impelled by many sacrificers for the purpose of summoning the gods to be worshipped— the messenger of the gods.
And likewise, the Taittirīyaka states: “Agni was the messenger of the gods” (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.1.13).

[Notes on variant readings: 1. For *na-la-sa*, [the reading is as follows]. 2. In the versions *kha-ga-gha-ca-ja-ṇa-na-bha-sa*, the phrase “*sa varuṇaḥ*” does not exist. 3. In the versions *kha-ga-gha-ca-ja-ṇa-na-bha*, the word “*apatyānām*” does not exist. 4. In the versions *kha-ga-ca-ja-ṇa-ta-na-bha*, there are reasons for the falling away [of the text]. 5. In *ja-ṇa*, it is “*tadahitāni*”; in *na*, it is “*ahitāni*. 6. In *ta*, it is a negative compound (*nañsamāsa*). 7. In *ca-ja-ṇa-sa-na*, it is “*naśvaraḥ*. 8. In *ja*, it is “*bahuprakāreṣu*. 9. In *ta*, it is “*vihṛtaḥ*. (Ṛgveda 2.57.450)
O Agni, when through you truth has been produced, may my fortune—my wealth—not perish;
moreover, may I attain the seat, the abode of riches and of abundant wealth.
Always; because of the acute accent on the first syllable in words such as *khara*, it is an acute-accented pada-initial (*pādādyudātta*). *Pitṛka*.
The root *pṛc* means "to join" (*saṃparke*).

In the imperative (*loṭ*), there is elision (*ślu*) of the suffix *śap* according to the rule "there is much [irregularity] in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*). Furthermore, according to the same rule "there is much [irregularity] in the Veda," there is the substitution of *i* for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).
*mṛdhyāḥ*. The root *mṛdh* has the meaning "to harm. In the *liṅ* (optative) mood, by the rule "the endings *ti*, *tas*, etc., become *si*, *thas*, etc.," the *tip* ending becomes *sip*.
For the animal sacrifice, the invitatory verse (*yājyā*) for the *puroḍāśa-sviṣṭakṛt* offering is "svadasva havyā.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "'svadasva havyā samipo didīhi' is the [verse] for the *puroḍāśa-sviṣṭakṛt*" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.5).
Taste the oblations; shine forth with nourishment; smilingly, measure out our glories. O Agni, conquer all enemies swiftly in battles; being well-disposed, shine upon us.
Taste the oblations; shine forth with nourishments; bestow upon us, as you are wont, glorious fame.
O Agni, conquer all those enemies in battles; being worthy and well-disposed, shine for us. 22.
O Agni, do thou relish—make savory—the *havyā*, the oblations worthy of being offered.
Do thou fully illuminate our *iṣaḥ*, our foods.
Having been illuminated, do thou measure out—bring together toward us—those *śravāṃsi*, those foods.
The meaning is "do so.
Then, in battles (*pṛtsu*), conquer (*jeṣi*) all those obstructing enemies.

Furthermore, being well-disposed (*sumanāḥ*), that is, having an auspicious mind, cause us (*naḥ*) to shine (*dīdihi*) throughout all days (*viśvā... ahāni*), making them fit for rituals such as the Agnihotra.
"Enjoy yourself. This is the form of the root *svad* in the sense of "tasting," in the imperative mood (*loṭ*).
In the accentuation of *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes, the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*) prevails.
[Thus we have] *didīhi*.
This is from the root *divu* (meaning "to play," etc. in the *loṭ* mood; the elision (*ślu*) of the *vikaraṇa* suffix occurs by the rule "frequently in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).
Because it is subsequent, once lengthening has been applied by the rule "hali ca," the elision of the *val* [consonant] follows;
then there is the *nighāta* (elision of accent);
and [the suffix] *asmadyak*.
The word *asmānatti* is formed from the root *ad* with the suffix *kvip*.
By the rule "viśvadevayoṣa ṭeḥ," the final vowel (*ṭi*) is replaced by the suffix *anta*.
Then, by the rule "supāṃ suluk," there is elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*).

Because the substitute *adya* is prescribed as having an udātta accent on its final syllable, when the *yaṇ* substitution is applied, the *yaṇ* becomes svarita according to the rule "udāttasvaritayoḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.4).
[The form is] *mimīhi*.
[The root is] *māṅ*, meaning "to measure" and "to sound."
The root *hu* (to sacrifice) and others;
in its imperative (*loṭ*) form, the active voice (*parasmaipada*) occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*);
there is elision of the accent (*nighāta*).
Sumanāḥ:
by the rule "somamanasī0," the first syllable of the final member [of the compound] is udātta.
Dīdihi.

When there is elision (*luk*) of *diver-yaṅ*, in the case of the imperative (*loṭ*), there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) due to the presence of *tu* and so forth; furthermore, there is elision (*lopa*) of *val*.
The second hymn, consisting of twenty-two verses beginning with "upasaḥ pūrvāḥ," is in the Triṣṭubh meter.

According to the Anukramaṇikā, [the seer] is Prajāpati. It is addressed to the Viśvedevas, for as stated regarding the previous hymn, "Prajāpati is indeed [the seer], and [it is] Vaiśvadeva," due to the use of the word "hi" (indeed) here.

The application of the hymn (*sūktaviniyoga*) is based on internal indicative marks (*laiṅgika*). Herein, first is the praise of Dawn (*uṣas*); after that, nine verses addressed to deities beginning with Agni; following those, verses addressed to the deities of Day and Night; then four verses addressed to Heaven and Earth (*rodasī*), or to Day and Night according to some; the fifteenth is addressed to the Viśvedevas, and the sixteenth is addressed to Indra (though some consider it to be for Agni or Tvaṣṭṛ). After that, there are six verses concerning the raining Indra.
1. *kha*, *ga*, *ja*, and *ṇa* have *mṛdh* in the sense of injury (*hiṃsārtha*); *ca* and *mṛdh* are in the sense of injury; *bha*, *la*, and *sa* have *mṛdh* in the sense of injury.
2. *kha*, *ga*, and *ca* are the same; *ja* and *ṇa* are the same as [their respective] *samāna*s; *na* is the same as *vanam*. 3. In *la*, "all" (*sarvān*) does not exist.
4. [The vowel] becomes long in those cases.
5. In the versions *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *sa*, the phrase "of the udātta and svarita [vowels]" is absent.
6. In the versions *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *sa*, the phrase "elision before *va*" (*vali lopaḥ*) is absent.
7. [From the rule regarding the application of the sounds *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *sa*, and *ha*: Maṇḍala 3, Adhyāya 5, Sūtra 55. Third Aṣṭaka, verse 453.
O Agni, many (*purutrā*)—that is, numerous—desires (*kāmāḥ*), that is, longings, of mine (*me*) fly apart (*vi patayanti*), meaning they go in various directions.
I meditate upon the ancient hymns for the sake of the *śamī*—the ritual characterized by the Agniṣṭoma and other sacrifices.
Thereafter, when the fire has been kindled for the purpose of the sacrifice, let us speak only the truth (*ṛta*);
for if there be untruthful speech, there would be a deficiency in the sacrifice.
*Purutrā*: the suffix *trā* is applied according to the rule beginning with "devamanuṣyapuruṣa" and so forth. *Patayanti*.
The root *palū* means "to go.
The suffix *ṇic* is added in its own sense (without changing the meaning).
The king, being one and the same, is distributed in many places; he lies among the reeds, moving through the forests.
One mother carries the calf and dwells [therein]. Great is the unique divine power of the gods.

He is common to all, a king, distributed in many places; lying among the reeds, he is far-reaching throughout the forests. One mother carries the calf, while another dwells [with him]; great is this power of the gods.

Even without being anointed, those who are pregnant—having become possessed of embryos by means of fire—bring forth and produce fruit and flowers. This indeed is the sovereign power (*aiśvarya*) of the gods. *Āśit*: from the root *kṣi* [in the sense of] "dwelling" or "going," with the suffix *kip*. *Anūrat*: from the root *rudh* [in the sense of] "desire," with the suffix *kip*; the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs according to the rule "it is seen in other cases as well. The accent is on the radical syllable. *Taraṇīṣu*: the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to the rule "the forms *taruṇī*, *talunī*, etc., are established [with this suffix]. *Antarvatīḥ*: the substitution of *vat* for *matup* occurs according to the rule "for *kṣaya*. *Suvate*: this is the form of the root *pūṅ* [in the sense of] "the release of the embryo of a living being" in the present tense (*laṭ*). [The word *nighataḥ* marks the end. 28.
The child lies in the east; now the one calf, having two mothers, wanders without kin.
These are the ordinances of Mitra and Varuṇa; great and unique is the divine sovereignty of the gods.
Lying down in front, now the child of two mothers wanders alone, friendless; these are the ordinances of Mitra and Varuṇa. Great is the singular divine sovereignty of the gods. 6.
Dvimātā: he who has two mothers, heaven and earth, is Dvimātā;
or alternatively, he who is the creator of the two worlds.

The Sun, having set in the western direction at the time of sunset, becomes reclined (*śayu*), lying down and inactive. But then, at the time of rising, he alone—the common child (*vatsa*) of Heaven and Earth due to his drawing up their essence—moves as one, unbound in his course and without support, traveling through the sky.
These indeed are the deeds (*vrata*) of Mitra and Varuṇa; they lie down [at rest].
The root *śīṅ* means "to sleep. By the rule *vbhṛmṛśītacari0*, etc., the suffix *ugra* is applied, and the vowel is elided. Thus, it has two vowels (*dvimātā*).
Regarding the word *nadyṛtaḥ*, there is the suffix *kap* prescribed by the rule “*nadyṛtaśca*”; however, there is a prohibition of this by the rule “*ṛtacchandasi*”.
The Hotṛ-priest, having two mothers, a sovereign in the sacrificial assemblies, moves ahead of others; he dwells as one who is well-established.
They bring forth delightful things for the one who speaks delightfully; great indeed is the singular divine sovereignty of the gods.

The son of two mothers, the Hotṛ-priest, the sovereign in the assemblies, moves along the forefront; he dwells in both worlds. They bring forth delightful things for the one who speaks delightfully; great indeed is the singular divine sovereignty of the gods. 7.

The creator of the two worlds, the Hotṛ priest who invokes the gods at the *vidathas*—the sacrifices—the sovereign ruler (*samrāj*) who shines perfectly in the rites, Agni moves first in the highest heaven as the Sun;
there he abides. He, the root of all action, dwells in the earth.
Or rather:
He moves toward— that is, he consumes— the foremost or principal portion, for the Śruti declares, "The Sviṣṭakṛt is indeed the foundation.
Furthermore, the singers, whose speech is *vraṇya*— that is, whose speech is delightful— bring forth, or perform with excellence, *vraṇyāni*— that is, delightful hymns of praise.
This is the sovereignty of the gods.
It moves;
there is no elision [of the accent] because of the rule "when *ca* and others are omitted."

1. In the *ta* [mantra], there is no long vowel. 2. In the *la* [mantra], it is at the time of sunset. 3. In the *kha*, *bha*, *ca*, and *pha* [mantras], it is "without support" (*anālambanaḥ*); in the *ca* and *pha* [mantras], it is "by means of power" (*balena*). 4. In the *ja* and *ṇa* [mantras], it concerns ritual actions (*karmāṇi*). This indeed is the sovereignty of the gods. 5. In the *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *bha*, and *sa* [mantras], it is in the lineage (*anvaye*). 6. In the *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, and *sa* [mantras], the word "he eats" (*bhakṣayāti*) is absent. 7. In the *na*, *la*, and *sa* [mantras], they lead forth (*praṇayanti*). 8. In the *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ja*, and *ṇa* [mantras], there is an absence of striking down (*nighātābhāvaḥ*).
As if of one fighting from close at hand, everything advancing was seen turned back. The thought of the nearest one moves toward the milk of the cow. Great is the unique asuric power of the gods. 8.
Like that of a hero fighting at the very front, everything moving toward him is seen; the thought moves within the cow to seize her. Great is the singular divine power of the gods. 8.

The entire multitude of beings (*viśvaṃ bhūtajātam*), being near the celestial fire (*dyāvāgneḥ*) situated at the end, came toward it facing it; it was seen turned away from them, with its back to them.
Therein is an illustration:
"like that of a hero."

Just as the enemy force, when facing a brave and capable king who is fighting and waging war, is seen turning its back, even so that Agni, being perceived by all, moves within and holds back the *goḥ*— that is, the scorching heat which is injurious to the water (*udaka*).

While fighting, Viṣṇu, the pervader, Vyāsa, the protector of all, bestowing upon himself beloved and most dear, immortal— that is, imperishable— abodes, which are splendors, that Agni protects the supreme path, the place.
Alternatively:
maintaining the *dhāmāni*—the supports of the worlds—and the *amṛtāḥ*—the waters—he protects the *paramaṃ pāthaḥ*, the highest place of water, namely the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
That *agni* knows, that is, understands, all those *viśvā bhuvanāni*, all the classes of beings.
*Gopāḥ*: from the root *gopāyati* with the suffix *kvip*, there is the elision of the vowel *a* and the elision of the *ya*.
In the word *agninā*, in the *saṃhitā* (continuous text), the substitution of *ru* occurs by the rule "In *yuṣmad*, *tad*, and *takṣan*, when followed by *su*, within the foot [of a verse]."

The twin sisters fashioned diverse forms; of these two, one is lovely and the other is black. When the dark and the ruddy sisters, though of different colors, attained a single common nature through their great power.

They have fashioned two distinct forms; of these two, one shines black, the other dark-brown. That which is the dark-brown sister and that which is the ruddy sister—great indeed is this singular divine power of the gods.
The two who are twins, identical in form, and joined as a pair—Day and Night—create various forms, such as white, black, and other colors.

When they become sisters to one another, the one is dark-colored and the other is ruddy, shining with whiteness. Of these two, one—the Day—is bright and shines through its connection with rays of light;
the other, characterized as Night, appears black due to its connection with darkness.
The feminine form is *yamyā*.
The substitution of *dā* occurs in place of the case-ending (*sup*).
It shines.
Because of the rule "ekānyābhyāṃ samarthābhyām," there is no *nighāta* (anudātta accent).
Where the mother and the daughter, like two milch-cows, suckle their young together; in the seat of Order, within the lap of the great ones, you alone possess the supreme sovereignty of the gods.

Where the Mother and the Daughter, both yielding their milk at once, suckle [the infant] together; in that seat of Truth, I praise those two who face each other. Between them lies the one great asuric power of the gods. 12.
"The Earth is the mother because she is the creator of all; and the Sky is the daughter, placed afar.
Regarding this, Yāska [states]: "The daughter is the one placed afar, who yields [milk] for these" (Nirukta 3.4).

These two, Heaven and Earth, who are like two cows yielding their own essence in the form of milk for the unconfined Sabara; therefore, they are the two "milch-cows" (*dhenū*) that must satisfy the world. Wherein, in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), being "united" (*asamīcī*)—that is, joined with one another—they "cause to suckle" (*dhāpayete*), making each other drink their own essence. I praise those two, Heaven and Earth, situated within that intermediate space which is the "seat" (*sadas*) of *ṛta*, the water. Or alternatively: Heaven causes the earth to suckle the essence characterized by rain, [and the earth causes heaven to suckle] the essence characterized by the oblation (*āhuti*).
1. Kha, ga, ca, and pha omit "rātri"; pa omits "rātri. 2. Kha, ga, gha, ca, ja, ṇa, na, bha, la, and sa do not have "nānā.
3. Ta has "binihitā."
4. [The reading] *gha* has *rasasya*; [the reading] *na-la-sa* has *kṣīrarūpasya*. 5. In *na-la-sa*, the word ‘*te*’ is not present.
6. In *kha-ga-ca-ja-ṇa-na-bha-sa*, it is *dyauḥ vṛtilakṣaṇaṃ rasam*.
The essence is the sky and the earth; thus mother and daughter become each other.
Standing in the seat of Order, in the place of the sacrifice, I praise you both.
Regarding *sabardughā*:

those learned in the tradition say that the word *saba* denotes milk. With this as an upapada, from the root *duh* (meaning "to fill"), the suffix *kap* is applied according to the rule *duhaḥ kaśca*, and the final syllable is replaced by *gha*.
Because the affix (*pratyaya*) has the marker *pittva*, it is *anudātta*; thus, the accent of the verbal root (*dhātu-svara*) remains.

In *dhāpayete*: from the root *dhed* meaning "to drink" with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), when the *laṭ* (present tense) suffix is applied, the rule "and [after roots] having the sense of swallowing or moving" would normally require the *parasmaipada* (active voice); however, by the supplementary rule "an addition regarding *dheṭ* among the roots beginning with *pā*," the *ātmanepada* (middle voice) is applied.
Non-prolation occurs due to the connection with the syllables of the *yati*.
Licking her calf, she has lowed; with what world has the cow placed herself on high?
She, the *iḷā*, swells with the milk of *ṛta*; she alone is the great sovereignty of the gods.

Licking another’s calf, she has lowed. With what world has the cow settled down? Upright, she has swelled with the milk of the cosmic order (*ṛta*). *Iḷā*—great is the sole sovereignty (*asuratva*) of the gods. 13.
The Earth’s calf is Agni; licking him with her tongue in the form of streams of water, the Great One—Dyaus—is lowing, making sound through the clouds;
she is Dyaus, the milch-cow who brings delight.
The wise one, having taken the water from that earth which was devoid of water, assumed his own form as a cloud (*megharūpa*) and deposited it with water.
That earth, previously devoid of water, becomes moistened during the rainy season by the milk—that is, the water—of the Sun, who is the embodiment of truth (*vṛta*);
for according to the Smṛti, "From the Sun rain is born" (Manu 3.76).
*rihatī* is the form of the present participle (*śatṛ*) from the root *lih* in the sense of "tasting" (*āsvādane*).
According to the rule *śataranumaḥ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied, and it bears the udātta accent.
*Apinvata*.
[The root] *pi* is used in the sense of "to sprinkle" (*secana*). It belongs to the *muc*-class and is conjugated in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*).
The elision of the accent.

The footless one clothes herself in many-colored forms; standing erect, licking her three-year-old calf, she has ascended. Knowing this, I move within the seat of Cosmic Order (*ṛta*), for the greatness of the gods is a singular sovereignty.

She who moves on foot, she who is clothed in many forms, she who stands erect displaying her bodies, licking the three-year-old calf—knowing this, I move through the seat of Truth; great indeed is the divine sovereignty of the gods, which is one. 14.
Padyā: Because she was born from the foot (padyā) of the Supreme Lord, the creator of the world, the earth is called Padyā.
Thus says a Vedic mantra: "The earth is Padyā" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.90.14).

Alternatively, the *padyā* is the ground suitable for the movement of feet; it "clothes" (*vaste*) itself in various forms (*vapūṃṣi*), that is, in manifold physical appearances consisting of both stationary and moving entities. This very earth, being elevated (*ūrdhvā*) upon the high altar (*uttara-vedi*), consumes (*tryavim*) the oblation (*havis*) which has become its own essence.
A calf one and a half years old is called a *tryavi*.
The sun is his measure.
Or, he is called *vṛtrahán* because he protects (*avati*) and pervades (*vyāpnoti*) the three worlds with his own splendor.
He stands licking (*lihānā*) those who seek to devour (*vrī*).
Knowing and understanding the dwelling place of the Sun, who is encompassed and has become the Truth, I move about with oblations; I serve that Āditya.
*padyā*: from the word *pāda*, the suffix *yat* is applied by the rule "in the Veda, for the sense of 'occurring therein'" (*bhave chandasi*).
By the rule "for the purpose of seeing that" (*paśyatadarthe*; Pāṇini 6.3.53), the substitution of *padya* for *pāda* occurs.
Alternatively,
[the suffix] *yat* is applied according to the rule "tatra sādhuḥ" (Pāṇini 4.4.98),
or according to the rule "yato ’nāvaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.213).

1. In the manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ja, ṇa, na, bha, and sa, the word *'dyām'* is absent. 2. [The reading is] *ta-jalāvarjitayā*. 3. In kha, ga, and ca, it is *pravarṣakāle*; in ta, it is *varṣākāle*. In kha, ga, ca, ja, ṇa, na, bha, and sa, the passage from *'ādityājjāyate'* to *'apinvata'* is absent. Regarding *aṃ*: it has the udātta accent on the first syllable (*āyudāttatvam*). Regarding *atrim*: [the root] *ava* is used in the sense of protection and so forth. The suffix *im* is added by the rule *'in'* (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.557). It takes the accent of the kṛt suffix (*kṛtsvaraḥ*). Regarding *rerihāṇā*: this is the form of the root *liha* (meaning "to taste") in the yaṅluk formation with the suffix *śānac*. It takes the accent of the reduplicated stem (*abhyastasvaraḥ*).
Like two steps placed within the wondrous one, one is hidden in secret and the other is manifest;
they move together yet extend in different directions—this is the sole, great divine power of the gods.

In one place, as it were; in another, as it were. It is placed, as it were. O Wondrous One! Between those two, one is hidden, the other is manifest. Moving together, yet spreading out in different directions—that is the great, singular divine power of the gods. 15.
*Pade*:
that which is stepped upon or known by means of its respective unique mark (*liṅga*) is a *pada*.
Day and night—these two, visible to all (*dasme*), exist as if placed within the sky, in the midst of it.
Of those two, day and night, one is characterized as night; it remains hidden, as if concealed, due to its lack of manifestation.
The other is the day; it becomes manifest, revealed by the light of the sun.
The *sadhrīcīnā* is the path (*pathyā*) consisting of the mutual union of day and night.
The meaning is "time.
She is *viṣūcī*;
she is called *viṣūcī* because she reaches both those who perform meritorious deeds and those who perform non-meritorious deeds.
All people exist within day and night;
or rather,
it exists within the intermediate space between heaven and earth, which serve as the foundation for the abodes of gods, humans, and others.
Of these two, one is the heaven, which remains hidden from us because it is concealed;
the other is the earth, which is manifest, being visible to all.
The word *sadhrīcīnā* is as explained previously.
*Sadhrīcīnā*: [derived] from *saṃpūrva-añjati* with the suffix *kin*; there is the substitution of *sadhi-* for *saha-* according to the rule "of *saha*, *sadhi-*".
The suffix *kha* is applied [to the root *añj*] optionally when preceded by a prefix, provided it denotes a feminine.

Let the milch-cows come, lowing, though they be without calves—those who yield nectar, the constant ones whose milk flows unceasingly; becoming ever new, young, and beautiful, this is the one great divine power of the gods.

Let the milch-cows low, though they be without calves—those who yield nectar, those who lie still, and those whose milk has been drawn; becoming ever new, ever young maidens, [they proclaim] the one great Asura-power of the gods. 16.
May the cows— the doors of increase, the gratifiers of the entire world— who are *aśiśvīḥ* (without calves,

or alternatively, those who do not become calves), who are *śaśayāḥ* (lying or dwelling in the sky), whose milk is never exhausted by anyone (*arpadugdhāḥ*), who yield water as their milk (*sabardughāḥ*), who are youthful (*yuvatayaḥ*), mingled with one another, and who are ever-new (*navyānbavyāḥ*)— may they shake down or milk forth the quarters or the clouds.
In the case of the *megha* [commentary], there is a change of gender in the phrase "becoming without young" (*aśiśvīr bhavantīḥ*).
1. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Gha, Ca, Ja, Ṇa, Na, Bha, and La, the word "in the middle" (madhye) is absent.
2. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Gha, Ca, Ja, Ṇa, Na, Bha, and Sa, it reads "of humans and so forth" (manuṣyādīnām).
3. In manuscript La, the word "other" (anyā) is absent. 4. In manuscript Ca, it is by way of being visible (dṛśyatayā); in Ja and Ṇa, it is by way of being invisible (adṛśyatayā).

5. *kha-ga-ca-ja-ṇa-na-bha-sa* is secret (*guhyam*); *na* is the cave (*guhā*); *la* is hidden (*gūḍham*). 6. *kha-ga-ca-ja-ṇa-na* is that which is being seen (*dṛśyamānā*); *sa* is by way of being seen (*dṛśyamānatayā*). 7. *kha-ga-ja-ṇa-na-bha-sa* is the vowel (*svaraḥ*); *ca-pha* is the substitution of *ī* (*īnādeśaḥ*).

The accent is that of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). [In the word] *dhunayantām*: from the root *dhūñ* in the sense of "shaking" (*kampane*). With the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the augment *nuk* is applied according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 7.2.37.1, which states: "The augment *nuk* is to be stated after roots ending in *dhṛ* and *ṇu*. The short vowel is Vedic (*chāndasa*). [In the word] *aśiśrīḥ*: the rule "the substitution of *śi* for *s* occurs in the common language (*bhāṣā*) when followed by *śī*" applies; however, by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*), it occurs here in the Veda.
When the bull bellows toward another [herd], he deposits his seed in another herd;
for he is the protector of the night, he is Bhaga, he is the king—his alone is the singular sovereignty over the great gods.

That bull bellows loudly among others; he deposits his seed in another herd. For he is the protector of the night, he is Bhaga, he is the King. Great is the singular divine sovereignty of the gods. 17.

When Parjanya, the self of Indra, the bull of the waters who rains, bellows loudly through the clouds in other directions, that Parjanya-Indra deposits his seed—water—in another herd, the multitude of the quarters; he rains there.
For in the world, a bull engages in mating for the sake of discharging seed among certain females and then pours his seed into another herd of cows; it is just like that.
That Indra is the protector of the night.
He is "possessing a thrower" (kṣepaṇavat) because he hurls his enemies or because he drives away [darkness] like water;
or else, *kṣapā* means night.
Likewise, "night" refers to that night which constitutes a portion of the sacrifices and hymns; he is possessed of that. He is "Bhaga," worthy of being honored by all.
He is indeed the king, for he is truly the king of all by bestowing various fruits in accordance with their respective actions.

*rورवीति* (roravīti) is the form of the root *ru* meaning "to sound" in the *laṭ* tense with the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix (*yaṅ-luk*). According to the rule *ekānyābhyāṃ samarthābhyām*, the first word does not undergo the *nighāta* (anudātta) accent.

In the word *yūtha*: [it is derived from] the root *yu* in the sense of "mixing. The lengthening of the vowel occurs because it is a conventional form (*nipāta*) ending in the suffix *thak*, according to the rule *tithapṛṣṭhathyūthaprothāḥ* (Uṇādi Sūtra 2.169).
*retaḥ*.

From the root *rīṅ* in the sense of “flowing” (*kṣaraṇe*), the suffix *asun* is applied according to the rule *surībhyāṃ tuṭ ca*, along with the augment *tuṭ*. Because the suffix is marked with *ṇi* (indicating it is *nit*), the word is accented on its first syllable.
O people, let us now proclaim the own-nature of the Hero, he who is known by the gods.
Six teams of animals, each with its own beast, draw him; great indeed is the unique asura-power of the gods.
O people, let us now proclaim the hero’s excellence in horses; the gods know it. Six teams, yoked horse by horse, bring him hither. Great indeed is the singular divine power of the gods. 18.

O people, let us now quickly proclaim with excellence the glorious possession of horses belonging to this heroic Indra; likewise, even the gods know quickly that same glorious possession of horses of this Indra. What is that glorious possession of horses?
This is explained:
at the time of the union of the pairs of months, the seasons (*ṛtavaḥ*), appearing sixfold, are designated as horses.
And those six seasons, joined five by five through the combination of Hemanta and Śiśira, carry the sacrificial horse (*aśvinam*) which is of the nature of Time.
This indeed is Indra’s possession of excellent horses, that he has mounted upon you.
*Ṣoḷhā*. From the word *ṣaṣ*, the suffix *dhā* is applied according to Pāṇini’s rule *saṃkhyāyā vidhārthe dhā*.
By the rule *ṣaṣa utvaṃ datadaśāsūtarpadādeḥ ṣutvaṃ ca* (Pāṇini 6.3.109), there is the substitution of *u* for the vowel and *ṣ* for the consonant. Thus, *ṣoḍhā*.
The accent of the conditional suffix.
In the animal sacrifice dedicated to Tvaṣṭṛ, the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the oblation is this: “O divine Tvaṣṭṛ...
As it is stated in the Sūtra: “‘O divine Tvaṣṭṛ,’ ‘Savitṛ who possesses all forms,’ and ‘O divine Tvaṣṭṛ, [make] this [sacrifice] beautiful’” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.8).
1. [The following consonants are single: kha, ga, gha, ca, ja, ṇa, pa, pha, bha, ya, tha.
2. [The following are double: kha-ca are *kṣipram*; na-la-sa are *anukṣipram*, which does not exist [here].

Devaḥ tvaṣṭā savitā viśvarūpaḥ pupoṣa prajāḥ purudhā jajāna | imā ca viśvā bhuvanānyasya mahad devānām asuratvam ekam || 19 || God Tvaṣṭṛ, the impeller, possessing all forms, has nourished offspring and has begotten them in many ways. And all these worlds belong to him; great is the unique divine power of the gods. || 19 ||
Savitar, the impeller of all by virtue of being the inner restrainer, the one of manifold forms, Tvaṣṭṛ—the deity named Tvaṣṭṛ—has generated, and continues to generate, progeny in many ways;
he has nourished, and continues to nourish, them.
And all these various worlds, the entire collection of beings, belong to this Tvaṣṭṛ.
*Viśvarūpa*: By the rule "In a *bahuvrīhi*, when it is a name, the final syllable of the first member is udātta," there is the acute accent on the final syllable of the first member.

The two great worlds, moving together in harmony, were set in motion by him; both were released through his wealth. The hero, finding riches, is heard [of]; great indeed is the unique sovereignty of the gods. 20. *Mahī* (great), *sam* (together), *airat* (set in motion), *camvā* (the two bowls/worlds), *samīcī* (moving together), *ubhe* (both), *te* (those), *asya* (his), *vasunā* (by wealth), *nyṛṣṭe* (released), *śruṇe* (is heard), *vīraḥ* (the hero), *vindamānaḥ* (finding), *vasūni* (riches), *mahat* (great), *devānām* (of the gods), *asuratvam* (sovereignty), *ekam* (unique). 20.
The two great ones, the earth and heaven, joined together;
they are called *camvā* because gods and humans take pleasure (*cam*) in one of them, while the other takes pleasure in them.
Or else: [the word *camvā* is derived from the root *cam*].
The two, Heaven and Earth, are called *camvau* because they are chewed upon and consumed by the multitude of beings.
Indra brought them together—that is, he properly joined them with Prajāpati and others.
Both of these, Heaven and Earth, become thoroughly pervaded (*nyṛṣṭe*) by his—Indra’s—*vasu*, whether it be splendor or wealth.
The Hero, the capable one, that Indra, having overcome his enemies, while obtaining—that is, acquiring—their riches, is heard by all;
for this is seen in such passages as, "This wealth of yours is known on every side" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.53.3).
*Airat* is the form of the root *īr* (meaning "to go") in the *laṅ* (imperfect) tense. *Nyṛṣṭe*.
The root *ṛ* means "to go.
The suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*). By the rule "the accent of the preceding *gati* [is retained]," the accent of the *gati* [remains].
*Śruṇe*:
this is the form of the root *śru* (in the sense of "hearing") with the suffix *ktu* used for the object by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*),
and the *ta* is elided according to the rule *lopasta ātmanepadeṣu*.
*vindamāna*:

this is the form of the root *vidl* (meaning "to obtain") in the present tense (*laṭ*) with the suffix *śānac*. Its accent is that of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*), because [the suffix] is a *lasārvadhātuka*.

And this earth dwells for us, O All-Sustainer, like a king with well-disposed friends; like heroes seated in their dwellings and seated in their strongholds—great indeed is the singular divine power of the gods. 21. And this earth dwells for us, O All-Sustainer, like a king with well-disposed friends; like heroes seated in their dwellings and seated in their strongholds—great indeed is the singular divine power of the gods. 21.

1. *ta* followed by another *saṃ*. 2. *kha-ga-ca-ja-ṇa-na-bha-devāḥ* [represent] humans. 3. *pha-prajāḥ* [represent] animals such as cattle and so forth. 4. *kha-ga-ca-ja-ṇa-na-bha-sa-lasārvadhātukasvaraḥ*.

The sustainer of all (*viśvadhāyāḥ*), meaning the supporter of the universe or the one who sees everything, our King Indra, dwells near this earth and the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). Therein lies the illustration: [the following phonetic rules apply].
Like a well-wishing friend (*hitamitra*): just as a benevolent counselor (*hitapadeṣṭṛ*) dwells near someone, so too [are they].

The *vīrāḥ* (heroes)—the capable Maruts who are companions in battle—are like those who sit in the front (*puraḥsadaḥ*), meaning those who go resolutely to the front for the sake of battle, like Indra’s *śarmasadaḥ* (those who dwell in his protection).
The meaning is "in destruction. They sit in comfort and in the home;
the sense is that wherever he is, they remain in close proximity there.
He dwells (*kṣeti*).

This is from the root *kṣi* in the sense of “dwelling” and “going,” in the present tense (*laṭ*), with the elision of the suffixal augment (*vikaraṇa*) according to the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*. There is also the *nighāta* (anudātta) accent.

May the plants be averter of [evil] for you, and may the waters [be so]; O Indra, the earth bears wealth for you. May we, your friends, be partakers of your favor. Great is the unique sovereignty of the gods. 22. [May] the plants be averters [of evil] for you; and the waters; O Indra, the earth bears wealth for you. May we, your friends, be partakers of your favor. Great is the unique sovereignty of the gods. 22.
O Indra, whose nature is Parjanya, the plants are your "niṣidhvarīḥ"—that is, they are exceedingly effective in their own inherent accomplishment.
Moreover, the waters have issued forth from you;
and the earth bears for you "rayim," wealth suitable for your enjoyment.
For there is a Vedic verse: "The earth bears many riches" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 3.51.5).

Therefore, O [Agni], may we—your friends, who assist you by the offering of oblations, we the singers—be "possessors of the desirable," that is, may we all become partakers of wealth worthy of being sought after.
This indeed is the great sovereignty of the gods.

*niṣidhvarīḥ*: [from] *ṣidhu* in the sense of "accomplishment" (*saṃrāddhi*). The suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) according to the rule for *saṃpad* and similar formations.
In the sense of "he has that," the suffix *vanip* is applied by the rule *chandasīvanipau*;
then, by the rule *vano ra ca*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* and the letter *ra* are added;
finally, there is a compound with *niḥ*.
Disregarding the *sakāra* of *nisaḥ* due to its being Vedic (*chāndasa*), the substitution of *patva* is applied according to the rule "upasargād ṛti sunoti" and so forth.
Since the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is *pit*, it is unaccented (*anudātta*), and thus the accent of the verbal root remains.
[The form is] *bibharti*.

From the root *ḍubhṛñ* in the sense of “sustaining and nourishing,” in the present tense (*laṭ*), the vowel substitution *it* is applied to the reduplication by the rule *bhṛñām it*; there is also the *nighāta* (anudātta) accent.
[The word is] *vāmabhājaḥ*.
The root *bhaj* is used in the sense of "service" (*sevā*).
By the rule *bhajo ṇviḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.2.62), the suffix *ṇvi* is applied.
The accentuation follows that of a compound where the final member is a *kṛt*-derived word.
By illuminating the meaning of the Vedas and dispelling the darkness of the heart,
may the Great Lord of the Sacred Fords (Yatīndra Maheśvara) bestow the four aims of human life.

Thus ends the third chapter of the third book in the Commentary on the Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, titled *Vedārthaprakāśa*, composed by Sāyaṇācārya, the upholder of the imperial sovereignty of the illustrious King Vīrabukka—the glorious Emperor, Supreme Lord, and promoter of the Vedic path.
1. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Gha, Ca, Ja, Na, Bha, and La, the phrase "niṣidhvaryo nitarām" does not exist.
2. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, Ja, Ṇa, Na, Bha, and Ha, [the word] "havir" is followed by "dānapradānopakārakāḥ".
3. In manuscript La, it is "stotāro vā".
Homage to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose breath is the Vedas and who created the entire universe from the Vedas.
The verse beginning with “na tā minanti” is the third [verse] of Viśvāmitra’s speech;
it is the son’s [hymn], belonging to Prajāpati, composed in the Triṣṭubh meter, and dedicated to the Viśvedevas.
Thus, the Anukramaṇikā states: “na tāthai.”
The application of this hymn is to be understood from its indicative mark (*liṅga*).
In this hymn, the year is generally praised together with the Ādityas.
Neither the deceitful nor the wise can violate those first, firm decrees of the gods; neither the two guileless worlds through their wisdom, nor the mountains that stand immovable, can bend them.

No, they do not violate the laws of the gods—the first and firm decrees—neither the guileless ones nor the wise, nor the two worlds through their knowledge, nor the mountains that stand immovable. || 1 ||

The *māyins*—the Asuras endowed with deceitful intellects—do not violate, nor do they harm, those various well-known *vratas* (vows) of the gods, Indra and the others; that is, the primary, primordial, and eternal duties such as the protection of the world, which are firm and impossible for anyone to shake.
Likewise, even the wise (*dhīras*) do not harm them.

Likewise, those deeds do not fail—that is, they do not cease to exist—“in the non-malicious,” meaning among creatures such as gods and humans who are free from malice; “in the two worlds,” meaning in heaven and earth; and “with the Vedyās,” meaning together with the creatures who are worthy of praise by all because they have their own support.
This is what is meant:
just as the establishment of humans and others upon heaven and earth as their support, and the establishment of mountains and the like in their height, this is the work of the gods.
Therefore, no one is able to alter that.
They harm. In the present tense (*laṭ*) of the root *mīṅ* in the sense of "harming," there is a short vowel according to the rule *mīnāter nigame*;
[the word] receives the *nighāta* accent.
By means of the *vedyās*. They deserve to be known (*vedana*). The suffix *yat* is applied according to the rule “*chandasi ca*” (Pāṇini 5.1.67).
Regarding *ninamaṃ*: in the word *namu prahve*, the suffix *ke* is added in the sense of a verbal action (*kṛtyārtha*).
It takes the accent of the *kṛt* suffix.
One, though not moving, bears six burdens; the cows have approached the highest and most exalted one.
Three great worlds stand near; two that were hidden within the cave have been revealed, while one remains concealed.
Six burdens one bears while moving; he carries the most exalted Truth. The cows have come near; three great ones stand close by. Of those two which were hidden in secret, one is visible. 2.

1. And [the reading] of Vācaspati. 2. Kha, Ga, Ca, Pha, Bha, and Sa read: "occurring immediately after the rain. 3. Ta reads: "the gifts. 4. Kha, Ga, Ca, Ja, Ta, Na, Bha, and Sa read: "accompanied by. 5. Gha, Ṇa, Na, Bha, and Na read: "to be bowed down to. 6. Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, Na, Bha, and Sa read: "the state. 7. Kha, Ga, Gha, Ca, Ṇa, Na, Bha, La, and Sa do not have the phrase: "'and whatever... the establishing'. 8. La reads: "of the deities. [The commentary explains: A year (*saṃvatsara*) is that which remains for a year (*vacaran sthāyī vekaḥ*). *Vṣaṭ* refers to the six seasons (*ṛtu*), so called because they are borne (*bhriyante*)—that is, characterized by the blooming of flowers and other such phenomena—in those [six] numbers. Thus, the *bhārāḥ* are the seasons.
He supports— that is, maintains as his constituent parts— the seasons (*vasantatān*).

Likewise, the rays (*gāvaḥ*), which are true and have become the rain (*vṛtam satyabhūtam varṣam*), reach (*upāvāguḥ*) that very same year (*saṃvatsaram*) which is more increased (*vṛddhataram*) and consists of the sun (*ādityātmakam*).
Furthermore, in that very year, three great worlds—characterized by movement, subject to the nature of coming and going, and situated one above the other—exist.
He shows these three worlds:
within the cave, that is, within one's own self, both heaven and the intermediate space are contained; they are not perceived [as external].

The earth is seen as the foundation for all beings; [it is called] *bhū* because it bears (*bhṛ*) burdens— [the root] *bhṛñ* meaning "to support and nourish"— with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
The word *kapāvataḥ* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*) by the rule "ghañarthe kavidhānam.
The word *nihita* is a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) derived from the root *dhā* with the prefix *ni*, used in the sense of the object (*karman*).
In the phrase "gatiranantaraḥ," the word *gati* retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). Regarding *daśi*: *daśir* means "to look."
In the *luṅ* (aorist) tense, with the *ciṇ* affix, there is the elision of the suffix according to the rule "ciṇo luk.
Due to the division of the sentence (*vākyabheda*), there is no loss of accent (*anighāta*).

He who has three bellies, the bull, possessing all forms; and he who has three udders, manifoldly rich in offspring; he who has three faces, the lord, possessed of greatness—he is the bestower of seed, the bull of the eternal ones. tripājasyaḥ | vṛṣabhaḥ | viśvarūpaḥ | uta | tryudhā | purudhā | prajāvān | tryanīkaḥ | patyate | māhināvān | saḥ | retodhāḥ | vṛṣabhaḥ | śaśvatīnām || 3 ||
*Tripājasyaḥ*: he whose *pājasya*, or chest, consists of three—the three seasons known as summer, the rainy season, and winter—is *tripājasyaḥ*; that is to say, he has three chests.
Furthermore, the word *pājasya* denotes the chest.

In the *Aśvamedha* mantra, "Indrasya kroḍo'dityai pājasyam" (*Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā* 25.8), because it is understood as referring to the chest (*uras*)— given the etymological derivation of *pājasi* as "that which is conducive to strength" (*bale sādhuh*) and because among all the limbs the chest is the strongest—

the bull (*vṛṣabhaḥ*) is the showerer of waters through its own part, the rain-cloud (*varṣatu*). It is "multiform" (*viśvarūpaḥ*), possessing various forms through the characteristic signs of its respective specific functions, such as the blooming of flowers and so forth.
Moreover,
he is "vnyudhā," meaning one who is attended by the three seasons known as spring, autumn, and winter;
he is possessed of progeny.
They are called *prajāḥ* (progeny) because they are born (*jāyante*) in abundance;
he possesses such progeny consisting of rice, barley, and other crops existing in many ways (*purudhā*).
Furthermore, he is *vanīkaḥ*, endowed with the three qualities known as the armies (*anīkāni*) of heat, rain, and cold.

The god who possesses a great ship—that is, who possesses greatness—and who presides over the year, approaches; he comes as a bull, capable of impregnating. That year becomes the depositor of seed—the sustainer of the seed, which is water—for the abundant production of flowers, fruits, and so forth, of the many plants.
He bestows [them].

In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, by the rule "anaṅ for *udhas*" (*udhaso'naṅ*), the substitution *anaṅ* occurs; since all grammatical rules are optional in the Vedic language (*chandasi*), this form also appears in the masculine.

The shortening of the vowel *u* is a Vedic feature (*chāndasa*). Furthermore, the acute accent on the final syllable of the second member follows the rule: "In the section concerning the acute accent on the final syllable of the second member, there is an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) of *tricakra* and others in the Vedic language. Thus, there is the acute accent on the final syllable of the second member.

In the encounter, the foot-soldier of these [gods] has awakened—the beautiful name of the Ādityas, O Ahi! Even the divine waters have stood still for him; moving separately, they have encompassed him on all sides. In the encounter, the foot-soldier of these [gods] has awakened—the beautiful name of the Ādityas, O Ahi! Even the divine waters have stood still for him; moving separately, they have encompassed him on all sides.

1. In the versions *kha*, *ga*, and *ca*, [the word] is "those in which all," while in *ṇa* it is "by which all. 2. In *gha*, *na*, *bha*, and *la*, there are two earths (*bhūmī*). 3. In *la*, [it is] "possessing offspring like rice, barley, and so forth" (*vrīhi-yavādi-haprajāvān*). 4. In *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *sa*, it is "endowed with the form of a cow" (*go-rūpetaḥ*). The year is the "path-leader" (*padavīḥ*) in the presence (*abhīke*, i.e., in the vicinity) of these plants. It is called "path-leader" because it produces (*prajanayati*) the "paths" (*padāni*), that is to say, the flowers, fruits, and so forth, which are not distinct from those [plants].
Having awakened, he awakens; he remains attentive.
Likewise, "of the Ādityas":
the Ādityas are the months, due to the identity of their number.
Alternatively,
because they are caused by the sun’s transit (*saṃkramaṇa*), the months are called *āditya*.
"Whichever lunar month is completed while the sun is in the chariot [sign] beginning with Aries..."
"that is to be known as Caitra and so forth," according to the traditional teaching (*smṛti*).
Of those months beginning with Caitra, I "invoke"—meaning I utter—the names such as Madhu and Mādhava, which are their beautiful designations.
I pronounce them; this is the meaning.

Moreover, the divine waters (*devīr āpaḥ*), shining by nature and moving separately hither and thither, have also delighted (*aramanta*) for this year; that is, they rejoice through the medium of growth for the satisfaction of the months belonging to the year.
Those waters [delight] him, this year, three times around. O Savitṛ, day after day, impel the heroic powers of heaven; impel them for three days.
O Lord of the three worlds, send down riches; O Resplendent One, Protector, bestow wealth upon us for our attainment.

Thrice from heaven, O Savitṛ, send forth your heroic powers day by day; thrice for us, throughout the day, send forth threefold wealth and treasures. O Radiant One, Protector, O Dhiṣaṇā, bestow them upon us for our gain. 6.

O Savitṛ, the impeller of all, O Āditya, having come from the sky (*divaḥ*), do thou impel—that is, bestow—upon us thrice each day, daily, heroic deeds, meaning riches worthy of being honored by all. This is further explained: O Bhaga, worthy of being honored by all, O Protector (*trātaḥ*), O Āditya, [grant] the threefold wealth (*rāyaḥ*); that is, riches consisting of three kinds of assets, distinguished as cattle, gold, and jewels.
They yield milk and other products, thus they are *rāyaḥ*, meaning cattle-wealth. Bestow those upon us—grant them—at the three daily pressings connected with each day.
O *dhiṣaṇā*, the intermediate Speech, grant us [them] for the sake of winning wealth; make us successful.
Three times. The suffix *suc* is applied according to Pāṇini Sūtra 5.4.18, *dvitricaturbhyaḥ suc*.
It has the accent of the *cit* suffix.
*Suva*: [the root] *bhū* in the sense of "impelling";
it belongs to the *tudādi* class.
The form is *loṭi*.
It is *tridhātu*. From the root *dhā* in the sense of "holding" and "nourishing," the suffix *tun* is applied according to the rule beginning with *sitanigabhimasi*, etc.
*dhīṣaṇe*:
because it is a vocative, it receives the *nighāta* (anudātta) accent.
Three times a day Savitar impels his own power; the two kings Mitra and Varuṇa, the fair-handed, [impel it].
Even the two wide worlds, Heaven and Earth, have come hither to beg for wealth at the impulse of Savitar.
Thrice from heaven Savitṛ impels; Mitra and Varuṇa, the two kings with beautiful hands—so [is it said], for even the two wide worlds, Heaven and Earth, beg for wealth at the impulse of Savitṛ. 7.
The god Savitṛ, from the sky—the sky—three times, at the three times of day, impels [us]; may he impel, may he send forth riches for us.
Furthermore, the two kings, the two with beautiful hands, Mitra and Varuṇa, [and] the waters.
The waters (*āpaḥ*) are so called because they pervade (*āpnoti*) the entire world;
they are expressed in the plural because that term is always used in the plural.

Furthermore, the two vast expanses (*urvī rodasī*), namely heaven and earth—these deities—at the impulse (*savāya*) of this god Savitṛ, the impeller, beg for and request the treasure (*ratnam*), that is, the desired object, by means of his impelling power (*savena*).
*soṣavīti*: this is the form of the root *bhū* in the sense of "impelling" (*preraṇe*) when used with the *yaṅluk* (elision of the *yaṅ* suffix) in the present tense (*laṭ*). *Mitrāvaruṇā*.

In the compound *devatādvandve ca*, there is the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of both members. *Bhikṣanta*: this is the form of the root *bhikṣ* (meaning "to beg") in the *laṅ* tense.
*Savāya*:
The final syllable is udātta because of the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) as ending in *a* by Pāṇini’s rule 3.3.56.4, which states *yava-savau ca*.
1. And *ca-mitrāvaruṇā* means Mitra and Varuṇa.
*Ṛgveda* 2.59:
"The three highest luminous realms are pierced; the three heroes of the Asura rule."
May the gods—upholders of cosmic order, vigorous, difficult to deceive, and eternal—be present at the divine assembly of heaven.
Thrice the highest firmament, the luminous realms—three heroes of the Asura reign there, observers of cosmic order, vigorous, and invincible. Thrice may the gods attend the assembly from heaven. 8.
The *rocanāni*—the shining ones, which are "difficult to destroy" (*dṛṇaśā*) meaning impossible for anyone to annihilate—exist in three supreme places.
In these three places resides the *asura*. He is called *asura* because he "casts forth" (*as-*) or "projects" (*kṣipati*) everything; he is Time (*kāla*), the year (*saṃvatsara*).
His "heroic sons," three in number, having the forms of Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya, "shine" or are resplendent. He further qualifies them as "upholders of the cosmic order (ṛta)."
*Ṛta* refers to the sacrificial acts such as the *agnihotra* which have become reality;

within that, these "eager ones" (*iṣirāḥ*)—meaning those who are swift for the sake of sacrifice, "difficult to deceive" (*duḥlabhāsaḥ*), meaning they cannot be overcome by anyone through their own splendor—all these "gods" (*devāḥ*) should be present "in our sacrifice" (*vidathe*) during the three pressings (*triḥ savaneṣu*) belonging to "heaven" (*divaḥ*), that is, the day, and they should be there in every way as those worthy of worship.
*Uttamā*: [The word] *uttama* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*) because it is listed among the words beginning with *uccha* in the rule "uttamaśca tamau sarvatra.
*Dṛṇaśā*.

The suffix *khal* is applied after the root *naś* in the sense of difficulty (*kṛcchra*). According to the rule "it should be stated that *u* replaces the *r* of *dāś*, *nāś*, *dabh*, and *pūrvam* when preceded by *duḥ*," the *r* is replaced by *u*. Then, the initial letter of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is changed to a retroflex (*ṣṭutva*).
The word *lit-svara* (acute accent on the first syllable) applies to *duḥ-bhāsaḥ* when there is the quality of being praised as difficult (*dur-u-vaṣṭutva*).

The fourth hymn, consisting of six verses beginning with "pra me vivikrān," has Viśvāmitra as its seer (ṛṣi), Triṣṭubh as its meter (chandas), and the Viśvedevas as its deity (devatā). Regarding this, the Anukramaṇikā states: "pra me pada. The application of this hymn is indicated by its internal characteristics (laiṅgika).
My inspired thoughts have found the cow who wanders alone, unherded and far-strayed;
she has yielded for me a vast abundance of nourishment. Indra and Agni shall be her praisers.

The discerning one has found my inspired thought, like a cow wandering at large, unherded, yet yielding much nourishment even from her own abundance; Indra and Agni are the ones who shall praise this deed of hers.
"Indra, the one who has stepped forth and possesses discernment, or Agni, has thoroughly perceived—has come to know with excellence—my *manīṣā*, my hymn of praise directed toward the deities.
In this regard, there is an illustration:

just as one might perceive a cow that is wandering here and there in the pasture, separated from the herd, solitary, without a keeper, roaming at will, and recently calved; even so has he perceived the hymn that gratifies the deities. This is the syntactical connection.

The cow that consists of praise "immediately" (sadyas) "bears" (dhāseḥ)—that is, it sustains the vital breaths; or, it is deposited (*dhīyate*) or bestowed (*dīyate*) upon the deities—thus it is *dhāsi*, meaning food. The genitive case is used in the sense of the object.

Indra, Agni, and the other gods have milked—that is, they have obtained—the abundant and much-desired fruit from this cow consisting of praise; or rather, Indra and Agni, as well as we who are the praisers, obtain the milk of this cow. They become the praisers (panitāraḥ) of that milk which has become their food. Or else, Indra and Agni, and we the praisers, obtain the milk of this cow.
*vivikrān*:
from the root *vic* in the sense of "separation" (*pṛthagbhāve*), this is the form [of the participle] with the suffix *kasu*.
*avidat*.

In the word *vidajjñāne*, the suffix *śa* is applied to the root *vida* in the sense of "knowledge" according to the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*. *Duduhe* is the form of the root *duha* (meaning "to milk") in the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
Because of its connection with the syllable *yad*, there is no elision (*anighāta*). It has the accent of a suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
[The word is] *panitāraḥ*.
The form [stotā] is derived from the root √stu in the sense of "praising," with the suffix tṛc.
1. [The rule] regarding those connected with *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, and *ahaḥ*.
2. [The rule regarding] the substitution of *ṣṭu* for *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, and *pūrvadatva*.
3. [The rule regarding] the root *dhāsi* having *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *bha*, and *prāṇa* as its [initial] consonants.
Indra and Pūṣan, the two bulls with skillful hands, like those pleased by heaven, have milked out the inexhaustible [soma];
when all the gods rejoiced in her, may we here obtain your favor, O Vasus.

Indra, Pūṣan, and the two bull-like ones with skillful hands—like those delighted by heaven—they have milked out the inexhaustible [milk]. When all the gods took delight in this [earth], may we here obtain your favor, O Vasus. 2.

O Vasus, you gods who cause all things to dwell; O Indra and Pūṣan, the two bulls who sprinkle the desired fruit; O Nāsatyas (the Aśvins) or Mitra and Varuṇa, who have beautiful hands—this being seen in such passages as "O kings Mitra and Varuṇa, of fair hands"—all these are the gods.
The word *na* is used here in the sense of an inquiry (*sampraśra*).
Now, being *prītāḥ* (delighted), they *sududuhe*—they milked well—from *divaḥ*, that is, from the sky, the *śaśayam* cloud lying in the firmament;
they effectively milked the desired fruit by means of rain.
Since all the gods take delight on this sacrificial altar—which belongs to you—in this world, may I obtain that which is pleasing, pleasant, and the desired fruit.
*Suhastā*:
From the root *has*, the suffix *tan* is applied according to the rule "asihasi," etc.;
it is ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable) because it begins with the prefix *ni*.
In the *bahuvrīhi* compound, the initial syllable of the final member is acute according to the rule "the first syllable of a two-syllable word is acute in the Veda.
[The form] *duduhe* [is derived from] the root *duh* "to milk," with the substitution of *ra* for *ir* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
*raṇayanta*: [This is] the form of the causative (*ṇyanta*) of the root *ram*, meaning "to play," in the imperfect (*laṅ*).
The attainment of color.
*Aśyāma*: from the root *aś* in the sense of "to pervade," in the *liṅ* mood, there is the elision of the suffix by the rule "there is frequently [elision] in the Veda."
The *parasmaipada* ending occurs by way of irregularity.
The sisters who desire the bull’s power, bowing down, recognize the embryo within him;
lowing toward their son, the milch-cows move about, bearing his great and wondrous forms.
The sisters who desire power for the bull, bowing down, perceive the embryo within him; like lowing milch-cows, they move toward their son, bearing the forms of greatness.
The *jāmayaḥ*— the sisters,
so called because they "give birth" (*jamanti*) by appearing during the rainy season,
namely the plants— desire *śaktim*, the power of pouring forth, for *vṛṣṇe*, Indra, the showerer of waters.
Bowing down in reverence, those plants recognize within this Indra the capacity for conception— characterized by flowers, fruits, and so forth— by means of rain;

yearning for their fruit, the milch-cows— the plants that satisfy all— move toward and reach their son, their offspring, who bears great and manifold forms consisting of the fruits of rice, barley, wild grain, and the like.
For in the world, cows making lowing sounds go toward their calves;
it is just like that.
Or else, [it refers to] sisters.
They are called *jāmayaḥ* because they "go everywhere" (*jamanti*) and spread forth; thus, they are the rays of the sun.
For the "bull" (*vṛṣṇe*), that is, for the showerer of waters;
the sun is the "showerer" (*varṣakaḥ*) because, having taken up formidable juices by means of his own rays, he showers them down again.
And from the Smṛti text, "From the Sun rain is born," they desire for him the power of rain;
those rays know the embryo— the capacity for the initial conception of the embryo— within this Sun.

*Jāmayaḥ*: [The word] *jāmayaḥ* is derived from the root *jam-* meaning "to go," by means of the suffix *iṇ* prescribed [by Pāṇini 3.2.17] as "after the roots *jan-* and *ghas-*, [the suffix] *iṇ* [is added]," due to the force of the term "variously" (*bahulavacanāt*); it is formed from this root as well. *Namasyantīḥ*: [meaning] "paying homage."

From the word *namaḥ*: 1. by the rule "namo-varivas-citraḥ kyac" [Pāṇini 3.1.19]; 2. with excellence (*pra*) and intensity (*su*); 3. because they cause delight (*ramayante*); 4. *la* refers to cows (*dhenavaḥ*), meaning cows that have recently calved; 5. *ṇa* refers to the power of rain (*varṣa-śakti*). 468.

*Ṛgveda*: [Aṣṭaka 3, Adhyāya 4, Varga 2]—the suffix *kyac* is applied; from that ending, the form is derived with the suffix *śatṛ*. It bears the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). *Jānate* is the form of the root *jñā* (meaning "to know") in the present tense (*laṭ*). *Acchā*: in the *saṃhitā*, there is a long vowel according to the rule *nipātasya ca*.
I clearly proclaim to the two well-established worlds, having yoked the pressing-stones with my mind at the sacrifice.
These, your lofty and visible sacrificial posts, O worshipful ones, rise up for Manu, providing abundant boons.

Clearly I speak to the two well-established worlds. Having yoked the pressing-stones at the sacrifice with inspired thought, these [stones] of yours, rich in boons for Manu, stand upright like visible objects, O worshipful ones. || 4 ||

At the sacrifice of the bridegroom, I—employing the pressing-stones (*grāvṇaḥ*) for the purpose of pressing the Soma—address with my mind’s impulse, that is, with speech characterized by praise, the two well-formed and beautiful worlds, Heaven and Earth (*dyāvāpṛthivī*).
O Agni, these [worlds] of yours are possessed of many boons (*bhūrivārāḥ*), being frequently chosen by the sacrificers;
they are displayed as objects of beauty, worthy of being beheld.

O Agni, that wondrous and unceasing stream of yours which swells like a torrent from a mountain—O God, O Jātavedas, O Vasu, grant us that providence and bestow upon us a benevolent favor that extends to all people. 6. yā | te | agne | parvatasya'iva | dhārā | asrantī | pīpayat | deva | citrā | tām | asmabhyam | pramatim | jātavedaḥ | vaso iti | rāsva | sumatim | viśva'janyām ||6||

O shining Agni, O God! Your manifold and various forms (*citrā*)—which do not cease and which establish their connection elsewhere than with us—possess a supreme intelligence (*pramati*) there that nourishes us by granting the fruits we require.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"the streams of the mountain."

Just as the torrents of water from a cloud upon a mountain, by uniting with the herbs, trees, and other vegetation, cause them to grow; even so, O *vaso*—O dweller of all—O *jātavedas*, O Agni whose wisdom is born, they bring forth *pramati* (insight) for the sake of the highest good. Through their devotion, they become expansive like the wisdom of the ancestors.
May our inspired thought return to us from afar; O you two who possess all desirable things, come hither toward us.

Well-yoked, they carry you both according to the Eternal Law; the prayers rise up like two parents. May you two grow old with us; from this inspired thought of ours, we have fashioned a hymn for you. Come hither toward us!

O Aśvins, the well-yoked horses have been properly harnessed to your chariot; by means of the *ṛta*, the truth-constituted chariot, they carry you both toward us. They sustain you for the sake of returning to the sacrifice.
The offerings and the sacrifice themselves stand uplifted, rising up toward you.
In this regard, there is an illustration:

just as sons go toward their parents—that is, toward both the mother and the father—so it is here. From us, from our presence, may you two utterly destroy the *paṇi*’s wisdom, that is, his demonic intellect.
We, however, have prepared the oblation characterized by food for you two;
come hither toward us.
*suyuk*:
[this is derived] from the root *yuj* with the suffix *kip*;
by the rule *supāṃ suluk*, there is elision (*luk*) of the nominal suffix (*sup*).
"Pitaraiva" [is explained as follows]: by the rule "pitā mātrā," there is the elision (śeṣa) of the word *pitṛ*;
the case-ending (*sup*) is replaced by the substitute *aṅ*.
*jarethām*. [The root] *jṛ* [is used] in the sense of "decay of age.
Because it is of the *pyanta* class, there is an absence of *vṛddhi* by virtue of the rule "*janījṛṣkasurao'mantāśca*" [which prescribes the substitution of *mi* for *liṭ*].
By the rule "chandasyubhayathā," the suffix *āthām* is treated as both [a sārvadhātuka and an ārdhadhātuka]; thus, because it is an *ārdhadhātuka*, there is the elision of the *ṇi*.
Since the *śap* is marked with *pittva*, it is unaccented (*anudātta*), and therefore the accent of the verbal root remains.
With well-yoked horses and on a well-rolling chariot, O Dastras, hear this song of praise from the mountain.
Why indeed, O Aśvins, do the ancient sages, who are most swift to come, turn back toward you?

With well-yoked horses, on your easy-rolling chariot, O Dāstṛs, hear this cry from the pressing-stone. Why indeed do the ancient inspired poets say that you, O Aśvins, are the swiftest to come to the aid of the distressed?
O Aśvins, with well-yoked, well-harnessed horses, and with a chariot that rolls smoothly— *suvṛkram* meaning it turns again and again—
come hither on your chariot equipped with beautiful wheels, O Dastras, you two destroyers of enemies, and protect us from the devourer.
He who is honored by all is *adriḥ*, the praiser;
listen to this verse, his hymn of praise.

O Aśvins, what do the wise, ancient seers say? They say that you two are the most excellent goers (*gamiṣṭhā*) toward our lack of livelihood (*avarti*), that is, toward the loss of our means of subsistence. What do they proclaim? What do they tell?
The meaning is that they do not speak.
This has already been explained in the eighth chapter of the first book [of the Ṛgveda Saṃhitā] in the passage beginning with "With a well-rolling chariot" (ṚV 1.118.3).
*gamiṣṭha*: the form *gantaḥ* is derived from the root *gam-* with the suffix *iṣṭhan*.
Take heed of us; come hither! All people, together with the gods, invoke you, O Aśvins.
For these honeyed draughts, mixed with milk, have been offered to you like friends at the beginning of the sacrifice.
Take heed! Come hither with whatever speeds you have! All people, O Aśvins, invoke you; for these honeyed draughts mixed with milk have been offered to you by the friends at the break of dawn. 4.
1. The wheel of sutras beginning with *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, and *pha*.
2. The *ṇa*-brāhmaṇas are the *vimas*. 3. *Na* and *sa* say thus.

"O Aśvins, take note of this; recognize this hymn worthy of praise. Moreover, come hither with your means of travel, your chariots, toward our sacrifice. All people, all the singers, invoke you both, O Aśvins, with words characterized by praise. Furthermore, the Adhvaryus and others present these oblations for you—honeyed drinks mixed with the milk of cows, intoxicating and resembling Soma. In this regard, there is an illustration: 'like friends. Just as friends give what is desired to their friends, so do they give to you. 'Usraḥ': one who dwells in the sky is *usraḥ*, the Sun; he rises at the very head of the dawn. Therefore, the sense is: 'come hither. *Manyethām*: from the root *man* (to know), belonging to the *divādi* class; this is the form in the imperative (*loṭ*). *Imā*: the substitution of *ḍā* for the case-ending (*sup*). *Goṛjīkā*: the preservation of the original form of the vowel *e* within the foot of the verse according to the rule "prakṛtyāntaḥpādam. *Dadhuḥ*: the form of the root *dāṇ* (to give) in the perfect tense (*liṭ*) with the suffix *usi*; it lacks the *udātta* accent due to being preceded by *hi*. *Usraḥ*: from the root *vas* (to dwell); the suffix *rak* is added by the rule "skāyatiñca," etc.; because of its *kit* nature, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*); the absence of the *ṣatva* change (the letter *ṣ*) is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
O Aśvins, lords of bounty among the people, you pass through even many realms at the will of the worshiper;
come hither by the broad paths traveled by the gods, O wonder-workers, for these offerings of yours are honeyed draughts.
Across even many realms, O Aśvins, you take pleasure among the people, O bounteous ones. Come hither by the paths traveled by the gods; O wonder-workers, here are your vessels of honeyed mead.
O Aśvins, you who by your own splendor pass across even many *rajāṃsi*—that is, numerous places—come hither to this rite by paths traveled by the gods.
O wealthy ones, O Aśvins, among the people who praise you, a hymn of praise that must be proclaimed on all sides (*ājñuṣaḥ*) is being offered to you both.
O destroyers of enemies, O Aśvins, these are the repositories of the sweet, intoxicating Soma juices for you both.
They are called *nidhayaḥ* because the Soma is deposited (*nidhīyate*) in them;
they are specific types of vessels.
They exist.
Therefore, the sense is: "Come from there."
Ājuṣaḥ: from the root *ghuṣ* preceded by *ā*, with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the object (*karman*). That which is proclaimed is "proclamation" (*āghoṣaḥ*).
For [the word] *gho* is a substitute for *g* due to its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group.
In the phrase “*āḍo’nunāsikaśchandasī*,” the nasalization (*anunāsika*) is Vedic; that is, it is not a constant feature but occurs by Vedic license.
Or else:
The meaning is "foremost.

From this [root], the word *aggūpa* is derived as a conventional form (*nipātita*) ending in the suffix *upa* by the rule “*aggūpaḥ*. It is called *aggūpa* because it goes (*añjati*) toward the gods; thus, it is a hymn of praise (*stotra*).
*Aggūpa* is indeed *ājñūpa*. The suffix *aṇ* is applied in its own sense (*svārthika*) because it belongs to the *prajñādi* group; it bears the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
The half-verse beginning with “Come, let us go” has been explained.
In the Acchāvāka’s *śastra* at the *atiriktokthya* sacrifice lasting twelve days (*asoyāma*), there are four optional *yājyā* verses beginning with “*purāṇam okaḥ*.
This is stated in the Sūtra: “If he has not studied [them], the four *yājyā* verses ‘*purāṇam okaḥ*, *sahyam*, and *śivam vām*’ [are to be used]” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 9.11).
O Heroes, the ancient dwelling, the auspicious chariot, and the wealth of you two were bestowed upon Jahnu;
making them once more auspicious and well-charioted, we, being of one mind, shall rejoice together with the honeyed mead.

The ancient home, the good chariot, the auspicious, that which is dear to you both— O heroes, having restored that wealth to Jahnu once again, making it a good chariot and auspicious, may you together now enjoy the exhilaration of the honeyed draught as one.

1. *kha-ga-gha-ṇa* read *madhukarāṇi*; 2. *ca-dadhuḥ* [is] indeed (*hi*); 3. *gha* reads *bhāvaḥ*; *hi* is a filler; 4. *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-ta-na-bha-sa* do not have the reading ‘*manyethām ... prakṛtibhāvaḥ*’; 5. *kha-ga-ṇa-na-bha-la-sa* do not have the reading ‘*ime*’.
O Aśvins, *vām*—of you two—the *purāṇam* ancient, *sakyam* friendship, is a *sedhyam okaḥ* (dwelling-place to be established), a *śivam* auspicious and beneficial thing.
Furthermore, O *narā* (two men), leaders of our ritual act, *draviṇam* wealth exists for *yuvayoḥ* you two in *jahakmyām*, born of the *jahaka* lineage.

Making your friendships—those auspicious and happiness-bringing bonds of friendship—everlasting once more, may we, becoming united as friends through our common service in offering oblations, together with you both, simultaneously and swiftly exhilarate ourselves with the intoxicating Soma.
Regarding *sakhyam*: in the sense of "the state of friendship," the suffix *ya* is applied [to *sakhi*] to form *sakhyam*. Regarding *jahāmyām*: [this refers to the dual ending].
The suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "belonging to" (*tasyedam*) to the word *jahru*, resulting in *jāhru*.
By the rule *orguṇaḥ*, the *u* is replaced by its *guṇa* vowel *o*.
Then, a metathesis (*vyatyaya*) occurs between the short and long vowels.
*Madama*: [This is derived] from the root *mad*, meaning "to rejoice," in the benedictive mood (*āśīrliṅ*); the suffix *aṅ* is applied according to the rule *liṅyāśiṣyaṅ*.
It is unaccented (*nighāta*).
O Aśvins, you who are most skillful, with Vāyu and your teams of horses, being of one mind, O youthful Nāsatyas—
enjoying the Soma that has passed the night, drink it readily, O bounteous givers!

O Aśvins, with Vāyu—ye who are most skillful, joined with your teams of horses, youthful Nāsatyas—rejoicing, drink the Soma that has passed through the filter, O ye who are unfailing and bounteous givers. 7.
O Nāsatyas— the two who possess no untruth— endowed with excellent skill (*sudakṣā*), ever-youthful (*yuvānā*),

givers of beautiful fruit (*sudānū*): O Aśvins, being in harmony (*sajoṣasā*) with Vāyu and with his teams of horses (*niyudbhiḥ*), taking pleasure (*juṣāṇā*) in the Soma, you two who are never-failing (*asidhrā*), drink this Soma which is being offered even though it is hidden beyond the day (*tiroahyam*).
With the *niyut* teams; from the root *yat*, the suffix *kvip*;
*tiroahyam*.
The suffix *yat* is applied according to the rule "in the Vedic language (*chandasi*), [the suffix *yat* is added] after *bhuva-*. That time in which I have become invisible is *tiroahyaḥ*.
The original accent of the first member [of the compound] remains.
O Aśvins, may our many foods and our unceasing hymns, striving together, encompass you.
Your chariot, born of the seasons and urged by the pressing-stones, traverses heaven and earth in an instant.

O Aśvins, many refreshments have come around you, striving with songs that are never-failing. Your chariot, born of the seasons and urged by the pressing-stones, traverses heaven and earth in an instant. 8.
O Aśvins, the *purucīḥ*— so called because they "go (*aśnanti*) to many places"—
many offerings characterized by oblations have gone around (*pari īyuḥ*) to you both.

Likewise, the singers— unwearied (amṛdhra), meaning not overcome by anyone, and striving (yatamānāḥ), meaning engaged in ritual action— serve you both with songs (gīrbhiḥ), that is, with words characterized by praise. You two are "born of the season" (ṛtujāḥ), meaning the progenitor of the seasonal water (ṛtu),
or else those who manifest in the sacrifice (ṛta).
Driven by the mountains—that is, drawn by the singers—your chariot, O you two, traverses heaven and earth instantly; indeed, at that very moment, it reaches them on all sides.
Regarding the swiftness of the Aśvins' chariot, there is a Vedic mantra:
"The leaders are the Aśvins" (in the *gha* recension); "O leaders, O Aśvins! (in the *ta* recension).
2. In the manuscripts na, la, and sa, "asaṃkhyā" is absent.
3. In manuscript ta, "punaḥpunaḥ" is present.
4. In the manuscripts kha, ga, gha, ca, ṇa, ta, na, bha, la, and sa, "aśvaiḥ" is absent.
5. In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member [is retained]; kha: in a *bahuvrīhi*, the accent of the first member [is retained].
6. ca: "the two Aśvins" (*aśvinā* = *aśvinau*).
7. kha-ga-gha-ca-ṇa-ma-sa: they go toward the great city; na: they go toward the great city; la: they go toward the most excellent city.
8. The mantra consisting of the syllables kha, ga, ca, ṇa, na, pha, and bha.

"Or he who, swifter than thought, comes to the clans with his own horses in a chariot" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.117.2). For this reason, the sense is: "Come to our sacrifice. *Īyuḥ*: From the root *iṇ* 'to go' in the perfect tense (*liṭ*), there is lengthening of the reduplication according to the rule *dīrgha iṇaḥ kiti*. Because it begins a quarter-verse (*pāda*), it is not subject to the *anighāta* (lack of suppression) accent. *Yatamānāḥ*: This is the form of the root *yat* 'to strive' in the present participle suffix *śānac*. Since the *śap* suffix is *pit*, it is *anudātta*; and since the *śānac* suffix is also *anudātta* by the accent of the *lasārvadhātuka*, the accent of the verbal root remains. *Ṛtajāḥ*: [The suffix] *viṭ* is added to the root *jan*. The rule beginning with *vid-manoh...* applies. *Adijūtaḥ*: *Jū* is a Vedic (Sautra) root. The suffix *kta* is added in the passive sense. By the rule *tṛtīyā karmaṇi*, the first member of the compound retains its original accent.

O Aśvins, you two for whom the most excellent honey-pressed Soma is intended—drink that; come to our dwelling. Your chariot indeed displays many forms; it is the best at arriving at the prepared place of him who possesses the pressed juice. 9. O Aśvins! The most excellent honey-pressed [Soma] is for you; the Soma is yours. Drink that; come to our home. Your chariot indeed performs many wonders; it is the swiftest to arrive at the prepared place of the one who has pressed the juice. 9.

O Aśvins, that Soma which is most excellent in sweetness (*madhusuttama*), which impels [the senses] with extreme sweetness, and which is *yuvāku*— that is, existing as one who desires you both; or alternatively, *yuvāku* means mixed with the *vasatīvarī* waters and other ingredients.
Drink this Soma! Drink it!
Come hither, come to our dwelling in our house!
Creating repeatedly for you both a vast, protective splendor, beauty, or wealth desirable by all, your chariot has reached the prepared place of the sacrificer who has pressed the Soma.
Yāska [says]: "In the place of *samidh* there is *nirithepa*" (Nirukta 12.7).
It is a purificatory term (*saṃskārin*).
Or else:
He has come to the conditioned house; he comes with exceeding intensity.
*Yuvākuḥ*. From the root *yu* (to join).
By the rule “*kaṭikuṣpibhyāṃ kākuḥ*,” this suffix *kāku* also occurs after this [root] due to its inclusion in the *bāhulaka* (variety) category.
By the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), it is *madhyodātta* (accented on the middle syllable).

Regarding *karikrat*: from the root *kṛ*, with *yaṅluk* and the *śatṛ* suffix, by the rule "dādharti dardharti dardharṣi," etc., when the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs in place of the reduplication (*cu*), since the root ends in a vowel (*akārāntatva*), the augment *ṛk* would not apply to the reduplication; therefore, that (*ṛk*) is also prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*).
The vowel has been practiced. "Niṣkṛtam" [is formed] with the suffix *kta* in the sense of the commencement of an action from the root *kṛ*.
The meaning is that the *saṃskṛta* has come into operation;
[this is] the accentuation according to the rule for *thā-thādi*.
The sixth hymn, consisting of nine verses beginning with “mitro janān,” belongs to Viśvāmitra; it is in the Triṣṭubh metre and is addressed to Mitra.
According to the Anukramaṇikā: “‘mitro mantraṃ’ [is the hymn] ending in four Gāyatrīs.
Of these, the first five are Triṣṭubhs, and the remaining four are Gāyatrīs.
The deity is Mitra.
When drops of rain fall into the milk intended for the Agnihotra, one should place a fuel-stick upon the fire with the verse, "Mitra impels the people" (*mitro janān*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "With the words 'Mitra impels the people as he speaks,' [one performs] the placing of the fuel-stick" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 3.11).

Mitra, speaking, impels men; Mitra has supported both the earth and the sky. Mitra gazes upon the people with unblinking eyes; offer an oblation rich in ghee unto Mitra. Mitra impels men as he speaks; Mitra has supported the earth and the sky. Mitra gazes upon the people with unblinking eyes; offer an oblation rich in ghee unto Mitra.
1. *ca-aśvinā* refers to the two Aśvins.
2. In the manuscripts *kha*, *gha*, and *ṇa*, it reads *madhurasamatyantam*; in *la*, it reads *madhurasamamṛtam*.
3. In *kha*, *ga*, and *ca*, it further reads *abhisutavataḥ*.
Ṛgveda 2.60:
Mitra is he who speaks, is praised, or utters sound;
or Mitra is the Sun (Sūrya), for he is measured (known) by all in an excellent manner, or he extends to all through the bestowing of rain.
He causes the people—the farmers and others—to labor;
he makes them exert effort in tasks such as agriculture.
Likewise, Mitra alone supports—that is, sustains—both these worlds, the earth and the heaven, by producing food and sacrificial offerings through rain.
This being so, Mitra, with his unblinking eye of grace, beholds and looks upon all *kṛṣṭīḥ*—that is, human beings who perform ritual actions.

Having known all this, O officiating priests (*ṛtvijaḥ*), offer, that is, present, the oblation (*havyam*) suitable for sacrifice—such as the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and other offerings—accompanied by the spreading and sprinkling of clarified butter (*ghṛtavat*), unto that god Mitra.
