Regarding this meaning, Yāska says: "Mitra stretches out [the world] like a mother, speaking—that is, making a sound."
"Mitra indeed sustains both the earth and the sky;
Mitra gazes upon the people with unblinking eyes.
"People" (*kṛṣṭayaḥ*) is a name for human beings; they are so called because they possess action (*karman*), or because their bodies are fashioned (*vikṛṣṭa*).
"Offer the oblation, rich in ghee, to Mitra"—this has been explained.
"The root *hu* signifies the act of giving" (Nirukta 10.22).
*yātayati* is the form of the root *yat* (meaning "to strive") in the *ṇic*-causative with the present tense (*laṭ*). *Dādhāra*.
By the rule "tujādīnām," there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable. *Juhotu*: in the imperative (*loṭ*) of the root *hu*, the suffix is replaced by *tu*.
The suffix is *guṇa*.
There is elision (*nighāta*).

The *yājyā* for the oblations of the *devasū* sacrifice is "pra sa mitra" [RV 3.59.2]. This same verse serves as the *yājyā* for the *maitra-caru* when the morning *homa* is performed after its proper time has passed.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "pra sa mitra matom astu prayasvān... mahimāya pṛcchate" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.11).
Then, when the sacrifice has been completed, [he recites] "tata iṣṭimitraḥ sūryo'bhi yo mahinā divam" and "pra sa mitra matoṃ astu prayasvān" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.12).
May he be beloved by Mitra, full of offerings; O Āditya, you bestow favor upon him through his sacred law.
He is neither slain nor conquered; no distress reaches him from near or from afar because of you.

May he be dear to Mitra, full of offerings, who exerts himself for you with sacred law (*vrata*), O Āditya; protected by you, he is not slain, nor is he overcome; neither from near nor from afar does distress reach him.
O Āditya, that mortal man who, joined with the vow and the sacrifice, bestows upon you a gift characterized by oblations— O Mitra, let that person be possessed of food,
let him prevail; protected by you, he is not slain nor oppressed by anyone,
nor is he conquered or overcome.
The evil (aṃhas) does not reach— that is, it does not attain— this man who has offered the oblation (havis) to you,
neither from nearby nor even from afar.
The root *śikṣati* means "the act of giving. The form is in the *parasmaipada* by way of grammatical substitution (*vyatyaya*).
Because it is connected with a preceding word (*yadvṛtta*), there is no elision of the accent (*anighāta*).
It is conquered (*jīyate*). In the passive form of the root *ji* with the suffix *yak*, there is lengthening by the rule "akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ.
[The word is] *tvotaḥ*.
The accent of the first member [of the compound] is determined by the rule *tṛtīyā karmaṇi*.
It pervades; [the root is] *aś* in the sense of "pervasion."
It begins with *sva-*;
the *parasmaipada* ending is used by way of transposition.
The invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the oblations of the *devasū* sacrifice dedicated to Mitra, the Truthful, is prescribed in the Sūtra as follows:
“Free from disease, rejoicing in nourishment—may he who honors Mitra be foremost, possessing sacrificial food” (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 4.11).

1. [The letters] kha, ga, gha, ca, ṇa, na, bha, la, and sa do not exist [as initial consonants]. 2. *ṇa* is followed by *vadhyate*. 3. *ta* signifies "to pervade. 4. *ta-na-la-sūtram*. Free from disease, rejoicing in nourishment, with measured steps upon the broad expanse of the earth, abiding in the ordinance of Āditya—may we abide in the benevolent favor of Mitra. (3) Free from disease; in nourishment; rejoicing; with measured steps; upon the broad expanse; of the earth; of Āditya; the ordinance; abiding in; may we; in the benevolent favor of Mitra; abide. (3)

O friends, free from affliction and devoid of disease, rejoicing and delighting in nourishing food (*iḷā*), upon the wide expanse of the earth, with well-knit knees— moving everywhere according to our desire— we, dwelling near and performing the ritual act (*vrata*) pertaining to Āditya, may we abide within the auspicious favor and benevolent thought of Mitra, the Sun.
*Madantaḥ*: [This is derived] from the root *mṛd* in the sense of "joy," with the suffix *śatṛ*; the *śap* [vocalization] occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*). *Mitajñvaḥ*.
In the word *jānu*, the form *ju* is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) substitution. Regarding *variman*:
from the word *uru*, the suffix *imanic* is applied according to the *pṛṣvādi* group.
By the rule "priyasthira" etc., there is the substitution of *vara*.
By the rule "supāṃ suluk" etc., there is the elision (*luk*) of the locative case ending.
The initial vowel is acutely accented by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).

This Mitra, worthy of homage, most gracious, a king of noble dominion, has been born as a wise ordainer. May we abide in the favor of that one worthy of sacrifice, and likewise in his auspicious goodwill. 4. This Mitra; worthy of homage; most gracious; a king; of noble dominion; has been born; as a wise ordainer; of him; may we; in the favor; of the one worthy of sacrifice; also; in the auspicious; goodwill; abide. 4.

This Mitra, the Sun, who was established in the preceding mantra, is worthy of homage (*namasya*), to be saluted by all; he is most gracious (*suśeva*), meaning he is to be served with ease. He is the king (*rājā*) of the entire world, the lord through the bestowing of light; he is of excellent power (*sukṣatra*), for by the word *kṣatra*, strength is expressed.

Endowed with beautiful strength, the Creator, the ordainer of the entire world—Sūrya, possessed of such qualities, was born; he manifested. May we, the sacrificers, abide in the auspicious thought, the beautiful intellect, the benevolent mind, and the mental well-being of that very Sūrya, who is endowed with such qualities and worthy of sacrifice.
*namasyaḥ* (one who is to be saluted);
*namasā sādhuḥ* (good through salutation).
The suffix *yat* is applied here according to the rule "tatra sādhuḥ" (good in that).
It has three *udātta* accents. *Ajaniṣṭa* is the form of the root *janī* (in the sense of "coming into existence") in the *luṅ* tense with the suffix *sic*.
In *saumanase*: the word *sumanas* [is used] in the sense of "belonging to this," and by the rule *tasyedam*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied; the accent is that of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).

Great is Āditya, to be approached with reverence; he who impels men is most gracious to the one who praises him. To him, the most excellent, offer this pleasing oblation in the fire for Mitra. 5. Great is Āditya, to be approached with reverence; he who impels men is most gracious to the one who praises him. To him, the most excellent, offer this pleasing oblation in the fire for Mitra. 5.

The great Āditya, who is to be approached with reverence, who disciplines men, and who is most gracious to the singer—to him, to Mitra, the most worthy of offerings, offer this pleasing oblation into the fire. 5.

1. Kha-ga-gha-ca-na-bha-sa: His work is as follows. This very Sun (Āditya), who is great, having been approached with homage—that is, with a gesture of salutation—he who is to be approached by all, and who is "yātayajana": he by whom people are to be set in motion toward their respective duties every morning; thus he is so described.

To that person who praises and offers hymns of praise, become a true friend; for him, the most excellent and most worthy of praise, a friend from of old, offer—yea, pour into the fire this oblation which is dear and pleasing.

*yātayajanaḥ*: this is the form of the root *yat* (meaning "to strive") in the present participle (*śatṛ*) with the suffix *pyan*. Although, in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent of the first member would normally apply, here the final syllable of the first member is acute due to its inclusion in the *marudvṛdhādi* group.
For *gṛṇate*: [from] the root *gṛ* in the sense of "sound.
The acute accent (*udātta*) of the case-ending is applied by the rule *śaturanumaḥ*.
[The suffix] *yat* is applied after the root *pan* because it belongs to the class beginning with *dhañ*;
by the rule “*yato ’nāvaḥ*,” there is acute accent on the first syllable.
*Juṣṭam*:
[The word] has the acute accent on the first syllable by the rule "nityaṃ mantre" (Pāṇini 6.1.210).

In the Abhīdhūpaḍaha and the Daśarātra, when there are seventeen, twenty, or more stomas, five, seven, or other such numbers of ṛks are to be inserted (*āvapanīya*) at the point of insertion (*āvāpasthāna*) for the recitations (*śastra*) of the Hotṛ and others.
Among these, in the *śastra* of the Maitrāvaruṇa, the verses beginning with “*mitrasya carṣaṇīdhṛtaḥ*” are intended for insertion.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “The four verses beginning with ‘*mitrasya carṣaṇīdhṛtaḥ*’ belong to Mitra” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.5).
The protection of the divine Mitra, the sustainer of the people, is victorious and brings gain; it possesses splendor with most wondrous fame.
The protection of the divine Mitra, the sustainer of the people, is winning and possesses most wonderful renown. 6.

Of the god Mitra, the sustainer of the people (*carṣaṇīdhṛtaḥ*)—that is, the supporter of human beings by means of bestowing rain—may his *avaḥ* (aid) come to me; may his food (*anna*), which is to be honored through sacrifices (*satraiḥ*), and his *śumna* (glory), that is, his wealth, which possesses most wonderful renown (*citraśravastama*)—meaning it is exceedingly praiseworthy—be granted.

*Mānasi*: From the root *man*, by the rule "mānasisparṇasi" etc., there is the substitution of the suffix *asic*; due to this irregular formation (*nipātana*), there is vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel. Because it ends in *i* (a *cit* suffix), it is oxytone.
By the rule "svamoḥ," there is elision (luk) of the case endings *su* and *am*.
If the time for the morning oblation (*prātarhoma*) has passed, the *Maitrīṣṭi* is performed.
For that sacrifice, the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) is “*abhi yo mahinā*.
This is also stated in the Sūtra: “‘*abhi yo mahinā divam*, ‘*pra ma mitra matom astu prayasvān*’” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.12).
He who by his greatness has surpassed the heavens, Mitra, the far-extending,
has surpassed the earth with his glories.
Mitra, who by his greatness has surpassed the sky, and by his glories has surpassed the earth, is far-extending. ||7||
That Mitra who by his own greatness—that is, by his majesty—overcomes, or surpasses, the sky and the intermediate space, that Mitra is all-pervading (*saprathas*). *Prathas* means renown or fame;
accompanied by that, he also overcomes the earth with his glories (*śravobhis*), which consist of the waters released through the medium of rain.
The meaning is that he makes it well-composed.
*Saprathāḥ*:
[from the root] *pratha* meaning "to become manifest," with the suffix *asun*.
By the rule "vopasarjanasya," the word *saha* becomes *sa-* when followed by *sabha*.
The five peoples have submitted to Mitra, who is powerful through his aid;
he sustains all the gods.
For Mitra, the five peoples have submitted themselves for his protective aid; he sustains all the gods. 8.
The five peoples—the four castes with the Niṣādas as the fifth—have submitted to Mitra, who is endowed with power (*śavas*) for the sake of overcoming enemies; they offer oblations to him.
Such a Mitra sustains all the gods by his very own nature.
1. In the *la*-mantra, at the point of the *yājyā* and *upasthāna*.
2. And the meaning is that they are to be inserted (*āvapanīyā*).
3. By all of us (*sarvair asmābhiḥ*).

It retains [the accent]. In the word *abhiṣṭi*, [the suffix] *kin* is applied by the rule "vṛṣa etc. in mantras" for the sense of strength (*śavas*) and nourishment (*iṣ*). By the rule "tādau ca niti," there is the acute accent on the final syllable of *abhi*. There is a substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) according to the *śakandhu*-class. In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the accent belongs to the first member.
Mitra has provided nourishment among the gods and among living beings for the person who has spread the sacrificial grass, according to his desired vows.
Among the gods, among the long-lived ones, for the person who has trimmed the sacrificial grass—may those whose vows are fulfilled grant nourishment; they are peerless. 9.

*Mitra* is the Lord Āditya. Among *devas*—those endowed with qualities such as radiance—and among *āyus*, that is, among human beings, he is the person who has "spread the sacrificial grass" (*vṛktabarhis*).
One by whom the *barhis* (sacrificial grass) has been "cut" (*vṛkta*) or mown;
the meaning is: a priest who offers the oblation after first cutting and arranging the *barhis*.
To that person for whom the sacrificial grass has been trimmed, he— whose vows are fulfilled— performs the *iṣṭis*,
meaning he performs those sacrifices by which desirable and auspicious vows (deeds) are accomplished;
that is to say, he grants them to him.

In *vṛktabarhiṣe*: the root *vraśc* means "to cut. Since it is used with the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) in the sense of the object (*karman*), the optional prohibition of *iṭ* applies by the rule *yasya vibhāṣā*.
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the accent belongs to the first member (*pūrvapada-svara*).
[The suffix] *aka* [is applied].
In the *luṅ* tense of the root *kṛ*, there is *kle*; by the rule "in a mantra, *ghas* etc. (*mantre ghasa*), there is elision (*luk*).
The elision of *sip* and the like by means of *halṅyādi-lopa*;
the *nighāta* (elision of accent).
The seventh hymn, consisting of seven verses beginning with "iheha vaḥ," belongs to Viśvāmitra. It is composed in the Jagatī meter and has the Ṛbhus as its deities;
the remaining three verses have Indra as their deity.
Thus it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: "iheha vaḥ consists of seven verses; it is in the Jagatī meter, and the last triplet has Indra as its deity."

The application of the hymn is based on its indicative mark (*laiṅgika*). There are four *āghā* verses belonging to the *vaiśvadeva-śastra* on the first day of both the *pṛṣṭhya* and *abhiplava* six-day periods; these are the *ābhava-nivid-dāniyā* verses.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The four beginning with 'iheha va'... (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.5).

O men, whatever kinship you have here through your mind, those eager ones have attained it by their wisdom; by means of those creative powers (*māyās*) and impetuous strength, O sons of Sudhanvan, you have obtained your share in the sacrifice.

Hither and thither, with their minds, the men, kinsmen and seekers, went toward those things by means of their wisdom—those magical powers through which the sons of Sudhanvan, impetuous in their vigor, obtained their share in the sacrifice. || 1 ||
O Ṛbhus, this is your kinship (*bandhutā*).
They are called *bandhavas* because they bind—that is, they connect one with the fruit [of action];
their collection is *bandhutā*.

In this world, everywhere, everything is known by the mind. O men, O Ṛbhus, you who are desirous of a share in the sacrifice—by means of *vedas*, that is, through knowledge concerning the ritual acts that procure a sacrificial portion, you have attained (*abhi jagmuḥ*), that is, you reach, those such rites.
Which ones are they?
By means of *māyās*: they are called *māyās* because they are measured (*mīyante*) or known; that is, ritual actions (*karmāṇi*).
By those *māyās*, by those very actions, [he is] one whose vigor and strength are ever-increasing.
They are endowed with the power of counteracting [defects], mastery, and moral vigor.
The Saudhanvanas:
there was a certain son of Aṅgiras named Sudhanvan.

His sons were the Saudhanvanas; and they were three—Ṛbhu, Vibhvan, and Vāja. By these names, you have obtained (*ānaśa*) a sacrificial portion (*yajñiyaṃ bhāgam*) worthy of sacrifice, characterized by the drinking of Soma and so forth. You are [those who] have attained it.
And thus says the wording of a mantra: "O Ṛbhu, Vibhvan, and Vāja, O gods, come hither; you who are skillful in work, attain your sacrificial portion" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.161.6).
This meaning is also clearly stated in the Brāhmaṇa, preceded by a narrative, in the passage: "The Ṛbhus indeed won the Soma-draught among the gods through austerity" (Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 3.30).
1. ta-na-udāttatvam | 2. kha-ga-gha-ca-ṇa-ta-na-bha-la-sa-bhāvaḥ | 3. kha-ga-gha-ca-ṇa-ta-na-bha-sa-sarvam | 4. kha-gha-ta-na-bha-vyāptāḥ |
Or rather:

O *Ṛbhus*, you leaders of men, desirous (*uśijaḥ*) and endowed with wealth characterized by the oblation (*vedasā*), the singers have approached—through kinship (*bandhutā*), that is, through truthfulness of mind—those deeds of yours, such as the churning of the cups and so forth;
they attain them.
In response to the question "Which ones?", he says:
those actions, such as the preparation of the cups (*camasa-kṣaṇa*) and so forth, by which you have obtained your share—they approach those;
the meaning is that your intellect contemplates those skillful deeds.
*iheha*: the doubling [of the word] occurs according to the rule *nityavīpsayoḥ*;
since the subsequent member is an *āmreḍita*, it is unaccented (*anudātta*), and thus the accent of the preceding member remains.
*Bandhutā*.
[Derived from] the root *bandh* in the sense of "binding.
By the rule *bhṛ-sṛ-snihi-* etc., the suffix *u* is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).
In the sense of "a collection," the suffix *tal* is applied according to Pāṇini’s sūtra 4.2.43, *agrāmajanabandhusahāyyebhyas tal*; this is the accent of the *liṅga*.

By those very powers with which you caused him to swell, by that wisdom with which you brought forth the cow from the hide, and by that mental skill with which you fashioned the two bay steeds— the Ṛbhus attained divinity through all of this together.
By those powers (*śacībhiḥ*), even though they are subject to death by virtue of being human, they now sustain their lives through friendship with Indra.
And so says the mantra: "The carriers [of oblations] maintained... (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.20.8).

The *Ṛbhus*, sons of the seer Sudhanvan—also called Saudhanvanas—being "well-doers" (*sukṛtaḥ*), that is, performers of beautiful deeds, attained divinity through "abundant *śamīs*," meaning actions that remove obstacles to the attainment of godhood, and through "beautiful work" (*sukṛtayā viṣṭī*), having pervaded [the ritual space], they "earned immortality" (*amṛtatvam erire*), that is, they attained divinity.
Accordingly, another mantra is recited: "Being mortal, they attained immortality" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.110.4).
*Napātaḥ*: By the rule *naāpnapāna* etc., there is the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of sandhi) for the negative particle *nañ*. *Dadhanvire*.
The root *dhav* has the sense of "to run. The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs by way of grammatical substitution; this is the form in the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
They moved. From the root *īr* meaning "to go," the suffix *ām* does not occur because it is a mantra.
The elision [of the suffix] is by *nighāta*.
[In the word] *sukṛtayā*,
the suffix *kyap* is applied after the root *kṛ* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*) by the rule "after *kṛ*, there is *śa* and *kyap*."
By the elision of the suffix *pratyaya*, there is udātta accent on the final syllable;
in a compound, however, the accent falls on the final syllable of the *kṛt*-suffix.

You travel on one chariot with Indra at the pressed juice; and thus you become possessed of the power and glory of the *vaśās*. O priests, O *Ṛbhus*, sons of Sudhanvan, your well-wrought deeds and heroic exploits are beyond compare. *indreṇa* (with Indra), *yātha* (you go), *saratham* (on one chariot), *sute* (at the pressed juice), *sacāṃ* (being together), *atho* (and so), *vaśānām* (of the *vaśās*), *bhavatha* (you become), *saha* (together with), *śriyā* (glory). *na* (not), *vaḥ* (your), *pratimai* (equals), *sukṛtāni* (well-wrought deeds), *vāghataḥ* (O priests), *saudhanvanāḥ* (O sons of Sudhanvan), *ṛbhavaḥ* (O *Ṛbhus*), *vīryāṇi* (heroic exploits), *ca* (and). 4.

O Ṛbhus, you—along with Indra, together upon a single common chariot—go to the sacrifice where the Soma has been pressed. Immediately thereafter, having mounted that same single chariot with Indra, you [approach] the *vaśas*. They are called *vaśas* because human beings are desired—that is, they are sought after—by the sacrificer for the sake of results characterized by heaven and so forth.
Together with their offerings consisting of praise, oblations, and so forth, you became [immortal], O Saudhanvanas—
sons of Sudhanvan— O Vāghatas.
According to Yāska, they are either "bearers of the fruit characterized by immortality and the like," or "wise ones."
O Ṛbhus, such are your excellent deeds (*sukṛtāni*)—those actions which bring about divinity—which are beyond compare;
they cannot be measured by anyone in terms of their magnitude.
Likewise, your heroic powers (*vīryāṇi*), your capacities, are likewise impossible to measure.
Of the *vaśas*.
[The root] *vaś* means "to desire.
The suffix *ap* is applied in the sense of the instrument (karaṇa) according to the rule: "An addition is made for the roots *vaś* and *raṇ*."
Because the suffix *pratyaya* has the marker *pitt*, it is unaccented (*anudātta*), and thus the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*) remains.
If the word *vaśā* signifies "barren cow," it is oxytone (*antodātta*), as in:
"The barren ewes have been released; they have been summoned" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 10.91.14).
*vaḥ*:
In the genitive plural of the pronoun *yuṣmad*, there is the substitution of *vas*; it is subject to the rule of *nighāta* (anudātta accent).
The root *māṅ* means "to measure";
[the suffix] *vic* [is applied].
*Pratimāḥ* is *pratimānam*.
In its dative singular form, the absence of elision of the final *ā* is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).
It takes the accent of the single substitute (*ekādeśasvara*).
On the fifth day of the *ābhilāvika* period, in the *vaiśvadeva* *śastra*, there are three verses beginning with "indra ṛbhubhiḥ" belonging to the *ābhīvarta* hymn.
This is prescribed in the Sūtra: "The two triplets 'ghṛtavatī bhuvanānām abhiśrīḥ' and 'indra ṛbhubhir vājabhiḥ' [are used]" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 7.7).
At the third pressing, the *prasthitayājyā* for the Hotṛ priest begins with the word "agnā."

And it is stated in the Sūtra: "O Indra, together with the Ṛbhus and Vājas, [drink] this well-mixed [soma]; O Indra and Varuṇa, drinkers of the pressed juice, [drink] this pressed juice" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.5).

1. The syllables *ga*, *gha*, *bha*, *la*, *sa*, and *ca* do not exist [in this recension]. 2. According to the recensions *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *bha*, and *sva*, the fruit is characterized by heaven and other such rewards. 3. According to the recensions *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, and *sa*, the word is accented on the final syllable (*antodātta*). 4. According to the recensions *kha*, *ga*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, *la*, and *sa*, the elision (*lopa*) is Vedic (*chāndasa*).

5. According to the recensions *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, *la*, and *sa*, the particle is *āthaḥ*. O Indra, drink the pressed Soma, which has been sprinkled together with the Vājins, the Ṛbhus;
urged by our devotion, O Maghavan, rejoice in the house of the donor along with the sons of Sudhanvan, the heroes.

O Indra, together with the R̥bhus who possess strength, pour down the pressed Soma that has been sprinkled; impelled by prayer, O Maghavan, drink it in the house of the donor, and rejoice with the sons of Sudhanvan, those heroic men.
He, O Indra, [is accompanied] by the Vājavadbhis;
Vāja is the name of the Ātā of the Ṛbhus.
Or rather:
*Vāja* means food.
With the *vṛdhvas* (increasers) accompanied by that [food], [the gods] seize the *soma*—which is *mahita* (honored), *samukṣita* (well-sprinkled), and *suta* (pressed)—with their *gabhastis*.
The *gabhastis* are the two arms, so called because they grasp objects with both hands, or because they hold things with both hands.
"Pour [the Soma] into their two arms; let it flow forth.
The meaning is: having grasped the Soma with both arms, drink it.

O Maghavan Indra, impelled by *dhī*—that is, by the hymn of praise—rejoice together with the *ṛbhus*, the human sons of Sudhanvan, in the house of the donor who has offered the oblation; be exhilarated by the drinking of Soma.
*Samukṣitam*. [The root] *ukṣ* means "to sprinkle. The suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).
In the word *gatiranantaraḥ*, the vowel [of the suffix] belongs to the verbal root (*gati*).
In *gabhastyoḥ*:
from the root *bhas* in the sense of "threatening" or "shining," the suffix *tip* is added by the rule *bhaserdvac*, and the augment *gaḍ* is applied to the root.
Alternatively,
this may be derived from the root *gṛh* (to seize) according to the *pṛṣodarādi* rule;
thus it should be understood as "be exhilarated" (*matsva*).
In the sense of "praising" (*madi*) and so forth,
in the *loṭ* [imperative] mood, there is elision of the *vikaraṇa* suffix by the rule "there is diversely [elision] in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).
There is also the suppression of accent (*nighāta*).
O Indra, accompanied by the Ṛbhus and Vāja, rejoice here at this libation with your power, O much-praised one!
These days have been set apart for you, according to the ordinances of the gods and the laws of men.

O Indra, accompanied by the Ṛbhus and Vāja, rejoice here at this libation with your power, O you who are praised by many! These days have been offered for you; the ordinances of the gods and the laws of men have been established through sacred rites. 6.

O Indra, praised by many (*puruṣṭuta*), you who possess the *Ṛbhus*—that is, endowed with the *Ṛbhus*, possessed of strength (*vāja*), joined with the brother of the *Ṛbhu*, and accompanied by *Śacī* (Indrāṇī) through her ritual action (*karman*)—rejoice in this our rite at this third pressing; be exhilarated!
O Indra, for your sake these days have been prepared;
they remain fixed for your drinking of Soma throughout the three pressings.

Furthermore, the *vratas*—the vows and ritual acts—of the gods, beginning with Agni, as well as those of human beings, remain fixed for your sake in accordance with their respective duties and actions.
O Indra, accompanied by the R̥bhus and the Vājins, come here to the singer’s hymn that wins the prize;
come to the sacrifice worthy of worship, with these hundred keen intentions for the sake of the living man, you who have a thousand ways of leading at the offering of the rite.

O Indra, with the R̥bhus, the winners of booty, come hither to the praiseworthy hymn of the singer who seeks gain; with a hundred keen intentions, for the sake of man, you whose guidance is a thousandfold, come to the offering of the sacrifice. 7.
1. [The syllables] kha, ga, gha, ca, ṇa, pha, bha, and samyagbhiṣikta.
2. [The syllables] ga, ca, and prakṣāraya.
3. [The syllables] ta, ma, ghavana, and dhanavan; [the syllables] na, la, sa, and maghavana he.

O Indra, accompanied by the swift steeds yoked for the prize and by the Ṛbhus, you who strive for the prize—bestowing food (vāja) upon the singer—come hither to this sacrifice, to the hymn of the praiser, which is worthy of sacrifice and fit for the rite.
Furthermore, how characterized?
By your banners (ketebhiḥ).
They are called *ketāḥ* because they are known (*jñāyate*) by all; thus, the *ketāḥ* are the wise Maruts.

Accompanied by those hundred—that is, by a number of hundred—vigorous horses skilled in running, [the Soma] comes for the sake of the living man, the sacrificer, as one possessing a thousand ways (*sahasranīthaḥ*), endowed with many modes of guidance, to the offering of the sacrifice (*adhvarasya*). "Sacrifice" (*adhvara*) is that in which harm (*dhvara*) does not exist; [he comes] to the oblation (*home*) of such Soma—this is the ellipsis.
In the word *vājayan*, the suffix *ṇic* is applied in the sense of "he produces strength" (*vājam karoti*).

Due to the rule "as if *iṣṭan*" (*ṇāviṣṭavat*), the status of *iṣṭan*-derivatives applies; consequently, by the rule "the *tṛ* [suffix] is elided before *iṣṭha*, *iman*, and *iyaṅ*" (*turiṣṭhemeyaḥsu*), there is the elision of the *ṭṛ*.
By means of the *ketas*.
[The root] *kit* means "to know"; [the suffix] *ghañ*.
Because of the substitution of *ñit*, the first syllable is udātta.
The eighth hymn, consisting of seven verses beginning with "upo vājena," is addressed to Uṣas and has Viśvāmitra as its seer.
Thus it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: "Uṣaḥ [is the deity]; [the hymn] pertains to Uṣas.
Its application is in the Prātaranuvāka during the ritual session for Uṣas, and in the Āśvina-śastra, within the Triṣṭubh meter.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Upo vājenedam u tyat" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.14).
O Dawn, rich in booty, O wise one, accept with joy the hymn of the singer, O bountiful lady!
Ancient yet ever-youthful goddess, full of wisdom, you move according to your law, O possessor of all boons.

O Dawn, rich in booty, wise one, graciously accept the hymn of the singer, O bountiful lady! Ancient goddess, yet ever youthful, bestowing abundance, you move according to your divine law, O possessor of all boons.
O Vājini, possessed of strength; O Ājñāvatī, endowed with command.
And thus says the mantra: "O Vājinīvatī, [come] together with strengths" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.48.16).

O Maghonī, possessor of wealth, O Uṣas, being Pracetā, possessed of excellent knowledge, do thou *juṣasva*—that is, accept and enjoy—the *stoma*, the hymn of praise, of the *gṛṇataḥ*, the singer who performs thy hymn of praise.

Alternatively, the connection is: "O Goddess Uṣas, ancient one, enjoy the hymn together with *vāja*—that is, the oblation characterized as *vāja*. O you who are praised by all (*viśvavāre*), O goddess, you who are from of old (*purāṇī*).
"Yuvatiḥ" is a simile;
she is likewise radiant, just as in the verse:
"A woman, well-adorned, as if polished by her mother" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.123.11).
Puraṃdhi: she whose [work] consists of many, abundant acts characterized by praise;
she who possesses manifold hymns of praise.
"Puraṃdhi means one of great wisdom," says Yāska; or, puraṃdhi means "shining.
Endowed with such qualities, you move toward the *vrata*, that is, the sacrifice, and you proceed by way of the sacrifice.
*Maghoni*:

from the word *magha*, the suffix *vanip* is applied in the sense of the possessive suffix *matup* according to the rule "In non-Vedic [usage], *ivan* and *van* are added"; in the feminine, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule "The suffix *ṅīp* is added after bases ending in *ṛ* or *n*."

In the case of *śruyavamaghonam atadvite*, once the semivowel substitution (*saṃprasāraṇa*) has been performed, there is *guṇa* [vṛddhi]. In the vocative singular, by the rule *ambārthanadyorhrasvaḥ*, there is shortening. There is also the *nighāta* (elision of accent).
*Purāṇī*:
The word *purāṇa* is established as having an udātta accent on the final syllable by the rule "purāṇaprokteṣu. The feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to the rule "ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...".

By the rule "anudāttasya ca yatrodāttalopaḥ," the word *puraṃdhiḥ* has its final syllable accented acute (*antodātta*). Due to its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group, the vowel *u* is replaced by *am*, and the vowel *ī* is shortened.
The initial acute accent (*ādyudātta*) is applied by the rule: "In the section on initial acute accents, there is an addition [to the list] for *divas* and so forth in the Vedic language.

[Variants]: kha-ga-gha-ca-ṇa-pha-bha read *vājibhiḥ*; kha-ga-gha-ca-ṇa-na-bha-sa omit *stotuḥ*. 3. gha-ca-ṇa-la read *prajñāḥ*. 4. ga-ca-pha read *tvam*; ṇa-na-la-sa read *satām*. 5. la reads *kurvāṇasya*. 6. kha-ga-gha-ca-ṇa-na-bha-sa omit *sevasva*. 7. kha-ga-gha-ca-ṇa-pha-bha: *yuvatiḥ* means "young woman. Ṛgveda 2.61: O immortal goddess Uṣas, shine forth with your radiant chariot, sending out pleasant truths.
May the well-governed horses, golden-hued and broad-backed, bring you hither.
O Goddess Uṣas, immortal one, shine forth upon us! O you whose chariot is radiant, stirring up pleasant truths, let your well-managed horses, broad-chested and golden-hued, bring you hither.

O Goddess, you who are immortal—free from the nature of death—and possessed of a golden chariot, a chariot made of gold; you who utter and cause to resound *sūnṛtāḥ*, words that are pleasant and true.
As it is said in the Vedic mantra: "The bestower of happiness, the *sūnṛtā*, causes [them] to resound" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.113.12).
Such as you are, shine forth; through connection with the rays of the sun, shine especially brightly.
May those horses of golden hue—broad-chested, endowed with great strength, reddish-brown in color, well-governed, and easily controlled when yoked to the chariot—bring you here.
*suyamāsaḥ* [is derived as follows]:
from the root *yama*, in the sense of "height," the suffix *khal* is applied;
the *liṭ* [augment] is unaccented.
O Dawn, facing all beings, you stand upright as the banner of immortality;
though pursuing the same goal to be attained, turn hitherward like a wheel with your newest form.
O Dawn, facing all beings, you stand upright as the banner of immortality. Moving toward your common goal, turn hither like a wheel, O most youthful one. 3.
O Goddess Uṣas, you face all beings;
you are "pratīcī," so called because you turn toward them or reach them.
You stand upright in the sky as the banner—the illuminator—of the immortal Sun, who is free from the nature of death.
O most new one, ever being born again, O goddess, come toward the goal (*artha*).
That which is sought and reached is the "goal," namely the path.
Desiring to traverse the same, single path—characterized by the time prior to sunrise—you have turned back; turn back once more upon this path.
In this regard, there is an illustration: like a wheel.
Just as the rim of the chariot of the sun, who moves through the sky, revolves again and again, so it is in this case.
*Pratīcī*. [This is derived from] *pratipūrvāt añcateḥ kvin*; the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule "the addition of *añcati* is also prescribed."
By the elision of the vowel *a* according to the rule "acaḥ," there is lengthening by the rule "cau"; [the word] is finally acute by the "udāttanivṛtti-svara" accent. [The word is] *ketuḥ*.
From the root *cāy* in the sense of "to worship" or "to observe," there is the substitution of *kī* according to the rule *cāyaḥ kī ca*;
the *guṇa* vowel is applied by the rule for initial accentuation (*ādyudāta*).
[The form is] *artham*.
The suffix *īyasun* occurs after a word ending in *ar*.
In the form *navyasi*, the word *nava* takes the suffix *īyasun* and the feminine suffix *ṅīp*.
The elision of the vowel *ī* is a Vedic (chāndasa) irregularity. [The form] *vavṛtasva* [is derived from] the root *vṛt*, meaning "to turn" (*vartane*).
By the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi," the *bhū* substitute is applied for the *vikaraṇa*.
1. You shine with the sounds gha, ca, ṇa, ta, na, bha, la, and sa.
2. With the sounds gha, ca, ṇa, na, pha, bha, and tva, you move like a wheel; turn toward, perform the turning toward, the equal goal, the supreme path—the goal.
That in which the path is sought and traversed is "artha"; [the word] *lasārtham*.
That in which the path is sought and traversed is "artha.
Wearing her woven garment, the bountiful Dawn, the mistress of the dwelling, approaches.
Self-born, fortunate, and of wondrous deeds, she has spread herself from the ends of heaven even unto the earth.
Like a needle that sews together, the Dawn comes, the mistress of the dwelling, rich in treasures.
Bringing forth the light, auspicious and wondrous in her deeds, she has spread herself from the ends of heaven to the ends of earth.

She who, like a shuttle (upāḥ), having gathered away (ava-cinavatī) the darkness spread out like a garment—causing its diminution (avacayam apakṣayam)—she who possesses wealth (maghonī) for the generous one, and who belongs to the *svasara* (the sun, or the day), being his wife (*patnī*), goes forth (*yāti*). *Svasaraḥ* means the sun or the day;
she goes as the wife of that.

9. *Svaḥ*: her own brilliance; 10. *janantī*: producing [light]; 11. *subhagā*: possessing great wealth; 12. or, endowed with good fortune; 13. *sudaṃsāḥ*: performing the beautiful act of the *āhuti* offering; 14. this very Dawn (Uṣas); 15. from the limit (*ā antāt*) of heaven (*divaḥ*), the celestial world; 16. and from the limit (*ā antāt*) of the earth (*pṛthivyāḥ*), up to its boundary; 17. *paprathe*: she spreads out, she shines forth—this is the meaning; 18. like a *syūmā*;
[the root] *syū* [is used] in the sense of "continuation of a thread" (*tantu-saṃtāne*).
The suffix *man* is applied by the rule "after the roots *ava*, *pi*, and *viśuṣi*, [the suffix *man* is added] with the *kit* designation.
By the rule "for *ch* and *y*, there is *ṅuṭ* and the nasal," *ūṭ* is substituted;
then the *yaṇ* replacement occurs.
By the rule "supāṃ suluk," there is elision (luk) of the nominative singular suffix *su*.
It is accented on the first syllable because it is a *nic* [ending].
Thus, it becomes *cinnavatī*.

In the word *śatanūmāḥ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is udātta. [The form] *janantī* is the present participle (*śatṛ*) form of the causative (*ṇyanta*) of the root *jan* (in the sense of "to be born").
By the rule *chandasyubhayathā*, the affix *śap* is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka*, resulting in the elision of the *ṇi*.
Bring forth with reverence your hymn of praise to the divine Dawn, who shines brightly for you!
The honey-bearer has sent her radiance upward to heaven; she, the delightful one, has illumined the luminous realms.

Hitherward [bring] for you the radiant goddess Dawn; with reverence offer to her a well-fashioned hymn. The honey-bearer has established her form aloft in heaven; she who sits in joy has shone forth through the luminous realms. 5.
O you worshippers, directed toward you, bring forth— perform— a beautiful hymn of praise together with reverence toward the goddess Uṣas, who shines resplendently;
she is the one who bestows honey, that is, she who imparts sweet words characterized by praise.
Soma is honey (madhu).
Or rather, it is so called because it sustains that [honey].
Or else:
It is the source of honey and other [nectars].
Or rather, this word is an indivisible name (*upānman*), whose constituent parts have arisen from the great emotion of *avahā* (disdain) and so forth. 16.
This Dawn has extended her luster upward in the sky, in the atmosphere—her luster, that is, her radiant energy, directed upward; she establishes it.
Likewise, she who is shining by nature, whose appearance is delightful, has shone forth preeminently.
Or alternatively: [the rest follows].
She has shone forth upon the worlds; she illuminates them intensely with her own splendor.
And thus says a Vedic mantra: "Shining forth with her rays, you indeed illuminate the entire radiant realm" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.49.4).
O giver of delightful joy!
The suffix *ac* is applied to the root *ravergatha*;
because it is marked with the indicator *it*, the augment *num* is added. The suffix *kin* is applied to the root *dṛś* preceded by the prefix *sam*.
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member prevails.

1. *ca-pha*: well-endowed with good fortune (*suṣṭhu saubhāgyayuktā*). 2. *ca-pha*: possessed of the beautiful *āhuti* ritual (*śobhanābhihotrakarmopetayā uṣasā*). 3. *kha-ga-gha-ca-ṇa-ta-na-sa*: from the word-final position (*avasānāt*). 4. *ta*: "O Goddess Dawn" (*uṣo devīm*). 5. *kha-ga-ta-na-pha-bha-sa*: shining beautifully (*śobhamānām*); *ca*: shining very well (*suṣṭhu śobhamānām*). 6. *ta*: honey (*madhuḥ*). 7. *kha-ga-gha-ca-ṇa-ta-na-bha-sa*: hymn of praise (*stomaḥ*). 8. *ga-ca-bha*: they sustain (*dhārayanti iti*). 9. *ca-pha*: this is true (*sad idam*). 10. *ca*: it takes refuge in (*āśrayati*). 11. *kha-ga-ca*: just as (*yathā ca*); *gha-ṇa-bha*: so too (*tathā ca*).
The observer of the cosmic order has been awakened by the rays of heaven; the wealthy goddess has risen with splendor across both worlds.
O Agni, seeking desirable wealth, you go toward the radiant Dawn who comes with her nourishment.

The observer of cosmic order, from the heights of heaven, has been awakened by her rays. Rich in bounty, she has risen with splendor across both worlds. O Agni, as you approach the dawning and radiant Dawn, you go toward her seeking desirable wealth.

This Dawn, who is faithful to the cosmic order (*ṛtāvarī*) and possessed of truth (*satyavatī*), has been awakened from the heavenly world (*divaḥ*) by her own rays of light (*akaiḥ*); she is made manifest to all.

Then this Revatī, the possessor of wealth, has stood pervading all around heaven and earth (Rodasī) in such a way as to be endowed with various wonderful forms. O Agni, seeking the radiant Dawn-goddess who approaches you and shines forth, and begging for oblations, you go toward—that is, you obtain—the desirable wealth characterized by the Agnihotra and other rites.
*Abodhi*. [This is derived from] the root *budh* in the sense of "understanding" (*avagamana*).
In the *luṅ* (aorist) tense, in the passive voice (*karmaṇi*), the suffix *ciṇ* is applied according to the rule *ciṇ bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*.
‘The suffix ciṇ is elided.
[Thus] *revatī* [is formed]: from the word *rayi*, the suffix *matup* is added.
The substitution of *v* [for *y*] occurs by the rule "chandasīraḥ.
Then, by the rule "rayematau bahulam," there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) followed by the substitution of the subsequent vowel (*parapūrvatva*). Finally, the *guṇa* [substitution takes place].
The suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ugitaśca*;
the acute accent (*udātta*) of the possessive suffix *matup* is established by the supplementary rule *reśabdāccopasaṃkhyānam*.
Seeking nourishment at the foundation of Cosmic Order, the Bull has entered the two great worlds, heaven and earth.
Great is the creative power of Mitra and Varuṇa; like the moon, he has distributed his light in many places.

Seeking nourishment at the foundation of Truth, the Bull has entered the two great worlds, Heaven and Earth. Great is the creative power (*māyā*) of Mitra and Varuṇa; like moons, they have spread their light in many places. 7.

The bull, the impeller of the waters through rain, the Sun, seeking nourishment at the base—the root—of *ṛta*, that is, at the foundation of the day which has become reality through the performance of rites such as the Agnihotra, has entered the two great worlds, Heaven and Earth, on all sides with his own splendors.
Or rather, the construction may be understood thus: the bull, beholding [the world] and moving everywhere, the mass of rays belonging to the dawns, has pervaded the two worlds, Heaven and Earth.
Then the great Dawn, the vast creative power (*māyā*) of Mitra and Varuṇa, appearing in the form of light like the moon, has distributed her own radiance in many places; she spreads it everywhere.
Mahī (is used for mahatī);
the absence of the suffix -lopa is Vedic;
purutrā (means "in many places").
In the phrase beginning with “devamanuṣya,” the suffix *apratyaya* is applied in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

The ninth hymn, consisting of eighteen verses beginning with "imā u vām," has the following index: "imā u vām [is dedicated] to Indra and Varuṇa, Bṛhaspati, Pūṣan, Savitṛ, Soma, and Mitra and Varuṇa; the last verse is by Jamadagni, or alternatively, the fourth is in the Gāyatrī meter.
Viśvāmitra is the seer (ṛṣi) of the first verse, while Jamadagni is the seer of the remaining triplet.
The first three verses are *triṣṭubh*s; the remaining fifteen are *gāyatrī*s.
Indra and Varuṇa are the deities of the first [verse], Bṛhaspati of the second, Pūṣan of the third, Savitṛ of the fourth, Soma of the fifth, and [Savitṛ] of the sixth. [Note:
In the first case, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) with subsequent form (*pararūpatva*); in the second case, there is no vocalization, but the preceding form (*parapūrvatva*).]
2. In the manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ṇa, ma, and sa, the word *apām* is absent. 3. In the manuscripts kha, ga, gha, ca, ṇa, ta, bha, and sa, the word *svatejobhiḥ* is absent.

4. In the manuscripts kha, ga, gha, ca, ṇa, pha, bha, and ma, the reading is *mitrasya varuṇasya māyā mahatī*, meaning "the great creative power (*māyā*) of Mitra and Varuṇa," which refers to that power belonging to both Mitra and Varuṇa.
Regarding Mitrāvaruṇa:

when there is an increase in the *stoma* at the third pressing during the *ābhiṣvikas* and *ukthya* sacrifices, the respective *hotṛ*-priests, having set aside another hymn (*sūkta*) from their own *śastra*, should insert (*āvapet*) as many verses beginning with "tvā" as are required for the chanting of the *stoma*. Among these, there are three verses for the insertion of the Maitrāvaruṇa.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "These indeed are your bees, thinking thus"—these are the three [verses] (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.9).
These very *bhramayas*, which we consider worthy of you, have not been easy to subdue for one like you;
O Indra and Varuṇa, what is that glory of yours by which you bring wealth to your friends?

These [are] yours; "Ūm"—thus [it is]. O you two, those who were thought to be wandering have not become impetuous for your protection. Where, O Indra and Varuṇa, is that glory of yours, by which you bring wealth to your friends? 1.

"O Indra and Varuṇa," [he says], "these subjects of yours, who are being oppressed by powerful enemies and are thus being tormented, are indeed 'bhramayaḥ,' prone to wandering. May they not be 'tujyāḥ,' to be harmed, by a powerful enemy—'yuvāvate,' meaning one possessing youth and strength (the fourth case used in the sense of the third). May this not happen.

Moreover, the construction is as follows: "O you two, where (*kva*) is that (*tyat*) such (*tādṛśaṃ*) fame (*yaśaḥ*) of yours? By which fame (*yena yaśasā*) you two used to bring (*bharathaḥ sma*) food (*sinam annam*) for us, your friends—that [fame], where does it exist? (i.e., it no longer exists).
Or alternatively:
O Indra and Varuṇa, these *bhramayaḥ*—the movements being performed by us which, thinking themselves capable of reaching you, are of the nature of wandering—are related to you both.
The root *man* is a verb meaning "to praise."
The hymns offered by those who praise you are for you two alone; they are not to be given to any other god, nor should they be bestowed upon another.
The root *tuj* here has the sense of "giving.
Let them not be granted to anyone else.
The rest is the same.
*bhramayaḥ* [is derived from] *bhramu anavasthāne* (to wander, to be unsettled). From *bhrām*,
by the rule *saṃpramāraṇaṃ ca*, there is *saṃprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) and the suffix *-thac*.
The acute accent on the final syllable occurs by way of transposition (vyatyaya).

[The form] *yuvāvate* is derived with the suffix *vatup*, according to the rule: "In the Vedic language (*chandas*), there is an addition [to the rule for *vatup*] when similarity (*sādṛśya*) is intended after the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*."
Even though they are not distinct [from the base], the substitution for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
[The form] *tujyāḥ* [is derived from] the root *tuja* in the sense of "injury," "giving," or "dwelling."
The suffix *yat* is applied by the rule "acyādayaśca";
its acute accent on the first syllable is established by the rule "yato'nāvaḥ";
[the form is] *sinam*.
The root *piñ* means "to bind. The suffix *na* is applied according to the rule *iṇ-piñ-ḍīṅ-guyi-vibhyo nak*.
The initial vowel is acute by virtue of metrical transposition (*vyatyaya*).
This man, most frequenting you both, constantly invokes you for protection.
O Indra and Varuṇa, being of one accord with the Maruts, hear my call from heaven and earth.
This one, most frequent, flowing forth, repeatedly invokes you for his sustenance. O Indra and Varuṇa, being of one accord with the Maruts, listen to my call from heaven and earth. 2.

O Indra and Varuṇa! This most excellent sacrificer—great indeed because of his intense engagement in Vedic rites—repeatedly invokes you both for protection or for the sake of the sacrifice, desiring wealth for himself. He calls upon you at all times, forever.

1. Kha, ga, ca, and ṇa [readings] include *stomātiśaṃsanārtham*; ta, na, bha, and sa [readings] have *stomātiśaṃsanārthāḥ*. 2. In na, la, and sa, "indrāvaruṇā" is absent. 3. Ṇa [reading]: *abhinandyamānāḥ*. 4. In kha, ga, ca, ṇa, na, bha, la, and sa, "u pūraṇaḥ" is absent. 5. In kha, ga, gha, ca, ṇa, na, bha, and sa, "api ca" is absent. 6. Kha, ga, ca, and ṇa [readings]: *etādṛśam*. 7. Na, la, and sa [readings]: *krāste*. 8. Gha [reading]: "ity anvayaḥ | u pūraṇaḥ". 9. Kha, ga, ca, ṇa, pha, bha, and sa [readings]: *kramaṇaśīlāḥ*. 10. He calls out intensely. O you two who are in harmony with the Maruts— those specific deities— and with Heaven and Earth, hear my invocation, your own call.
*Purutamaḥ*:
by the rule *tamapó dhyayayena*, it has the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudāttatva*).
He calls out repeatedly.
This form arises from the root *haya* (to call) after the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix, when the *saṃprasāraṇa* substitution has been applied by the rule "and [the vowel] of a reduplicated stem.
By day.
In the word *ūdidam*, the case ending (*vibhakti*) is acute (*udātta*). In the word *pṛthivyāḥ*, the acute accent occurs according to the rule “*udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt*” [Pāṇini 6.1.174].
*Havam*. It is derived from the root *hve* (to call), with the suffix *ap* according to the rule *bhāve 'nupasargasya*;
the suffix is *anudātta* because it is marked with *pittva*.
O Indra and Varuṇa, may that wealth be ours; O Maruts, may there be for us riches consisting of all-heroic sons.
May the protectors guard us with their shelters; may Hotrā Bhāratī favor us with sacrificial gifts.

May that wealth be ours, O Indra and Varuṇa; may riches be ours, O Maruts, consisting of all heroic sons. May the protectors aid us with their shelters; may Hotrā Bhāratī aid us with sacrificial gifts. 3.
O Indra and Varuṇa—O Indra and Varuṇa—may that desired wealth (*vasu*) be ours; may it be so for us.
O Maruts, [grant] a *rayi*—a wealth consisting of a multitude of cattle accompanied by sons and grandsons, one who is a hero (*sarvavīraḥ*), capable in all tasks.
For the Taittirīyaka states: “Cattle indeed are *rayi*.”
May he be ours;
may the wives of the gods, who are most protective (*varūtarīḥ*) and worthy of being honored by all, be our *śaraṇaiḥ*—
for *śaraṇa* refers to houses, so called because they hear [and protect from] the afflictions of cold and other hardships.
May they protect us. *Hotrā*:
that in which oblations (*havīṃṣi*) are offered.
Alternatively, the *hotrā* is speech (*vāk*), because the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is offered (*hūyate*) therein.
And thus says the Śruti: "For we offer the vital breath into speech, or speech into the vital breath."
Alternatively,
"hotrā" is a name for the sacrifice,
because the oblation (*havis*) is offered (*hūyate*) therein.

And sacrifice is called speech; for the Brāhmaṇa states: "They restrain their speech, for speech is indeed the sacrifice" (AiB 5.24). Such is Bhāratī Sarasvatī, together with the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) in the form of cows.
Or rather, may he protect us with his noble and powerful arms.
In the word *vasudhyā* in this *saṃhitā*, the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by the rule *pūrvapadāt*.
Regarding *varūtaraḥ*,
its formation is established through the specific grammatical derivation (*nipātana*) as ending in the feminine suffix *ṅīp* according to the rule beginning with *prasitaskabhita*.
*Hotrā*:
[derived from] the root *hu*, meaning "to give" or "to eat.
By the rule *huyāmāśubhasibhyaśchan*, the suffix *an* is applied in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
O Bṛhaspati, enjoy our oblations which are dear to all the gods;
bestow jewels upon the donor.
O Bṛhaspati, enjoy our oblations which are dear to all the gods; bestow jewels upon the donor. 4.
O Bṛhaspati, friend of all the gods (*viśvadevya*), please enjoy—that is, accept with favor—our offerings (*havyāni*) such as the *puroḍāśa* cakes, which are worthy of being invoked.
Then, grant to me, the sacrificer who has offered the oblation, the most excellent treasures (*ratnāni*).
*rāsva* (imperative):
from the root *rā* in the sense of "giving. The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used here due to the suffix *dhyaya*.
1. In *ga*, *gha*, *ṇa*, *bha*, and *ha* there are Indra and Varuṇa (*indrāvaruṇau*); in *ca*, *na*, *sa*, and *ha* there are Indra and Varuṇa.

2. In *ca*, *pha*, and *bha* there is Vīra. 3. In *kha*, *ga*, and *ca* he is a hero in all rites (*sarvakarmavīraḥ*); in *gha*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, and *sa* he is a hero in all rites (*sarvakarmasu vīraḥ*).
4. [The syllables] kha, ga, ca, gha, ṇa, na, pha, bha, la, sa [indicate] a multitude of sons and cattle.
5. [If] kha, ga, ca, ṇa, sa [are present], there is no [offering].
6. [If] kha, ga, ca, ṇa, na, bha, sa [are present], or alternatively... [the word] *havis* is not present.
7. May she protect;
or rather, may the three goddesses—the Hotrā of Agni the Hotṛ, Bhāratī, and Sarasvatī who has the Sun as her consort—protect [us].
8. [The substitution of] *sa*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *na*, and *bha* occurs in the case of giving (*dāna*) and taking (*ādāna*).
9. The sacrificial offerings such as the *gha-ta-la* and the *puroḍāśa*.

Worship Bṛhaspati with hymns at the sacrifices; he has willed toward himself unyielding vigor. (5) Worship the pure Bṛhaspati with hymns at the sacrifices; he has willed toward himself unyielding vigor. (5)
O priests, you who are present at the sacrifices, worship and serve the pure Bṛhaspati with hymns worthy of praise;
I entreat him from all sides for that invincible power, his strength which is unbending and unassailable by others.
*bṛhaspatim*: because it belongs to the *vanaspati*-class, it has the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) on both syllables. *cake*.
In the third person singular of the periphrastic future, the elision of the letter 'm' is a Vedic anomaly.
The bull of the people, omniform, invincible, Bṛhaspati, the most excellent. 6. The bull; of the people; omniform; invincible; Bṛhaspati; the most excellent. 6.

The bull (*vṛṣabha*) of the *carṣaṇīs*, that is, of human beings—one who showers desired fruits; the one of universal form (*viśvarūpa*), meaning the one whose form is Vyāsa. Or alternatively, the one endowed with the cow as his vehicle named Viśvarūpa.
And thus says a Vedic mantra: "Bṛhaspati begot Viśvarūpā" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.161.6). [The meaning is:
"I pray for my desired fruit from Bṛhaspati—who is *adābhya* (unassailable by anyone), *vareṇya* (worthy of being honored by all)—this is the connection with the preceding [verse]."
*Viśvarūpam*. [The accentuation is] by the rule "In a *bahuvrīhi*, when it is a proper name, the final syllable of the first member is udātta.
Alternatively:
The term *viśvarūpa* contains the suffix *ac* according to the rule for words beginning with *arśas*;
because it belongs to the class beginning with *marut*, the final syllable of the first member of the compound is udātta.
[The word is] *adābhya*.
The suffix *ṇya* is applied [to form the word *dāmya*] according to the rule: "It should be stated that [the suffix applies] after the root *dam*."
O Pūṣan, O radiant god, this most excellent hymn of praise is being recited for you by us. 7. This—O Pūṣan—O glowing one—this well-spoken hymn—O god—most human—by us—for you—is being recited. 7.
O glowing one, O radiant Pūṣan, O god, this newest, most recent, and beautiful hymn of praise—this speech consisting of excellent laudation—is addressed to you.
This very praise is recited and performed by us, the worshippers, for your sake. "Accept it"—thus it connects with the following verse.

Be pleased with this my song that seeks for strength; favor my prayer as one desiring a bride favors a young woman. 8. Be pleased with that; [be pleased with] my song; [be pleased with] that which seeks for strength; favor the prayer; like one desiring a bride, [favor] the young woman. 8.
O Pūṣan, graciously accept—that is, favor—this speech of mine, characterized by praise, as I offer it.
Delighted by the hymn, come toward this prayer (*dhī*) which seeks nourishment (*vāja*), desires food, and brings joy.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
Like a suitor;
just as a suitor desiring fortune approaches a young woman, so too [he approaches] her who seeks booty.

1. [The variants] kha, ga, gha, ṇa, na, pha, bha, and sa read *yayāce*. 2. [The variants] ca, pha, and adābhyaṃ read *ahiṃsyaṃ vareṇyaṃ varaṇīyaṃ bṛhaspati namasyata*, which connects with the preceding [verse]. [The variants] kha, ga, and bha read *ācake*. 3. [The variant] bha reads *satīti*. 4. [The variant] la reads *dīptimān*. 5. [The variants] kha, ga, gha, ṇa, na, bha, and sa read *śobhanā stutirūpā*. 6. [The variants] ta, na, and sa read *vāṇī* [in the sense of] "by us. 7. [The variants] kha, ga, ca, ṇa, bha, la, and sa do not have the word *kriyate*. 8. [The variants] kha, ga, gha, ca, ṇa, pha, bha, do not have the word *prati*.

The suffix *ayac* is applied after the word *vāja* in the sense of "one who desires"; from that form, when the suffix *śatṛ* follows, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added, resulting in the form [vājayan]. Since *ṅīp* is anudātta, the accent falls on the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). The word *ava* is the form of the root *ava*, meaning "to protect" and so forth, in the imperative (*loṭ*).

He who looks out upon all beings and beholds them together—may that Pūṣan be our protector. 9. He who... all... looks out upon... beings... and... beholds... together... he... may that Pūṣan... be our protector. 9.
Pūṣan, who gazes upon all beings— that is, all worlds— with direct vision, seeing them in their particularity;
and furthermore, who beholds them together, meaning he correctly knows the true nature of each respective object—
may that such Pūṣan, the god, be our protector and guardian.
He perceives clearly,
just as a yogin is free from affliction.
Since the suffix *śap* is marked with *pit*, it is unaccented, and thus the accent of the verbal root remains.
In the case of *tiṅ* [suffixes] that possess the udātta accent, there is the suppression (*nighāta*) of the verbal root (*gati*).
He sees.
Here, because it is transitive (*sakarmaka*), the *parasmaipada* ending is used.

We meditate upon—that is, we contemplate—that *bhargas*, which is to be honored as the object of worship and as that which is to be known; *bhargas* is that which burns away ignorance and its effects; it is self-luminous light, whose essence is the Supreme Brahman. Alternatively, the word "that" (*tat*) is an epithet of *bhargas*.
We meditate upon that such splendor (*bharga*) of the divine Savitṛ.
In response to the expectation "What is that?", he says: "He" (*yaḥ*), with a change of grammatical gender.
"That splendor which shall impel our intellects—may we meditate upon that. This is the synthesis.
Or alternatively:

May we meditate upon—that is, may we hold in our minds as an object of meditation—the *bharga* (splendor) of that god Savitṛ, the Sun, who impels all *dhiyaḥ* (thoughts) and actions; of him, the progenitor of all, the radiant one, that well-known *bharga* which is to be chosen by all (*vareṇya*), worthy of being honored by everyone, and which is the circle of light that consumes sins.
Alternatively, by the word *bharga*, food is denoted.
We meditate upon—that is, we hold fast to—the fruit characterized by *bhargas* and so forth, through the grace of that divine Savitṛ who impels our thoughts (*dhiyaḥ*).
The meaning is: "May we become the support for that [fruit].

If the word *bhargas* refers to food (*anna*) and the word *dhī* refers to ritual action (*karman*), then according to the Atharvaṇa: "The sages call the Veda, the meters, and the excellent *bhargas* of the divine Savitṛ, 'food'."
"I shall declare those actions of yours, by which Savitṛ is impelled" (Gopatha Brāhmaṇa 1.32).
*Bhargaḥ*:
[derived] from the root *bhṛj* (meaning "to ripen" or "to burn") with the suffix *asun*.

By the rule *astrajo ropadhayo ramyantarasyām* (Pāṇini 6.4.47), there is elision of the letters following the *r* and the penultimate vowel, and the augment *ram* is inserted. Due to its inclusion in the *nyaṅku*-class, the substitution of *ku* for *j* occurs.
Thus: *dhīmahi*.
In the case of the root *dhyai* with the suffix *liṅ*, there is a vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) according to the rule "in the Veda [it occurs] abundantly" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).
The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
Alternatively:
‘Dhīṅ’ is used in the sense of a support (locative). In the optative (liṅ), there is elision of the verbal suffix (vikaraṇa) according to the rule ‘bahulaṃ chandasi’. [Thus:
‘pracodayāt’.
The augment *byāṭ* is added to the root *codayati*.
Due to its connection with that [augment], there is no *nighāta* (elision of accent).
Since the augment is unaccented (*anudātta*), the accent belongs to the suffix *ṇic*.
Seeking strength through the wisdom of the divine Savitṛ, we implore the bounty of Bhaga. 11. Of the divine Savitṛ; we; seeking strength; through the wisdom; of Bhaga; the bounty; we implore. 11.

Seeking vigor, may we come here desiring food and strength. Through the *purandhi*—the wisdom or the abundance—of the radiant god Savitṛ, we implore and beg for the gift, the bestowal, of *bharga*, the wealth worthy of being enjoyed.
*rātiṃ*:
by the rule *mantre vṛṣa* etc., the suffix *kin* is acute-accented.

The sages, impelled by their inspired thoughts, worship the divine Savitṛ with sacrifices and well-fashioned hymns. 12. The divine one; men; Savitṛ; the sages; with sacrifices; with well-fashioned hymns; they worship; impelled by their inspired thoughts. 12.

Men who are leaders of actions—wise sages such as the Atharvans and others, impelled by their intellects or by their ritual acts—worship and serve the divine Savitṛ with their own sacrifices consisting of oblations worthy of worship, and with beautiful hymns of praise.
They pay homage. [The suffix] *kyac* is applied according to the rule: “*namas-varivas-citradah kyac*” (Pāṇini 3.1.19).

In the *agnīṣomapraṇayana* (the leading forward of Agni and Soma), there are three verses beginning with "Somo jigāti. This is stated in the Sūtra: "‘Somo jigāti gātuvit...’; [the Adhvaryu] should cause the Hotṛ to recite these three verses for Varuṇa, the King of the gods" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 4.10).

1. Kha, ga, gha, ca, ṇa, bha: *tadbhargaḥ* (its splendor). 2. Kha, ga, ca, ṇa, bha: *avidyābhañjanāt tatkāryayorbhajanam* (the breaking [or parching] of ignorance and its effects); Na, pha: *avidyātatkāryayoḥ bhañjane* (in the breaking of ignorance and its effects). 3. Kha, ga, ca, ṇa, bha, sa: *svayaṃjyotiḥ tejaḥ* (self-luminous light).
4. *ta-na-la-dhīmahi*:
"I am he, he is I"—thus may we meditate.
5. *kha-ga-ca-dhyāyāmi*; *ṇa-dhyāyāma*; *na-bha-sa-dhyāyāma*.
6. In manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ṇa, pha, bha, and sa, the word *yaḥ* is absent.
7. In manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ṇa, bha, and la, the phrase *sarvasya prasavituḥ* is absent. 8. Because it is visible (*taddṛśyatayā*).
9. And [the form] *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-vareṇya*.
10. *Kha-ga-ca-ṇa-bha-sa*: [the term] “*adhīśabda*” does not exist when it has the sense of an object (*karmaparatve*).
11. *Ta*: because it belongs to the *nyaṅku*-class (*nyaṅkādi*).
12. The *ta* is always grave (*anudātta*).
13. The letters *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *bha*, *la*, *sī*, and the word *arāti* do not exist [as *udātta*].
Rule 1–62.

40.0 O Mitra and Varuṇa, you two of excellent wisdom, sprinkle our pasture with clarified butter and the regions with honey. 16. O Mitra and Varuṇa, sprinkle our pasture with clarified butter; sprinkle the regions with honey, O you two of excellent wisdom. 16.

O Mitra and Varuṇa, you two of noble intellect and beautiful deeds, sprinkle our pasture—the path of the cattle, the place where the cows dwell—with clarified butter, that is, with flowing milks; drench it on all sides. The sense is: "Grant us cattle.
Sprinkle our dwelling places, the regions, with sweet nectar.
*gavyūtim*:
the substitution of *vānt* [i.e., *au*] occurs by the rule "in the Veda, [the word] *gavyūti* [is formed with *au*]. *madhvā*.
Because all case endings are optional in the Vedic language (*chandas*), there is an absence of the *num* augment here.

O you of wide renown, strengthened by homage, you two rule as great lords through the power of skill, with your most rapid [aid], O you whose vows are pure. 17. O you of wide renown, strengthened by homage, great, you rule over skill, with your most swift [powers], O you of pure vows. 17.
O Mitra and Varuna, you two who possess pure vows and purified actions, whose praise is wide— that is, worthy of being praised by many— or rather,
you two for whom the recitation (śaṃsa) is wide, that is, great.

Increasing through reverence, through homage, through oblation, through food, or through praise; joined with most swift [prayers] characterized by exceedingly long hymns, you two rule by the greatness of *dakṣa*—
*dakṣa* being wealth or strength—
over that, you possess sovereign power.
*Uruśaṃsā*:
from the root *śaṃsu* meaning "to praise," with the suffix *ghañ* used in the sense of the object (*karman*).

The word *kṛtsvaraḥ*. [In the formation of] *drāviṣṭhābhiḥ*, when the suffix *iṣṭhan* follows words beginning with *dīrgha*, the substitute *drāghīyas* occurs according to the rule "priyasthira... and so forth.
Because it is a *nittva* [term], it is udātta on its first syllable.
The *yājyā* for the offering to Mitra and Varuṇa is this verse: “*gṛṇānā jamadagninā*” (being praised by Jamadagni).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “The Hotṛ, sacrificing to Mitra and Varuṇa, [recites] ‘*gṛṇānā jamadagninā*’” (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 5.5).
At the commencement of the study of the Veda (*adhyāyopākaraṇa*), during the oblation within the Maṇḍala, this same verse “*gṛṇānā jamadagninā*” is used (*Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra* 3.5.7).

Praised by Jamadagni, sit in the womb of Cosmic Order; drink the Soma, O you who increase Truth! 18. Praised by Jamadagni, sit in the womb of Cosmic Order; drink the Soma, O you who increase Truth! 18.

O Mitra and Varuṇa, being praised (gṛṇānā)—that is, being extolled by the great seer named Jamadagni; or alternatively, being praised by Viśvāmitra, whose fire was kindled (jamadagni)—may you two sit down (sīdatam) in the womb of Ṛta, that is, in the place called the sacrificial ground (devayajana). O increasers of Ṛta (ṛtāvṛdhā), those who cause the fruit of ritual action to increase, may you two drink (pātam) the Soma. Regarding *gṛṇānā*: from the root *gṛ* "to sound," the suffix *śānac* is used in the sense of the object (passive) by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*); because of its *cit* nature, it is accented on the final syllable. Regarding *sīdatam*: from the root *sad*, in the imperative (*loṭ*), the substitution of *sīda-* occurs according to the rule "pāghrā... etc. Regarding *pātam*: from the root *pā* "to drink"; the elision of the suffix *śap* occurs by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi. || 11 ||
Thus ends the fifth Anuvāka in the third Maṇḍala of the Ṛgveda Saṃhitā Bhāṣya, composed by Sāyaṇācārya in the Mādhavīya Vedārthaprakāśa; and the third Maṇḍala is also completed.

1. With the sweet flavor of honey (*la-madhurarasena*). 2. Kha, ga, gha, ca, ṇa, bha, and śuddhakarmāṇau. 3. *Na*—this is the [reading]. And thus it is stated in the Sūtra: "O bird, announce what is auspicious; proclaiming [it], [say] 'by Jamadagni'. This [verse] is also used for the *utsarjana* (concluding rite), according to the Sūtra rule: "Then, at the *utsarga*... 4. Kha, ga, ca, ṇa, bha, and sa—there is no [reading] by way of transposition (*vyatyayena*). 5. *Saṃ*.
